LB1-1.claim: According to a case the US embassy in Dhaka filed against five Bangladeshis, reported in a Prothom Alo editorial of 25 February 2024, two Bangladeshis named Mofizur Rahman and Ashraful Alam Bhuiyan admitted at their US visa interview on 11 February that they were involved in trafficking people from Bangladesh to various countries, and they had submitted fake documents to the embassy.
LB1-1.target_section: Forged documents and impersonation > What happens
LB1-1.why_new: An embassy itself filing a case over fake documents and an admission made at the visa interview; the section has no embassy-filed case.

LB1-2.claim: According to the same US embassy case (editorial of 25 February 2024), one of the two men admitted that an immigration officer at Hazrat Shahjalal International Airport in Dhaka helped him in exchange for money.
LB1-2.target_section: Departure day at the airport > Documented cases
LB1-2.why_new: A recorded admission of a paid immigration officer at Dhaka airport helping a trafficker.

LB1-3.claim: A Prothom Alo editorial of 25 February 2024 stated that BRAC's Migration Programme rescued and brought home 629 people in 2022 who had been living in misery abroad without valid papers, and that they had been taken to Libya with the promise of attractive jobs in Europe.
LB1-3.target_section: Libya to Italy by boat > The numbers
LB1-3.why_new: A returns figure for BRAC's programme for 2022; the section gives only IOM-assisted returns.

LB1-4.claim: According to UNHCR, as cited in a Prothom Alo editorial of 25 February 2024, 13 per cent of the 5,236 refugees and migrant workers who went to Italy by sea were Bangladeshi citizens (the editorial does not state the period).
LB1-4.target_section: Libya to Italy by boat > The numbers
LB1-4.why_new: An early-2024 share figure; the period is not printed, so it needs a check against UNHCR before use.

LB1-5.claim: On 15 February 2024 a boat carrying 52 migrants caught fire and sank in the Mediterranean off the Tunisian coast; 8 Bangladeshis died, 26 others were rescued and one was seriously injured, according to a Prothom Alo editorial of 25 February 2024.
LB1-5.target_section: Libya to Italy by boat > What happens
LB1-5.why_new: The February 2024 Tunisia boat deaths are not in the Death list.

LB1-6.claim: The Counter Terrorism and Transnational Crime unit identified a Libya-based trafficker who had appointed 40 brokers across Bangladesh whose job was to find young people wanting to go abroad, according to a Prothom Alo editorial of 25 February 2024.
LB1-6.target_section: Libya to Italy by boat > The path
LB1-6.why_new: Shows the scale of one Libya-based trafficker's recruiting network in Bangladesh (40 brokers).

LB1-7.claim: A Home Ministry report on trafficking from the previous year (2023) said that in the nine months from January to September, courts disposed of 332 cases under the trafficking Act; in 316 of them (95.18 per cent) all the accused were acquitted, and in 16 cases 56 people were punished, only two of them with life imprisonment, according to a Prothom Alo editorial of 25 February 2024.
LB1-7.why_new: The guide states penalties but not how trafficking cases actually end; this is the acquittal rate.

LB1-8.claim: The father of a woman from Savar said the people he had sued for trafficking his daughter to India on the promise of taking her to Canada were all released, and that he himself spent four months in jail in a case the defendants filed against him, according to a Prothom Alo editorial of 25 February 2024.
LB1-8.why_new: A complainant jailed in a counter-case after the accused were acquitted; the guide has no counter-case example.

LB1-9.claim: Salma Ali, president of the Bangladesh National Women Lawyers' Association, said trafficking cases are not investigated properly because ring members are very influential, and the Prothom Alo editorial of 25 February 2024 adds that they threaten victims into compromise settlements.
LB1-9.why_new: A named expert's explanation of why cases fail: influence, and threats that force compromise.

LB1-10.claim: According to relatives, police and local sources, several young men from Rajoir, Madaripur, and Muksudpur, Gopalganj, left home for Italy on 14 January 2024, flew through Dubai to Libya, and on 14 February left Libya on an engine boat through brokers; eight of them died on the boat in the Mediterranean off Tunisia (five from Rajoir and three from Muksudpur), along with one Pakistani.
LB1-10.target_section: Libya to Italy by boat > What happens
LB1-10.why_new: Home districts, dates and route of the February 2024 Tunisia boat deaths.

LB1-11.claim: Relatives of the eight dead told journalists at Dhaka airport on 2 May 2024 that brokers had put 52 people on a small boat that could take 30, that the eight who died had been forced to stay below the deck, and that when they tried to come out for lack of oxygen the brokers beat them and sent them back down; the relatives said they died of the torture and lack of oxygen.
LB1-11.target_section: Libya to Italy by boat > What happens
LB1-11.why_new: How people die on these boats without the boat sinking: overloading and being held below deck.

LB1-12.claim: The brother of Sajal Bairagi (22) of Sendia village, Rajoir, Madaripur, one of the eight who died on the boat off Tunisia in February 2024, told Prothom Alo the family gave BDT 14 lakh to a broker named Mosharraf by selling land and cows and borrowing.
LB1-12.target_section: Libya to Italy by boat > The contract price and the final price
LB1-12.why_new: A 2024 price and how it was raised (land, cattle, loans).

LB1-13.claim: Sajal Bairagi's brother said in May 2024 that the broker was telling the family not to file a case and had said he would return some money but was not giving it, and that, being poor and unable to afford a case, the family was trying to settle with the broker.
LB1-13.target_section: Libya to Italy by boat > The law
LB1-13.why_new: Shows why no case follows a death: the broker discourages it with a refund promise and the family cannot afford one.

LB1-14.claim: The Madaripur Superintendent of Police, Masud Alam, told Prothom Alo in May 2024 that police would give all legal help if relatives of the eight dead filed a case, but that the victims had little interest in filing cases.
LB1-14.target_section: Libya to Italy by boat > The law
LB1-14.why_new: Police position: they act only if the family files, and families mostly do not.

LB1-15.claim: The bodies of the eight Bangladeshis who died on a boat off Tunisia in February 2024 reached Dhaka's Hazrat Shahjalal International Airport on a Saudia flight on 2 May 2024, and were sent to the Dhaka Medical College morgue for post-mortem before being handed to the families.
LB1-15.target_section: How is the body brought home?
LB1-15.why_new: The bodies came home about two and a half months after the deaths, and went to a post-mortem before release to families.

LB1-16.claim: Azmir Hossain (24) of Mirsarai, Chattogram, said Libya-based Shahadat Hossain kept tempting his mother with a job in Italy paying BDT 50,000 a month, took BDT 1.5 lakh in advance, and had Azmir carry the rest of the money himself; a local union parishad member said Shahadat is from the same area.
LB1-16.target_section: Libya to Italy by boat > How it is sold
LB1-16.why_new: The seller is a neighbour living in Libya who pitches the mother, names a salary and takes a small advance.

LB1-17.claim: Azmir Hossain said he reached Dubai on 21 March 2024, where the broker's men met him at the airport and kept 30 to 35 people together in a room of a small house for two days, then flew them to Egypt, held them 24 hours in a warehouse-like place in the airport area, and put them on another plane to Libya.
LB1-17.target_section: Libya to Italy by boat > The path
LB1-17.why_new: Stop-by-stop detail of the Dubai and Egypt legs: who meets them, how many per room, how long at each.

LB1-18.claim: Azmir Hossain said everyone's passport was taken as soon as they reached Libya, that he was beaten whenever he mentioned the promised job, and that BDT 6 lakh was collected from his family in stages by phone.
LB1-18.target_section: Libya to Italy by boat > What happens
LB1-18.why_new: A survivor's first-person account of what follows arrival.

LB1-19.claim: Azmir Hossain said that after collecting BDT 6 lakh from his family the broker sold him to another group at a high price and left him in a Libyan desert to be handed over; he said he escaped with a Libyan citizen's help and took shelter with a Bangladeshi he knew, and that the broker then came and took him back.
LB1-19.target_section: Libya to Italy by boat > What happens
LB1-19.why_new: Being sold on after the ransom is paid, by the same Bangladeshi who recruited him.

LB1-20.claim: Azmir Hossain said he was locked in a room and beaten regularly for trying to escape, went eight days without food, and reached home on 5 May 2024 in a critical condition, 41 days after leaving home according to Prothom Alo; his mother said he is now mentally ill from blows to the head and that she owes BDT 6 lakh.
LB1-20.target_section: Libya to Italy by boat > What happens
LB1-20.why_new: The whole trip lasted 41 days and never left Libya; the outcome for the family.

LB1-21.claim: Abdullah Al Zobayer (24) of Mirsarai, Chattogram, told Prothom Alo in June 2024 that he trusted a friend who was the younger brother of a Libya-based broker and a member of the ring, was taken to Libya on the promise of Italy, and that the ring collected BDT 4 lakh from his family.
LB1-21.why_new: The recruiter was the victim's own friend; the section lists standing and track record but not friendship.

LB1-22.claim: Abdullah Al Zobayer, who returned from captivity in Libya in 2024, said the ring that took him has many members and also targets Bangladeshi expatriates in the Middle East, taking people to Libya with talk of good jobs or passage to Europe and holding them hostage to collect money from their families.
LB1-22.target_section: Recruited while abroad or just back
LB1-22.why_new: A survivor stating that the ring recruits among expatriates already in the Middle East.
LB1-22.h3: Recruited while abroad or just back

LB1-23.claim: After returning, Azmir Hossain filed a case in a Chattogram court against six people, including the Libya-based broker and his brother; his lawyer told Prothom Alo in June 2024 that it was a criminal case over cheating and torture in Libya and that the court took cognisance of the complaint and ordered an investigation.
LB1-23.target_section: Libya to Italy by boat > The law
LB1-23.why_new: A returnee filing directly in court, and what the court did.

LB1-24.claim: A union parishad member in Karerhat, Mirsarai, said he phoned the Libya-based broker several times to get Azmir Hossain sent home and saw the marks of beating on Azmir's head and body on a video call.
LB1-24.target_section: Libya to Italy by boat > Where to get help
LB1-24.why_new: An elected local representative negotiating directly with the broker in Libya, and a witness to the injuries.

LB1-25.claim: Prothom Alo reported on 13 July 2024 that at least 24 people from Bhairab and elsewhere in Kishoreganj, Habiganj and Narsingdi went to Libya at about the same time through a broker ring led by Rasel Mia of Bhairab to cross to Italy by sea, that none had reached Italy, and that some were hostages of kidnappers and others were in Libyan jails.
LB1-25.target_section: Libya to Italy by boat > What happens
LB1-25.why_new: A whole batch from one broker stranded; two outcomes, kidnappers or Libyan jail.

LB1-26.claim: Prothom Alo reported in July 2024 that Rasel Mia took BDT 24 lakh from the father of Faruk Mia of Bhairab and BDT 22 lakh each from Tofayel Ahmed and Sabuj Mia for Italy; the father of Shafiqul Islam of Shibpur, Narsingdi, said Rasel took BDT 23 lakh and that BDT 10 lakh was now being demanded to free his son.
LB1-26.target_section: Libya to Italy by boat > The contract price and the final price
LB1-26.why_new: 2023-24 prices of BDT 22 to 24 lakh paid up front to a Bhairab broker, then a further demand to free the hostage.

LB1-27.claim: Families of two hostages in the Bhairab case said in July 2024 that large ransoms were being demanded but that they could find no one who could assure them that paying would get the men released.
LB1-27.target_section: Libya to Italy by boat > What happens
LB1-27.why_new: Families' own statement that nobody guarantees release after payment.

LB1-28.claim: According to local people in Bhairab, when the hostages phoned home begging to be freed, the broker Rasel Mia and his ring members hid and cut off contact with the families; the families then went to community leaders for a remedy and got no result.
LB1-28.target_section: Libya to Italy by boat > What happens
LB1-28.why_new: What the local broker does once people are taken hostage, and that village arbitration failed.

LB1-29.claim: Local people in Bhairab, Kishoreganj, said in July 2024 that several broker rings sending people to Italy by sea through Libya had been active there for 10 years and that many people did reach Italy through them; the most active, Rasel Mia's ring, then took several crore taka from 24 people, none of whom reached Italy.
LB1-29.why_new: Adds to 'People he has already sent': a ten-year local track record, followed by a batch of 24 none of whom arrived.

LB1-30.claim: Prothom Alo reported that on 5 July 2024, when Rasel Mia came to his home in Jagannathpur, Bhairab, victims' families surrounded and beat him and handed him to police, who sent him to Kishoreganj district jail under the trafficking Act; the officer-in-charge of Bhairab police station said the father of one victim filed a case after the arrest and Rasel was sent to jail in that case.
LB1-30.target_section: Libya to Italy by boat > The law
LB1-30.why_new: The case and arrest came only after the families themselves caught the broker.

LB1-31.claim: Rasel Mia admitted under police questioning that he took money on the promise of sending people to Italy, and said he had made all the arrangements but could not send everyone because new problems had arisen on the sea route, at which everyone grew impatient.
LB1-31.target_section: Libya to Italy by boat > The law
LB1-31.why_new: The broker's own explanation, on record.

LB1-32.claim: Prothom Alo reported on 21 September 2024 that a broker ring sent 26 young men from 25 families in Goalnagar union, Nasirnagar, Brahmanbaria, and Ratani village, Austagram, Kishoreganj, to Libya on the promise of Italy, each paying BDT 11 lakh; nine came home after torture and harassment, some of the rest were captive and several were missing.
LB1-32.target_section: Libya to Italy by boat > What happens
LB1-32.why_new: A village cluster case with the outcome counted: 9 of 26 back, none in Italy.

LB1-33.claim: Returnees from Nasirnagar, Brahmanbaria, and Austagram, Kishoreganj, said each of them gave the broker Farhad Mia BDT 4 lakh before leaving, that he took BDT 4.5 lakh more from each while holding them in a camp in Libya, and that after they were caught on the boat and jailed and he got them out, he again took BDT 2.5 lakh from each family promising to send them to Italy through the 'game' (the boat crossing).
LB1-33.target_section: Libya to Italy by boat > The contract price and the final price
LB1-33.why_new: The instalment structure of one deal: before departure, in the camp, and again for each new boat attempt.

LB1-34.claim: Returnees from Nasirnagar, Brahmanbaria, and Austagram, Kishoreganj, said that two and a half to three months after the last payment the broker sold them, that after three months in jail they reached their families through a Pakistani man with the help of a man from Bhairab, and could come home only after each paid a further BDT 1 lakh 20 thousand for the air ticket and other costs; they returned between 7 August and 14 September 2024 after release from Libyan jail.
LB1-34.target_section: Libya to Italy by boat > What happens
LB1-34.why_new: Getting out of Libyan jail and home cost each man a further BDT 1.2 lakh, paid by the family.

LB1-35.claim: Suman Mia of Nasirnagar told Prothom Alo he paid the broker BDT 11 lakh in all and was told he would be taken to Italy within a week; he said 60 people were put on a boat from Benghazi, and after it had run for an hour they understood they had all been sold.
LB1-35.target_section: Libya to Italy by boat > What happens
LB1-35.why_new: A 'boat to Italy' that was in fact the handover to buyers.

LB1-36.claim: Suman Mia said the 60 were held in a camp for a month and a half, beaten every day and fed once in 24 hours, given two litres of salt water for bathing and the toilet and one bread at night, and made to do cleaning work from morning to evening at the house of a man named Ahammad, whose son beat them with a pistol when they did not work.
LB1-36.target_section: Libya to Italy by boat > What happens
LB1-36.why_new: Conditions and forced unpaid labour in the camp, in a survivor's words.

LB1-37.claim: Enamul Haque of Lalurtuk village, Nasirnagar, said he spent BDT 22 lakh to send two sons (land sold for BDT 7 lakh, a BDT 12 lakh loan and savings), that one son was 'sold four times', and that he last spoke to the other a year earlier; both were missing in September 2024.
LB1-37.target_section: Libya to Italy by boat > What happens
LB1-37.why_new: Repeated resale of one person (four times), and disappearance for a year.

LB1-38.claim: The Nasirnagar Upazila Nirbahi Officer told Prothom Alo in September 2024 that the administration had not known of the 26 men's cases until journalists told them, that none of the victims had complained to it, and that legal action would follow an investigation if a complaint came; relatives had held a human chain demanding the brokers' trial and compensation.
LB1-38.target_section: Libya to Italy by boat > The law
LB1-38.why_new: What did not happen: no complaint, so no official action, 26 victims notwithstanding.

LB1-39.claim: One man the Nasirnagar families accuse, a cousin of the alleged ring leader, told Prothom Alo he had himself gone to Libya through that cousin, spent a month and a half in jail there with the others and 18 months in Libya in all, and took money from no one.
LB1-39.target_section: Libya to Italy by boat > The law
LB1-39.why_new: The accused's denial; also shows a relative of the broker travelling in the same batch.

LB1-40.claim: Faridul Alam of Chandanaish, Chattogram, who had worked in Dubai since 2003, told a columnist writing in Prothom Alo in December 2024 that he made a verbal contract of BDT 5 lakh with a Bangladeshi broker from Noakhali to be taken as far as Greece: BDT 50,000 in advance, BDT 1.5 lakh after reaching Iran and the remaining BDT 3 lakh after reaching Turkey.
LB1-40.target_section: NEW: From the Gulf overland through Iran and Turkey to Greece
LB1-40.why_new: A stage-payment contract tied to borders crossed (advance, Iran, Turkey) on a route the guide does not cover.
LB1-40.h3: NEW: From the Gulf overland through Iran and Turkey to Greece

LB1-41.claim: By Faridul Alam's account, at the end of 2010 the smugglers put him and several others in a taxi in Dubai that crossed the UAE border into a coastal hill area of Oman though the passengers had no passport or visa, and from there about thirty young men were put on a boat to Bandar Abbas in Iran, where another Bangladeshi broker received them.
LB1-41.target_section: NEW: From the Gulf overland through Iran and Turkey to Greece
LB1-41.why_new: First legs of the Gulf-to-Greece route: Dubai, Oman by taxi, boat to Bandar Abbas.
LB1-41.h3: NEW: From the Gulf overland through Iran and Turkey to Greece

LB1-42.claim: By Faridul Alam's account, after he reached Iran a relative in Dubai deposited BDT 1.5 lakh into an Iranian bank account the brokers gave, and the balance of the contract was paid into a bank account the brokers gave while the group was held in Istanbul.
LB1-42.target_section: NEW: From the Gulf overland through Iran and Turkey to Greece
LB1-42.why_new: How the stage payments are collected: bank accounts supplied by the brokers in the transit country.
LB1-42.h3: NEW: From the Gulf overland through Iran and Turkey to Greece

LB1-43.claim: Faridul Alam said the group was kept about seven days in Iran and taken by taxi and then bus into Turkey, that police took them off the bus on the way to Istanbul and sent them back to the border six times, and that the broker's men sent them again each time until they reached Istanbul on the seventh attempt.
LB1-43.target_section: NEW: From the Gulf overland through Iran and Turkey to Greece
LB1-43.why_new: Iran-Turkey leg, with six failed attempts inside Turkey.
LB1-43.h3: NEW: From the Gulf overland through Iran and Turkey to Greece

LB1-44.claim: Faridul Alam said that in Istanbul many people were kept crammed in one room and not allowed outside for more than a month, and that about a hundred people were then loaded for Greece into a closed lorry-like vehicle with room for 25 to 30 at most.
LB1-44.target_section: NEW: From the Gulf overland through Iran and Turkey to Greece
LB1-44.why_new: Holding house in Istanbul and the overloaded closed lorry across the Greek border.
LB1-44.h3: NEW: From the Gulf overland through Iran and Turkey to Greece

LB1-45.claim: By Faridul Alam's account, Greek soldiers or border guards caught the group where the lorry dropped them and put them in jail, UN refugee agency staff then moved them to a refugee camp, and after about ten days they were given a document called a 'stay paper' and took a bus to Athens with the EUR 60 per person the smugglers had handed them in Istanbul.
LB1-45.target_section: NEW: From the Gulf overland through Iran and Turkey to Greece
LB1-45.why_new: What arrival in Greece looked like on this route.
LB1-45.h3: NEW: From the Gulf overland through Iran and Turkey to Greece

LB1-46.claim: Faridul Alam said he presented himself as Rohingya in all his asylum applications in Greece because the smuggling ring's brokers advised that asylum might be easier that way; the court did not accept his application and stamped his stay paper, which let him stay one month, and he never got asylum in Greece despite four or five interviews.
LB1-46.target_section: NEW: From the Gulf overland through Iran and Turkey to Greece
LB1-46.why_new: Brokers coaching a false nationality for asylum, and that it did not work.
LB1-46.h3: NEW: From the Gulf overland through Iran and Turkey to Greece

LB1-47.claim: Faridul Alam said he lived about four years in Athens hawking and doing manual work, with police at times detaining him and taking his goods, and that what he earned fed him and left nothing to send to his family in Bangladesh.
LB1-47.target_section: NEW: From the Gulf overland through Iran and Turkey to Greece
LB1-47.why_new: The economic outcome: no remittance after reaching Europe.
LB1-47.h3: NEW: From the Gulf overland through Iran and Turkey to Greece

LB1-48.claim: Faridul Alam said that at the end of 2014 he left Athens by bus with two or three other Bangladeshis for Macedonia, then Serbia, then Hungary, where the bus of Afghan, Pakistani and Bangladeshi refugees was taken to a refugee camp; he then left for Austria and Germany, and in the Czech Republic police held him eight to ten days and took the money and papers in his bag and pockets and did not return them.
LB1-48.target_section: The Balkans and Eastern Europe > The path
LB1-48.why_new: The Greece-Macedonia-Serbia-Hungary overland leg, from a man who did it.

LB1-49.claim: Faridul Alam's asylum applications were rejected in Germany, where he lived on EUR 350 a month from a refugee camp from 2015 to 2018, and again in Paris, where the process took from 2018 to 2021; in December 2024 he was cooking for a mess of Bangladeshis in La Courneuve, Paris.
LB1-49.target_section: NEW: From the Gulf overland through Iran and Turkey to Greece
LB1-49.why_new: Fourteen years after leaving Dubai: three countries' asylum refusals and no legal status.
LB1-49.h3: NEW: From the Gulf overland through Iran and Turkey to Greece

LB1-50.claim: Faridul Alam said the Bangladesh embassy in Paris took his application and fingerprints for a passport and, after a long wait, told him it could not issue a new passport unless he submitted his old Bangladeshi one, which he had thrown away when he set out from Dubai because, he said, an asylum application cannot be made while holding it.
LB1-50.target_section: NEW: From the Gulf overland through Iran and Turkey to Greece
LB1-50.why_new: The cost of destroying the passport for an asylum claim: he cannot get a new one to go home.
LB1-50.h3: NEW: From the Gulf overland through Iran and Turkey to Greece

LB1-51.claim: According to their families, three men from Noli Joynagar village, Mathbaria, Pirojpur, left for Libya through a broker in July 2023 on a contract of BDT 3 lakh and went first to Dubai, after which contact was lost; some time later they called on imo from Libya to report torture, and the ring demanded BDT 12 lakh ransom per person.
LB1-51.target_section: Libya to Italy by boat > The contract price and the final price
LB1-51.why_new: A BDT 3 lakh contract turned into a BDT 12 lakh ransom demand; the article does not say Italy was promised.

LB1-52.claim: The wife of one of the three Mathbaria men said in January 2025 she had sold 15 katha of land to raise the BDT 12 lakh ransom, and the father of another said he had paid BDT 15 lakh since his son left and did not know how much more he would have to pay.
LB1-52.target_section: Libya to Italy by boat > The contract price and the final price
LB1-52.why_new: Five times the contract already paid by one family, eighteen months on, with the men still held.

LB1-53.claim: The wife of one Mathbaria hostage refused to name the brokers to Prothom Alo in January 2025, saying she wanted her husband back, and the family of another refused to speak at all, believing someone known to the brokers lived near their home and that the torture would increase if word got out.
LB1-53.target_section: Libya to Italy by boat > What happens
LB1-53.why_new: Why families stay silent while a relative is held: the ring has eyes in the village.

LB1-54.claim: The wife of one Mathbaria hostage filed a case under the trafficking Act at Mathbaria police station in 2024; the station's officer-in-charge said in January 2025 that the investigation had been given to the district detective branch and that it could say what progress there was.
LB1-54.target_section: Libya to Italy by boat > The law
LB1-54.why_new: A case filed while the men were still hostages, with no reported result months later.

LB1-55.claim: The Deputy Commissioner of Pirojpur, asked in January 2025 about three local men held for ransom in Libya, said the administration has little it can do in such cases, but that if the family complains it can inform the Ministry of Foreign Affairs in writing.
LB1-55.target_section: Libya to Italy by boat > Where to get help
LB1-55.why_new: What a district administration says it can actually do for a hostage's family: forward a written complaint to the Foreign Ministry.

LB1-56.claim: According to the Bangladesh embassy in Libya, a boat carrying 56 people trying to reach Italy from Libya sank in the Mediterranean on 25 January 2025 and 23 bodies washed up on the beach between 28 and 31 January; the bodies were decomposed and not formally identified, but the embassy, citing local sources, said nearly all were Bangladeshi.
LB1-56.target_section: Libya to Italy by boat > What happens
LB1-56.why_new: The January 2025 sinking (23 bodies) is not in the Death list.

LB1-57.claim: The brother of Abul Bashar Akon (32) of Rajoir, Madaripur, who died with his nephew Titu Howlader (19) in the January 2025 sinking, said a BDT 14 lakh contract had been made a year and a half earlier with a broker from Mahendradi to send the two to Italy on an agricultural visa, and that when that broker could not deliver they were forced to decide on the Libya route and made a new contract through another broker.
LB1-57.target_section: Libya to Italy by boat > How it is sold
LB1-57.why_new: A named case of a paid-for legal visa (agricultural, Italy) failing and the family being moved onto the boat route.

LB1-58.claim: The same brother said the broker had told the family the two men would reach Italy without any problem, that the family first heard of the nephew's death from the broker, and that the broker could no longer be found; the mother said both had told her by phone that they were fine and the broker would give them a 'game' very soon.
LB1-58.target_section: Libya to Italy by boat > How it is sold
LB1-58.why_new: The reassurance given before the boat and the broker's disappearance after it.

LB1-59.claim: The boat crossing from Libya to Europe is known as the 'game'; small boats are mainly used and are loaded beyond capacity, Prothom Alo wrote in February 2025.
LB1-59.target_section: Libya to Italy by boat > The path
LB1-59.why_new: The guide uses 'game houses' without saying that the crossing itself is called the 'game'.

LB1-60.claim: According to relatives, police and local sources, the two Rajoir men left home on 1 January 2025, flew from Dhaka through Dubai to Libya, were sent by the broker to the coast, and left the Libyan coast on an engine boat on 24 January.
LB1-60.target_section: Libya to Italy by boat > The path
LB1-60.why_new: Timing: 23 days from leaving home in Madaripur to the boat.

LB1-61.claim: According to police and local sources in Madaripur in February 2025, the ringleaders of the broker ring taking people to Italy through Libya, from Rajoir and from Bhanga in Faridpur, take BDT 18 to 25 lakh from each person under a contract for Europe, and several times more must be paid if the person is caught by Libyan police or held by mafia there.
LB1-61.target_section: Libya to Italy by boat > The contract price and the final price
LB1-61.why_new: The 2025 Madaripur price range, with the police's own statement that capture multiplies it.

LB1-62.claim: After the January 2025 sinking, local brokers in Rajoir went into hiding for fear of arrest, Prothom Alo reported; Madaripur's Additional Superintendent of Police said police were investigating the broker ring, and the Additional Deputy Commissioner said the district administration had started work through the embassy to bring the bodies home.
LB1-62.target_section: Libya to Italy by boat > The law
LB1-62.why_new: What the authorities did in the first days: investigation announced, no arrest reported, repatriation of bodies through the district administration.

LB1-63.claim: Intelligence sources said in February 2025 that, besides the two dead, eight more people from Rajoir upazila, all aged 20 to 30, were reported missing, though it was not confirmed whether they were on the boat that sank on 25 January.
LB1-63.target_section: Libya to Italy by boat > The numbers
LB1-63.why_new: Concentration in one upazila: ten dead or missing from Rajoir around one sinking.

LB1-64.claim: The father of Hridoy Howlader of Kamarkhali, Faridpur, said the group was to be taken to Italy by ship on the night of 24 January 2025, that many refused to board when a small boat was offered instead, and that those who refused were shot dead while those who boarded drowned, according to a Prothom Alo editorial of 6 February 2025.
LB1-64.target_section: Libya to Italy by boat > What happens
LB1-64.why_new: A family's allegation that people who refused the small boat were shot; the guide has no account of forced boarding.

LB1-65.claim: Sujan Faraji of Madaripur, who died in the January 2025 sinking, set out with BDT 16 lakh taken from his aunt without telling his father, who had not agreed to the journey; a broker named Monir Sheikh of Majumdarkandi, Rajoir, had contracted to take him to Italy for BDT 15 lakh, according to a Prothom Alo editorial of 6 February 2025.
LB1-65.target_section: Libya to Italy by boat > The contract price and the final price
LB1-65.why_new: A young man leaving against his father's wishes on a relative's money; a BDT 15 lakh contract.

LB1-66.claim: Relatives said at least 12 people from Madaripur and Faridpur were among those killed in Libya, according to a Prothom Alo editorial of 6 February 2025 that discussed the January 2025 boat sinking.
LB1-66.target_section: Libya to Italy by boat > The numbers
LB1-66.why_new: District concentration of the dead in the January 2025 sinking.

LB1-67.claim: According to Bangladesh embassy sources in Tripoli cited in a Prothom Alo editorial of 6 February 2025, 4,200 Bangladeshis had been freed from various detention centres in Libya and sent home in the previous year and a half, and more than a thousand irregular Bangladeshis were still held in Libya.
LB1-67.target_section: Libya to Italy by boat > The numbers
LB1-67.why_new: An embassy figure for returns from detention (mid-2023 to early 2025) and the number still held.

LB1-68.claim: A Prothom Alo editorial of 6 February 2025 stated that 84,000 Bangladeshis went to Europe by sea from 2009 to 2024 and that on average at least 100 Bangladeshis die each year when boats sink (it gives no source for either figure).
LB1-68.target_section: Libya to Italy by boat > The numbers
LB1-68.why_new: A Bangladeshi death estimate per year; the guide gives only all-nationality deaths. Unsourced in the article, so needs a source before use.

LB1-69.claim: The migration analyst Asif Munir told Deutsche Welle that each person needs BDT 16 to 20 lakh for this journey and that international as well as local rings are involved, as quoted in a Prothom Alo editorial of 6 February 2025.
LB1-69.target_section: Libya to Italy by boat > How it is sold
LB1-69.why_new: A named analyst's price range in taka for early 2025.

LB1-70.claim: A Prothom Alo editorial of 6 February 2025 stated that some licensed manpower-exporting firms are behind these broker rings and send people abroad through them, and that cases against many such firms in the past led to no action because many of those involved were influential people linked to the then ruling party.
LB1-70.target_section: Libya to Italy by boat > The law
LB1-70.why_new: The newspaper's own assertion, not a sourced finding, that licensed agencies sit behind the boat brokers; flag as editorial opinion.

LB1-71.claim: According to relatives and police, 24 young men from Shariatpur and Madaripur who were taken from home in 2022 and 2023 to be sent to Italy from Libya by an illegal route went missing in Libya; relatives claim none of the 24 has contacted family since 21 and 22 March 2024.
LB1-71.target_section: Libya to Italy by boat > What happens
LB1-71.why_new: A batch of 24 from one broker lost on the same two days with no word for 11 months.

LB1-72.claim: The 24 Shariatpur and Madaripur men were sent first to the United Arab Emirates, then through Egypt to Libya, according to Palong Model police station and relatives.
LB1-72.target_section: Libya to Italy by boat > The path
LB1-72.why_new: Confirms the UAE-Egypt-Libya routing for 2022-24 departures from Shariatpur.

LB1-73.claim: In the Shariatpur case the broker ring took BDT 12 lakh to 20 lakh from the 24 families in various ways; some of the men were detained by police in Libya on two occasions and jailed, some were held hostage and tortured, and they were freed from captivity and jail after money was collected from their families.
LB1-73.target_section: Libya to Italy by boat > The contract price and the final price
LB1-73.why_new: Money taken both for release from hostage-takers and for release from Libyan jail.

LB1-74.claim: The man arrested in the Shariatpur case, Rashed Khan of Charjadabpur village, Shariatpur Sadar, works at sending manpower to various countries and has a firm named Lamisa Enterprise, according to police and relatives; one wife said her husband left home with him on 3 February 2024.
LB1-74.why_new: A broker with a named firm and a known manpower business in the district; the article gives no licence.

LB1-75.claim: Fatema Akter, whose husband Shahin Sikdar (26) went missing on the way to Italy, said he left home with the broker on 3 February 2024, phoned some days later to say they would be sent from Libya to Italy illegally by sea, last spoke to the family on the night of 22 March 2024, that the broker took BDT 18 lakh from them at various times, and that she could not stay in her area because of debt pressure.
LB1-75.target_section: Libya to Italy by boat > How it is sold
LB1-75.why_new: The family learned the journey was the illegal sea route only by phone after he had left.

LB1-76.claim: Riaz Akon said his family gave the broker BDT 20 lakh, raised by selling land and a cattle farm, to send his younger brother to Italy, had had no trace of him for a year, and that the broker gave no information when asked.
LB1-76.target_section: Libya to Italy by boat > What happens
LB1-76.why_new: A second family's payment and the broker's silence.

LB1-77.claim: Relatives of the 24 missing men filed 11 cases against Rashed Khan and his associates in the Shariatpur court and at Palong Model police station; the CID arrested him in Jatrabari, Dhaka, on 14 February 2025 in a case under the trafficking Act filed by the father of a missing man from Kalkini, Madaripur, and a Shariatpur magistrate sent him to jail the next day, fixing a later date to hear the police's remand request and his bail application.
LB1-77.target_section: Libya to Italy by boat > The law
LB1-77.why_new: Eleven cases by families led to a CID arrest in Dhaka; shows the route from family case to arrest.

LB1-78.claim: On 15 February 2025, on hearing of the arrest, relatives of the missing men began a hunger strike in the grounds of the Shariatpur District and Sessions Judge's court demanding exemplary punishment and the tracing of the missing men.
LB1-78.target_section: Libya to Italy by boat > Where to get help
LB1-78.why_new: Arrest did not produce information on the missing; families resorted to a hunger strike.

LB1-79.claim: BDT 15 lakh, then BDT 30 lakh more: according to his family, Md Rasel Mia (25) of Dharmandal village, Nasirnagar, Brahmanbaria, went to Libya in early 2024 through a broker from his own village for BDT 15 lakh, raised by selling the ancestral homestead and borrowing from relatives; he was sold to a local ring on arrival, which sent videos of his torture to Bangladesh and took a further BDT 30 lakh from the family in rounds.
LB1-79.target_section: Libya to Italy by boat > The contract price and the final price
LB1-79.why_new: A further contract-versus-final-price case: BDT 15 lakh agreed, BDT 45-50 lakh paid, and the man died.

LB1-80.claim: According to Rasel Mia's family, the ring demanded BDT 10 lakh more a few days before his death, and when the family could not pay he was tortured and died in Libya on 21 February 2025; the family learned of the death the next day through an expatriate, and his father, who said he had paid BDT 50 lakh in stages by selling his homestead and farmland, alleged his son was killed with a poisonous injection.
LB1-80.target_section: Libya to Italy by boat > What happens
LB1-80.why_new: Death after the family ran out of money, having paid BDT 50 lakh; guide's Death list has boats only, plus the two contract-price cases.

LB1-81.claim: After Rasel Mia's death the broker from his village fled with his family, Prothom Alo reported on 22 February 2025; the officer-in-charge of Nasirnagar police station said legal steps would be taken if the victim's family gave a written complaint.
LB1-81.target_section: Libya to Italy by boat > The law
LB1-81.why_new: No case at the time of death: police wait for a written complaint while the broker absconds.

LB1-82.claim: Khurshed Mia (35), a vegetable seller in Bhairab, Kishoreganj, said he first went to Libya on 14 June 2023 for BDT 4 lakh on the understanding that the broker would find him work in Libya until he went on to Italy, and that he got work there as a painter.
LB1-82.target_section: Libya to Italy by boat > How it is sold
LB1-82.why_new: A named case of the 'work in Libya first' offer, with the entry price (BDT 4 lakh).

LB1-83.claim: Khurshed Mia said that in Libya, after a month without work, he got a job at a shopping mall 'in exchange for 500 dinars' that was to pay 1,400 dinars at the end of the month but paid him half, and then worked four months at an oil company for 1,200 dinars a month.
LB1-83.target_section: Libya to Italy by boat > What happens
LB1-83.why_new: What work in Libya paid in 2024, the fee to get a job, and wage theft.

LB1-84.claim: Khurshed Mia said that while working in Libya he agreed with a broker to be taken by sea to Italy for BDT 9 lakh and paid BDT 6 lakh in two rounds without reaching Italy; he said the whole attempt cost him BDT 19 lakh, plus several lakh for treatment, and that he had to sell the land his house stood on.
LB1-84.target_section: Libya to Italy by boat > The contract price and the final price
LB1-84.why_new: The price of the sea leg alone when bought inside Libya (BDT 9 lakh) against the total spent (BDT 19 lakh).

LB1-85.claim: Khurshed Mia said law-enforcement officers raided the fourth-floor flat where 11 of them lived at about 1:30 am on 10 July 2024 and he hid for two hours on the window ledge; later he was kept in a place with 210 other people, where a raid at 10 pm took away 160 while he hid for four hours in a tree.
LB1-85.target_section: Libya to Italy by boat > What happens
LB1-85.why_new: Raids by Libyan forces on migrants' housing and on a holding house of over 200 people.

LB1-86.claim: Khurshed Mia said a mafia group attacked the building the broker had moved him to and he jumped from the first floor to save himself, injuring his arm and leg; he got no treatment for five days, the broker's men moved him from a private hospital to a government hospital because they could not bear the cost, he had five operations in three and a half months there, and he came home on 13 February 2025 unable to walk.
LB1-86.target_section: Libya to Italy by boat > What happens
LB1-86.why_new: Permanent disability as an outcome, and what medical care looked like for an injured migrant in Libya.

LB1-87.claim: A Prothom Alo editorial of 1 April 2026 said the family of Shayek Ahmed (23) of Sunamganj gave brokers BDT 12 lakh by selling their cows and land, that the rubber boat he left on from Libya for Greece on 21 March lost its way and drifted for six days, that he died of starvation when the food ran out, and that 12 young men from Sunamganj died on that journey and their bodies were thrown into the sea.
LB1-87.target_section: Libya to Italy by boat > What happens
LB1-87.why_new: Adds to the March 2026 Greece boat already in the Death list: rubber boat, six days adrift, death by starvation, 12 of the dead from Sunamganj, price paid.

LB1-88.claim: According to CID information cited in a Prothom Alo editorial of 1 April 2026, 17,000 Bangladeshis were sent to Italy by illegal routes in the previous year.
LB1-88.target_section: Libya to Italy by boat > The numbers
LB1-88.why_new: A CID figure for the year to March 2026; differs from the 20,164 sea arrivals for 2025 the section already gives, so note the source.

LB1-89.claim: According to Home Ministry data cited in a Prothom Alo editorial of 1 April 2026, about 4,500 cases were filed under the trafficking Act in the five years 2020 to 2024, and 94 to 95 per cent of the accused in them were acquitted; the editorial added that in most incidents no case is filed at all.
LB1-89.why_new: Five-year case count and acquittal rate under the old Act.

LB1-90.claim: Speakers at a roundtable held by BRAC and Prothom Alo in Sylhet on 18 April 2026 said there is no legal way to go abroad by sea and that no one can lawfully leave Bangladesh for work abroad except through the Dhaka, Chattogram and Sylhet airports.
LB1-90.target_section: The Overseas Employment and Migrants Act 2013
LB1-90.why_new: States in plain words which exits are lawful; the guide cites section 34 ('official exit point') without naming them.

LB1-91.claim: Shahriar Zaman, a returnee from the United Kingdom (introduced as having stayed 10 years, though the article also says he was there about eight years), told a roundtable in Sylhet on 18 April 2026 that he went there to study through brokers who said he could work legally alongside his studies, that he found nothing of the kind and had to work illegally, and that he was paid GBP 1 an hour where others got GBP 8.
LB1-91.target_section: Student visas used as work routes > What happens
LB1-91.why_new: A returnee's wage figure for undocumented work after a broker-arranged student route to the UK.
LB1-91.h3: Student visas used as work routes

LB1-92.claim: Joni Lal Deb, Assistant Superintendent of Police with 7 APBn (Armed Police Battalion) at Sylhet's Osmani International Airport, said on 18 April 2026 that an active group of human traffickers and smugglers operates in the airport area and tries to mislead ordinary passengers with various inducements.
LB1-92.target_section: Departure day at the airport > Who gets stopped
LB1-92.why_new: A named airport police officer on touts working the airport area at Sylhet.

LB1-93.claim: According to an account by Bangladesh's ambassador to Libya, Major General Habib Ullah, quoted by former foreign affairs adviser Md Touhid Hossain in Prothom Alo on 27 April 2026, among 113 irregular migrants sent home from Libya one had paid brokers and mafia BDT 82 lakh in stages and another BDT 73 lakh, and when asked how many had paid a broker more than BDT 20 lakh, over fifty of the 113 raised their hands.
LB1-93.target_section: Libya to Italy by boat > The contract price and the final price
LB1-93.why_new: The highest totals on record in these articles (BDT 82 and 73 lakh), and a share: nearly half of one return flight had paid over BDT 20 lakh.

LB1-94.claim: By the ambassador's account, about two-thirds of the 113 returnees on that flight identified themselves as from Madaripur.
LB1-94.target_section: Libya to Italy by boat > The numbers
LB1-94.why_new: How concentrated the route is in one district, from a head count on a return flight.

LB1-95.claim: Returnees told the ambassador to Libya before their flight home in spring 2026 that one had eaten rice once after twenty days, five men sharing one bowl with no curry, that another got a handful after twenty-five days, and that a piece of bread was thrown at them 'the way food is given to a dog' and they were beaten as well.
LB1-95.target_section: Libya to Italy by boat > What happens
LB1-95.why_new: Detainees' own words on food in captivity.

LB1-96.claim: One of the 113 returnees told the ambassador he had lived in Libya for 14 years before deciding, in old age, to try the 'game' (the boat crossing to Italy).
LB1-96.target_section: Recruited while abroad or just back
LB1-96.why_new: Long-settled workers in Libya also take the boat; the section has Gulf and Russia examples only.
LB1-96.h3: Recruited while abroad or just back

LB1-97.claim: The 113 migrants reached Dhaka the next day, and IOM paid the whole cost from the airfare to their travel back to their own villages, Md Touhid Hossain wrote in Prothom Alo on 27 April 2026; they went home with nothing.
LB1-97.target_section: Libya to Italy by boat > Where to get help
LB1-97.why_new: Says exactly what IOM covers on a return flight: airfare and onward travel to the village.

LB1-98.claim: On 4 April 2026 a wooden boat that left Tajoura, Libya, for the Italian island of Lampedusa with about 105 passengers sank; 32 people were rescued alive and 2 bodies recovered, the other 71 were missing, and Bangladeshis were among both the rescued and the missing, Md Touhid Hossain wrote in Prothom Alo on 27 April 2026.
LB1-98.target_section: Libya to Italy by boat > What happens
LB1-98.why_new: The April 2026 Tajoura sinking is not in the Death list; names Tajoura as a departure point.

LB1-99.claim: Md Touhid Hossain wrote in Prothom Alo on 27 April 2026 that a boat that left Libya for Greece on 21 March 2026 with 48 passengers drifted for six days before 26 people were rescued alive, 21 of them Bangladeshis, and that 20 of the 22 dead or missing were reported to be Bangladeshi.
LB1-99.target_section: Libya to Italy by boat > What happens
LB1-99.why_new: Different counts from the guide's for the same March 2026 boat (guide: 43 aboard, 38 Bangladeshis, at least 18 dead); record the conflict.

LB1-100.claim: Md Touhid Hossain, the former foreign affairs adviser, wrote in April 2026 that because surveillance and restrictions on the route to Italy had recently increased, traffickers were now using the Greece route.
LB1-100.target_section: Libya to Italy by boat > The path
LB1-100.why_new: A named former official on the 2026 shift from Italy to Greece as the destination from Libya.

LB1-101.claim: Md Touhid Hossain wrote that the main route to Italy by sea used to be a flight to Kenya, then overland to Libya, then the boat, and that a person boards the plane to Kenya on a false story of a safari or tourism; along the way people change hands several times like goods.
LB1-101.target_section: Libya to Italy by boat > The path
LB1-101.why_new: A Kenya entry point and the cover story used at departure; the guide's path lists only Dubai, Egypt, India and Sri Lanka.

LB1-102.claim: Md Touhid Hossain wrote that many Bengalis are among those who torture the hostages in Libya, and that the people who collect ransom from families in Bangladesh by showing torture videos live undisturbed in the same society.
LB1-102.target_section: Libya to Italy by boat > What happens
LB1-102.why_new: A former foreign adviser stating that Bangladeshis do the torturing and the ransom collection is done at home.

LB1-103.claim: The Minister for Expatriates' Welfare and Overseas Employment, Ariful Haque Chowdhury, said at a roundtable in Sylhet on 18 April 2026 that the government is building a system to stop people being cheated by paying brokers, and plans, in discussion with the Bangladesh Bank governor, to introduce a 'Probashi card' so that migrants are served through a set system instead of cash transactions.
LB1-103.target_section: The staged-payment trap, and no receipts
LB1-103.why_new: A stated government plan (not yet a scheme) to replace cash payments; the guide has nothing on it.
LB1-103.h3: The staged-payment trap, and no receipts

LB1-104.claim: The Minister for Expatriates' Welfare said on 18 April 2026 that the government had declared zero tolerance of the 'mafia syndicate' at home and abroad and was determined to identify the Bangladeshi members of trafficking rings in Libya and elsewhere, bring them back and try them.
LB1-104.target_section: Libya to Italy by boat > The law
LB1-104.why_new: A ministerial commitment on Bangladeshi traffickers based in Libya; a statement of intent, not an action taken.

LB1-105.claim: Shariful Islam Hasan, associate director of BRAC's Migration Programme, said on 18 April 2026 that Bangladeshis are the largest group in the world crossing the Mediterranean to Europe, a situation that has lasted a decade, and that people from 8 to 10 districts, among them Madaripur, Shariatpur, Sylhet, Sunamganj and Habiganj, are losing their lives going this way.
LB1-105.target_section: Libya to Italy by boat > The numbers
LB1-105.why_new: The source districts, named by BRAC; the guide gives no district list for the boat route.

LB1-106.claim: Shariful Islam Hasan of BRAC's Migration Programme said on 18 April 2026 that the programme had helped about 39,000 people at the airport in the previous eight years, and gives returnees reintegration support and training, followed by counselling and help to set up as entrepreneurs.
LB1-106.target_section: Where victims and families get help
LB1-106.why_new: Scale of BRAC's airport help (39,000 in eight years) for the BRAC item in the help list.
LB1-106.h3: Where victims and families get help

LB1-107.claim: Roksana Akter of Bishwanath, Sylhet, said on 18 April 2026 that she went to Saudi Arabia through a broker from Sunamganj, was abused in various ways at her workplace and had to borrow to come home, where she faced insult and neglect; she said the EU and BRAC's Prottasha-2 project then helped her set up a shop, whose income now runs her household.
LB1-107.target_section: Where victims and families get help
LB1-107.why_new: Evidence from a returnee that BRAC's reintegration help (Prottasha-2) produced a working livelihood.
LB1-107.h3: Where victims and families get help

LB1-108.claim: Joni Lal Deb, Assistant Superintendent of Police with 7 APBn at Osmani International Airport, Sylhet, said on 18 April 2026 that various rings use people going abroad for the first time as easy targets, especially to draw them into carrying drugs or smuggled goods, and that many do not realise they are becoming part of a crime ring.
LB1-108.target_section: Departure day at the airport > Who gets stopped
LB1-108.why_new: A specific airport risk for first-time migrants (being used as carriers), stated by airport police.

LB1-109.claim: The same officer said the armed police unit at Sylhet's Osmani airport should have more than three hundred members but has about one hundred, and that intelligence and plain-clothes members work the airport to stop anyone luring passengers.
LB1-109.target_section: Departure day at the airport > Who checks what
LB1-109.why_new: Staffing at Sylhet airport security: a third of sanctioned strength.

LB1-110.claim: Md Nazmus Sakib, assistant director of the District Employment and Manpower Office in Sylhet, said on 18 April 2026 that about 2,900 licensed agencies send workers abroad but all are Dhaka-centred, that only a few agencies work directly in Sylhet and the rest work as brokers under the cover of travel agencies, and that money beyond the set limit is being taken as a result.
LB1-110.target_section: The chain from the village to the visa seller
LB1-110.why_new: A DEMO official saying that outside Dhaka the 'agency' a migrant meets is usually a travel agency acting as broker.

LB1-111.claim: Mohammad Nasir Uddin, general secretary of the Sylhet District Press Club, said on 18 April 2026 that Sylhet has over 150 licensed travel agencies but more than 500 agencies are in fact active illegally, taking BDT 8 lakh to 20 lakh to send people abroad (he gave no source for the figures).
LB1-111.target_section: The chain from the village to the visa seller
LB1-111.why_new: A local estimate of unlicensed travel agencies in Sylhet and what they charge; unsourced, attribute to the speaker.

LB1-112.claim: The assistant director of Sylhet's District Employment and Manpower Office said on 18 April 2026 that the office gives people who want to go abroad through the government channel registration, fingerprinting and a three-day pre-decision training covering legal migration, avoiding brokers and safety, that many people fall in with brokers before the training, and that the office completed registration and biometrics for 35,290 people in 2025 and 6,290 up to March 2026.
LB1-112.target_section: How do I register on OEP?
LB1-112.why_new: The three-day pre-decision training at the DEMO, and one district's registration volume.

LB1-113.claim: Md Salah Uddin, deputy director of the Divisional Passport and Visa Office in Sylhet, said on 18 April 2026 that the regular-service passport fee is BDT 4,025 for five years and BDT 5,750 for ten years and the super-express fee is BDT 10,350, and that with super-express service a person who completes biometrics in the morning can get the passport in Dhaka by the afternoon.
LB1-113.why_new: Ten-year fee and a super-express figure not in the guide (which gives 4,025 / 6,325 / 8,625); check the 10,350 figure against the official fee table.

LB1-114.claim: The same passport official said a person aged 18 or over can apply with a national ID card and a person under 18 with a birth registration, paying the set fee at a bank and giving fingerprints.
LB1-114.why_new: Plain statement of the identity document needed by age, from a passport office head.

LB1-115.claim: Zakir Hossain, senior instructor at the Sylhet government Technical Training Centre, said on 18 April 2026 that the centre runs regular Japanese, Italian, Korean and Arabic language courses and, with International Labour Organization support, level-three training in electrical installation and maintenance and in food preparation that combines language with the trade, with a possibility of work in Italy after the training.
LB1-115.target_section: How do I join a TTC course?
LB1-115.why_new: A concrete legal alternative in a boat-route district: Italian-language and ILO-backed trade courses at Sylhet TTC.

LB1-116.claim: The Sylhet TTC instructor said that many of the people who most need the training do not come, that college and university students with no immediate need to go abroad come instead, and that in the centre's experience about 99 per cent of people go abroad without acquiring any skill.
LB1-116.target_section: How do I join a TTC course?
LB1-116.why_new: A trainer's estimate that almost nobody who migrates from Sylhet has trained first.

LB1-117.claim: Mahbubul Mannan Chowdhury, acting regional head of Probashi Kallyan Bank (PKB, the state bank for migrants) in Sylhet, said on 18 April 2026 that by the ministry's list going abroad through the government channel costs about BDT 1 lakh 60 to 70 thousand, but that most people in practice spend more than BDT 4 to 5 lakh, and that agencies' profit reaching BDT 2.5 to 3 lakh cannot be justified.
LB1-117.target_section: What people pay, and to whom
LB1-117.why_new: A PKB regional head's figure for the gap between official cost and what borrowers actually pay, and his estimate of the agency margin.

LB1-118.claim: The PKB acting regional head in Sylhet said on 18 April 2026 that many people come to the bank and have to take loans of BDT 3 to 4 lakh, with a monthly instalment of about BDT 14,000, and that many take four to five months or longer to get work after going abroad, during which the loan weighs on them more.
LB1-118.target_section: Can I get a government loan to go abroad?
LB1-118.why_new: Typical PKB migration loan size and instalment, and the gap before the first wage, from the bank itself.

LB1-119.claim: The PKB acting regional head in Sylhet said on 18 April 2026 that the bank tries to help returnees who come back having suffered losses with loans at 8 per cent interest, but that in many cases this is not succeeding.
LB1-119.target_section: What help is there when I come back?
LB1-119.why_new: The bank's own admission that its returnee loans often do not work.

LB1-120.claim: The director of Osmani International Airport, Sylhet, said on 18 April 2026 that many of the victims heard at that day's roundtable had spent BDT 10 to 15 lakh, and up to BDT 20 lakh, to go abroad.
LB1-120.target_section: Libya to Italy by boat > The contract price and the final price
LB1-120.why_new: A Sylhet-side spending range for irregular journeys, from survivors' testimony at one meeting.

LB1-121.claim: The general secretary of the Sylhet District Press Club said on 18 April 2026 that over the previous 10 years at least 10,000 people had died or gone missing, more than two and a half lakh had been trafficked abroad by illegal routes and at least 15,000 had been jailed in various countries (he gave no source).
LB1-121.target_section: Libya to Italy by boat > The numbers
LB1-121.why_new: Ten-year totals from a speaker with no source given; usable only with attribution or after checking.

LB1-122.claim: Sujan Mia of Simtola village, Chhatak upazila, said on 18 April 2026 that he first went from Bangladesh to Oman for construction work, moved to Dubai after a problem with his iqama (residence permit) and then worked in Qatar, and later returned to Dubai to head for Europe, going through Oman to Iran, Turkey, Greece, North Macedonia and Serbia, working illegally to survive.
LB1-122.target_section: NEW: From the Gulf overland through Iran and Turkey to Greece
LB1-122.why_new: A second, later account of the Dubai-Oman-Iran-Turkey-Greece route, supporting a section for it.
LB1-122.h3: NEW: From the Gulf overland through Iran and Turkey to Greece

LB1-123.claim: Sujan Mia said that, finding no chance of legal work in the countries he passed through, he went back to Greece and from there travelled through Bulgaria, Albania and Bosnia and across Italy to France, where he worked about four years and eight months and tried to regularise; though he paid tax and completed the process, he was caught before he got legal papers and came back to Bangladesh.
LB1-123.target_section: The Balkans and Eastern Europe > The path
LB1-123.why_new: A Greece-Bulgaria-Albania-Bosnia-Italy-France overland path, and deportation after nearly five years.

LB1-124.claim: Sujan Mia of Chhatak upazila, who said he was caught in France and returned to Bangladesh, said on 18 April 2026 that when he later tried for an Australian visa a broker and an agency took BDT 17 lakh from him and gave him a fake visa.
LB1-124.target_section: Fake visa, demand letter or job offer
LB1-124.why_new: A deportee cheated again at home: BDT 17 lakh for a fake Australian visa.
LB1-124.h3: Fake visa, demand letter or job offer

LB1-125.claim: Mizanur Rahman of Phulsuti village, Nagarkanda, Faridpur, alleged at a human chain outside the Faridpur Deputy Commissioner's office on 14 October 2026 that a Faridpur trafficking ring, having promised to take him to Italy, held and tortured him in Libya and took BDT 60 lakh in three rounds.
LB1-125.target_section: Libya to Italy by boat > The contract price and the final price
LB1-125.why_new: BDT 60 lakh in three rounds, the largest named single-victim total in the 2026 cases here.

LB1-126.claim: Mizanur Rahman said that, still not released after the payments and seeing how severe the torture was, he broke a window, escaped and gave himself up to Libyan police, and later came home in 2026 through IOM; eleven people tortured by the same ring came home from Libya through IOM in 2026 and joined the human chain.
LB1-126.target_section: Libya to Italy by boat > What happens
LB1-126.why_new: A way out that worked: escaping and surrendering to Libyan police, then return through IOM.

LB1-127.claim: At the same human chain, Taslima Begum said her husband Habib was killed because the family could not pay a ransom of BDT 10 lakh; she now lives with their three children at her father's house.
LB1-127.target_section: Libya to Italy by boat > What happens
LB1-127.why_new: A killing alleged over an unpaid BDT 10 lakh ransom.

LB1-128.claim: Asked about the returnees' demand for trial of the Faridpur ring, the Additional Superintendent of Police (Crime and Ops) of Faridpur said on 14 October 2026 that legal action would be taken if the victims' families complained, and that steps would follow investigation if anyone had filed a case; one victim at the human chain asked, 'Where do I go to get justice?'
LB1-128.target_section: Libya to Italy by boat > The law
LB1-128.why_new: Eleven returnees protesting publicly and the police still asking for a complaint: no case or arrest is reported.

LB1-129.claim: According to investigators, on 5 August 2025 the wife of Md Saiful (39) of Sundarganj, Gaibandha, who had gone to Libya about two years before November 2026 through a Bangladeshi broker, got a call from a Libyan mobile number saying he was in the callers' custody, that BDT 30 lakh ransom must be paid or he would be killed, and that no one in the family would be allowed to speak to him until half the ransom was paid.
LB1-129.target_section: Libya to Italy by boat > What happens
LB1-129.why_new: A ransom demand with no proof of life: half must be paid before the family may hear the man's voice.

LB1-130.claim: The CID said the family sent BDT 5 lakh in all between 10 and 25 August 2025 from a bKash shop at Bamandanga Hall Mor, Sundarganj, to several mobile numbers the accused gave, and that even after the money was received the family was not put in touch with Saiful.
LB1-130.target_section: Libya to Italy by boat > What happens
LB1-130.why_new: How ransom is paid inside Bangladesh: mobile-wallet transfers from a local agent shop to several numbers.

LB1-131.claim: According to the CID, after the family of a man held in Libya had paid BDT 5 lakh in August 2025, a man named Sohel contacted the hostage's wife, said he had all the information and would if necessary go to Libya himself to rescue him, and told her to come to the Kadamtali area of Dhaka; when she went there his phone was switched off.
LB1-131.target_section: People who offer to get your money back
LB1-131.why_new: A 'rescuer' approaching a hostage's family; extends the section from debt recovery to hostage recovery.
LB1-131.h3: People who offer to get your money back

LB1-132.claim: According to the CID, the father of the Gaibandha hostage was then contacted from another number and asked for a further BDT 42 lakh in the name of rescuing his son, and was told his son was held by two men in Libya named Mokarram and Anwar from whom the caller had got the father's number; the father said he would pay nothing more unless he could speak to his son directly, and no more calls came to him or to his son's wife.
LB1-132.target_section: Libya to Italy by boat > What happens
LB1-132.why_new: Successive callers demanding rising sums (30, then 42 lakh) with no proof of life; when the family insisted on speaking to him, the calls stopped.

LB1-133.claim: The father of the Gaibandha hostage filed a case under the trafficking Act at Sundarganj police station on 5 September 2025, the case was sent to the CID for investigation, and on 12 November 2026 the CID arrested two men from Chandpur village, Singra, at Singra Bazar, Natore; the CID said it was still gathering information on where in Libya the son was held and on rescuing him.
LB1-133.target_section: Libya to Italy by boat > Where to get help
LB1-133.why_new: A second example of a family's police case reaching the CID and producing arrests, here 14 months after filing, with the hostage still not found.

LB1-134.claim: In its statement on the Gaibandha case on 13 November 2026 the CID asked everyone to verify the legality of the person, the agency, the visa and the employing firm before going abroad.
LB1-134.target_section: Libya to Italy by boat > Where to get help
LB1-134.why_new: The CID's stated advice (it does not say how to verify).

AB2-1.claim: In a Prothom Alo column published on 26 May 2026, Dr Selim Reza, associate professor and coordinator of the Centre for Migration Studies at North South University, wrote that workers who spend BDT 4 to 7 lakh on a Qatar "free visa" find on arrival that there is no assured job for them: a company's name is on the papers but in reality there is no work.
AB2-1.target_section: Free visas and visa trading in the Gulf
AB2-1.why_new: The section says free-visa workers find no job; it does not say that the visa papers still carry a company name that has no work behind it.
AB2-1.h3: Free visas and visa trading in the Gulf

AB2-2.claim: In a Prothom Alo column published on 26 May 2026, Dr Selim Reza, associate professor and coordinator of the Centre for Migration Studies at North South University, wrote that in practice a "free visa" means sending a worker without any specific job, and that the arrangement is a form of visa trading from which brokers, recruiting agencies and some dishonest businessmen profit.
AB2-2.target_section: Free visas and visa trading in the Gulf
AB2-2.why_new: Names who profits (brokers, recruiting agencies, some businessmen), attributed to a named migration researcher.
AB2-2.h3: Free visas and visa trading in the Gulf

AB2-3.claim: In a Prothom Alo column published on 26 May 2026, Dr Selim Reza, associate professor and coordinator of the Centre for Migration Studies at North South University, wrote that in Doha and the areas around it countless Bangladeshi workers now wait for temporary work, some get no work for weeks on end, and many go unpaid for months.
AB2-3.target_section: Free visas and visa trading in the Gulf
AB2-3.why_new: Ground-level detail on what joblessness in Qatar looks like (waiting for casual work around Doha, weeks without work); the section only says they hunt for illegal day labour.
AB2-3.h3: Free visas and visa trading in the Gulf

AB2-4.claim: In a Prothom Alo column published on 26 May 2026, Dr Selim Reza, associate professor and coordinator of the Centre for Migration Studies at North South University, wrote that thousands of Bangladeshi workers in Qatar are now without work or pay, that a large share of them are jobless after being cheated through visa trading and broker rings, that some have become undocumented and that many lack food and medical care.
AB2-4.target_section: Free visas and visa trading in the Gulf
AB2-4.why_new: A dated (May 2026) expert statement on the scale and condition of jobless Bangladeshis in Qatar; the author gives no count beyond 'thousands'.
AB2-4.h3: Free visas and visa trading in the Gulf

AB2-5.claim: In a Prothom Alo column published on 26 May 2026, Dr Selim Reza, associate professor and coordinator of the Centre for Migration Studies at North South University, wrote that after the 2022 football World Cup ended, employment fell in a large part of Qatar's construction sector, many companies wound up their projects and many laid off workers, so new job openings are fewer than before.
AB2-5.target_section: Free visas and visa trading in the Gulf
AB2-5.why_new: Explains why a Qatar free-visa holder now finds no work: the post-World Cup fall in construction jobs. The section has no such explanation.
AB2-5.h3: Free visas and visa trading in the Gulf

AB2-6.claim: Qatar's labour minister, Dr Ali bin Samikh Al Marri, said during his visit to Dhaka that began on 17 May 2026 that about 4 lakh 73 thousand Bangladeshis work in Qatar and about 30 percent of them work on development projects, according to a Prothom Alo column of 26 May 2026.
AB2-6.target_section: Free visas and visa trading in the Gulf
AB2-6.why_new: The section's numbers have no figure for how many Bangladeshis work in Qatar.
AB2-6.h3: Free visas and visa trading in the Gulf

AB2-7.claim: According to data from the overseas employment ministry, as cited in a Prothom Alo column of 26 May 2026, 1 lakh 7 thousand 598 workers went from Bangladesh to Qatar in 2023.
AB2-7.target_section: Free visas and visa trading in the Gulf
AB2-7.why_new: Annual outflow to Qatar; not in the section.
AB2-7.h3: Free visas and visa trading in the Gulf

AB2-8.claim: At the seventh Bangladesh-Qatar joint committee meeting on 18 May 2026 Qatar showed interest in recruiting technical workers, especially electricians, plumbers, welders and AC technicians, and its labour minister said Qatar wants to take skilled workers directly from five specific Technical Training Centres (TTCs) in Bangladesh, according to a Prothom Alo column of 26 May 2026.
AB2-8.target_section: Free visas and visa trading in the Gulf
AB2-8.placement: other: what Qatar says it is hiring
AB2-8.why_new: Sets what Qatar officially asked for (named skilled trades, direct from five TTCs) against the no-job 'free visa'; the column does not name the five TTCs.
AB2-8.h3: Free visas and visa trading in the Gulf

AB2-9.claim: In a Prothom Alo column published on 26 May 2026, Dr Selim Reza of North South University's Centre for Migration Studies wrote that he learned from talking to many Bangladeshi workers in Qatar that to go there some sold land, some borrowed at high interest and some left their families in debt, and separately that a large share of workers went abroad on loans and, without regular work, cannot send money to their families at home.
AB2-9.why_new: A Qatar example of land sale and high-interest borrowing for a visa with no job; based on the author's own conversations with workers, no names or counts given.

AB2-10.claim: In a Prothom Alo column published on 26 May 2026, Dr Selim Reza, associate professor and coordinator of the Centre for Migration Studies at North South University, wrote that it must be ensured that no worker can go abroad without a contract for a specific job, and that sending workers in the name of a "free visa" or uncertain employment must stop.
AB2-10.target_section: Free visas and visa trading in the Gulf
AB2-10.why_new: A warning quoted from a named expert, which the spec asks for.
AB2-10.h3: Free visas and visa trading in the Gulf

AB2-11.claim: In a Prothom Alo column published on 26 May 2026, Dr Selim Reza, associate professor and coordinator of the Centre for Migration Studies at North South University, wrote that many people, from village-level middlemen to licensed recruiting agencies, are part of the broker ring that controls Bangladesh's overseas employment sector, and that overcharging workers, false promises, fake contract papers and supplying illegal visas have become a "normal" business process.
AB2-11.placement: other: expert statement on the chain
AB2-11.why_new: A named researcher's statement that licensed agencies, not only village brokers, are part of the chain; opinion, to be used as an attributed statement.

AB2-12.claim: In a Prothom Alo column published on 26 May 2026, Dr Selim Reza, associate professor and coordinator of the Centre for Migration Studies at North South University, wrote that Qatar free-visa workers who find no job go around looking for day labour or temporary work illegally and many are at risk of police harassment, arrest or being sent home.
AB2-12.target_section: Free visas and visa trading in the Gulf
AB2-12.why_new: The section already states this; the draft supplies the Prothom Alo quote and date in case the existing sentence needs a second source.
AB2-12.h3: Free visas and visa trading in the Gulf

AB2-13.claim: Dipta Rakshit, Bangladesh country representative of Winrock International, told a Prothom Alo roundtable in Dhaka in July 2026 that of 473 people who returned from scam centres in Cambodia, 80 percent had gone through a recruiting agency in the regular migration process.
AB2-13.target_section: Cambodia, Myanmar and Laos: scam compounds
AB2-13.why_new: The section says 'many went with BMET clearance' and cites BRAC's 66% through middlemen; it lacks this 80%-through-agencies figure and its base of 473 returnees.
AB2-13.h3: Cambodia, Myanmar and Laos: scam compounds

AB2-14.claim: A concept paper presented by Shariful Islam Hasan, associate director of BRAC's Migration Programme and Youth Platform, at a roundtable at the Prothom Alo office in Dhaka in July 2026 said traffickers now lure people by spreading fake job advertisements and posts about successfully reaching abroad on social media.
AB2-14.target_section: Online job adverts, Facebook and WhatsApp scams, and fake government sites
AB2-14.why_new: Adds 'posts about successful arrival abroad' as a lure, attributed to BRAC.
AB2-14.h3: Online job adverts, Facebook and WhatsApp scams, and fake government sites

AB2-15.claim: According to a concept paper presented by BRAC's Shariful Islam Hasan at a roundtable at the Prothom Alo office in Dhaka in July 2026, about 1 thousand 800 Bangladeshis had returned home up to June 2026 after falling victim to such fraud, as trafficking of Bangladeshis lured with work in cyber scam centres in Cambodia and on the Myanmar border has risen.
AB2-15.target_section: Cambodia, Myanmar and Laos: scam compounds
AB2-15.why_new: The section gives June 2026 returns (583) but no cumulative 2026 figure for returnees.
AB2-15.h3: Cambodia, Myanmar and Laos: scam compounds

AB2-16.claim: Mannan Soyal, who was cheated in Cambodia, told a Prothom Alo roundtable in Dhaka in July 2026 that after he filed a case against the people through whom he was cheated, the accused side filed a counter-case, and he alleged that the fraudsters are now pressing him to take money and withdraw the case.
AB2-16.placement: other: what happens after a victim files a case
AB2-16.why_new: The guide states the penalty for pressuring a victim to settle but has no reported case of a counter-case or of pressure to withdraw.

AB2-17.claim: Ali Akbar Khan, acting additional inspector general of police at the CID, told a Prothom Alo roundtable in Dhaka in July 2026 that Bangladeshis are being used in scam centres in Cambodia and other countries, and that many who were first victims of the fraud later become part of the same ring and get involved in trafficking and cheating others.
AB2-17.target_section: Cambodia, Myanmar and Laos: scam compounds
AB2-17.why_new: The section does not say that victims are turned into recruiters for the same ring; this is the CID's statement.
AB2-17.h3: Cambodia, Myanmar and Laos: scam compounds

AB2-18.claim: Salma Ali, adviser to the Bangladesh National Women Lawyers' Association, alleged at a Prothom Alo roundtable in Dhaka in July 2026 that trafficking cases drag on for lack of skilled public prosecutors and judges, although good laws and policies exist.
AB2-18.why_new: The law section describes the Act and tribunals but says nothing on why cases are slow.

AB2-19.claim: Mannan Soyal, a Bangladeshi who returned from a scam centre in Cambodia, told a roundtable on technology-driven fraud and human trafficking held at the Prothom Alo office in Dhaka on 22 July 2026 that he went to Saudi Arabia in 2022, came home after three years, and was then sent to Cambodia by a relative from his own area for BDT 5 lakh on the promise of a restaurant job, travelling on 5 December 2025 after training.
AB2-19.target_section: Cambodia, Myanmar and Laos: scam compounds
AB2-19.why_new: A named, dated survivor account (recruiter a relative, restaurant job, BDT 5 lakh, pre-departure training) not in the section.
AB2-19.h3: Cambodia, Myanmar and Laos: scam compounds

AB2-20.claim: Mannan Soyal, a Bangladeshi who returned from a scam centre in Cambodia, told a roundtable on technology-driven fraud and human trafficking held at the Prothom Alo office in Dhaka on 22 July 2026 that he went to Saudi Arabia in 2022, stayed there three years and decided to go abroad again after coming home, and that a relative from his area then sent him to Cambodia for BDT 5 lakh with talk of a restaurant job.
AB2-20.target_section: Recruited while abroad or just back
AB2-20.placement: other: new bullet (a Gulf returnee recruited for Cambodia)
AB2-20.why_new: The section has returnees recruited for Libya and Russia but none recruited for Cambodia after a Gulf stint.
AB2-20.h3: Recruited while abroad or just back

AB2-21.claim: Mannan Soyal, a Bangladeshi who returned from a scam centre in Cambodia, told a roundtable on technology-driven fraud and human trafficking held at the Prothom Alo office in Dhaka on 22 July 2026 that a few days after arriving he was taken to a Chinese establishment where he saw thousands of people working at computers, and was told to introduce himself as "Maria", build relationships with people on Instagram and get money out of them by fraud.
AB2-21.target_section: Cambodia, Myanmar and Laos: scam compounds
AB2-21.why_new: The section says people are 'forced to scam' but never says what the work is; this gives the actual task (a female persona on Instagram, relationship fraud) and the scale of one compound.
AB2-21.h3: Cambodia, Myanmar and Laos: scam compounds
