AB2-22.claim: Mannan Soyal, a Bangladeshi who returned from a scam centre in Cambodia, told a roundtable on technology-driven fraud and human trafficking held at the Prothom Alo office in Dhaka on 22 July 2026 that when he said he had not been told about this work, his passport was already with them, and he was told that if he did not want to work he should pay the money back and take his passport, which was not possible; he was then made to work by force.
AB2-22.target_section: Cambodia, Myanmar and Laos: scam compounds
AB2-22.why_new: Shows the lever used on a worker who refuses: repay the money to get the passport back. Not in the section.
AB2-22.h3: Cambodia, Myanmar and Laos: scam compounds

AB2-23.claim: Mannan Soyal, a Bangladeshi who returned from a scam centre in Cambodia, told a roundtable on technology-driven fraud and human trafficking held at the Prothom Alo office in Dhaka on 22 July 2026 that he was beaten for failing to meet the set target and locked in a small room, and was later rescued in a police raid.
AB2-23.target_section: Cambodia, Myanmar and Laos: scam compounds
AB2-23.why_new: A first-person account of punishment for missed targets and of release through a police raid; the section has beatings from another source but no account of how a victim got out through a raid.
AB2-23.h3: Cambodia, Myanmar and Laos: scam compounds

AB2-24.claim: Mannan Soyal, a Bangladeshi who returned from a scam centre in Cambodia, told a roundtable on technology-driven fraud and human trafficking held at the Prothom Alo office in Dhaka on 22 July 2026 that because he had no passport his return home became complicated, and that he came back after BRAC helped arrange a travel pass and a ticket.
AB2-24.target_section: Cambodia, Myanmar and Laos: scam compounds
AB2-24.why_new: Says what a compound victim without a passport needs to get home (a travel pass) and who arranged it; the section lists BRAC only for the 2025 Myanmar rescue.
AB2-24.h3: Cambodia, Myanmar and Laos: scam compounds

AB2-25.claim: Mannan Soyal, a Bangladeshi who returned from a scam centre in Cambodia, told a roundtable on technology-driven fraud and human trafficking held at the Prothom Alo office in Dhaka on 22 July 2026 that after his human trafficking case the accused side filed a counter-case, that he is now himself an accused in a case, and that he does not have the money to fight it.
AB2-25.placement: other: what happens after a victim files a case
AB2-25.why_new: A reported instance of a trafficking complainant becoming an accused through a counter-case; the guide has none.

AB2-26.claim: Naznin Akter, a Bangladeshi woman who returned from Malaysia, told a roundtable on technology-driven fraud and human trafficking held at the Prothom Alo office in Dhaka on 22 July 2026 that she separated from her husband five years ago, was struggling to support two children and decided to go to Malaysia to get free of debt; an acquaintance offered her restaurant work at about BDT 60 thousand a month, and she had to pay more than BDT 2.5 lakh to go, which she raised by selling jewellery and borrowing.
AB2-26.target_section: Trafficking disguised as a job, especially for women
AB2-26.why_new: A named 2025 Malaysia case of a woman (restaurant job, wage promised, sum paid, how raised); the section's cases are Jordan, Saudi Arabia, Dubai and Cambodia.
AB2-26.h3: Trafficking disguised as a job, especially for women

AB2-27.claim: Naznin Akter, a Bangladeshi woman who returned from Malaysia, told a roundtable on technology-driven fraud and human trafficking held at the Prothom Alo office in Dhaka on 22 July 2026 that she was taken to Malaysia on a visit visa on 15 November 2025 for a promised restaurant job, and that she had been taught beforehand what to say at immigration.
AB2-27.target_section: A visit or tourist visa sold as a job
AB2-27.why_new: A dated Malaysia visit-visa case and a mechanism the section lacks: the traveller is coached on what to tell immigration.
AB2-27.h3: A visit or tourist visa sold as a job

AB2-28.claim: Naznin Akter, a Bangladeshi woman who returned from Malaysia, told a roundtable on technology-driven fraud and human trafficking held at the Prothom Alo office in Dhaka on 22 July 2026 that after she reached Malaysia on a visit visa on 15 November 2025 her passport, ticket and papers were taken and she was told she would get no work unless she paid the balance, although she had kept BDT 5 thousand unpaid on the agreement that she would pay it after starting work.
AB2-28.target_section: Visit and tourist visas sold as jobs
AB2-28.why_new: Adds to the Malaysia bullet a survivor's account of what happens on landing: documents seized and work withheld over an agreed unpaid balance of BDT 5,000.
AB2-28.h3: Visit and tourist visas sold as jobs

AB2-29.claim: Naznin Akter, a Bangladeshi woman who returned from Malaysia, told a roundtable on technology-driven fraud and human trafficking held at the Prothom Alo office in Dhaka on 22 July 2026 that in Malaysia her family was also pressed for money, she was kept in a hotel and then moved to a closed room where she was held for six days in a row and tortured only for asking where she was, and that she managed to come home on 21 November through her brothers' efforts.
AB2-29.target_section: Trafficking disguised as a job, especially for women
AB2-29.why_new: Completes the case: confinement, pressure on the family, and return within a week through her brothers, with no mention of any help from authorities.
AB2-29.h3: Trafficking disguised as a job, especially for women

AB2-30.claim: Naznin Akter, a Bangladeshi woman who returned from Malaysia, told a roundtable on technology-driven fraud and human trafficking held at the Prothom Alo office in Dhaka on 22 July 2026 that on arrival in Malaysia on 15 November 2025 her passport, ticket and papers were taken from her and she was told there would be no work until the balance was paid.
AB2-30.target_section: The passport kept by the dalal
AB2-30.why_new: A case of the passport (and return ticket) being seized abroad as leverage for more money; the section's cases are in Bangladesh and Cambodia.
AB2-30.h3: The passport kept by the dalal

AB2-31.claim: Shakirul Islam, chairperson of OKUP (Ovibashi Karmi Unnayan Program), told a roundtable on technology-driven fraud and human trafficking held at the Prothom Alo office in Dhaka on 22 July 2026 that at a recent consultation meeting in Madaripur the deputy commissioner said he knows the traffickers but does not have the power to act against them.
AB2-31.why_new: A reported admission by a district's top administrator, in the main Libya-route district, that known traffickers are not acted against.

AB2-32.claim: Shakirul Islam, chairperson of OKUP, told a roundtable on technology-driven fraud and human trafficking held at the Prothom Alo office in Dhaka on 22 July 2026 that OKUP supported the case of an abused woman who returned from the Middle East in 2019, that the long investigation found elements of human trafficking, and that in 2025 the judge at the special tribunal proposed an out-of-court settlement; he said the victim stated clearly that she wanted justice and dignity, not money, but the case was in the end settled for a little over BDT 4 lakh.
AB2-32.why_new: The guide says trafficking offences can't be settled privately; this is a reported case, six years long, where a tribunal judge proposed settlement and the case ended with about BDT 4 lakh.

AB2-33.claim: Shakirul Islam, chairperson of OKUP, told a roundtable on technology-driven fraud and human trafficking held at the Prothom Alo office in Dhaka on 22 July 2026 that workers are going abroad on BMET's clearance, so the state must also take responsibility for that process.
AB2-33.target_section: When the visa, the agency and the clearance are all real
AB2-33.why_new: An NGO head's attributed statement tying BMET clearance to state responsibility; opinion, usable only as attributed.
AB2-33.h3: When the visa, the agency and the clearance are all real

AB2-34.claim: Mahmudul Hasan, legal coordinator of RMMRU (the Refugee and Migratory Movements Research Unit), told a roundtable on technology-driven fraud and human trafficking held at the Prothom Alo office in Dhaka on 22 July 2026 that a human trafficking case takes two to three years to go from investigation to the trial stage, that many victims cannot keep the case going in that time because they are left with nothing after spending lakhs of taka to go abroad, and that many lose a day's income each time they appear in court.
AB2-34.why_new: How long a trafficking case takes to reach trial and why victims drop out; the guide only notes that workers often can't keep a case going.

AB2-35.claim: Mahmudul Hasan, legal coordinator of RMMRU (the Refugee and Migratory Movements Research Unit), told a roundtable on technology-driven fraud and human trafficking held at the Prothom Alo office in Dhaka on 22 July 2026 that there is no designated or separate investigation agency for the human trafficking tribunals, so investigation reports are not submitted on time and in many cases a proper investigation is not done, and that the Dhaka human trafficking tribunal has had no judge for five months.
AB2-35.why_new: A dated (July 2026) fact about the Dhaka tribunal having no judge and about who investigates; the section lists the courts but not their working state.

AB2-36.claim: Salma Ali, chairperson of ATSEC South Asia and adviser to the Bangladesh National Women Lawyers' Association, told a roundtable on technology-driven fraud and human trafficking held at the Prothom Alo office in Dhaka on 22 July 2026 that a suspicious passenger can be identified at the airport in a few minutes of observation, and that recently a young woman bound for Nepal was suspected, steps were taken, and she was rescued and brought back to the country.
AB2-36.why_new: The section records women stopped on Nepal trips as a problem; this is a women's-rights lawyer citing a Nepal-bound woman who, she says, was rescued. No date or details are given.

AB2-37.claim: Salma Ali, chairperson of ATSEC South Asia and adviser to the Bangladesh National Women Lawyers' Association, told a roundtable on technology-driven fraud and human trafficking held at the Prothom Alo office in Dhaka on 22 July 2026 that trials are long in many cases and many victims in the end do not want to continue the case over the question of confidentiality, so organised criminals get away, and that trafficking in the name of migration is still going on through land ports, airports and sea routes.
AB2-37.why_new: Gives confidentiality as a reason victims drop cases; the 2026 Act's confidentiality duty is in the guide but not how it plays out.

AB2-38.claim: Ali Akbar Khan, acting additional inspector general of police at the CID, told a roundtable on technology-driven fraud and human trafficking held at the Prothom Alo office in Dhaka on 22 July 2026 that many people go abroad on tourist visas and are then cheated, and some go from being victims to later becoming traffickers themselves.
AB2-38.target_section: Visit and tourist visas sold as jobs
AB2-38.why_new: The CID chief's own statement linking tourist-visa travel to later fraud, and that some victims become traffickers.
AB2-38.h3: Visit and tourist visas sold as jobs

AB2-39.claim: Ali Akbar Khan, acting additional inspector general of police at the CID, told a roundtable on technology-driven fraud and human trafficking held at the Prothom Alo office in Dhaka on 22 July 2026 that many people who were tortured abroad compromise after returning home or do not want to give evidence, which obstructs trials.
AB2-39.target_section: Refund refusals after a failed departure
AB2-39.why_new: The section cites the CID on Cambodia returnees bargaining with brokers; this is a broader CID statement that returnees settle or refuse to testify and that it blocks trials.
AB2-39.h3: Refund refusals after a failed departure

AB2-40.claim: Ali Akbar Khan, acting additional inspector general of police at the CID, told a roundtable on technology-driven fraud and human trafficking held at the Prothom Alo office in Dhaka on 22 July 2026 that the biggest challenge in investigating human trafficking is collecting information and evidence across countries and identifying technology-based money transactions, and that investigating cryptocurrency, hundi and online transactions needs modern software, training and international cooperation.
AB2-40.why_new: The CID itself says trafficking payments through hundi, cryptocurrency and online transfers are hard for it to trace.

AB2-41.claim: Rebeka Khan, joint secretary (Political-1) at the Home Ministry, told a roundtable on technology-driven fraud and human trafficking held at the Prothom Alo office in Dhaka on 22 July 2026 that the new 2026 law covers, alongside human trafficking, migrant smuggling and fraud through fake job advertisements online, and that the biggest challenge now is implementing the law and preventing fraud within the regular migration process.
AB2-41.why_new: A Home Ministry official's statement that the Act reaches fraud through fake online job adverts; the section lists advertising for smuggling but not this official reading.

AB2-42.claim: Rebeka Khan, joint secretary (Political-1) at the Home Ministry, told a roundtable on technology-driven fraud and human trafficking held at the Prothom Alo office in Dhaka on 22 July 2026 that the government is working on implementing a national referral system and on drawing up a National Plan of Action (NPA) 2026-30 so that victims get protection, legal aid and services in a coordinated way.
AB2-42.target_section: Where victims and families get help
AB2-42.why_new: The help section lists existing contacts; it does not mention the national referral system or the NPA 2026-30, both described as work in progress in July 2026.
AB2-42.h3: Where victims and families get help

AB2-43.claim: Rebeka Khan, joint secretary (Political-1) at the Home Ministry, told a roundtable on technology-driven fraud and human trafficking held at the Prothom Alo office in Dhaka on 22 July 2026 that the use of modern technology at airports, including the Passenger Name Record and Advance Passenger Information systems, is being expanded to detect fake travel documents.
AB2-43.why_new: Names two passenger-data systems being expanded at airports to catch fake travel documents; not in the airport section.

AB2-44.claim: Rebeka Khan, joint secretary (Political-1) at the Home Ministry, told a roundtable on technology-driven fraud and human trafficking held at the Prothom Alo office in Dhaka on 22 July 2026 that bilateral and regional cooperation to suppress cyber fraud centres in Cambodia and other countries has been strengthened, and that quick legal action is being taken against people involved in human trafficking even if they are government officials.
AB2-44.target_section: Cambodia, Myanmar and Laos: scam compounds
AB2-44.why_new: The government's stated position in July 2026; the official gave no case, number or name.
AB2-44.h3: Cambodia, Myanmar and Laos: scam compounds

AB2-45.claim: Tanvir Hassan Zoha, prosecutor and special investigating officer at the International Crimes Tribunal, told a roundtable on technology-driven fraud and human trafficking held at the Prothom Alo office in Dhaka on 22 July 2026 that fieldwork shows that in many cases a trafficking victim is taken abroad, tortured and a ransom is demanded, and that with quick, coordinated steps it is possible to bring the victim back and arrest the trafficker.
AB2-45.why_new: A prosecutor's statement confirming the torture-for-ransom pattern and that fast action has brought victims back.

AB2-46.claim: Dr B M Mainul Hossain, professor and director of the Institute of Information Technology at Dhaka University, told a roundtable on technology-driven fraud and human trafficking held at the Prothom Alo office in Dhaka on 22 July 2026 that traffickers use fake job advertisements, videos made with artificial intelligence, cryptocurrency, identity-hiding technology and secure messaging apps, and that even mainstream media are sometimes misled when trying to detect artificial videos.
AB2-46.target_section: Online job adverts, Facebook and WhatsApp scams, and fake government sites
AB2-46.why_new: Adds AI-generated video to the tools used in online recruitment fraud; the section describes Facebook pages and photos only.
AB2-46.h3: Online job adverts, Facebook and WhatsApp scams, and fake government sites

AB2-47.claim: Dipta Rakshit, Bangladesh country representative of Winrock International and director of its Ashshash project, told a roundtable on technology-driven fraud and human trafficking held at the Prothom Alo office in Dhaka on 22 July 2026 that information from people who returned from Cambodia shows that 80 percent went abroad through the legal migration process.
AB2-47.target_section: When the visa, the agency and the clearance are all real
AB2-47.why_new: A share (80%) for the section's central point that Cambodia victims went through the legal process.
AB2-47.h3: When the visa, the agency and the clearance are all real

AB2-48.claim: Dipta Rakshit, Bangladesh country representative of Winrock International and director of its Ashshash project, told a roundtable on technology-driven fraud and human trafficking held at the Prothom Alo office in Dhaka on 22 July 2026 that the channels used to move money, including bKash, Nagad, hundi and cryptocurrency, must be effectively monitored and held accountable, and that the flow of human trafficking money must be brought under strict watch.
AB2-48.placement: other: NGO statement on payment channels
AB2-48.why_new: Names the payment channels (bKash, Nagad, hundi, cryptocurrency) an anti-trafficking NGO says carry trafficking money.

AB2-49.claim: Shariful Islam Hasan, associate director of BRAC's Migration Programme and Youth Platform, told a roundtable on technology-driven fraud and human trafficking held at the Prothom Alo office in Dhaka on 22 July 2026 that many Bangladeshis and Rohingya are trying to go to Malaysia across the Bay of Bengal, and that reports of the deaths of about 500 Rohingya had come in the previous week.
AB2-49.why_new: The section treats the boat route as the 'older route' (2012-15) and asks whether boats still leave; BRAC said in July 2026 that Bangladeshis and Rohingya are attempting the Bay of Bengal crossing now. He gave no source or place for the 500 deaths.

AB2-50.claim: Shariful Islam Hasan, associate director of BRAC's Migration Programme and Youth Platform, told a roundtable on technology-driven fraud and human trafficking held at the Prothom Alo office in Dhaka on 22 July 2026 that many people who are in Malaysia are being drawn into a trap of fraud with assurances that they will be sent on to Australia.
AB2-50.why_new: A new onward-migration fraud aimed at Bangladeshis already in Malaysia (Australia promised); not in the guide.

AB2-51.claim: Shariful Islam Hasan, associate director of BRAC's Migration Programme and Youth Platform, told a roundtable on technology-driven fraud and human trafficking held at the Prothom Alo office in Dhaka on 22 July 2026 that many people who are in Malaysia are being cheated with assurances that they will be sent to Australia.
AB2-51.target_section: Recruited while abroad or just back
AB2-51.why_new: The section covers recruitment in the Gulf, on the flight home and in Russia; this adds Malaysia with an Australia promise.
AB2-51.h3: Recruited while abroad or just back

AB2-52.claim: Shariful Islam Hasan, associate director of BRAC's Migration Programme and Youth Platform, told a roundtable on technology-driven fraud and human trafficking held at the Prothom Alo office in Dhaka on 22 July 2026 that 583 people returned from Cambodia in June alone and 1 thousand 800 so far in 2026 as victims of cyber fraud, and that of them 88 percent were held captive, 87 percent had forged papers, 38 percent suffered serious mental trauma and 27 percent were physically tortured.
AB2-52.target_section: Cambodia, Myanmar and Laos: scam compounds
AB2-52.why_new: The section has BRAC's 66% (middlemen) and 98% (no promised job); it lacks 88% confined, 87% forged papers, 38% trauma, 27% physical torture, and the 1,800 total for 2026.
AB2-52.h3: Cambodia, Myanmar and Laos: scam compounds

AB2-53.claim: Shariful Islam Hasan, associate director of BRAC's Migration Programme and Youth Platform, told a roundtable on technology-driven fraud and human trafficking held at the Prothom Alo office in Dhaka on 22 July 2026 that social media is a major tool of traffickers and that research says 82 percent of Bangladesh's young people want to leave the country if they get the chance.
AB2-53.target_section: Online job adverts, Facebook and WhatsApp scams, and fake government sites
AB2-53.why_new: BRAC's statement on social media as the traffickers' tool; the 82% figure is cited without naming the research.
AB2-53.h3: Online job adverts, Facebook and WhatsApp scams, and fake government sites

AB2-54.claim: Md Al-Amin Noyon, president of Anirban Survivors' Voice, told a roundtable on technology-driven fraud and human trafficking held at the Prothom Alo office in Dhaka on 22 July 2026 that in the past year and a half 56 thousand Bangladeshis went through BMET to 28 countries where Bangladesh has no embassy or consulate, and that there is no information on how they are or whether they are safe.
AB2-54.target_section: When the visa, the agency and the clearance are all real
AB2-54.why_new: A count of workers cleared to countries with no Bangladesh mission; the guide has the Cambodia clearance figure but not this.
AB2-54.h3: When the visa, the agency and the clearance are all real

AB2-55.claim: Md Al-Amin Noyon, president of Anirban Survivors' Voice, told a roundtable on technology-driven fraud and human trafficking held at the Prothom Alo office in Dhaka on 22 July 2026 that 16 thousand workers went to Cambodia in the same year and a half, and that in working with them he found many were shown an employment visa when being taken and were later given a tourist visa and sold to fraud rings, although they had gone following the government's rules.
AB2-55.target_section: Cambodia, Myanmar and Laos: scam compounds
AB2-55.why_new: The mechanism of the swap: an employment visa is shown before departure and a tourist visa is what the worker ends up with. The section says only that the worker flies in on a visit visa.
AB2-55.h3: Cambodia, Myanmar and Laos: scam compounds

AB2-56.claim: Md Al-Amin Noyon, president of Anirban Survivors' Voice, told a roundtable on technology-driven fraud and human trafficking held at the Prothom Alo office in Dhaka on 22 July 2026 that it is also BMET's responsibility to monitor whether workers reached the workplace and whether their pay and housing are right, and that the state, if it wished, could identify how many people went on tourist visas and did not return.
AB2-56.target_section: When the visa, the agency and the clearance are all real
AB2-56.why_new: A survivor-led organisation's statement on what BMET is responsible for after departure; opinion, usable as attributed.
AB2-56.h3: When the visa, the agency and the clearance are all real

AB2-57.claim: Md Al-Amin Noyon, president of Anirban Survivors' Voice, told a roundtable on technology-driven fraud and human trafficking held at the Prothom Alo office in Dhaka on 22 July 2026 that people who return from scam centres must be seen as survivors, not criminals, and need regular follow-up, rehabilitation and mental health care so that they do not get drawn back into criminal rings.
AB2-57.target_section: Cambodia, Myanmar and Laos: scam compounds
AB2-57.why_new: A survivors' organisation on how scam-centre returnees should be treated; pairs with the Act's rule that a trafficking victim cannot be charged.
AB2-57.h3: Cambodia, Myanmar and Laos: scam compounds

AB2-58.claim: Tasneem Binte Karim, national programme coordinator at UNODC South Asia, told a roundtable on technology-driven fraud and human trafficking held at the Prothom Alo office in Dhaka on 22 July 2026 that Bangladesh lacks a reliable national database, research and evidence-based analysis on scam-centre trafficking, including how many Bangladeshis are trafficked through deceptive recruitment, return home, and get rehabilitation and justice.
AB2-58.target_section: Cambodia, Myanmar and Laos: scam compounds
AB2-58.why_new: A caveat for every figure in the section: UNODC says there is no reliable national data on scam-centre trafficking.
AB2-58.h3: Cambodia, Myanmar and Laos: scam compounds

AB2-59.claim: Tofayel Ahmed, who returned from a scam centre in Cambodia, told a roundtable on safe migration and the reintegration of returnees held at the Prothom Alo office in Dhaka on 18 August 2026 that he had come to Dhaka to go to Saudi Arabia but, at a friend's instigation, went to Cambodia through two brokers, and that he travelled with a BMET smart card.
AB2-59.target_section: Cambodia, Myanmar and Laos: scam compounds
AB2-59.why_new: A named survivor who was diverted in Dhaka from a Saudi plan to Cambodia by a friend and two brokers, and who held a BMET smart card.
AB2-59.h3: Cambodia, Myanmar and Laos: scam compounds

AB2-60.claim: Tofayel Ahmed, who returned from a scam centre in Cambodia, told a roundtable on safe migration and the reintegration of returnees held at the Prothom Alo office in Dhaka on 18 August 2026 that he went to Cambodia with a BMET smart card and was sold to a scam centre there.
AB2-60.target_section: When the visa, the agency and the clearance are all real
AB2-60.why_new: A second first-person Cambodia account (besides Md Shafiqul Islam) of a smart-card holder sold to a scam centre.
AB2-60.h3: When the visa, the agency and the clearance are all real

AB2-61.claim: Tofayel Ahmed, who returned from a scam centre in Cambodia, told a roundtable on safe migration and the reintegration of returnees held at the Prothom Alo office in Dhaka on 18 August 2026 that he was kept for three days in a restaurant in Phnom Penh and then taken late at night to a scam centre for an "interview"; when he realised what it was and contacted the people who had sent him, they told him this was the work he had to do there and that he would later be sent to a European country.
AB2-61.target_section: Cambodia, Myanmar and Laos: scam compounds
AB2-61.why_new: Adds steps the section lacks: a holding stay in a Phnom Penh restaurant, a night-time 'interview' at the compound, and brokers promising onward travel to Europe to keep him working.
AB2-61.h3: Cambodia, Myanmar and Laos: scam compounds

AB2-62.claim: Tofayel Ahmed, who returned from a scam centre in Cambodia, told a roundtable on safe migration and the reintegration of returnees held at the Prothom Alo office in Dhaka on 18 August 2026 that he was held in the scam centre for about one month and 27 days before he managed to escape, that he was never given the one-year visa and work permit, and that he became illegal when his one-month single-entry visa ran out.
AB2-62.target_section: Cambodia, Myanmar and Laos: scam compounds
AB2-62.why_new: States the papers gap precisely: a one-year visa and work permit promised, a one-month single-entry visa given, then overstay. The section mentions the one-month visit visa but not what was promised or the overstay.
AB2-62.h3: Cambodia, Myanmar and Laos: scam compounds

AB2-63.claim: Tofayel Ahmed, who returned from a scam centre in Cambodia, told a roundtable on safe migration and the reintegration of returnees held at the Prothom Alo office in Dhaka on 18 August 2026 that after police began raids he applied to return home through the Bangladesh embassy on Facebook, and that he came home on 14 June after the application was approved.
AB2-63.target_section: Cambodia, Myanmar and Laos: scam compounds
AB2-63.why_new: A working route home used by a survivor: applying to the Bangladesh embassy through Facebook. The section gives the Bangkok embassy's address and phones only. He does not say which embassy page.
AB2-63.h3: Cambodia, Myanmar and Laos: scam compounds

AB2-64.claim: Hridoy Chowdhury, a Bangladeshi who returned from Libya, told a roundtable on safe migration and the reintegration of returnees held at the Prothom Alo office in Dhaka on 18 August 2026 that friends who had gone to Libya told him there would be work there and that later one could go on to Greece or Italy, and that he went with the help of a broker from his own area, Habiganj in Sylhet, whom he trusted because he knew him; the broker is still in Libya.
AB2-64.why_new: A first-person account of the pitch coming from friends already in Libya (work first, Greece or Italy later) and of a broker from the same area who operates from Libya.

AB2-65.claim: Hridoy Chowdhury, a Bangladeshi who returned from Libya, told a roundtable on safe migration and the reintegration of returnees held at the Prothom Alo office in Dhaka on 18 August 2026 that after reaching Libya he worked for a company for two months in a row, was then taken to Benghazi and boarded a boat for Greece, and that after about 14 hours on the boat the coast guard detained them and sent them back to Libya, where he was held as a prisoner in a jail in Tobruk.
AB2-65.why_new: A survivor account of the eastern Libya (Benghazi) to Greece crossing ending in interception and a Tobruk jail; the section's path describes the western route to Lampedusa and mentions the Tobruk-Greece boat only for deaths.

AB2-66.claim: Hridoy Chowdhury, a Bangladeshi who returned from Libya, told a roundtable on safe migration and the reintegration of returnees held at the Prothom Alo office in Dhaka on 18 August 2026 that he finally got out of the jail in Tobruk, Libya, by contacting his broker, and that he had to come home empty-handed despite spending a huge amount of money.
AB2-66.why_new: Shows release from a Libyan jail going through the broker; he does not say what it cost or what he paid in all.

AB2-67.claim: Ariful Haque Chowdhury MP, the Expatriates' Welfare and Overseas Employment Minister, told a roundtable on safe migration and the reintegration of returnees held at the Prothom Alo office in Dhaka on 18 August 2026 that action is being taken against unauthorised and fake recruiting agencies and that the recruitment process is being brought online.
AB2-67.target_section: Refund refusals after a failed departure
AB2-67.placement: other: what the government says it is doing
AB2-67.why_new: The minister's August 2026 statement; he gave no number of agencies or names.
AB2-67.h3: Refund refusals after a failed departure

AB2-68.claim: Ariful Haque Chowdhury MP, the Expatriates' Welfare and Overseas Employment Minister, told a roundtable on safe migration and the reintegration of returnees held at the Prothom Alo office in Dhaka on 18 August 2026 that Dubai is taking 6 thousand drivers and that the ministry is arranging for its representatives to come to Bangladesh and recruit workers directly once they are satisfied with the training, which he said would leave middlemen no scope for fraud.
AB2-68.target_section: The chain from the village to the visa seller
AB2-68.placement: other: a recruitment channel without middlemen
AB2-68.why_new: A specific demand (6,000 drivers for Dubai) and a direct-recruitment arrangement announced by the minister in August 2026; the article gives no detail on how to apply.

AB2-69.claim: Ariful Haque Chowdhury MP, the Expatriates' Welfare and Overseas Employment Minister, told a roundtable on safe migration and the reintegration of returnees held at the Prothom Alo office in Dhaka on 18 August 2026 that when a Bangladeshi citizen dies abroad, whether the person went by a legal or an illegal route, the government brings the body home and also gives the family financial help and help with the children's education, and that work is under way to introduce a welfare card for expatriates carrying various services.
AB2-69.target_section: How is the body brought home?
AB2-69.why_new: The minister's statement that repatriation of the body does not depend on having gone legally, and that a welfare card is being prepared (not yet issued as of August 2026).

AB2-70.claim: Ariful Haque Chowdhury MP, the Expatriates' Welfare and Overseas Employment Minister, told a roundtable on safe migration and the reintegration of returnees held at the Prothom Alo office in Dhaka on 18 August 2026 that a returnee who is jobless at home can apply to the ministry or the Wage Earners' Welfare Board, and that the government wants to give financial and logistic support according to the person's occupation and will also monitor it; he described this as something the government is planning.
AB2-70.why_new: Where the minister says a jobless returnee should apply; stated as a plan, with no form, amount or deadline given.

AB2-71.claim: Shariful Islam Hasan, associate director of BRAC's Migration Programme and Youth Platform, told a roundtable on safe migration and the reintegration of returnees held at the Prothom Alo office in Dhaka on 18 August 2026 that recruiting agencies are Dhaka-centred, that there is no agency in Sylhet, Tangail, Munshiganj or the other districts from which most people go abroad, and that people there are connected to Dhaka through middlemen; because of these middlemen at home and abroad and workers' lack of skills, he said, Bangladeshi workers' cost of going abroad is the highest in the world and their income comparatively low.
AB2-71.target_section: The chain from the village to the visa seller
AB2-71.placement: other: why the village needs a middleman
AB2-71.why_new: Explains the root of the chain: no agencies in the high-migration districts (three named), so the link to Dhaka is the middleman. The section describes the layers but not why they exist.

AB2-72.claim: Shariful Islam Hasan, associate director of BRAC's Migration Programme and Youth Platform, told a roundtable on safe migration and the reintegration of returnees held at the Prothom Alo office in Dhaka on 18 August 2026 that people from eight to ten districts, including Madaripur, Shariatpur, Sylhet, Sunamganj, Habiganj, Kishoreganj and Narsingdi, try to reach Europe across the Mediterranean, that many first go to Libya through Egypt or Dubai and are physically tortured there, and that some pay BDT 25 lakh, some BDT 30 lakh, and some as much as BDT 65 to 67 lakh.
AB2-72.why_new: Names the source districts and gives BRAC's top-end figure of BDT 65 to 67 lakh; the section's highest quoted figure is Tk 45 lakh taken from one family.

AB2-73.claim: Shariful Islam Hasan, associate director of BRAC's Migration Programme and Youth Platform, told a roundtable on safe migration and the reintegration of returnees held at the Prothom Alo office in Dhaka on 18 August 2026 that BRAC has started a campaign with the slogan "No going abroad by sea", trying to raise awareness through police, mosque imams, religious leaders, schools and social media.
AB2-73.why_new: Minor: names BRAC's campaign against the sea route; include only if the section wants it.

AB2-74.claim: A T M Mahbubul Karim, joint secretary and project director of the RAISE project, told a roundtable on safe migration and the reintegration of returnees held at the Prothom Alo office in Dhaka on 18 August 2026 that the RAISE project has so far brought 2 lakh 53 thousand returnees under its reintegration programme, gives referral, training and counselling across the country through 35 district offices, and works with seven NGOs including BRAC and IOM.
AB2-74.why_new: The guide's returnee help covers airport desks and PKB loans; it does not mention the RAISE project's 35 district offices offering referral, training and counselling. The article does not say where the offices are.

AB2-75.claim: A T M Mahbubul Karim, joint secretary and project director of the RAISE project, told a roundtable on safe migration and the reintegration of returnees held at the Prothom Alo office in Dhaka on 18 August 2026 that many women returnees cannot come under reintegration support because of family and society: the family sends them abroad but suspects them and does not value them after they return; he said the project is thinking of naming a responsible officer at union level so that it is known which woman has returned to which house and when.
AB2-75.why_new: Why women returnees miss out on support, from the official running the government's reintegration project; the union-level officer is an idea under consideration, not a decision.

AB2-76.claim: A T M Mahbubul Karim, joint secretary and project director of the RAISE project, told a roundtable on safe migration and the reintegration of returnees held at the Prothom Alo office in Dhaka on 18 August 2026 that domestic work abroad is not the same as at home, and that working in 50-degree heat, cooking local food and using modern appliances need training.
AB2-76.placement: other: official on why training is needed
AB2-76.why_new: A government official's concrete description of what differs in domestic work abroad.

AB2-77.claim: Dr Md Al-Mamunul Ansari, DIG (Operations) of the Airport Armed Police Battalion at APBn headquarters, told a roundtable on safe migration and the reintegration of returnees held at the Prothom Alo office in Dhaka on 18 August 2026 that during checks at immigration officers can often tell that a person travelling on a tourist visa is in fact going for work, and that they then verify and, if needed, report it or try to stop the person; if there is a case against someone, he said, the database is checked and action is taken.
AB2-77.why_new: A senior airport police officer stating in his own words that tourist-visa travellers judged to be going for work are stopped, and that passengers are checked against a case database.

AB2-78.claim: Dr Md Al-Mamunul Ansari, DIG (Operations) of the Airport Armed Police Battalion at APBn headquarters, told a roundtable on safe migration and the reintegration of returnees held at the Prothom Alo office in Dhaka on 18 August 2026 that the Airport Armed Police Battalion has worked at the airport since 2013, and that the air force and police, APBn, the Special Branch's immigration police and an anti-human-trafficking investigation team currently work there.
AB2-78.placement: other: who works at the airport
AB2-78.why_new: The section lists SB immigration and the welfare desk; it does not mention APBn or an anti-trafficking investigation team at the airport.

AB2-79.claim: Dr Md Al-Mamunul Ansari, DIG (Operations) of the Airport Armed Police Battalion at APBn headquarters, told a roundtable on safe migration and the reintegration of returnees held at the Prothom Alo office in Dhaka on 18 August 2026 that the airport police counsel trafficking victims and victims returning from abroad, try to get them rehabilitated through BRAC and other organisations, take cases from victims and investigate them, have brought victims back from Iran, Libya and Greece by sending officers abroad or by other arrangements, and try to identify and arrest accused persons who are in Bangladesh even when the crime took place abroad.
AB2-79.target_section: Where victims and families get help
AB2-79.why_new: Adds the Airport Armed Police Battalion as a body that says it takes and investigates victims' cases and has brought victims back from Iran, Libya and Greece; the help list has the CID and local police only. No contact number is given.
AB2-79.h3: Where victims and families get help

AB2-80.claim: A T M Abu Asad, additional director general of the Department of Immigration and Passports, told a roundtable on safe migration and the reintegration of returnees held at the Prothom Alo office in Dhaka on 18 August 2026 that the department has cases where one person took passports by repeatedly changing name, date of birth and other information, and that this is reducing the acceptance of Bangladeshi passports with foreign embassies and immigration authorities.
AB2-80.why_new: The passport authority's own statement on identity changes in passports and their effect abroad; relevant to the FAQ on agents changing a woman's age.

AB2-81.claim: A T M Abu Asad, additional director general of the Department of Immigration and Passports, told a roundtable on safe migration and the reintegration of returnees held at the Prothom Alo office in Dhaka on 18 August 2026 that passports have been issued in a much safer way since e-passports were introduced in 2020, that passports are now issued after verifying the NID or birth registration, and that because an e-passport takes the prints of all 10 fingers, the same person can no longer get a passport under a different identity.
AB2-81.why_new: The section gives fees and the matching rule; it does not say that ten fingerprints now block a second passport under another name or age.

AB2-82.claim: A T M Abu Asad, additional director general of the Department of Immigration and Passports, told a roundtable on safe migration and the reintegration of returnees held at the Prothom Alo office in Dhaka on 18 August 2026 that super express passports are being delivered within 24 hours or two days, and that the department has no scope to give a passport without valid information and documents even to someone who went abroad by an illegal route.
AB2-82.why_new: Adds '24 hours' for super express (the section says within 2 working days) and the rule for people abroad irregularly who need a passport.

AB2-83.claim: Squadron Leader Rakib Ahmed Tawab, deputy director (QA and I) of the Civil Aviation Authority of Bangladesh, told a roundtable on safe migration and the reintegration of returnees held at the Prothom Alo office in Dhaka on 18 August 2026 that in many cases passengers arrive at the airport with fake BMET cards, fake visas or other fake papers, and that 24 agencies working at the airport, including immigration and the airlines, check these in coordination.
AB2-83.target_section: Fake BMET cards and fake clearance
AB2-83.why_new: An August 2026 statement from the airport's own regulator that fake BMET cards and visas keep turning up; goes to the section's open question on whether fake cards have been caught since 2024 (he gives no count).
AB2-83.h3: Fake BMET cards and fake clearance

AB2-84.claim: Squadron Leader Rakib Ahmed Tawab, deputy director (QA and I) of the Civil Aviation Authority of Bangladesh, told a roundtable on safe migration and the reintegration of returnees held at the Prothom Alo office in Dhaka on 18 August 2026 that the Probashi Kallyan desk at the airport is open 24 hours and works on solving various problems, and that people going abroad are now also offered luggage wrapping at low cost.
AB2-84.target_section: At the airport: the welfare desk
AB2-84.why_new: The section lists the desk's services and phones but not that it is open 24 hours; the wrapping price is not given.

AB2-85.claim: Squadron Leader Rakib Ahmed Tawab, deputy director (QA and I) of the Civil Aviation Authority of Bangladesh, told a roundtable on safe migration and the reintegration of returnees held at the Prothom Alo office in Dhaka on 18 August 2026 that videos of cut or damaged luggage often spread on social media, but the authority's investigations found that in 95 percent of cases the incidents happened not at Bangladesh's airport or a transit airport but at the airport of the country where the journey began.
AB2-85.why_new: The civil aviation authority's own finding on where returnees' luggage is cut open; this is the authority's claim about its own airport, with no method given.

AB2-86.claim: Md Badrul Haque, administrator of BAIRA (the Bangladesh Association of International Recruiting Agencies), told a roundtable on safe migration and the reintegration of returnees held at the Prothom Alo office in Dhaka on 18 August 2026 that not all recruiting businessmen are dishonest and many send workers following the rules, while some fraud rings spread their nets in remote areas and take people's money.
AB2-86.why_new: The recruiting agencies' association's own position on fraud rings; generic, usable only as an attributed statement.

AB2-87.claim: Ali Haider Chowdhury, former secretary general of BAIRA, told a roundtable on safe migration and the reintegration of returnees held at the Prothom Alo office in Dhaka on 18 August 2026 that dependence on brokers would fall if the list of legal recruiting agencies and correct information about jobs reached upazila level.
AB2-87.target_section: The chain from the village to the visa seller
AB2-87.why_new: A former BAIRA official conceding that agency lists and job information do not reach upazila level; a recommendation, not an existing service.

AB2-88.claim: Dr Jahangir Hossain, director (skills standards and curriculum) of the National Skills Development Authority, told a roundtable on safe migration and the reintegration of returnees held at the Prothom Alo office in Dhaka on 18 August 2026 that under the authority's agreement with Probashi Kallyan Bank, returnees who hold a skills certificate can get a collateral-free loan of up to BDT 5 lakh, that recognition of prior learning (RPL) can create upskilling and reskilling opportunities using returnees' skills, and that work has begun to bring workers in Saudi Arabia and Singapore under RPL.
AB2-88.target_section: What help is there when I come back?
AB2-88.why_new: The FAQ says PKB lends up to Tk 3 lakh without collateral; an NSDA director says a skills certificate raises the collateral-free limit to Tk 5 lakh under an NSDA-PKB agreement. Needs checking against PKB's own terms.

AB2-89.claim: Md Jahangir Hossain, deputy managing director of Probashi Kallyan Bank, told a roundtable on safe migration and the reintegration of returnees held at the Prothom Alo office in Dhaka on 18 August 2026 that the bank began operating on 20 April 2011 and from 2011-12 to June 2025 gave migration loans to 2 lakh 63 thousand 689 people, lending BDT 384 crore.
AB2-89.target_section: Can I get a government loan to go abroad?
AB2-89.why_new: Scale of PKB migration lending over 14 years, from the bank itself; not in the guide.

AB2-90.claim: Md Jahangir Hossain, deputy managing director of Probashi Kallyan Bank, told a roundtable on safe migration and the reintegration of returnees held at the Prothom Alo office in Dhaka on 18 August 2026 that the bank has several kinds of rehabilitation loan for returnees (rehabilitation, women's rehabilitation, special rehabilitation and self-employment loans), also lends where migrants run a business at home through their families, and has lent BDT 702 crore to 24 thousand 971 people under these rehabilitation loans.
AB2-90.target_section: What help is there when I come back?
AB2-90.why_new: Names PKB's returnee loan types and the number of borrowers (24,971), from the bank itself; the FAQ gives terms but no scale beyond the 2% pandemic figure.

AB2-91.claim: Mahsin Hamuda, national programme officer at the ILO (International Labour Organization), told a roundtable on safe migration and the reintegration of returnees held at the Prothom Alo office in Dhaka on 18 August 2026 that 94 percent of returnee workers want to become entrepreneurs after coming home but do not get loans easily because of complicated procedures and too much paperwork, and that to solve this an arrangement has now been made to give loans across the country through Karmasangsthan Bank at 7 percent interest on submission of only three documents.
AB2-91.target_section: What help is there when I come back?
AB2-91.why_new: A second lender for returnees not in the guide: Karmasangsthan Bank, 7% interest, three documents. The article does not name the three documents or the loan ceiling.

AB2-92.claim: Mahsin Hamuda, national programme officer at the ILO (International Labour Organization), told a roundtable on safe migration and the reintegration of returnees held at the Prothom Alo office in Dhaka on 18 August 2026 that the government recently drew up a reintegration policy for returned migrant workers, that many people do not know Probashi Kallyan Bank gives loans, and that reintegration support is usually project-based and stops when the project ends.
AB2-92.target_section: What help is there when I come back?
AB2-92.why_new: Notes the new reintegration policy and why returnee support is unreliable (project-based, little known).

AB2-93.claim: Anwar Hossain Chowdhury, managing director of the SME Foundation, told a roundtable on safe migration and the reintegration of returnees held at the Prothom Alo office in Dhaka on 18 August 2026 that the foundation is training returnees in business planning, financial literacy, the papers needed, trade licence, TIN and BSTI certificate and product markets, and that this work is still at a very early stage.
AB2-93.target_section: What help is there when I come back?
AB2-93.why_new: Another body said to train returnees (SME Foundation), described by its own head as at an early stage; no location or enrolment route is given.

AB2-94.claim: Nurul Kader, programme manager at the European Union delegation in Dhaka, told a roundtable on safe migration and the reintegration of returnees held at the Prothom Alo office in Dhaka on 18 August 2026 that EU-funded work on reintegrating returnees in Bangladesh began in 2017, and that the projects running through BRAC and IOM are essentially a pilot initiative.
AB2-94.why_new: The section mentions the EU-BRAC Prottasha-2 project; the EU's own programme manager calls these projects a pilot.

AB2-95.claim: Shariful Islam Hasan, associate director of BRAC's Migration Programme and Youth Platform, told a roundtable on safe migration and the reintegration of returnees held at the Prothom Alo office in Dhaka on 18 August 2026 that many people return empty-handed after finding no work, and that many have no savings even after 20 to 25 years abroad.
AB2-95.placement: other: who comes back with nothing
AB2-95.why_new: BRAC's statement on returnees' finances; generic, low priority.

AB2-96.claim: On 3 September 2026 Cambodia's immigration police detained 32 Bangladeshis at the airport in Phnom Penh when they went there to fly home; two were later released and the other 30 were held in an immigration detention centre, Prothom Alo reported on 19 October 2026.
AB2-96.target_section: Cambodia, Myanmar and Laos: scam compounds
AB2-96.why_new: The section says nothing about what happens to people who leave a compound and try to fly home: here 32 were detained at the airport and 30 held about a month and a half.
AB2-96.h3: Cambodia, Myanmar and Laos: scam compounds

AB2-97.claim: The 30 Bangladeshis held in Cambodia's immigration detention centre had gone to the airport on 3 September 2026 to return home under the process set by the Cambodian government, but were detained during immigration checks because of illegal stay and other complications, Prothom Alo reported on 19 October 2026.
AB2-97.target_section: Cambodia, Myanmar and Laos: scam compounds
AB2-97.why_new: Gives the reason for detention (illegal stay) even though they were following the government-set return process; the article does not describe that process.
AB2-97.h3: Cambodia, Myanmar and Laos: scam compounds

AB2-98.claim: The 30 Bangladeshis detained in Cambodia in September 2026 had been taken there through a broker ring with the lure of an attractive salary, many were forced into cyber scamming after arrival, and it is alleged that those who tried to escape from the centres were tortured, Prothom Alo reported on 19 October 2026.
AB2-98.target_section: Cambodia, Myanmar and Laos: scam compounds
AB2-98.why_new: Background of this group; the torture for escape attempts is reported as an allegation.
AB2-98.h3: Cambodia, Myanmar and Laos: scam compounds

AB2-99.claim: After an application by Anirban Survivor Voice Foundation, the expatriate welfare branch of the Wage Earners' Welfare Board sent a letter, signed by its deputy director (IRP) Mohammad Zakir Hossain, asking the First Secretary of the labour wing at the Bangladesh embassy in Bangkok to arrange the release and quick return of the Bangladeshis detained in Cambodia, Prothom Alo reported on 19 October 2026.
AB2-99.target_section: Cambodia, Myanmar and Laos: scam compounds
AB2-99.why_new: Shows the actual chain that got detainees out: survivors' NGO applies to the Welfare Board, the Board writes to the labour wing of the Bangkok embassy. The section lists the embassy but not this route.
AB2-99.h3: Cambodia, Myanmar and Laos: scam compounds

AB2-100.claim: Thirty Bangladeshis who had fled scam centres in Cambodia and were detained on their way home landed in Dhaka at 12:10 pm on Tuesday 20 October 2026 on Thai Airways flight TG-321, after being held in Cambodia's immigration detention centre since 3 September, Prothom Alo reported.
AB2-100.target_section: Cambodia, Myanmar and Laos: scam compounds
AB2-100.why_new: Confirms the return actually happened (the 19 October report only said it was due) and fixes the length of detention: 3 September to 20 October 2026.
AB2-100.h3: Cambodia, Myanmar and Laos: scam compounds

AB2-101.claim: Following an application by Anirban Survivor Voice Foundation, the Wage Earners' Welfare Board had written to the First Secretary of the labour wing at the Bangladesh embassy in Bangkok asking for arrangements to free and quickly return the 30 Bangladeshis held in Cambodian immigration detention, who flew home on 20 October 2026, Prothom Alo reported.
AB2-101.target_section: Where victims and families get help
AB2-101.placement: other: example of the Welfare Board route
AB2-101.why_new: A completed example for the help list: an application to the Welfare Board through a survivors' organisation ended in release and return.
AB2-101.h3: Where victims and families get help

AB2-102.claim: According to a press release from Anirban Survivor Voice Foundation reported by Prothom Alo on 21 October 2026, eight Bangladeshi workers went to Cambodia and Laos for work at various times in 2025, were made to work there for some time, and were then taken by road through Thailand and sold to a scam centre in Myanmar.
AB2-102.target_section: Cambodia, Myanmar and Laos: scam compounds
AB2-102.why_new: The section says victims are taken across the Thai border; this case shows workers who first held jobs in Cambodia or Laos being moved overland through Thailand and sold on to Myanmar.
AB2-102.h3: Cambodia, Myanmar and Laos: scam compounds

AB2-103.claim: According to a press release from Anirban Survivor Voice Foundation reported by Prothom Alo on 21 October 2026, the eight Bangladeshis sold to a scam centre in Myanmar were forced to work there under torture and abuse, at one point escaped to Thailand, surrendered to the immigration police because they had no visa, and were then kept in a safe home on a charge of illegal entry.
AB2-103.target_section: Cambodia, Myanmar and Laos: scam compounds
AB2-103.why_new: What happens after escaping a Myanmar compound into Thailand: surrender to immigration police and a stay in a safe home for illegal entry. Not in the section.
AB2-103.h3: Cambodia, Myanmar and Laos: scam compounds

AB2-104.claim: According to a press release from Anirban Survivor Voice Foundation reported by Prothom Alo on 21 October 2026, the Foundation took up the return of the eight on the basis of complaints from the victims and their families and applied to the Wage Earners' Welfare Board for help on 24 August 2026, after which a letter signed by the Board's director Md Saidur Rahman instructed the First Secretary (Labour) at the Bangladesh embassy in Bangkok to take steps to free the eight Bangladeshis staying in a safe home under the referral mechanism of Mae Sot immigration in Thailand and send them home.
AB2-104.target_section: Cambodia, Myanmar and Laos: scam compounds
AB2-104.why_new: A second documented use of the route: family complains to a survivors' organisation, it applies to the Welfare Board, the Board instructs the Bangkok labour wing. Also names where Myanmar escapees are held (the Mae Sot immigration safe home).
AB2-104.h3: Cambodia, Myanmar and Laos: scam compounds

AB2-105.claim: Three Bangladeshis who escaped from a scam centre in Myanmar, Md Saidur Rahman, Robiul and Md Sohel Rana, were due to land in Dhaka at 4:20 pm on Thursday 22 October 2026, while the rest of the eight held in a safe home under the referral mechanism of Mae Sot immigration in Thailand were still in the legal process for returning, according to a press release from Anirban Survivor Voice Foundation reported by Prothom Alo on 21 October 2026.
AB2-105.target_section: Cambodia, Myanmar and Laos: scam compounds
AB2-105.why_new: Timeline: application on 24 August, first three due home on 22 October, about two months later, with five still waiting. The article reports the return as scheduled, not as completed.
AB2-105.h3: Cambodia, Myanmar and Laos: scam compounds

AB2-106.claim: Two young Bangladeshi men who went to Cambodia hoping for good jobs had about BDT 6 lakh taken from each of them, had their passports taken on arrival and were then "sold" to a scam centre for USD 5 thousand, Prothom Alo reported on 27 October 2026 on the CID's arrest of two alleged members of the trafficking ring.
AB2-106.target_section: Cambodia, Myanmar and Laos: scam compounds
AB2-106.why_new: The section has a USD 5,000 ransom for two youths from another source; this adds what they paid in Bangladesh (about BDT 6 lakh each) and the sale price to the compound (USD 5,000).
AB2-106.h3: Cambodia, Myanmar and Laos: scam compounds

AB2-107.claim: Citing its preliminary inquiry, the CID said on 27 October 2026 that two Bangladeshi youths sold to a scam centre in Cambodia were tortured if they refused to take part in online fraud or made even a small mistake, and had no chance to leave of their own will or return home safely.
AB2-107.target_section: Cambodia, Myanmar and Laos: scam compounds
AB2-107.why_new: CID's account that torture followed refusal and even small mistakes, not only missed targets.
AB2-107.h3: Cambodia, Myanmar and Laos: scam compounds

AB2-108.claim: The CID said on 27 October 2026 that after two Bangladeshi youths were sold to a scam centre in Cambodia, a further USD 5 thousand was demanded from their families as ransom to free them and the families paid it, that the traffickers kept the two under their own control even after release, and that money was collected once more for the air tickets home.
AB2-108.target_section: Cambodia, Myanmar and Laos: scam compounds
AB2-108.why_new: Shows that paying the ransom did not end it: the traffickers kept control and charged again for the tickets. The section's ransom bullet stops at the demand.
AB2-108.h3: Cambodia, Myanmar and Laos: scam compounds

AB2-109.claim: According to the CID, the two Bangladeshi youths freed from a scam centre in Cambodia stayed in a local hotel there for about two months after their release and returned to Bangladesh on 3 September 2026 with the help of the BRAC Migration Centre, which they reached online.
AB2-109.target_section: Cambodia, Myanmar and Laos: scam compounds
AB2-109.why_new: A case where victims stuck in Cambodia after release got home by contacting BRAC online; the section lists BRAC only for the 2025 Myanmar rescue and gives no online route.
AB2-109.h3: Cambodia, Myanmar and Laos: scam compounds

AB2-110.claim: A case over the trafficking of two youths to Cambodia was filed at Paltan police station in Dhaka on 26 October 2026 naming Md Shaon Molla (23) and Md Sakib Sarkar (26), both from the Pubail area of Gazipur, and the CID arrested the two in a raid in the Paltan area on 27 October 2026 on the charge of trafficking the youths and forcing them into fraud work; the CID said the investigation is continuing.
AB2-110.target_section: Cambodia, Myanmar and Laos: scam compounds
AB2-110.why_new: A case where a returnee's complaint led to arrests the next day; the section's law part has no arrest for a Cambodia case. The article does not say under which Act the case was filed.
AB2-110.h3: Cambodia, Myanmar and Laos: scam compounds

AB2-111.claim: After two youths trafficked to Cambodia returned home on 3 September 2026, a case was filed at Paltan police station in Dhaka on 26 October naming two men, and the CID arrested both the next day, 27 October, according to the CID.
AB2-111.target_section: Where victims and families get help
AB2-111.placement: File a criminal case with the local police (example)
AB2-111.why_new: A second example, beside the Chandpur one, of a police case by returnees leading to an arrest, here within a day.
AB2-111.h3: Where victims and families get help

AB2-112.claim: According to BMET data reported by Prothom Alo on 27 October 2026, 12 thousand 263 Bangladeshis took clearance to go to Cambodia in 2025, making it the 8th largest destination for Bangladeshi workers that year, while 4 thousand 727 went to the Russian Federation, which ranked 13th.
AB2-112.target_section: Cambodia, Myanmar and Laos: scam compounds
AB2-112.why_new: A calendar-year BMET figure and rank for Cambodia (the section has 15,921 in 18 months) and the 2025 figure for Russia.
AB2-112.h3: Cambodia, Myanmar and Laos: scam compounds

AB2-113.claim: According to BMET data reported by Prothom Alo on 27 October 2026, 4 thousand 727 Bangladeshis went to the Russian Federation in 2025, placing Russia 13th among destinations for Bangladeshi workers that year.
AB2-113.why_new: A 2025 BMET outflow figure for Russia; check against the Russia section's existing numbers.

AB2-114.claim: Prothom Alo reported on 27 October 2026 that Bangladeshis are taken to Cambodia in the name of call-centre jobs and then made to do online fraud, that Cambodian law enforcement recently raided and shut these scam centres under international pressure, and that 646 Bangladeshi workers came back in June after that.
AB2-114.target_section: Cambodia, Myanmar and Laos: scam compounds
AB2-114.why_new: Gives 646 June returnees, which differs from the 583 the section cites from BRAC for June 2026; the article names no source for 646. The conflict should be noted or resolved.
AB2-114.h3: Cambodia, Myanmar and Laos: scam compounds

AB2-115.claim: People in the sector told Prothom Alo in October 2026 that Cambodia's economy is no better than Bangladesh's and job opportunities there are few, yet workers are sent there for the scam centres; the paper also reported that, with the Middle East labour market shrinking somewhat, people who are a little better off have in recent years been going to countries such as Russia and Cambodia, where many are cheated.
AB2-115.target_section: Cambodia, Myanmar and Laos: scam compounds
AB2-115.why_new: Who is targeted (somewhat better-off people looking beyond the Gulf) and the sector's own view that Cambodia has few real jobs; sources are unnamed 'people in the sector'.
AB2-115.h3: Cambodia, Myanmar and Laos: scam compounds

FV1-1.claim: On the Wednesday before a report dated 22 February 2024, the Airport Armed Police Battalion (APBn) and Dhaka detective police (DB) arrested five people in front of Terminal 2 of Hazrat Shahjalal International Airport, Dhaka: two alleged ringleaders, Mohammad Asaduzzaman and Mohammad Kabir Hossain, and three men, Jane Alam, Sabbir Mia and Samrat Saudagar, who were trying to leave for Europe on fake visas.
FV1-1.placement: other: How it is sold (Fake visas)
FV1-1.why_new: A dated airport case of fake visas for a Europe route; the section has the May 2026 Italy case but not this one.

FV1-2.claim: A DB deputy commissioner, Mashiur Rahman, told Prothom Alo in February 2024 that the three arrested travellers admitted they were first going to Qatar on fake visas and were then to go on illegally to France, Italy and Greece, and that each had paid a broker BDT 16 to 18 lakh.
FV1-2.placement: other: How it is sold (Fake visas)
FV1-2.why_new: Price (BDT 16-18 lakh) and route (fake visa to Qatar, then irregularly to France, Italy, Greece).

FV1-3.claim: According to DB in February 2024, low-ranking employees of various agencies working at Dhaka airport and people from private airlines had formed a ring that sent people from Bangladesh to the Middle East, Europe and elsewhere on fake visas for lakhs of taka; one of the two arrested men, Kabir Hossain, was a booking assistant of Qatar Airlines (printed as 'Qatar Airlines') and the other, Asaduzzaman, a security worker at Shahjalal airport, the DB officer said.
FV1-3.why_new: Insider involvement: an airline booking assistant and an airport security worker named as ringleaders (the section has only the 2026 Biman ground officer).

FV1-4.claim: In the February 2024 Dhaka airport case, police seized three passports, three fake visas, a special card for entering Hazrat Shahjalal International Airport, mobile phones, e-tickets, and work permit and visa papers from those arrested.
FV1-4.why_new: What the ring held, including a special airport entry card.

FV1-5.claim: In the February 2024 Dhaka airport case, the three men who were trying to travel on fake visas were arrested along with the two alleged ringleaders, a case of fraud and forgery was filed against them, and a court granted one day's remand.
FV1-5.why_new: Shows the travellers holding the fake visas were themselves arrested and charged, not treated only as victims.

FV1-14.claim: The CID said in May 2024 that Jannat Trade International took BDT 5 lakh 12 thousand each from three people with a promise of well-paid jobs in Kyrgyzstan and gave them so-called Kyrgyzstan visas and air tickets; when they went to Hazrat Shahjalal International Airport on 7 April, immigration police found no record of their visas online and their journey was stopped.
FV1-14.target_section: Fake visa, demand letter or job offer
FV1-14.why_new: A dated Kyrgyzstan fake-visa case with the price and how it was caught (immigration's online visa check).
FV1-14.h3: Fake visa, demand letter or job offer

FV1-15.claim: In the Jannat Trade International case, a case was filed at Paltan police station, Dhaka, under the Prevention and Suppression of Human Trafficking Act, and the CID arrested three people, including the firm's proprietor, Ibrahim Mallik Nahid, whom it called the head of the ring (reported 7 May 2024).
FV1-15.target_section: Fake visa, demand letter or job offer
FV1-15.why_new: Shows a fake-visa airport case registered as trafficking, not only as fraud.
FV1-15.h3: Fake visa, demand letter or job offer

FV1-6.claim: A Prothom Alo report from Canada dated 23 April 2024 said the Canadian government had announced that people who found an LMIA-approved job (a job for which no one already allowed to work in Canada could be found; LMIA is the Labour Market Impact Assessment) could come and work temporarily, and that many Bangladeshis who came on visit visas without understanding this found no such job, claimed political asylum and were now in trouble.
FV1-6.target_section: Visit and tourist visas sold as jobs
FV1-6.placement: other: The path, country by country (new Canada item)
FV1-6.why_new: The guide has no Canada item for visit visas sold as a way to work.
FV1-6.h3: Visit and tourist visas sold as jobs

FV1-7.claim: According to the 23 April 2024 Prothom Alo report from Canada, each person spent BDT 5 to 15 lakh on the Canadian visit visa, because the visa is document-based and dishonest rings made the financial and other documents for them and took this money.
FV1-7.target_section: Visit and tourist visas sold as jobs
FV1-7.why_new: Price of a Canada visit-visa package and the mechanism (rings fabricate bank and other documents).
FV1-7.h3: Visit and tourist visas sold as jobs

FV1-8.claim: The April 2024 report said visit-visa applicants had shown a good job or business, large bank balances, and country and family ties at home, and that because they got the visa on one set of documents and then told a different story to claim asylum, many would lose their asylum cases and be removed from Canada.
FV1-8.target_section: Visit and tourist visas sold as jobs
FV1-8.why_new: Why asylum after a document-built visit visa fails.
FV1-8.h3: Visit and tourist visas sold as jobs

FV1-9.claim: According to the April 2024 report, an asylum claimant in Canada must prove that his life is under threat in his own country and must hire an immigration lawyer, lawyers are charging at least CAD 7,000 to 10,000, and a claimant who loses the case is removed from Canada.
FV1-9.target_section: Visit and tourist visas sold as jobs
FV1-9.why_new: Cost and outcome of the asylum route after arrival.
FV1-9.h3: Visit and tourist visas sold as jobs

FV1-10.claim: The April 2024 report said asylum claimants in Canada get roughly 700 dollars a month from the government until they find work, that they had to hand their passports to the government and so could not go home, and that thousands of Bangladeshis could find no work because they lacked English, relevant work experience and education.
FV1-10.target_section: Visit and tourist visas sold as jobs
FV1-10.why_new: What life is like after claiming: allowance, passport surrendered, no work.
FV1-10.h3: Visit and tourist visas sold as jobs

FV1-11.claim: The April 2024 report said such people were surviving on food banks, which run on local donations and had cut what they give as crowds grew, and that many, struggling to fight their asylum cases, were bringing large amounts of money from home through hundi.
FV1-11.target_section: Visit and tourist visas sold as jobs
FV1-11.why_new: Families at home keep paying after arrival, by hundi.
FV1-11.h3: Visit and tourist visas sold as jobs

FV1-12.claim: The April 2024 report said travellers were lately being turned back at various airports before entering Canada, that documents are checked again on landing in Canada, and that those who came with fake invitation letters and fake documents were being sent home at once.
FV1-12.target_section: Visit and tourist visas sold as jobs
FV1-12.why_new: Refused entry on arrival for fake invitation letters.
FV1-12.h3: Visit and tourist visas sold as jobs

FV1-13.claim: According to the April 2024 report, a ring inside Canada was arranging to send these people on to the United States across unguarded border points near Montreal, and various sources said many were now held in US jails.
FV1-13.target_section: Visit and tourist visas sold as jobs
FV1-13.why_new: An onward-smuggling step (Canada to the US) not in the guide.
FV1-13.h3: Visit and tourist visas sold as jobs

FV1-16.claim: Recruiting agency owners told Prothom Alo in June 2024 that after the Covid pandemic the UAE began taking workers on travel visas, with the employer applying after arrival to change the visa to an employment visa, and that a ring used this facility to cheat workers: many found no work after arriving and lived on the streets and in parks.
FV1-16.target_section: Visit and tourist visas sold as jobs
FV1-16.placement: other: The path, country by country (UAE)
FV1-16.why_new: Explains how the UAE visit-visa route began and why it collapsed; the section only says conversion is closed.
FV1-16.h3: Visit and tourist visas sold as jobs

FV1-17.claim: According to the June 2024 Prothom Alo report, under UAE labour law an employer found to be connected with a worker who has become illegal is fined AED 50,000, and this was one reason UAE employers became unwilling to take Bangladeshi workers.
FV1-17.target_section: Visit and tourist visas sold as jobs
FV1-17.placement: other: The path, country by country (UAE)
FV1-17.h3: Visit and tourist visas sold as jobs

FV1-18.claim: Shakirul Islam, chairperson of the migrant organisation OKUP (Ovibashi Karmi Unnayan Program), told Prothom Alo in June 2024 that workers who went to the UAE on travel visas had to pay brokers again to get an employment visa.
FV1-18.target_section: Visit and tourist visas sold as jobs
FV1-18.placement: other: The path, country by country (UAE)
FV1-18.why_new: A second payment after arrival, from a named NGO head.
FV1-18.h3: Visit and tourist visas sold as jobs

FV1-19.claim: Tipu Sultan, joint secretary general of BAIRA (the recruiting agencies' association), told Prothom Alo in June 2024 that many who went to the UAE on travel visas for employment found no work, which damaged Bangladesh's image and reduced interest in taking its workers.
FV1-19.target_section: Visit and tourist visas sold as jobs
FV1-19.placement: other: The path, country by country (UAE)
FV1-19.h3: Visit and tourist visas sold as jobs

FV1-20.claim: BAIRA's secretary general, Ali Haider Chowdhury, told Prothom Alo in June 2024 that the UAE does not give visas for hiring in the unskilled sector and wants workers in professional categories, where Bangladeshi workers lack certificates, although the visa type can be changed after arriving.
FV1-20.target_section: Visit and tourist visas sold as jobs
FV1-20.placement: other: The path, country by country (UAE)
FV1-20.why_new: Why UAE jobs are sold on other visa types.
FV1-20.h3: Visit and tourist visas sold as jobs

FV1-21.claim: BMET data analysed by Prothom Alo in June 2024 showed about 8,500 workers a month going to the UAE in 2022, an average of 8,200 a month in 2023 and an average of 6,500 a month in the first four months of 2024.
FV1-21.target_section: Visit and tourist visas sold as jobs
FV1-21.why_new: Flow figures for the UAE before the July 2024 restriction.
FV1-21.h3: Visit and tourist visas sold as jobs

FV1-22.claim: According to the June 2024 report, the UAE labour market closed to Bangladeshis in 2012 after various complaints about workers, about 25,000 a year went in 2014 and 2015, the number fell to 1,000 in 2020, and sending resumed in 2021.
FV1-22.target_section: Visit and tourist visas sold as jobs
FV1-22.placement: other: The path, country by country (UAE)
FV1-22.why_new: Earlier closure history of the UAE market.
FV1-22.h3: Visit and tourist visas sold as jobs

FV1-23.claim: Officials said the state minister for expatriates' welfare, Shafiqur Rahman Chowdhury, met heads of foreign employers in the UAE on 25 May 2024 and discussed sending more workers as motorbike riders and car drivers.
FV1-23.target_section: Which countries can I go to for work right now?
FV1-23.why_new: Which trades the government was pushing for the UAE in 2024; low priority.

FV1-24.claim: Kawsar Khan, an immigration lawyer in Sydney, wrote in Prothom Alo on 26 November 2024 that the main condition of Australia's work visas is that an Australian business sponsors the applicant, that only an 'approved sponsor' approved by Australia's immigration department can nominate someone, that getting a job through such a sponsor from Bangladesh is in practice very hard, and that there are precedents of lakhs of taka being taken in the name of a sponsor.
FV1-24.target_section: NEW: Fake Australia and Canada work visas
FV1-24.why_new: The real rule the scam imitates: only an approved sponsor can nominate.
FV1-24.h3: NEW: Fake Australia and Canada work visas

FV1-25.claim: Kawsar Khan wrote in November 2024 that proof of English skill is a mandatory condition for an Australian work visa, and that immigration experts say anyone who claims the visa can be had without proof of English should be identified as a fraud ring.
FV1-25.target_section: NEW: Fake Australia and Canada work visas
FV1-25.why_new: A concrete red flag from a named immigration lawyer.
FV1-25.h3: NEW: Fake Australia and Canada work visas

FV1-26.claim: Kawsar Khan wrote in November 2024 that Australian immigration law changes almost every year, and that fraud rings use wrong explanations of such changes and flashy news to cause financial loss to many people who want to go abroad.
FV1-26.target_section: NEW: Fake Australia and Canada work visas
FV1-26.why_new: Mechanism: scams ride on news of real rule changes (see also the 2026 farm-visa rumour).
FV1-26.h3: NEW: Fake Australia and Canada work visas

FV1-27.claim: According to Kawsar Khan in November 2024, an applicant for Australia's subclass 482 work visa at that time needed at least two years' experience in the same occupation within the previous five years (for example, a Bangladeshi applying as a restaurant manager), and the immigration department had proposed cutting this to one year.
FV1-27.target_section: NEW: Fake Australia and Canada work visas
FV1-27.why_new: The experience requirement a real 482 applicant had to meet in 2024; a proposal, so the current rule needs an official source.
FV1-27.h3: NEW: Fake Australia and Canada work visas

FV1-28.claim: Abdul Gani (30) of Shushuti village, Fulbaria, Mymensingh, said he gave Shafiqul Islam, known locally as a manpower broker, a total of BDT 6 lakh 10 thousand to go to Turkey; Shafiqul took his passport and money, kept him waiting a year and a half, then said Turkey was not possible and he would be sent to Saudi Arabia within 20 days, and on 18 February (2025) gave him an air ticket in the name of 'Jazeera Airways' and a visa, both of which turned out to be fake.
FV1-28.target_section: Fake visa, demand letter or job offer
FV1-28.why_new: A dated village-level case with the destination switched and both ticket and visa forged.
FV1-28.h3: Fake visa, demand letter or job offer

FV1-29.claim: RAB said in May 2025 that Shafiqul Islam (42) of Patira village, Fulbaria, Mymensingh, cheated people by making fake tickets in the names of 'Jazeera Airways', 'Air Arabia', 'Salam Air', 'Egypt Air' and others.
FV1-29.target_section: Fake visa, demand letter or job offer
FV1-29.why_new: Fake airline tickets in named airlines' names as part of the package.
FV1-29.h3: Fake visa, demand letter or job offer

FV1-30.claim: Abdul Gani said that after the fake ticket and visa Shafiqul Islam was to return his money but fled the area from 10 April (2025), and that under pressure from his dadon loan and with no refund he filed a written complaint with RAB; another complainant said he had sold all he had and borrowed through dadon to pay, was not sent abroad, and was threatened when he asked for his money.
FV1-30.target_section: Refund refusals after a failed departure
FV1-30.why_new: Refund promised, broker absconds, threats when money is asked for; the victim's route was a written complaint to RAB.
FV1-30.h3: Refund refusals after a failed departure

FV1-31.claim: RAB-14 detained Shafiqul Islam at Technopara, Joydebpur, Gazipur, on the night of 29 May 2025 and handed him to Fulbaria police station; RAB-14's commander, Naymul Hasan, said he had been cheating village people for about three years and a case would be filed under the regular law, and the Fulbaria officer-in-charge said the complaint would be verified and legal action taken.
FV1-31.target_section: Fake visa, demand letter or job offer
FV1-31.why_new: What the authorities did, and that no case had yet been registered when reported.
FV1-31.h3: Fake visa, demand letter or job offer

FV1-32.claim: Local residents alleged that Shafiqul Islam took nearly BDT 1 crore in a few years on promises of sending people abroad for work, and the two complainants said many people in nearby areas had been cheated through him.
FV1-32.target_section: Fake visa, demand letter or job offer
FV1-32.why_new: Scale of one village broker, as alleged.
FV1-32.h3: Fake visa, demand letter or job offer

FV1-41.claim: On 13 August 2025 the Dhaka Chief Metropolitan Magistrate Court granted 13 more days of remand for Khairul Bashar, chairman of BSB Global Network, in five separate fraud cases, after Gulshan police asked for 31 days saying he had embezzled a huge amount in the name of sending people abroad for higher education.
