FV1-41.target_section: Study-abroad firms that take the fee
FV1-41.why_new: What happened after the July 2025 arrest: five separate fraud cases and further remand.
FV1-41.h3: Study-abroad firms that take the fee

FV1-42.claim: The CID filed a money-laundering case against Khairul Bashar at Gulshan police station on 4 May 2025, arrested him in Dhanmondi, Dhaka, the day before 15 July 2025, and questioned him on 10 days' remand in that case.
FV1-42.target_section: Study-abroad firms that take the fee
FV1-42.why_new: The money-laundering case and its date; the guide has only the arrest.
FV1-42.h3: Study-abroad firms that take the fee

FV1-43.claim: According to the CID's preliminary inquiry, from 2018 to 2024 Khairul Bashar, with his wife Khandaker Selima Rowshan and son Arosh Ibne Bashar, built an organised ring that took large sums from students in the name of admission to foreign universities, scholarships and visa processing, drawing them in with fake visa processing, made-up claims of representation and flashy adverts.
FV1-43.target_section: Study-abroad firms that take the fee
FV1-43.why_new: Period, family members named by CID, and the three things sold (admission, scholarship, visa processing).
FV1-43.h3: Study-abroad firms that take the fee

FV1-44.claim: The CID said in August 2025 that 448 victims of BSB Global Network had so far reported being cheated, that the real number could be higher, that several victims had filed fraud and forgery cases at different police stations, and that many students who did go abroad were cheated in various ways there.
FV1-44.target_section: Study-abroad firms that take the fee
FV1-44.why_new: Victim count (448) and that some were cheated after travelling.
FV1-44.h3: Study-abroad firms that take the fee

FV1-45.claim: The CID said Khairul Bashar and his family members kept the money collected from students in various bank accounts and withdrew it to buy immovable property, run businesses and transfer money illegally.
FV1-45.target_section: Study-abroad firms that take the fee
FV1-45.why_new: Where the money went, per CID; relevant to whether refunds are recoverable.
FV1-45.h3: Study-abroad firms that take the fee

FV1-33.claim: Afaz Uddin Molla (58), a Bangladeshi worker in Kuwait for 30 years, told Prothom Alo in June 2025 that in August 2024 he saw a social media advert saying 'a chance to go to Canada for little money' and rang the mobile number in the Facebook advert; the man who answered called himself Asadul Islam, said he was in Canada, could take him from Kuwait to Canada quickly, and that the salary there would be BDT 4 to 5 lakh.
FV1-33.target_section: Online job adverts, Facebook and WhatsApp scams, and fake government sites
FV1-33.why_new: A Canada Facebook-advert case aimed at a worker already in the Gulf.
FV1-33.h3: Online job adverts, Facebook and WhatsApp scams, and fake government sites

FV1-34.claim: According to the case statement, the man calling himself Asadul took BDT 24 lakh from Afaz Uddin between August and December 2024 as the cost of a Canada visa, sent to several bKash numbers he supplied; Afaz Uddin was told again and again that the visa would come very soon, and then the phone number was switched off.
FV1-34.target_section: Online job adverts, Facebook and WhatsApp scams, and fake government sites
FV1-34.why_new: Amount, period, payment channel (several bKash numbers) and how contact ended.
FV1-34.h3: Online job adverts, Facebook and WhatsApp scams, and fake government sites

FV1-35.claim: Roksana Akter, the complainant and wife of the Kuwait-based victim in the 2024 Canada case, told Prothom Alo that she asked many times to speak to 'Asadul' on a video call and he never agreed.
FV1-35.target_section: Online job adverts, Facebook and WhatsApp scams, and fake government sites
FV1-35.why_new: A red flag the article itself shows: the recruiter refuses video calls.
FV1-35.h3: Online job adverts, Facebook and WhatsApp scams, and fake government sites

FV1-36.claim: Roksana Akter filed a case at Jatrabari police station, Dhaka, on 22 May 2025 naming a man called Asadul as the main accused with 20 to 25 unnamed associates, and police sources said the court ordered the CID to investigate.
FV1-36.target_section: Online job adverts, Facebook and WhatsApp scams, and fake government sites
FV1-36.why_new: What was done: a case in Dhaka by the family while the victim is abroad, sent to CID.
FV1-36.h3: Online job adverts, Facebook and WhatsApp scams, and fake government sites

FV1-37.claim: When Prothom Alo rang the phone number named in the case on the evening of 4 June 2025, the person who answered said he was not Asadul, that his name was Hanif, and cut the call.
FV1-37.target_section: Online job adverts, Facebook and WhatsApp scams, and fake government sites
FV1-37.why_new: The identity given to the victim was not confirmed; the name may be false.
FV1-37.h3: Online job adverts, Facebook and WhatsApp scams, and fake government sites

FV1-38.claim: Afaz Uddin said the BDT 24 lakh he paid in 2024 for a promised Canada job was all his savings plus loans from acquaintances and relatives, and his wife said the family was still paying interest on the money they borrowed.
FV1-38.why_new: Debt left behind by an online scam.

FV1-39.claim: Omar Faruq Faruqi, chief public prosecutor of the Dhaka Metropolitan Sessions Judge Court, told Prothom Alo in June 2025 that the CID should identify and arrest every member of the ring by tracing the bKash numbers named in the case, that no one should put money in on the strength of flashy social media adverts, and that people should go abroad through institutions that have a licence and regularly send people.
FV1-39.target_section: Online job adverts, Facebook and WhatsApp scams, and fake government sites
FV1-39.why_new: Advice from a named prosecutor, and that the bKash numbers are the investigative lead.
FV1-39.h3: Online job adverts, Facebook and WhatsApp scams, and fake government sites

FV1-40.claim: Afaz Uddin Molla, a worker in Kuwait, told Prothom Alo that in August 2024 he answered a Facebook advert offering a cheap route to Canada and was promised he would be taken from Kuwait to Canada, and according to the case statement the man calling himself Asadul took BDT 24 lakh from him by December 2024.
FV1-40.target_section: Recruited while abroad or just back
FV1-40.why_new: Another worker targeted while in the Gulf, this time online.
FV1-40.h3: Recruited while abroad or just back

FV1-46.claim: On 22 September 2025 the Bangladesh Embassy in Abu Dhabi said in a press release that UAE authorities had confirmed no UAE authority had announced a visa ban on Bangladeshis, and that the news reports of a ban cited an article on the website of a so-called visa processing centre, uaevisaonline.com, whose information was not correct.
FV1-46.target_section: Online job adverts, Facebook and WhatsApp scams, and fake government sites
FV1-46.why_new: A named fake 'visa processing centre' website and an embassy denial of a rumoured ban. Check against the guide's statement that the UAE restricted work and visit visas in July 2024: the embassy denial concerns a September 2025 'ban' report only.
FV1-46.h3: Online job adverts, Facebook and WhatsApp scams, and fake government sites

FV1-47.claim: The Bangladesh Embassy in Abu Dhabi said in September 2025 that it had reviewed uaevisaonline.com and found the registrant's and technical contact's addresses and telephone numbers were in the United Kingdom, the registrar's contact number was in the United States, the company contact number on the site was Indian, and the head office address given was in Dubai, where the embassy confirmed the building or house number does not exist.
FV1-47.target_section: Online job adverts, Facebook and WhatsApp scams, and fake government sites
FV1-47.why_new: How an embassy checked a visa website: domain registration contacts and a physical address that does not exist.
FV1-47.h3: Online job adverts, Facebook and WhatsApp scams, and fake government sites

FV1-48.claim: The embassy said it held customer reviews of uaevisaonline.com's past activity and that most customers complained of having been cheated financially.
FV1-48.target_section: Online job adverts, Facebook and WhatsApp scams, and fake government sites
FV1-48.why_new: Embassy's finding on the site's customers.
FV1-48.h3: Online job adverts, Facebook and WhatsApp scams, and fake government sites

FV1-49.claim: On 23 September 2025 the CID arrested Josna Khatun (35), of Daljitpur village, Narail, in Ibrahimpur, Kafrul, Dhaka; the CID said she is the named main accused in a fraud case at Paltan police station and that the ring first lured people with jobs abroad, then took large sums through several bank accounts and gave them fake visas.
FV1-49.target_section: Fake visa, demand letter or job offer
FV1-49.why_new: A dated Italy fake-visa ring with payment through bank accounts, not only cash or mobile money.
FV1-49.h3: Fake visa, demand letter or job offer

FV1-50.claim: According to the September 2025 report, the Josna Khatun ring promised high-paid jobs in Italy and handed over forged visas, and also took money on promises of placing people in important government posts; its network covers Faridpur, Narail, Narsingdi, Kishoreganj, Chandpur, Chattogram and other districts.
FV1-50.target_section: Fake visa, demand letter or job offer
FV1-50.why_new: Destination (Italy), the districts covered, and that the same ring also sold government jobs.
FV1-50.h3: Fake visa, demand letter or job offer

FV1-51.claim: According to the September 2025 report, an earlier-arrested active member of the same ring, Milon Mia of Faridpur, was found in the investigation to have collected people from different areas in the name of sending them abroad, and the ring took several crore taka from more than a hundred people.
FV1-51.target_section: Fake visa, demand letter or job offer
FV1-51.why_new: The division of roles (a district-level collector feeding a Dhaka ring) and the scale. Note: the article's opening line says 'hundreds of crores' while the CID detail says several crore from over a hundred people.
FV1-51.h3: Fake visa, demand letter or job offer

FV1-52.claim: The CID said in September 2025 that the Josna Khatun ring, which took money for jobs abroad and gave fake visas, also held on to many victims' passports to harass them.
FV1-52.target_section: The passport kept by the dalal
FV1-52.why_new: Another dated case of passports held as a lever.
FV1-52.h3: The passport kept by the dalal

FV1-62.claim: Investigators said in July 2026 that a ring advertising Australia and Canada jobs on social media used fake work permits, visa approval letters, LMIAs (Canada's Labour Market Impact Assessment) and a fake visa verification website made to look like an Australian government site: when a passport number was entered, it showed a message that the visa had been approved.
FV1-62.target_section: Online job adverts, Facebook and WhatsApp scams, and fake government sites
FV1-62.why_new: A fake 'verify your visa' site that returns 'approved' for the victim's passport number: the section has a fake police-clearance site but not this.
FV1-62.h3: Online job adverts, Facebook and WhatsApp scams, and fake government sites

FV1-53.claim: Tanzim Ul Haque, a senior officer at the Sandwip branch of Probashi Kallyan Bank, told Prothom Alo in May 2026 that in many cases they see fraudulent contracts between a fake employer and the worker, and that many people still sell their homestead to go abroad and end up in trouble.
FV1-53.target_section: Fake visa, demand letter or job offer
FV1-53.why_new: A bank loan officer's first-hand statement that fake employer-worker contracts reach PKB.
FV1-53.h3: Fake visa, demand letter or job offer

FV1-54.claim: Prothom Alo reported in May 2026 that Arif Hossain of Santoshpur, Sandwip, was cheated after going to Saudi Arabia and had to return home after only 27 days, and Arif said he had sold his electronics shop to get the visa and now has nothing left.
FV1-54.why_new: A dated case of a business sold for a visa and a return within 27 days (the article does not say how he was cheated).

FV1-55.claim: The principal of the government technical training centre near the Sandwip upazila complex, Muhammad Sharfuddin, said 750 people trained there last year (2025) and about 300 trainees were currently enrolled, and according to BMET data 2,080 people from Sandwip went abroad in 2025.
FV1-55.target_section: Is there a job for someone with no skills?
FV1-55.why_new: Local numbers only; included for completeness.

FV1-56.claim: Citing the case, the CID said that in December 2025 an acquaintance contacted an Oman-based Bangladeshi offering to arrange work in Australia and put him in touch with a man calling himself 'Khaja Mohammad Ali', who, by phone, imo, WhatsApp and Messenger, promised to take him to Australia and took BDT 1 lakh 46 thousand 400 in stages through bKash for processing, online application, form filling and visa costs.
FV1-56.target_section: Online job adverts, Facebook and WhatsApp scams, and fake government sites
FV1-56.why_new: A dated Australia online case with the fee labels used and the amount.
FV1-56.h3: Online job adverts, Facebook and WhatsApp scams, and fake government sites

FV1-57.claim: The CID said on 18 June 2026 that an arrested 19-year-old from Taraganj, Rangpur, Md Roni Islam, ran a fake Facebook page posing as an Australia-based expatriate named 'Khaja Mohammad Ali', posted attractive videos about Australian jobs, work permits and immigration, and, to build credibility, contacted people through an imo account using an Australian number.
FV1-57.target_section: Online job adverts, Facebook and WhatsApp scams, and fake government sites
FV1-57.why_new: The persona trick: a recruiter in Bangladesh posing as an expatriate, with a foreign number on imo.
FV1-57.h3: Online job adverts, Facebook and WhatsApp scams, and fake government sites

FV1-58.claim: In the June 2026 Australia case, the CID said that after taking money through bKash the accused also gave a bank account number to collect more, that the second arrested man, Md Rakibul Hossain (26) of Saidpur, Nilphamari, helped receive, move and transact the money through various mobile banking accounts, and that six mobile phones and 12 SIM cards were seized.
FV1-58.target_section: Online job adverts, Facebook and WhatsApp scams, and fake government sites
FV1-58.why_new: The money-handling role and the many SIMs behind one persona.
FV1-58.h3: Online job adverts, Facebook and WhatsApp scams, and fake government sites

FV1-59.claim: In the June 2026 Australia case the phone numbers went dead and all contact stopped; the victim's nephew filed a case at Jatrabari police station, Dhaka, on 2 June 2026, and the CID arrested the two accused at Kamarpukur Bazar, Saidpur, Nilphamari, on 17 June.
FV1-59.target_section: Online job adverts, Facebook and WhatsApp scams, and fake government sites
FV1-59.why_new: A relative in Bangladesh can file the case for a victim abroad; arrest followed in 15 days.
FV1-59.h3: Online job adverts, Facebook and WhatsApp scams, and fake government sites

FV1-60.claim: The CID asked people in June 2026 not to make any payment on an offer of a job abroad or migration without properly checking the institution concerned, the recruiting body and the visa process.
FV1-60.target_section: Online job adverts, Facebook and WhatsApp scams, and fake government sites
FV1-60.why_new: CID's own warning (it gives no method).
FV1-60.h3: Online job adverts, Facebook and WhatsApp scams, and fake government sites

FV1-61.claim: The victim in the June 2026 Australia online case was a Bangladeshi working in Oman, approached in December 2025 through a person he already knew.
FV1-61.target_section: Recruited while abroad or just back
FV1-61.why_new: Another Gulf-based worker targeted for an onward move.
FV1-61.h3: Recruited while abroad or just back

FV1-63.claim: Dhaka Metropolitan Police said that Md Sayedul Haque, hoping for a job in Australia, paid about BDT 4 lakh 80 thousand in stages through bKash for a medical fee, visa processing fee, document charge and other heads, that more was then demanded with no real arrangement to send him, and that he filed a case at Pallabi police station.
FV1-63.target_section: Online job adverts, Facebook and WhatsApp scams, and fake government sites
FV1-63.why_new: A dated case with the amount and the fee heads used.
FV1-63.h3: Online job adverts, Facebook and WhatsApp scams, and fake government sites

FV1-64.claim: After the Pallabi case, the DB's Cyber and Special Crime (North) division located the accused and on Tuesday 28 July 2026 arrested Mariful Islam (21) and Bachcha Bau alias Hasinur (28) in the Kishoreganj police station area of Nilphamari, seizing a laptop, seven mobile phones, 13 SIM cards and nine forged Bangladeshi passports; a DMP additional deputy commissioner, Niaz Mehedi, said the ring had cheated more than 72 people in the same way.
FV1-64.target_section: Online job adverts, Facebook and WhatsApp scams, and fake government sites
FV1-64.why_new: Arrests, seizures (nine forged passports) and the victim count. The date 28 July is worked out from 'last Tuesday' in a report dated Friday 31 July 2026.
FV1-64.h3: Online job adverts, Facebook and WhatsApp scams, and fake government sites

FV1-65.claim: Police said the Nilphamari ring arrested in July 2026 took money in stages by mobile banking under the heads of medical fee, visa processing fee, document verification, ticket and other incidental costs, after assuring people the job abroad was confirmed.
FV1-65.target_section: The staged-payment trap, and no receipts
FV1-65.why_new: Adds 'medical fee' and 'ticket' to the fee labels, from a police account.
FV1-65.h3: The staged-payment trap, and no receipts

FV1-66.claim: A Prothom Alo explainer of 6 August 2026 set out the real Canadian work permit process: a genuine job offer from a Canadian organisation; the employer applies to the Canadian government for an LMIA (Labour Market Impact Assessment, proof that no citizen or permanent resident was found for the post) and gets it approved; the applicant submits the job offer, passport, proof of education and professional qualification, proof of language skill and, as required, a health examination; after biometrics, security checks and assessment the immigration authority decides; and the work permit itself is issued on arrival on the border officer's final approval.
FV1-66.target_section: NEW: Fake Australia and Canada work visas
FV1-66.why_new: The real five-step process against which a Canada offer can be compared; the guide has none.
FV1-66.h3: NEW: Fake Australia and Canada work visas

FV1-67.claim: The August 2026 explainer said not every Canadian job needs an LMIA: work permits are also given without one under international agreements, special programmes and for certain occupations.
FV1-67.target_section: NEW: Fake Australia and Canada work visas
FV1-67.why_new: Qualifies the LMIA rule so the guide does not overstate it.
FV1-67.h3: NEW: Fake Australia and Canada work visas

FV1-68.claim: According to the August 2026 explainer, Canada has nothing like Saudi Arabia's kafil (sponsor) system in which a sponsor can arrange a visa: only the federal government issues Canadian visas, and even provincial governments have no power to issue one.
FV1-68.target_section: NEW: Fake Australia and Canada work visas
FV1-68.why_new: Corrects the Gulf-shaped belief that a visa can be bought from a sponsor.
FV1-68.h3: NEW: Fake Australia and Canada work visas

FV1-69.claim: The August 2026 explainer listed what Canada fraudsters claim: '100 per cent guaranteed visa' (১০০ শতাংশ গ্যারান্টি ভিসা), 'a job without an interview' (ইন্টারভিউ ছাড়াই চাকরি), 'Canadian permanent residence (PR) in two or three months', 'a high-paid job with no qualifications', 'a special government quota' (সরকারি বিশেষ কোটা) and 'no language skill needed'.
FV1-69.target_section: NEW: Fake Australia and Canada work visas
FV1-69.why_new: The sales phrases used for Canada, in Bangla.
FV1-69.h3: NEW: Fake Australia and Canada work visas

FV1-70.claim: The August 2026 explainer said the Canadian government or immigration department gives no one an advance assurance of a visa, every application is checked separately, and no person, agency or representative can guarantee visa approval.
FV1-70.target_section: NEW: Fake Australia and Canada work visas
FV1-70.why_new: A guarantee is itself the red flag.
FV1-70.h3: NEW: Fake Australia and Canada work visas

FV1-71.claim: Analysing recent incidents and various past frauds, the August 2026 explainer said Canada fraudsters typically make fake job offer letters using well-known organisations' logos, show copies of forged LMIAs or work permits, send fake visa approval letters, build copies of government websites, use the photos or identities of people living in Canada on social media, and press for a quick decision and an advance payment.
FV1-71.target_section: NEW: Fake Australia and Canada work visas
FV1-71.why_new: The full kit of trust-building devices for Canada offers.
FV1-71.h3: NEW: Fake Australia and Canada work visas

FV1-72.claim: The August 2026 explainer said a fraudster calls on WhatsApp or imo from a number with Canada's country code (+1), and that anyone outside Canada can make a call from a Canadian country-code number online.
FV1-72.placement: other: new item (A foreign phone number)
FV1-72.why_new: A foreign country code is not proof the caller is abroad (the June 2026 CID case shows the same with an Australian number on imo).

FV1-73.claim: The August 2026 explainer said to check four things on a Canada job offer: that the employer really exists, by matching its address, phone number and website; that the pay, workplace, duties and contract terms in the offer letter are realistic; that the email came from the organisation's own domain and not a free email service; and, if told to verify the visa on a website, that it really is a government website.
FV1-73.target_section: NEW: Fake Australia and Canada work visas
FV1-73.why_new: Four concrete checks for a Canada offer.
FV1-73.h3: NEW: Fake Australia and Canada work visas

FV1-74.claim: Experts cited in the August 2026 explainer advised against sending large sums to a personal bank account or mobile banking number, said receipts for every payment should be kept and any document read and understood before signing, and said that in case of doubt a Canada-authorised immigration consultant or lawyer can be consulted.
FV1-74.target_section: NEW: Fake Australia and Canada work visas
FV1-74.why_new: Payment advice and who can give a second opinion.
FV1-74.h3: NEW: Fake Australia and Canada work visas

FV1-75.claim: The August 2026 explainer said a Canadian work permit is a temporary permission and never a right to live there permanently, so advertising that 'a work permit means guaranteed PR' is misleading; permanent residence can be applied for later only on meeting qualification, work experience, language and programme conditions.
FV1-75.target_section: NEW: Fake Australia and Canada work visas
FV1-75.h3: NEW: Fake Australia and Canada work visas

FV1-76.claim: The August 2026 explainer said about 6 per cent of Canada's population was unemployed and lakhs of international students already in Canada were looking for jobs, and that without a good score in IELTS (English) or in TEF or TCF (the French tests) a Canadian job visa 'is not for you'.
FV1-76.target_section: NEW: Fake Australia and Canada work visas
FV1-76.why_new: Why a no-qualification Canada job offer is implausible: competition and the language-test bar.
FV1-76.h3: NEW: Fake Australia and Canada work visas

FV1-77.claim: Kawsar Khan reported on 11 August 2026 that law enforcers had recently arrested several rings in Dhaka and elsewhere accused of building copies of Australian government websites and giving fake sponsorships and 'work visit visas'.
FV1-77.target_section: NEW: Fake Australia and Canada work visas
FV1-77.why_new: Shows the pattern is repeated across several rings, not one case.
FV1-77.h3: NEW: Fake Australia and Canada work visas

FV1-78.claim: The Australian High Commission in Dhaka said in a recent warning, reported on 11 August 2026, that to avoid fake migration agents people should go to a registered migration agent or a lawyer for any visa advice.
FV1-78.target_section: NEW: Fake Australia and Canada work visas
FV1-78.why_new: An official warning from the destination's mission.
FV1-78.h3: NEW: Fake Australia and Canada work visas

FV1-79.claim: Under Australian law an agent giving visa advice or services must be registered with OMARA (the Office of the Migration Agents Registration Authority), and any registered agent's name or number can be checked free on the online list at www.mara.gov.au, Kawsar Khan wrote in August 2026.
FV1-79.target_section: NEW: Fake Australia and Canada work visas
FV1-79.why_new: A check that exists, with where and the cost (free).
FV1-79.h3: NEW: Fake Australia and Canada work visas

FV1-80.claim: According to Kawsar Khan in August 2026, a registered Australian migration agent must charge only a fair and reasonable fee, give the client a written agreement or written information on the cost and scope of the service before starting, and tell the applicant the result of the application as soon as it is received.
FV1-80.target_section: NEW: Fake Australia and Canada work visas
FV1-80.why_new: What a genuine agent is bound to do, so its absence can be spotted.
FV1-80.h3: NEW: Fake Australia and Canada work visas

FV1-81.claim: Kawsar Khan wrote in August 2026 that there is no way to get an Australian work visa directly without a language test or skills assessment, that the Department of Home Affairs alone has authority to grant a visa and no person, employer, organisation or lawyer can guarantee one, and that an Australian employer can apply to sponsor a worker from abroad only when suitable skilled people are not available locally, which is costly and slow.
FV1-81.target_section: NEW: Fake Australia and Canada work visas
FV1-81.why_new: The real rule behind Australian work visas, and that visas are not bought and sold as in the Gulf.
FV1-81.h3: NEW: Fake Australia and Canada work visas

FV1-82.claim: Australian government visa portals carry .gov.au in the address, and fraudsters offer fake visa-verification on .com or .net domains with almost the same name, Kawsar Khan wrote in August 2026.
FV1-82.target_section: Online job adverts, Facebook and WhatsApp scams, and fake government sites
FV1-82.why_new: How to tell the fake verification site from the real one: the domain ending.
FV1-82.h3: Online job adverts, Facebook and WhatsApp scams, and fake government sites

FV1-83.claim: Kawsar Khan listed in August 2026 the promises that mark an Australia fraud: 'recruitment for over a hundred posts with no experience', 'guaranteed permanent citizenship in two months from a work visa' and 'no interview or English skill needed'.
FV1-83.target_section: NEW: Fake Australia and Canada work visas
FV1-83.why_new: The sales phrases used for Australia.
FV1-83.h3: NEW: Fake Australia and Canada work visas

FV1-84.claim: According to Kawsar Khan in August 2026, Australia fraudsters make wholly forged job appointment letters on the letterhead and logo of a well-known Australian organisation and then demand an advance, and use overseas or internet phone numbers to make it seem the call came from Australia.
FV1-84.target_section: NEW: Fake Australia and Canada work visas
FV1-84.why_new: Forged offer letters and spoofed numbers for Australia.
FV1-84.h3: NEW: Fake Australia and Canada work visas

FV1-85.claim: Kawsar Khan's August 2026 checklist: check the agent's registration number before paying anything for a visa; send no large sum to a personal bank or mobile banking number and collect a written receipt for every payment; follow only the government's official immigration website, immi.homeaffairs.gov.au; and on a job offer from an employer, go to that organisation's own website, take the contact details from there and verify the offer.
FV1-85.target_section: NEW: Fake Australia and Canada work visas
FV1-85.why_new: Four concrete checks with the official site named.
FV1-85.h3: NEW: Fake Australia and Canada work visas

FV1-86.claim: Tanvir Ahmed, one of the Bangladeshis living in Australia quoted in an August 2026 Prothom Alo article, said many in Bangladesh think a visa comes for lakhs of taka but a work visa is impossible there without proof of skill and language, and Sharmin Sultana said fraudsters now send fake links that look exactly like government websites.
FV1-86.target_section: NEW: Fake Australia and Canada work visas
FV1-86.why_new: Expatriates' own account of what they see; low priority.
FV1-86.h3: NEW: Fake Australia and Canada work visas

FV1-87.claim: Kawsar Khan wrote on 20 August 2026 that fraud rings usually pick Australian visa categories such as Working Holiday (subclass 417) or eVisitor (subclass 651), whose list of eligible countries does not include Bangladesh: they enter an eligible country in the online application to get a quick digital visa, then use the facility for correcting details to add the applicant's Bangladeshi passport number.
FV1-87.placement: other: new item (A visa that shows online)
FV1-87.why_new: The exact mechanism by which a real Australian government check comes to show a 'granted' visa against a Bangladeshi passport.

FV1-88.claim: As a result, Kawsar Khan wrote, the government's preliminary checking system shows the visa as granted, but in reality it is impossible to travel directly on that visa; people he warns answer 'but the visa is showing online!'.
FV1-88.placement: other: new item (A visa that shows online)
FV1-88.why_new: An online 'granted' result on the official system is not proof.

FV1-89.claim: According to Kawsar Khan in August 2026, Australia fraud rings sometimes use the Maritime Crew (subclass 988) visa, and then send the victim first to a country where Bangladeshis usually need no visa, such as Nepal, the Maldives, Fiji or Indonesia; he wrote that an offer to route a person through another country instead of a direct Dhaka to Australia ticket is a sure sign of danger.
FV1-89.target_section: A flight to a different country first
FV1-89.why_new: Explains why Australia offers are routed through Nepal (the guide has the Jashore-Kathmandu case but not the reason), and names the other transit countries.
FV1-89.h3: A flight to a different country first

FV1-90.claim: Tabarak Khan, a resident of Botany, Sydney, said his nephew fell into an agency's trap: the government checking system showed a visa, but from its type he was sure it was fake; the nephew ignored repeated warnings, and the fraud was caught at the last moment when the ticket to Nepal was being bought.
FV1-90.target_section: A flight to a different country first
FV1-90.why_new: A named relative's account linking the 'visa shows online' trick to a Nepal ticket.
FV1-90.h3: A flight to a different country first

FV1-91.claim: Harun ur Rashid, a businessman in Leppington, Sydney, said a ring made a contract of about BDT 16 lakh with a relative of his to bring him on an agricultural visa with the lure of permanent citizenship in three years, though the relative lacked even the minimum English or occupational qualification for an ordinary work visa; the forgery became clear when the application number and the grant number were matched.
FV1-91.target_section: NEW: Fake Australia and Canada work visas
FV1-91.why_new: A price (about BDT 16 lakh) for an Australia 'agricultural visa', and how it was caught.
FV1-91.h3: NEW: Fake Australia and Canada work visas

FV1-92.claim: Kawsar Khan wrote in August 2026 that the biggest bait of Australia visa fraudsters is 'visa first, money later' (আগে ভিসা, পরে টাকা).
FV1-92.placement: other: "Pay the balance after the visa."
FV1-92.why_new: Confirms from an immigration lawyer that 'pay after the visa' is itself the bait, alongside the section's two cases.

FV1-93.claim: Kawsar Khan wrote in August 2026 that OMARA has taken disciplinary action against more than 61 registered migration advisers since 2021-22, and that in Australia itself several advisers' licences have been cancelled over allegations of lending their licences to unregistered fake brokers.
FV1-93.target_section: NEW: Fake Australia and Canada work visas
FV1-93.why_new: Even a registered adviser's number can be lent to an unregistered broker; action taken in Australia.
FV1-93.h3: NEW: Fake Australia and Canada work visas

FV1-94.claim: Kawsar Khan advised in August 2026 that all Australian immigration business is done on the government's one official portal (homeaffairs.gov.au), that the truth of an offer can be checked by speaking on a government number or through the embassy, that no money should be sent to a personal bank or mobile account, and that the health examination should be done nowhere except at the clinic designated by the Australian High Commission in Dhaka.
FV1-94.target_section: NEW: Fake Australia and Canada work visas
FV1-94.why_new: Adds the medical rule: only the High Commission's designated clinic (compare the fake medical tests in 'Proof that is not proof').
FV1-94.h3: NEW: Fake Australia and Canada work visas

FV1-95.claim: Kawsar Khan wrote in August 2026 that people who are told a document is forged often reply 'I have spent so much already, let me pay a bit more and see what happens', and call again only when stuck at the airport or abroad after losing their savings and homestead.
FV1-95.target_section: NEW: Fake Australia and Canada work visas
FV1-95.why_new: Why victims keep paying after a warning, from a practitioner of 17 years.
FV1-95.h3: NEW: Fake Australia and Canada work visas

FV1-96.claim: Kawsar Khan wrote on 21 September 2026 that some intermediary agencies in Dhaka and other cities used to run flashy campaigns saying 'you can go on a travel visa and become a student' or 'once you get in, you can enrol in some private college, renew the visa and stay', and that the Australian government's new measures closed those routes.
FV1-96.target_section: Student visas used as work routes
FV1-96.why_new: The Australia pitch (visit visa to student visa, cheap college to stay on), not in the section.
FV1-96.h3: Student visas used as work routes

FV1-97.claim: Under the Australian reforms announced by immigration and home affairs minister Tony Burke, as described by Kawsar Khan on 21 September 2026, a mandatory 'No Further Stay' condition is being attached to tourist and visitor visas, so the chance to come on a visit visa and apply onshore for a student or other visa is in effect over.
FV1-97.target_section: Student visas used as work routes
FV1-97.why_new: Australia item: no switching from a visit visa inside the country. Needs the official source and effective date.
FV1-97.h3: Student visas used as work routes

FV1-98.claim: Under the same reforms, Kawsar Khan wrote, 'visa hopping' is being stopped: a student can move only to a higher-level qualification (for example bachelor's to master's) and can no longer enrol in a lower-level vocational or diploma course to keep a visa alive.
FV1-98.target_section: Student visas used as work routes
FV1-98.why_new: Closes the 'enrol in a cheap course to stay' route sold by agencies.
FV1-98.h3: Student visas used as work routes

FV1-99.claim: Under the same reforms, newly arriving international students in Australia can no longer bring a husband, wife or children, the same applies to the graduate visa, and only doctoral (PhD) researchers are exempt; families already in Australia will not be separated, Kawsar Khan wrote.
FV1-99.target_section: Student visas used as work routes
FV1-99.why_new: Bringing a spouse to work and pay the fees was the family plan the article describes; it is closed for new students.
FV1-99.h3: Student visas used as work routes

FV1-100.claim: Kawsar Khan wrote in September 2026 that many Bangladeshi families sell land or break savings to send a child to Australia in the hope that the husband or wife will work there to pay the study costs and that they will somehow become permanent.
FV1-100.target_section: Student visas used as work routes
FV1-100.why_new: The family calculation behind the student route.
FV1-100.h3: Student visas used as work routes

FV1-101.claim: According to Kawsar Khan, the September 2026 reforms include identifying about 77,000 people who stayed on after their visas expired and making them leave quickly, with 100 new border force officers and use of Melbourne's old quarantine centre.
FV1-101.target_section: Student visas used as work routes
FV1-101.why_new: What overstaying in Australia now risks.
FV1-101.h3: Student visas used as work routes

FV1-102.claim: Kawsar Khan advised in September 2026 that people should drop the idea, sold by agents in Dhaka, of 'reaching Australia any way first and seeing later', because the days of passing years on visa changes or drawn-out appeals are over, and that those whose main aim is simply to work or to live with family would do better not to come under the current rules.
FV1-102.target_section: Student visas used as work routes
FV1-102.why_new: A named practitioner's advice against using study as a work route.
FV1-102.h3: Student visas used as work routes

FV1-103.claim: Kawsar Khan wrote in September 2026 that the reforms give construction trade skills the same points as a higher university degree and prioritise shortage sectors such as health care, teaching and farm labour, and that construction engineering, nursing, health care, specialised teaching and technical occupations still need skilled migrants.
FV1-103.target_section: Student visas used as work routes
FV1-103.why_new: Which skills Australia still takes; low priority, needs an official source.
FV1-103.h3: Student visas used as work routes

FV1-104.claim: Kawsar Khan, a registered Australian migration consultant, wrote on 2 October 2026 that there is no direct agricultural visa to Australia for Bangladeshis and that the brokers' trade in one is a fraud from start to finish; social media posts were claiming Australia was giving fast visas to Bangladeshi farm workers and that a visa would come in 10 to 15 days with no experience or English certificate.
FV1-104.target_section: NEW: Fake Australia and Canada work visas
FV1-104.why_new: A current (autumn 2026) scam and a flat statement that the visa does not exist for Bangladeshis.
FV1-104.h3: NEW: Fake Australia and Canada work visas

FV1-105.claim: Kawsar Khan traced the rumour to real news: from July 2026 Australia slowed processing of Working Holiday Maker visas, and on 17 September minister Tony Burke announced that agriculture and fisheries would be added to the priority list for skilled visa processing and that first-year Working Holiday applications would again be processed at normal speed; what Australian media called 'faster visas for farms' became 'agricultural visas for Bangladeshis' in Bangladesh, though the announcement covered only people already eligible and citizens of specified countries.
FV1-105.target_section: NEW: Fake Australia and Canada work visas
FV1-105.why_new: Shows how a real announcement was twisted into the sales pitch.
FV1-105.h3: NEW: Fake Australia and Canada work visas

FV1-106.claim: The main route for foreign farm workers into Australia is the Pacific Australia Labour Mobility scheme (PALM), which is open only to nine Pacific island countries (Fiji, Kiribati, Nauru, Papua New Guinea, Samoa, Solomon Islands, Tonga, Tuvalu and Vanuatu) and Timor-Leste; workers are selected through those countries' government labour-sending offices, and stay up to 9 months for seasonal work or one to four years on long-term contracts, Kawsar Khan wrote in October 2026.
FV1-106.target_section: NEW: Fake Australia and Canada work visas
FV1-106.why_new: The real farm-work scheme and why a Bangladeshi cannot be in it.
FV1-106.h3: NEW: Fake Australia and Canada work visas

FV1-107.claim: Kawsar Khan wrote that the PALM scheme's official website itself says no one has to pay money or give a gift to join and the employer pays the airfare at the start, while people in Dhaka, Chattogram or Khulna were asking lakhs of taka in the name of an 'agricultural visa'.
FV1-107.target_section: NEW: Fake Australia and Canada work visas
FV1-107.why_new: The real scheme is free to the worker; any fee is the flag.
FV1-107.h3: NEW: Fake Australia and Canada work visas

FV1-108.claim: According to Kawsar Khan in October 2026, brokers most often use the name of the Working Holiday visa and say anyone aged eighteen to thirty can apply; the visa goes only to citizens of specified countries, it has two types, subclass 417 and 462, and Bangladesh is in neither; India entered the list in 2024 under a trade agreement, and by lottery.
FV1-108.target_section: NEW: Fake Australia and Canada work visas
FV1-108.why_new: The half-truth brokers use (the age rule) and the fact that undoes it (Bangladesh is not on either list).
FV1-108.h3: NEW: Fake Australia and Canada work visas

FV1-109.claim: Kawsar Khan wrote that the legal routes to Australia for Bangladeshis are the study visa, skilled migration visas and employer-nominated work visas, the employer-sponsored temporary one being the Skills in Demand visa (subclass 482) in force since December 2024; these need an occupation on the approved list, proof of skill, work experience, English, and an employer eligible to sponsor, and there is no easy, direct way to bring people from Bangladesh for ordinary work such as fruit picking or clearing fields.
FV1-109.target_section: NEW: Fake Australia and Canada work visas
FV1-109.why_new: The legitimate routes, stated once, against which offers can be compared.
FV1-109.h3: NEW: Fake Australia and Canada work visas

FV1-110.claim: When an Australian visa is granted the approval letter carries a number that can be matched on the Australian government's checking service VEVO, Kawsar Khan wrote in October 2026, adding that new tricks keep appearing and in some cases more checking is needed even when the visa shows on VEVO.
FV1-110.target_section: NEW: Fake Australia and Canada work visas
FV1-110.why_new: The official check (VEVO) and its limit, which ties to the 'visa shows online' trick.
FV1-110.h3: NEW: Fake Australia and Canada work visas

FV1-111.claim: Kawsar Khan wrote that the conversation should end if someone cannot show a registered migration professional's number, cannot state the visa subclass and details, or talks of a 'visa in ten days'.
FV1-111.target_section: NEW: Fake Australia and Canada work visas
FV1-111.why_new: Three questions to put to anyone selling an Australian visa.
FV1-111.h3: NEW: Fake Australia and Canada work visas

FV1-112.claim: In the same 17 September 2026 speech, according to Kawsar Khan, the minister said second-year Working Holiday visas would now go by lottery with 45,000 places against about 57,000 who qualified the year before, and third-year places would be only 5,000 against about 31,000; the National Farmers' Federation says these visa holders do one in seven farm jobs.
FV1-112.target_section: NEW: Fake Australia and Canada work visas
FV1-112.why_new: Shows Australia is tightening, not opening; low priority, needs an official source.
FV1-112.h3: NEW: Fake Australia and Canada work visas

FV1-113.claim: Kawsar Khan wrote in October 2026 that BMET (the Bureau of Manpower, Employment and Training) and the Bangladesh High Commission in Canberra should issue regular, plainly worded warnings about the 'agricultural visa' fraud.
FV1-113.target_section: NEW: Fake Australia and Canada work visas
FV1-113.placement: other: what authorities have not done
FV1-113.why_new: A gap: no Bangladeshi official warning is reported.
FV1-113.h3: NEW: Fake Australia and Canada work visas

FV1-114.claim: On Friday 9 October 2026 the Special Response Battalion (SRB-4) arrested 12 members of a ring at Technical Mor, Dhaka, accused of taking money on promises of jobs abroad, working visas and a guaranteed pass in the written test; a mobile court then sentenced seven of them to between seven days and three months in jail and fined five.
FV1-114.why_new: Possibly the same raid as the section's '9 Oct 2026, 20 arrested in Shyamoli' case from another source: this report gives 12 arrested at Technical Mor, the unit (SRB-4) and the sentences; reconcile before adding.

FV1-115.claim: SRB said the ring arrested on 9 October 2026 guaranteed people wanting to go abroad a worker visa at low cost and a pass in the written test, took between BDT 40,000 and BDT 10 lakh from candidates depending on the case, and then kept the money on various excuses.
FV1-115.why_new: The price range (BDT 40,000 to 10 lakh) for a 'guaranteed pass'.

FV1-116.claim: According to the SRB press conference of 9 October 2026, BOESL's test is held every Friday and Saturday at the venue of the Bangladesh-Korea Technical Training Centre (BKTTC), and the broker ring worked mainly by targeting the candidates who gathered there for the test.
FV1-116.why_new: Where and when the brokers find their targets: outside the exam venue on exam days.

FV1-117.claim: The SRB press conference said BOESL, under the Ministry of Expatriates' Welfare and Overseas Employment, recruits workers for abroad on the government's behalf, takes no fee from candidates in the recruitment process, and that a person with only a passport can get overseas work through the test at no cost.
FV1-117.why_new: As stated by SRB; compare with the guide's wording that BOESL takes a fee only after final selection by pay order.

FV1-118.claim: SRB-4's commander, Lieutenant Colonel Hafizur Rahman, said BKTTC is a training centre teaching 24 trades in courses of various lengths, that its certificates help in getting a job abroad, but that it does not send workers or arrange jobs, so taking training and getting a job are not the same thing.
FV1-118.why_new: A training centre's name is used to sell jobs; the centre sends no one.

FV1-119.claim: The 9 October 2026 action began with complaints from BKTTC and BOESL, after which SRB ran a shadow investigation and raided with an executive magistrate present; SRB asked anyone cheated in this way to inform the authorities quickly and to verify information through government offices and approved agencies.
FV1-119.why_new: How the enforcement was triggered (the institutions themselves complained) and the mobile-court route.

FV1-120.claim: The UAE Ministry of Human Resources and Emiratisation (MOHRE) named five signs of a fake job offer, Gulf News reported (Prothom Alo, 22 November 2026): being asked to open a new bank account in your own name as part of recruitment; being asked for confidential bank account details by an unverified person or company; a demand for money to confirm the job or complete recruitment; being asked to receive money into your account or transfer it on to another account; and insistence on contact only through WhatsApp or another messaging app with no institutional phone number or address.
FV1-120.target_section: Fake visa, demand letter or job offer
FV1-120.why_new: Five official red flags from the UAE ministry; the section's UAE content covers only the offer check.
FV1-120.h3: Fake visa, demand letter or job offer

FV1-121.claim: MOHRE says every valid job offer issued through its system carries a specific serial number and a barcode, and a job seeker can verify an offer on the ministry's official website, in the 'MOHRE UAE' mobile app or by calling 600590000 (Prothom Alo, 22 November 2026, citing the ministry).
FV1-121.target_section: Fake visa, demand letter or job offer
FV1-121.why_new: Adds what a real UAE offer looks like (serial number, barcode) and two more ways to check (app, phone 600590000) beyond inquiry.mohre.gov.ae.
FV1-121.h3: Fake visa, demand letter or job offer

FV1-122.claim: MOHRE said that anyone meeting these conditions after a job offer should stop the process at once and verify, and should give no money or personal information until the offer letter is confirmed genuine.
FV1-122.target_section: Fake visa, demand letter or job offer
FV1-122.why_new: The ministry's instruction on what to do when a flag appears.
FV1-122.h3: Fake visa, demand letter or job offer

FV1-123.claim: Two of the five signs of a fake UAE job offer named by MOHRE in November 2026 are being told to open a new bank account in your own name as part of recruitment, and being asked to receive money into your bank account or move it from there to another account.
FV1-123.why_new: Bears on the section's open question about job seekers' accounts being used to move other people's money: an official warning that fake job offers ask for exactly this.

FV1-124.claim: MOHRE's labour market observatory said more than 26 lakh people contacted the ministry through its channels for services and verification in the third quarter of 2026 (July to September); according to BMET, more than 70 per cent of workers who leave Bangladesh each year go to Middle Eastern countries.
FV1-124.target_section: Fake visa, demand letter or job offer
FV1-124.why_new: Scale of use of the UAE verification channels; low priority.
FV1-124.h3: Fake visa, demand letter or job offer

RU1-1.claim: The Ministry of Expatriates' Welfare said in a notice reported on 6 February 2025 that, because a tourist or visit visa gives no legal scope to work, the people sent on one suffer financial and mental harm and are put at risk, and that deaths are occurring on illegal routes to various countries.
RU1-1.target_section: Visit and tourist visas sold as jobs
RU1-1.why_new: The guide cites this notice for the list of countries and the two rules; it does not give the Ministry's stated consequences (no legal scope to work, harm, deaths).
RU1-1.h3: Visit and tourist visas sold as jobs

RU1-2.claim: The same February 2025 notice of the Ministry of Expatriates' Welfare also told people to confirm with BMET (the Bureau of Manpower, Employment and Training) that the job and the recruiting agency are genuine, and not to go abroad for work through any person or organisation other than a valid recruiting agency.
RU1-2.target_section: Visit and tourist visas sold as jobs
RU1-2.why_new: The guide gives items 1 and 2 of the notice (no tourist/visit visa, no travel without BMET clearance) but not items 3 and 4.
RU1-2.h3: Visit and tourist visas sold as jobs

RU1-3.claim: The Ministry of Expatriates' Welfare's February 2025 notice stated that under the existing memorandum of understanding between Bangladesh and Malaysia there is no scope for women workers to be employed in Malaysia.
RU1-3.target_section: Trafficking disguised as a job, especially for women
RU1-3.why_new: A ministry statement that any Malaysia job offer to a woman worker falls outside the agreement; not found in the scam or illegal-routes chapters.
RU1-3.h3: Trafficking disguised as a job, especially for women

RU1-4.claim: The Ministry of Expatriates' Welfare's February 2025 notice said that, to avoid being cheated by fake overseas job adverts circulated on social media such as Facebook and YouTube, the recruiting agency's or employer's information can be verified from BMET's website or the Probashbandhu call centre.
RU1-4.target_section: Online job adverts, Facebook and WhatsApp scams, and fake government sites
RU1-4.why_new: Names the two official channels the Ministry itself points to for checking an online job advert; the section's check points only to the fake-visa section.
RU1-4.h3: Online job adverts, Facebook and WhatsApp scams, and fake government sites

RU1-5.claim: According to his family, Jafar Sardar (35) of Bara Meghla village, Jashore Sadar, left home on 17 August 2024 bound for Cyprus through a Dhaka agency named 'Dream Home Travels', which had submitted his papers to the Cyprus embassy; when no visa came in two years it took him to Saudi Arabia with talk of a job in Russia, and two months later he was taken to Russia through Dubai, Libya or Turkey.
RU1-5.target_section: A flight to a different country first
RU1-5.why_new: A second, named member of the group of 10 the guide describes through Akram Hossain, with the agency's name, the Cyprus embassy filing and the switch of destination from Cyprus to Russia.
RU1-5.h3: A flight to a different country first

RU1-6.claim: Jafar Sardar's family said they paid Dream Home Travels BDT 8 lakh in all, raised from a BDT 4 lakh NGO loan, the sale of his mother's and wife's jewellery and money borrowed at interest.
RU1-6.target_section: A flight to a different country first
RU1-6.why_new: What this family paid, to whom, and how it was financed.
RU1-6.h3: A flight to a different country first

RU1-7.claim: According to the family of Jafar Sardar of Jashore, reported on 17 February 2025, the broker took 10 Bangladeshis to Russia together; one, a young man from Narsingdi named Akram, escaped and came home, and the other nine were forced to the battlefield in Ukraine to fight for Russia, where one was killed and one was shot.
RU1-7.why_new: The outcome for the whole group of 10 sent in 2024 (one escaped, nine sent to the front, one dead, one shot); the guide's Russia section covers only the May 2026 group in detail.

RU1-8.claim: Jafar Sardar's wife, Khadija Akter, told Prothom Alo in February 2025 that the broker ring forcibly took her husband to the Russian battlefield, that he was kept in a barracks, given an army haircut and war training, and that his last message said 'bring me home at any cost'.
RU1-8.why_new: A family account of what happens between arrival and deployment.

RU1-9.claim: Relatives of nine Bangladeshis sent to the Ukraine battlefield formed human chains in Dhaka several times, went more than once to the Russian embassy and to Bangladesh's Foreign Ministry and wrote to the Expatriates' Welfare Ministry, and on 16 February 2025 Jafar Sardar's family wrote to the Chief Adviser's office asking for his return and the money; the report of 17 February 2025 records no result.
RU1-9.why_new: Shows which doors families actually tried in early 2025 and that the article reports no outcome.

RU1-10.claim: The wife of Bazlur Rahman Sardar (30) of Jashore said in February 2025 that he returned to Malaysia two months earlier after an earlier two-year stay, that police there detained more than a hundred people together while he was at work, and that because nobody appeared on behalf of the recruiting agency he had gone through, a red seal was put in his passport and he was to be sent home within about a week; Prothom Alo reported he had been in a Malaysian jail for a month and a half after a fault was found in his papers.
RU1-10.target_section: When the visa, the agency and the clearance are all real
RU1-10.why_new: A worker sent through a recruiting agency who was detained at work in Malaysia and deported because the agency did not show up for him.
RU1-10.h3: When the visa, the agency and the clearance are all real

RU1-11.claim: A report by BRAC's Migration Programme, 'Promises Written in Blood: How Legal Migration Turned into Forced Recruitment in the Russia-Ukraine War', published on the Monday before 5 November 2025 and based on survivors' accounts, family testimony and document checks, says brokers lured workers with false promises of high-paid work, that many went hoping for work in oil, construction or logistics, and that after arrival in Russia their passports were confiscated and they were forced to join the military.
RU1-11.why_new: Adds the BRAC report by name, its evidence base, and the oil and logistics job pitches (the guide has construction and welding).

RU1-12.claim: BRAC's November 2025 report says the Bangladeshis spent BDT 7 to 8 lakh to go to Russia for work, and that international facilitators as well as local brokers are involved in trapping them.
RU1-12.why_new: A 2025 price point (BDT 7 to 8 lakh) below the BDT 9.5 to 10 lakh the guide gives for 2026, and BRAC's finding of international facilitators.

RU1-13.claim: Shariful Hasan, BRAC's associate director (migration and youth), told Prothom Alo in November 2025 that 10 families had so far asked BRAC to bring relatives back from Russia and that these men had gone to Russia on valid visas to work; BRAC's report says there are more such Bangladeshis but the number could not be confirmed.
RU1-13.why_new: BRAC's own caseload as of November 2025 and its statement that the true number is unknown.

RU1-14.claim: According to Prothom Alo in November 2025, BRAC's Migration Programme began receiving many applications from families from late 2024 with almost the same account, submitted applications to the Foreign Ministry for the victims' rescue, gave case documents to the police's Criminal Investigation Department (CID), and gives the families legal and psychological support.
RU1-14.why_new: Says concretely what BRAC does with a family's application (Foreign Ministry rescue application, case papers to CID, legal and psychosocial support); the guide only says BRAC asked the government to trace the men.

RU1-15.claim: Shariful Hasan of BRAC said in November 2025 that a Bangladeshi using the name MD Sohel was campaigning on Facebook about the benefits available for joining the Russian army and fighting, and that because of this many people were being newly lured to go to Russia to fight.
RU1-15.why_new: A recruitment channel the section lacks: open Facebook promotion of army service by a Bangladeshi.

RU1-16.claim: BRAC's November 2025 report records that Ayon Mondal of Bagerhat, who went to Russia on a valid visa, said in his last message that he was being taken towards the Ukrainian border and has not been traced since, and that Amit Barua of Cumilla has been missing since a photo showed him in Russian military uniform.
RU1-16.why_new: Two named missing men from 2025 who went on valid visas.

RU1-17.claim: Ali Hossain of Mymensingh told Prothom Alo in November 2025 that his son Afzal Hossain Meraj, who went to Russia on 10 August 2024 through the travel agency Friendship and Co-operative Recruitment, worked four months at the company he was recruited for, was then laid off, and then went to fight through a ring; he was wounded in a mine blast and spent 25 days in hospital.
RU1-17.target_section: Recruited while abroad or just back
RU1-17.placement: other: In Russia, after the job ends
RU1-17.why_new: Another dated, named case of the lay-off-then-army pattern, with the agency named and the four-month gap.
RU1-17.h3: Recruited while abroad or just back

RU1-18.claim: Ali Hossain applied to the Foreign Ministry on 22 April 2025 to bring his son Afzal Hossain Meraj home, alleging in the letter that his son had been sold to the Russian army, and told Prothom Alo in November 2025 that his son had been able to return two months earlier with the help of the Bangladesh Embassy in Moscow.
RU1-18.why_new: A second documented return through the Moscow embassy, with the route the family used (a written application to the Foreign Ministry) and the time it took (about five months).

RU1-19.claim: Tasneem Siddiqui, executive director of RMMRU (the Refugee and Migratory Movements Research Unit), told Prothom Alo in November 2025 that besides people going to Russia directly for work, many are first taken to Saudi Arabia on tourist or Umrah visas and are later made to sign a contract and forced to go to the battlefield.
RU1-19.why_new: Names Saudi Arabia on a tourist or Umrah visa as a first leg; the guide's path lists Dubai and unnamed third countries.

RU1-20.claim: An AFP report of 12 April 2025, as cited by Prothom Alo, quoted the Bangladesh Embassy in Moscow as saying about a dozen families had contacted it to get their sons back, all alleging the sons were deceived into the Russian army, and reported that Mohammad Yasin Sheikh, 22, was killed on 27 March 2025 while fighting for Russian forces.
RU1-20.why_new: The embassy's own caseload in April 2025 and a named, dated death earlier than any in the guide.

RU1-21.claim: Foreign Ministry spokesperson Mohammad Rafiqul Alam said at a Dhaka briefing on 9 February 2025 that some Bangladeshis had been forced into the Russia-Ukraine war after falling into the hands of human traffickers, that the Ministry had asked the Embassy in Moscow for details, that the relevant ministries had been asked to act against the recruiting and travel agencies involved, and that one member of a ring trafficking people to Russia had been arrested.
RU1-21.why_new: The government's first public acknowledgement and first arrest, in February 2025; the guide's law entries start in June 2026.

RU1-22.claim: According to the Foreign Ministry spokesperson's 9 February 2025 briefing, the authorities concerned were asked to take special caution at Bangladesh's international airports over Bangladeshis going to Russia on travel visas during the war and those with a valid Russian travel visa in their passports.
RU1-22.why_new: An airport-side measure: a passenger for Russia on a travel visa can expect extra scrutiny at departure since February 2025.

RU1-23.claim: Prothom Alo reported in November 2025 that RMMRU (the Refugee and Migratory Movements Research Unit) had prepared a report from interviews with victims about a month and a half earlier and given it to the adviser for the Information Ministry with a call to raise awareness.
RU1-23.why_new: Existence of a second victim-interview report (RMMRU, about September 2025) besides BRAC's.

RU1-24.claim: A Prothom Alo editorial of 4 February 2026, citing an Associated Press (AP) investigation, says people from disadvantaged areas were taken to Russia with the lure of work as cooks or cleaners and, after arriving, were forced to sign military contracts written in Russian.
RU1-24.why_new: Adds cook and cleaner as job pitches, from the AP investigation.

RU1-25.claim: According to the AP investigation as summarised in a Prothom Alo editorial of 4 February 2026, a Russian commander told one victim directly that he had in fact been 'sold'; returned workers said they were made to collect bodies from the battlefield and move the wounded, and those who refused were tortured.
RU1-25.why_new: Tasks the men were put to (body collection, evacuating the wounded) and the 'sold' statement.

RU1-26.claim: A Prothom Alo editorial of 4 February 2026 said it was believed that at least 40 Bangladeshis had lost their lives in the previous few months after being deceived by recruiting agencies into the Russia-Ukraine war.
RU1-26.why_new: A February 2026 death estimate, earlier than the guide's figures (34 by March 2026 from Fortify Rights, 20 of the May group).

RU1-27.claim: A Prothom Alo editorial of 4 February 2026 said, citing the investigation, that a Bangladeshi living in Moscow is the main organiser of the trafficking ring, that investigators suspect the ring has links with the Russian government, and named 'SP Global' as one of the firms that ran such trafficking openly.
RU1-27.why_new: Who is said to run the chain (a Moscow-based Bangladeshi) and one firm named.

RU1-28.claim: Jahangir Alam of Lakshmipur, who was sent to Russia in 2025 on the promise of work as a cook in a cantonment and was instead sent straight to the battlefield, told Prothom Alo in July 2026 that he was handed a weapon without training and then taught to use it for one day, that 16 men were together in the war camp, and that he lived in fear after four of them died.
RU1-28.why_new: A named survivor with the job pitch 'cook in a cantonment', one day of weapons training and 4 deaths among 16.

RU1-29.claim: Jahangir Alam of Lakshmipur escaped from the battlefield and came home through the Bangladesh embassy seven months after going, according to Prothom Alo in July 2026.
RU1-29.why_new: Another return through the embassy after an escape; the guide has one (August 2026).

RU1-30.claim: RMMRU says 4,727 Bangladeshis went to Russia in 2025 against 993 the year before, and that 2,125 workers took clearance for Russia in the first six months of 2026, Prothom Alo reported on 30 July 2026.
RU1-30.why_new: Year-by-year figures; the guide gives only one combined total (7,449 from January 2025 to 27 October 2026). Note the 2024 figure here (993) differs from the BMET figure in the 21 October 2026 article (1,395).

RU1-31.claim: Expatriates' Welfare Minister Ariful Haque Chowdhury told Prothom Alo in July 2026 that the licences of three agencies that sent workers to Russia had been cancelled, that the licences of 49 agencies linked to irregularities in sending workers to Malaysia had been withdrawn, and that BMET had been told to be more careful before giving clearance for Cambodia.
RU1-31.why_new: The Minister's own statement of the three actions together; the 49 Malaysia licences are not in the scam chapter.

RU1-32.claim: According to the Home Ministry's human trafficking report, 1,126 new cases were filed under the trafficking law in 2025, and 5,284 cases including older ones were pending up to May 2026, of which 3,306 were under trial and 1,978 still under investigation.
RU1-32.why_new: The backlog a new trafficking case joins; the guide has only the CID unit's own caseload.
RU1-32.h3: Where to complain and get help

RU1-33.claim: Prothom Alo reported on 30 July 2026 that 71 new trafficking cases were filed in January 2026, 66 in February, 110 in March, 130 in April and 123 in May, and that only 17 cases were disposed of in that period.
RU1-33.why_new: Monthly filings against disposals in 2026: 500 filed, 17 disposed.
RU1-33.h3: Where to complain and get help

RU1-34.claim: Home Ministry data show that in 4,427 cases under the Prevention and Suppression of Human Trafficking Act over the five years 2020 to 2024, 94 to 95% of the accused were acquitted.
RU1-34.why_new: The acquittal rate; the guide says nothing on how trafficking cases end.
RU1-34.h3: Where to complain and get help

RU1-35.claim: UNHCR (the UN refugee agency) data show that Bangladeshis were again in 2026 the top nationality among people crossing the Mediterranean to Italy, and for the first time the top nationality among sea crossings to Greece, Prothom Alo reported on 30 July 2026.
RU1-35.why_new: Bangladesh first on the Greece sea route for the first time; the guide's numbers cover Italy only.

RU1-36.claim: BRAC, citing Frontex (the EU border agency), said 20,259 Bangladeshis entered Europe across the Mediterranean in 2025, and that in the first six months of 2026, 4,249 Bangladeshis entered Italy this way and 3,608 went from Libya to Greece by sea.
RU1-36.why_new: First-half 2026 figures and the Libya-to-Greece count (3,608), which the guide lacks.

RU1-37.claim: People in the migration sector told Prothom Alo in July 2026 that workers bound for Italy or Greece are sent to Libya, tortured in many camps there, and held hostage until BDT 25 to 30 lakh is extracted.
RU1-37.why_new: Raises the reported ransom range to BDT 30 lakh (the guide has BDT 25 lakh) and names Greece as a destination sold through Libya.

RU1-38.claim: Of the at least 18 Bangladeshis who died in March 2026 on the way from Libya to Greece, 12 were from Sunamganj.
RU1-38.why_new: The home district of 12 of the 18 dead; the guide has the incident but not where the men came from.

RU1-39.claim: BRAC says that, of the people who returned from Cambodia, 88% said they had no freedom of movement, 86% had their passports and papers taken, 27% suffered severe physical torture and 38% mental torture, Prothom Alo reported on 30 July 2026.
RU1-39.target_section: Cambodia, Myanmar and Laos: scam compounds
RU1-39.why_new: Four more findings of the BRAC returnee study; the guide cites only the 98% and 90% figures.
RU1-39.h3: Cambodia, Myanmar and Laos: scam compounds

RU1-40.claim: Prothom Alo reported on 30 July 2026 that Cambodia's law enforcement had recently shut the scam centres under international pressure, after which 583 workers returned in June alone.
RU1-40.target_section: Cambodia, Myanmar and Laos: scam compounds
RU1-40.why_new: Why the June 2026 returns happened (a Cambodian crackdown under international pressure).
RU1-40.h3: Cambodia, Myanmar and Laos: scam compounds

RU1-41.claim: Shariful Hasan, associate director of BRAC, said in July 2026 that trafficking used to be done by force but is now done mainly in the name of migration, with people lured through job advertisements, and that traffickers do not get exemplary punishment.
RU1-41.target_section: Trafficking disguised as a job, especially for women
RU1-41.why_new: A named expert's description of the shift from forced trafficking to trafficking through migration offers.
RU1-41.h3: Trafficking disguised as a job, especially for women

RU1-42.claim: Prothom Alo reported in July 2026 that cheated workers returning from various countries are filing human trafficking cases, and that in some cases the families of migrants killed abroad file them.
RU1-42.why_new: That families of the dead, not only returnees, file trafficking cases.
RU1-42.h3: Where to complain and get help

RU1-43.claim: Jahangir Alam of Lakshmipur told Prothom Alo in September 2026 that after four men in his war camp died he fell ill and spent two months in hospital, escaped from there, and returned home through the Bangladesh embassy.
RU1-43.why_new: How this survivor got out: escape from hospital, then the embassy.

RU1-44.claim: According to BMET, 4,727 Bangladeshis went to the Russian Federation in 2025, which put Russia 13th among Bangladesh's overseas labour markets that year, ahead of Malaysia, South Korea and Lebanon.

RU1-45.claim: According to BMET, 12,263 Bangladeshis took clearance for Cambodia in 2025, making it the eighth-largest destination for Bangladeshi workers that year.
RU1-45.target_section: Cambodia, Myanmar and Laos: scam compounds
RU1-45.why_new: The 2025 calendar-year figure and Cambodia's rank; the guide has an 18-month total.
RU1-45.h3: Cambodia, Myanmar and Laos: scam compounds

RU1-46.claim: Prothom Alo reported on 5 September 2026 that after Cambodian law enforcement raided and shut scam centres, 646 Bangladeshi workers came back in June alone, with more returning daily.
RU1-46.target_section: Cambodia, Myanmar and Laos: scam compounds
RU1-46.why_new: A different June 2026 return count (646) from the 583 in the guide and in the 30 July 2026 article; the conflict needs resolving.
RU1-46.h3: Cambodia, Myanmar and Laos: scam compounds

RU1-47.claim: People in the sector told Prothom Alo in September 2026 that Cambodia's economy is no better than Bangladesh's and has few jobs, yet workers are sent there for the scam centres.
RU1-47.target_section: Cambodia, Myanmar and Laos: scam compounds
RU1-47.why_new: The sector's own explanation of why a Cambodia job offer is implausible.
RU1-47.h3: Cambodia, Myanmar and Laos: scam compounds

RU1-48.claim: Prothom Alo reported on 5 September 2026 that 66,316 people of all nationalities crossed the Mediterranean to Italy in 2025 and 1,126 of them died or went missing at sea, and that of 14,194 who crossed up to June 2026 the largest share, 32% or 3,691 people, were Bangladeshis.
RU1-48.why_new: Half-year 2026 arrivals with the Bangladeshi share (32%); the article names no source for these figures.

RU1-49.claim: Prothom Alo reported on 5 September 2026 that only 100 people took clearance to go to Libya in 2025 and 63 in 2026, which it reads as meaning the workers reach Libya through the Middle East and other countries.
RU1-49.why_new: Shows almost nobody on the Libya route leaves with clearance for Libya.

RU1-50.claim: Mashiur Rahman of Madaripur, who came home on 1 September 2026 with a group of Bangladeshis returned from detention in Libya with IOM's help, said he had left his own restaurant business to try for Italy and came back having lost BDT 32 lakh.
RU1-50.why_new: A named returnee with the total lost (BDT 32 lakh) and what he gave up.

RU1-51.claim: Airport sources told Prothom Alo that 15,245 people returned to Bangladesh on travel passes in the first three months of 2026 and 8,215 in April alone; the paper says these are workers who lost everything, have no passport and return on a travel pass after being detained by police.
RU1-51.why_new: 2026 counts of outpass returns; the guide has no current figure.

RU1-52.claim: The CID's Trafficking in Human Being (THB) unit counts 1,657 people charged in 536 cases from 2018 to 2025, of whom only 353 could be arrested.
RU1-52.why_new: Arrest rate in CID trafficking cases (353 of 1,657 accused).
RU1-52.h3: Where to complain and get help

RU1-53.claim: Ali Haider Chowdhury, former secretary general of BAIRA (the recruiting agencies' association), claimed in September 2026 that 70% of workers going to Saudi Arabia go for a short term and that many find no work after arriving; Prothom Alo added that there are complaints of workers not getting work according to their contracts in Saudi Arabia and that there is not work there at the rate workers are going.
RU1-53.target_section: When the visa, the agency and the clearance are all real
RU1-53.why_new: An industry insider on Saudi Arabia, the one market still growing: real visas without work behind them.
RU1-53.h3: When the visa, the agency and the clearance are all real

RU1-54.claim: Migration expert Asif Munir told Prothom Alo in September 2026 that indifference to sending workers by the rules has not stopped, that responsibility for approving clearance lies with the government, and asked why workers are sent to countries whose appointment letters cannot be verified and how clearance is given for countries like Russia and Cambodia.
RU1-54.target_section: When the visa, the agency and the clearance are all real
RU1-54.placement: other: why clearance is no guarantee
RU1-54.why_new: A named expert stating that appointment letters for Russia and Cambodia cannot be verified, yet clearance was given.
RU1-54.h3: When the visa, the agency and the clearance are all real

RU1-55.claim: RMMRU says India has 192 recruiting agencies, Pakistan 464, Nepal 416 and Sri Lanka 248, while Bangladesh, which once had 850 to 900, was taken to nearly 2,400 under the last Awami League government; the interim government approved 252 new licences in 2025 and 2,646 agencies in all have taken licences, Prothom Alo reported on 5 September 2026.
RU1-55.why_new: The number of licensed agencies against neighbours'; RMMRU's point is that fewer agencies are easier to monitor.

RU1-56.claim: In July 2026 the BNP government withdrew the licences of 49 recruiting agencies after a charge sheet was filed in court in a case over corruption and irregularities in sending workers to Malaysia.
RU1-56.target_section: When the visa, the agency and the clearance are all real
RU1-56.why_new: The licence action that followed the Malaysia syndicate case, with its trigger (the charge sheet).
RU1-56.h3: When the visa, the agency and the clearance are all real

RU1-57.claim: Prothom Alo reported on 5 September 2026 that Malaysia's labour market closed in June 2024 over irregularities, Oman's has been effectively closed since 2024, and workers going to the UAE fell from about 1 lakh in 2023 to 47,000 in 2024 and 13,750 in 2025; analysts told the paper that the closure or shrinking of these markets is a major reason workers have become interested in risky countries.
RU1-57.why_new: UAE year-by-year figures and the stated link between closed markets and the risky new ones.

RU1-58.claim: BMET says about 5 lakh workers took clearance to go abroad in January to August 2026 against about 7 lakh 40 thousand in the same period of 2025; Prothom Alo reported that about 6.25 lakh Bangladeshis went to Saudi Arabia for work in 2024, over 7 lakh 55 thousand in 2025 and about 2 lakh 15 thousand in the first six months of 2026, and recruiting agencies say the rise may not continue from next year.
RU1-58.why_new: Overall and Saudi clearances falling in 2026.

RU1-59.claim: Of the 30 Bangladeshis who flew from Dhaka to Russia on 7 May 2026, Prothom Alo reported that after 21 days of training they were split into groups of 16, 8 and 6 and sent to the war, and that many died around 12 and 13 June; two who were hospitalised, Adnan Hossain of Narayanganj and Rajon Hossain of Jhenaidah, later escaped and came home and gave the paper the information about the others' deaths.
RU1-59.why_new: The timeline of the May 2026 group (21 days' training, three groups, deaths around 12-13 June) and the two named survivors who are the source.

RU1-60.claim: Prothom Alo reported that Rajon Hossain (21) of Jhenaidah, who went to Russia with the group of 30 on 7 May 2026, paid a broker BDT 10 lakh for a high-paid job, got no job, and after four days in a hotel was sent to an army camp after his signature was taken on a paper; he told the paper that after 21 days' training he was sent to the front line with five other Bangladeshis, that four were killed in a drone attack, and that he was wounded, admitted to hospital and escaped from there to come home.
RU1-60.why_new: The survivor's own sequence and the fate of his six-man group (four dead); the guide has his account of the contract but not what followed.

RU1-61.claim: Prothom Alo reported that Adnan Hossain of Narayanganj was admitted to a Moscow hospital with a splinter in his abdomen from the battlefield, had three operations, could not get out of bed for a month and a half, and after two months in hospital escaped and went to the embassy, then came home on 15 September 2026 on a travel pass (a valid travel permit).
RU1-61.why_new: The practical way out that worked: reach the embassy in person from hospital and leave on a travel pass.

RU1-62.claim: Adnan Hossain said Russia does not publish information on Bangladeshis' deaths in the war and does not bring back the bodies, and that anyone who does not return from the front line is declared missing; Prothom Alo reported that those it spoke to said the bodies of foreigners killed are not recovered but left on the field.
RU1-62.why_new: Explains why families get neither a body nor a death record: the dead are recorded as missing.

RU1-63.claim: Abdul Majid of Lalmonirhat told Prothom Alo that his son Abdullah Al Mamun phoned his younger brother the day before being sent to fight after training, that there was no contact afterwards, and that a man who went with him, Al Amin, later said Mamun had died; a funeral in absentia was arranged in the village, but because the death was not confirmed the people who came prayed instead of performing the funeral prayer, and five months had passed by October 2026.
RU1-63.why_new: How a family learns of a death (from a fellow recruit) and is left without confirmation.

RU1-64.claim: Prothom Alo reported on 21 October 2026 that it had received news of at least 54 deaths of Bangladeshis in the Russia-Ukraine war over the previous three years.
RU1-64.why_new: The newspaper's own running count (54 in three years), higher than the 34 the guide cites from Fortify Rights.

RU1-65.claim: According to a letter the labour wing of the Bangladesh Embassy in Russia sent to the Expatriates' Welfare Ministry on 25 May 2026, the recruiting agency Jabale Noor sought permission on 5 May to send 70 workers and the embassy did not attest it, and RS International was at first told it could bring 10 workers but that was suspended when suspicion arose.
RU1-65.target_section: When the visa, the agency and the clearance are all real
RU1-65.why_new: The embassy had refused attestation to both agencies before the 30 flew; the guide says only that the three firms sent them.
RU1-65.h3: When the visa, the agency and the clearance are all real
