RU1-66.claim: The embassy's 25 May 2026 letter says that the two agencies, unable to get attestation, sent the workers in the name of TS Overseas, and asks the Ministry to check how workers were sent without the embassy's permission.
RU1-66.target_section: When the visa, the agency and the clearance are all real
RU1-66.why_new: The mechanism: a refused agency uses a third agency's name to get the workers out with clearance.
RU1-66.h3: When the visa, the agency and the clearance are all real

RU1-67.claim: According to the embassy's 25 May 2026 letter, on 18 May a worker's family phoned the Bangladesh Embassy in Russia to say that 30 people had come through Jabale Noor and RS International and were being sent to the battlefield, and the embassy was sending a letter to Russia's Foreign Ministry asking that the workers be returned to work under their appointment letters instead of being sent to war.
RU1-67.why_new: A family's phone call on 18 May is what alerted the embassy, 11 days after arrival and before deployment; the embassy's response was a letter to the Russian Foreign Ministry.

RU1-68.claim: Foreign Ministry sources told Prothom Alo in October 2026 that for four to five months the Russian government had been informing the embassy about Bangladeshis missing and killed on the battlefield, 40 people so far, without separating the dead from the missing, and had not yet said anything about the latest 20 deaths.
RU1-68.why_new: The only official Russian-side figure: 40 dead or missing notified to the embassy.

RU1-69.claim: Foreign Ministry sources told Prothom Alo in October 2026 that compensation can be claimed if someone dies in the war or is missing for more than six months, but that getting it from Russia means a complicated process that includes establishing who the heir is and the heir going to Russia and staying at least six months, and that the bodies cannot be recovered.
RU1-69.why_new: The compensation rule and why families cannot use it; the guide has nothing on compensation from Russia.

RU1-70.claim: Bangladesh's ambassador to Russia, Md Nazrul Islam, told Prothom Alo in October 2026 that more than 90% of the workers go to the war of their own accord, that Russia has said the latest 30 also went voluntarily and holds written proof of it, and that the bodies cannot be sent home because the Russian authorities are not handing them over.
RU1-70.why_new: The embassy's and Russia's position: the signed contract is treated as written proof of volunteering.

RU1-71.claim: Two wounded returnees and six families told Prothom Alo that the workers pleaded with their families before being sent to war in June 2026, that when the families contacted the agency it promised to take responsibility, and that from the first week of June the men began to go missing; the families got news of deaths but no proof.
RU1-71.why_new: What the agency told families when they called before deployment: a promise to take responsibility, and nothing after.

RU1-72.claim: The Wage Earners' Welfare Board says it bears the cost of bringing home the body of a worker who went with BMET clearance or took membership registration from the embassy after going abroad, on the family's application, and that a family with neither can still apply, in which case the Board sends a proposal to the Expatriates' Welfare Ministry, which pays from a yearly budget allocation.
RU1-72.placement: other: bodies and compensation in Bangladesh
RU1-72.why_new: The body-repatriation rule stated for this context, including the route for a worker with no clearance or membership.

RU1-73.claim: According to the Wage Earners' Welfare Board, it gives BDT 35,000 cash for the burial of each body brought home and then a BDT 3 lakh grant, but by October 2026 no application to bring a body home from Russia had reached it, because with no proof of death nobody can apply, and so nobody is getting any compensation.
RU1-73.placement: other: bodies and compensation in Bangladesh
RU1-73.why_new: Why families of the Russia dead get none of the Welfare Board's death benefits: every benefit starts from proof of death.

RU1-74.claim: The Special Response Battalion (SRB) said that Mizanur Rahman, founder of Jabale Noor International and described as one of the leaders of the trafficking ring, and Abu Taher alias Lentu were arrested on 13 October 2026 over the sending of the 30 men.
RU1-74.why_new: Names, role and date of the two arrests the guide mentions without detail.

RU1-75.claim: CID sources said at least six cases had been filed over the trafficking of Bangladeshis to Russia, Prothom Alo reported on 21 October 2026.
RU1-75.why_new: Number of criminal cases on the Russia route.

RU1-76.claim: BMET data show 37 people took clearance for Russia in 2023, 1,395 in 2024, 4,725 in 2025 and 3,105 in 2026 up to 15 October.
RU1-76.why_new: The year-by-year BMET series; the guide has a single combined figure.

RU1-77.claim: Md Palash Sheikh, one of the 30, was wounded in his first spell at the war, was sent back after recovering and lost a hand, and in October 2026 was being treated in a Moscow hospital; his cousin Abu Saleh Islam told Prothom Alo that asking the embassy and the Ministry had brought no help to get him home, that he cannot escape the hospital because it is under army guard, and that the family, which spent BDT 10 lakh to send him, has received no money.
RU1-77.why_new: A wounded man is sent back to the front; a case where the embassy and Ministry did not help, and the hospital is guarded.

RU1-78.claim: Prothom Alo obtained 28 separate letters that families submitted to the Expatriates' Welfare Ministry in July 2026 to get missing relatives back; the letters say Jabale Noor International of Khilkhet and RS International of Ashulia sent the men to Russia through brokers, that they were sold to the Russian army with the lure of high pay, and ask for their quick and safe return and for financial help.
RU1-78.why_new: 28 written applications to the Ministry in July 2026, with the two agencies' locations as the families give them (Khilkhet and Ashulia); the article reports no result.

RU1-79.claim: Prothom Alo reported in October 2026 that travel to Russia has not decreased, and that because staying six months at the war brings a chance of Russian citizenship and pay of BDT 3 to 4 lakh a month, many go to the war of their own accord.
RU1-79.why_new: The open pitch for army service itself: citizenship after six months and BDT 3 to 4 lakh a month.

RU1-80.claim: A Prothom Alo investigation found that clearances to send workers to Russia were taken in the names of 93 recruiting agencies over four years, that only 17 agencies took clearance for more than a hundred workers each, and that Bonna Bijoy Overseas alone took the most, 27% of the workers or about 2,500.
RU1-80.why_new: How concentrated the Russia business is: one agency with over a quarter of all clearances.

RU1-81.claim: Prothom Alo reported on 21 October 2026 that Bonna Bijoy Overseas, the agency that sent the most workers to Russia, is accused of trafficking in the name of sending workers to Algeria, has a human trafficking case against it and faces allegations over sending workers to Russia too, and that its server has been locked so it can take no new clearances; its managing director, Barun Debnath, did not answer the paper's call or text message.
RU1-81.why_new: Action against the largest Russia sender: its BMET server access locked.

RU1-82.claim: Of the three agencies the SRB accuses over the 30 men, Prothom Alo found that TS Overseas had taken clearance in the names of 266 workers for Russia and that the names of the other two could not be found in BMET's database.
RU1-82.target_section: When the visa, the agency and the clearance are all real
RU1-82.why_new: Two of the three firms named in the case do not appear in BMET's database as Russia senders at all; the clearances ran through the third.
RU1-82.h3: When the visa, the agency and the clearance are all real

RU1-83.claim: A responsible official of BOESL, the government recruiting agency, which took the second-highest number of Russia clearances at 771, told Prothom Alo in October 2026 that it had been sending workers to three Russian companies, that after one worker ran off with a vehicle and another became involved in the war two of the companies stopped taking workers, that 14 more people were still due to go to the third company on its old demand letter, and that BOESL had received no new demand letter for a year.
RU1-83.target_section: When the visa, the agency and the clearance are all real
RU1-83.why_new: Even among workers sent by the government's own agency, one ended up in the war.
RU1-83.h3: When the visa, the agency and the clearance are all real

RU1-84.claim: Research on labour migration to Russia done by BRAC's Migration Programme in November 2025 found, as Prothom Alo summarises it, that the deception begins in Bangladesh: the men left with valid visas, job contracts and the required papers, and were sent to the war after being taken there.
RU1-84.target_section: When the visa, the agency and the clearance are all real
RU1-84.why_new: BRAC's finding that the papers were valid and the fraud started at home.
RU1-84.h3: When the visa, the agency and the clearance are all real

RU1-85.claim: Expatriates' Welfare Minister Ariful Haque Chowdhury told Prothom Alo in October 2026 that nobody is being given clearance without verification and attestation of confirmed job information, that many people are going by various means through different countries, and that all embassies have been alerted and instructed to keep watch by staying in touch with the expatriate community.
RU1-85.why_new: The Minister's stated rule (no clearance without attestation) and his admission that people still go through third countries.

RU1-86.claim: Shariful Hasan, head of BRAC's Migration Programme, said in October 2026 that the agencies accused of trafficking are sending the most workers to Russia and that nobody has a count of how many found work, where the rest are or how many have died; he advised opening a hotline and drawing up a list of the missing.
RU1-86.why_new: As of October 2026 there is no hotline and no list of the missing; BRAC proposes both.

RU1-87.claim: The SRB, the detective branch and others concerned told Prothom Alo that the men sent from Bangladesh have neither the physical fitness, the training nor the tactics for war, and that when the enemy attacks them with drones Russian soldiers identify the enemy's position.
RU1-87.why_new: How the 'bait' use works in practice (drawing drone fire so positions can be located); the guide states the fact without the mechanism.

RU1-88.claim: Prothom Alo reported on 21 October 2026 that of the 30 Bangladeshis sent to Russia on 7 May 2026, 20 were reported dead, two were wounded and under treatment in Russian hospitals (Palash Sheikh and Ali Hasan Sohel), two had managed to return to Bangladesh (Rajon Hossain and Adnan Hossain), and six were still being made to fight.
RU1-88.why_new: The full accounting of the 30 (20 dead, 2 in hospital, 2 home, 6 still at the front); the guide gives only the deaths.

RU1-89.claim: According to the SRB's 14 October 2026 press conference, 17 of the 30 died in a drone attack on their first day on the battlefield and three more died later at different times.
RU1-89.why_new: States the cause (a drone attack) and how the 20 divides into 17 and 3.

RU1-90.claim: Pabitra Chandra (30), a carpenter from a very poor family in Gopalpur, Tangail, and one of the 30, went to Russia with BDT 1 lakh 30 thousand from selling his wife's jewellery and BDT 9.5 lakh borrowed from an NGO and local moneylenders, according to Prothom Alo.
RU1-90.why_new: How one of the 30 raised the money: BDT 10.8 lakh, almost all of it debt.

RU1-91.claim: Pabitra Chandra's brother-in-law, Tapan Chandra Sutradhar, told Prothom Alo that in the first few days after reaching Russia Pabitra said he and several others were being kept in a hotel and would be given work once the papers were sorted out, that contact then stopped for some time, and that on 29 May 2026 he phoned to say 'we are being taken to the war by force; the chance of dying there is 95 per cent'.
RU1-91.why_new: What the men were told while held in the hotel ('work after the papers are done') and the date families learned the truth.

RU1-92.claim: Prothom Alo reported that after 29 May 2026 Pabitra Chandra contacted the Bangladesh embassy and asked it to arrange for him and the others to be brought home, that his family later heard of his death through his companions, and that as of 21 October 2026 the family had not had it confirmed by the embassy or any government channel.
RU1-92.why_new: A direct request to the embassy before deployment that did not stop it, and no official confirmation of death five months on.

RU1-93.claim: Tapan Chandra Sutradhar said in October 2026 that lenders come and stand behind Pabitra Chandra's family for their money when they sit down to eat, and that the family is thinking of selling its remaining 3 decimals of land, which would still not clear the debt.
RU1-93.why_new: What the debt does to the family after the death.

RU1-94.claim: Rahat Chowdhury, nephew of Robin Mir, a Siddhirganj (Narayanganj) autorickshaw driver who was one of the 30, told Prothom Alo that for the first three or four days in Russia his uncle was given good food and shown around, that there was then no news for five or six days, that on 15 May 2026 he said they were being taken to work, that on 17 May he was seen in an army camp in a video, and that on 29 May he phoned in tears to say they had been taken through deep forest on the promise of work and sold.
RU1-94.why_new: A day-by-day timeline from arrival to the army camp (good treatment, silence, 'going to work', camp within 10 days).

RU1-95.claim: Robin Mir of Siddhirganj went to Russia for work after selling his village land and cattle and borrowing, with three other men from Narayanganj, through whom his family learned of his death, according to Prothom Alo.
RU1-95.why_new: Another of the 30, financed by selling land and cattle; four men recruited from one district.

RU1-96.claim: Taslim Sardar, who keeps in regular contact with his brother-in-law Sourav Molla of Gopalganj through the messaging app imo, told Prothom Alo in October 2026 that Sourav was three to four kilometres behind the front line being made to dig earth for bunkers, and had twice tried to escape without success.
RU1-96.why_new: What the six survivors still in the army are doing, and that escape attempts fail.

RU1-97.claim: According to Taslim Sardar, of the six men from the group of 30 still at the war in October 2026, Kamal was digging bunkers with Sourav, Roni Sheikh and Al Amin were carrying food, water and weapons on foot from the camp to the front line, and Hanif and Helal had no fixed task and were made sometimes to dig bunkers and sometimes to carry food.
RU1-97.why_new: The support tasks the men are used for.

RU1-98.claim: Taslim Sardar, a relative of one of the six men still at the war, organised a human chain in Dhaka with the affected families shortly before 21 October 2026, Prothom Alo reported.
RU1-98.why_new: Families of the May 2026 group are organised and reachable through a named relative.

RU1-99.claim: A draft report by the UN's Independent International Commission of Inquiry on Ukraine, published on the website of the UN human rights office (OHCHR) on 26 October 2026, examined information on the recruitment of nationals of 48 countries into Russia's forces and found evidence of deception or coercion for 29, Bangladesh among them; the report gives no separate figures on Bangladeshi recruits, their names or what happened to them.
RU1-99.why_new: Identifies the report, its date and its limits; the guide cites only '29 countries'.

RU1-100.claim: The UN commission obtained copies of business visas of recruited Bangladeshis that mention an invitation from a Russian civilian company, Prothom Alo reported on 28 October 2026.
RU1-100.why_new: The visa type actually used for Bangladeshis: a business visa on a civilian company's invitation, not a work visa.

RU1-101.claim: The UN commission's report describes a group of 30 who were given a letter of assurance saying they would not be sent to the Russia-Ukraine battlefield; by the time the report was written 17 of the group had been killed on the front line, 5 were missing and 1 had returned wounded; the report does not name the group's country.
RU1-101.why_new: A written 'you will not be sent to the war' guarantee was given and was worthless.

RU1-102.claim: According to the UN commission, men abroad got Russian job offers through social media adverts or through recruiting agents and firms, for work as security guards, drivers, mechanics, electricians, construction workers, welders, repair workers, transport workers and technicians, and in some cases in IT, medicine, sport or agriculture; some recruiters said the work was under the military but civilian.
RU1-102.why_new: The full range of jobs used as bait, and the 'under the military but civilian' line.

RU1-103.claim: The UN commission says the job offers spoke of high pay, Russian citizenship, comfortable housing, a pension after leaving the job and other benefits, and that some recruits were shown photos or a catalogue of the housing.
RU1-103.why_new: What is promised and the props used (housing photos, a catalogue).

RU1-104.claim: According to the UN commission, the Russia job offers seemed credible to recruits because of the recruiters' assurances, their own earlier experience of working abroad, information from others who said they had got the same work, and documents showing the recruiting firm's government approval; in some cases an acquaintance had told them about the job.
RU1-104.why_new: A UN finding on what made the offer believable, including the firm's government approval papers.

RU1-105.claim: The UN commission found that after accepting, many recruits were pressed to travel to Russia within a few days; agents arranged the visa, air ticket, housing and the rest of the journey; some paid in advance and others were told the money would be deducted from their pay later; and visa types varied by country and region between business visas, short-term tourist visas and no visa at all.
RU1-105.why_new: Pressure to leave within days, the 'pay later from salary' variant and the visa types.

RU1-106.claim: Testimony and documents obtained by the UN commission name Bahrain, Brazil, Ethiopia, France, Kenya, Mexico, Morocco, Oman, Panama, Spain, Turkey and the United Arab Emirates as transit countries; in some cases agents travelled with the recruits or met them in the transit country, and some recruits were told to go by road to a neighbouring country and fly from there so as not to be caught at the airport.
RU1-106.why_new: Transit countries and the instruction to leave from a neighbouring country to avoid airport checks.

RU1-107.claim: The UN commission says the recruiting agents in the various countries were local, regional or Russian nationals who operated as travel or tourism businesses; some firms held local licences, some presented themselves as legal or government-approved, and in many cases visas issued by the Russian embassy were handed over through the agents.
RU1-107.why_new: Who the recruiters are (travel and tourism firms, some licensed) and that the embassy visa itself comes through them.

RU1-108.claim: According to the UN commission, many recruits had no freedom of movement after reaching the airport in Russia: they were kept in temporary accommodation, handed to the Russian armed forces, and within hours or days of arriving made to sign a one-year military service contract with Russia's Defence Ministry.
RU1-108.why_new: The contract is with the Russian Defence Ministry, for one year, and is signed within hours or days.

RU1-109.claim: The UN commission found the contracts were written in Russian, most recruits did not know Russian and so could not understand the terms, and they could not use translation because their phones were not in their hands.
RU1-109.why_new: Why the men could not translate the contract: the phones had already been taken.

RU1-110.claim: The UN commission's report says recruits who refused to sign the contract were pressured, threatened or tortured; one recruit said four people were shot dead in front of him and he was told he would be next if he did not sign, after which he signed.
RU1-110.why_new: What refusal to sign leads to.

RU1-111.claim: The UN commission says foreigners already in Russia were also taken into the armed forces by deception or coercion: some were in police custody or in temporary detention centres for foreign nationals and some were serving prison sentences, and several were told that signing a military contract would spare them prosecution, a long sentence, solitary confinement or torture, with threats of torture or a longer sentence if they did not sign.
RU1-111.target_section: Recruited while abroad or just back
RU1-111.placement: other: In Russia, after the job ends
RU1-111.why_new: A recruitment point the guide lacks: foreigners in Russian police custody, immigration detention or prison.
RU1-111.h3: Recruited while abroad or just back

RU1-112.claim: According to the UN commission, initial military training lasted from 20 minutes to a few days, in some cases up to a month; the recruits were then sent to battlefields in Ukraine, where they were made to dig trenches, guard areas, deliver food and water and collect bodies, their main tasks being to carry out assaults and advance; they also reported days without food and water, beatings, detention and death threats.
RU1-112.why_new: Training length (as little as 20 minutes) and the tasks, from a UN source.

RU1-113.claim: The UN commission found that recruits were taken to open bank accounts, but many were not paid and some got little; money was withdrawn from some accounts without permission, some salaries were withheld or accounts closed, and in some cases recruiting agents or military personnel took the bank cards; many recruits lost contact with their families after going to the war.
RU1-113.why_new: How the pay disappears: the bank card is taken by the agent or military staff.

RU1-114.claim: The UN commission concluded that the Russian authorities committed human trafficking together with recruiting agents; that because trafficked people became members of the Russian armed forces on signing the contract they cannot be called mercenaries; and that if they surrender or are captured they are entitled to prisoner-of-war protection until the war ends.
RU1-114.why_new: The men's legal status under international law (not mercenaries; prisoner-of-war protection on capture or surrender).

RU1-115.claim: The UN commission recommended that Russia stop recruiting foreign nationals through deception or coercion, discharge trafficked people who are in its forces and assist them, and investigate and prosecute those involved in the recruitment; according to international media citing its UN mission, Russia does not recognise the commission's mandate and says the report is based on false information.
RU1-115.why_new: The recommendation to discharge trafficked recruits, and Russia's rejection of the report.

RU1-116.claim: The UN commission's findings on recruitment rest on 245 testimonies from recruits detained by Ukrainian authorities or who got home, family members, lawyers, local authorities, researchers and journalists, plus invitation letters, itineraries, air tickets, visas, Russian entry documents, hotel bookings, military contracts and Russian Defence Ministry documents; the victims were all men aged 18 to 60, mostly from financially weak and marginal groups.
RU1-116.why_new: How the UN figure was established and who the victims are.

RU1-117.claim: Expatriates' Welfare Minister Ariful Haque Chowdhury told Prothom Alo in October 2026 that extra caution is being taken over sending workers to Russia, that instructions have been given to check appointment letters much more thoroughly, and that action has begun against the recruiting agencies involved.
RU1-117.why_new: The government's response to the UN report.

RU1-118.claim: Selim Reza, coordinator of North South University's Centre for Migration Studies, told Prothom Alo in October 2026 that the government went on giving clearance for Russia even after learning that people were being taken to the war by force, and that the demand in Russia's labour market had not been properly assessed.
RU1-118.why_new: An academic's statement that clearances continued after the forced recruitment was known.

RU1-119.claim: As Prothom Alo reported it on 5 November 2026, the Expatriates' Welfare Ministry's letter of 4 November 2026 to BMET's Director General names Serbia, Moldova, Belarus, Congo, Russia, Japan, Iraq, Laos, Vietnam, Cambodia, Ukraine and Libya, and BAIRA (the recruiting agencies' association) sent a copy of the instruction to all its member agencies the same day.
RU1-119.why_new: Prothom Alo's version of the 12-country list (with Congo, Russia and Cambodia), which bears on the guide's open question about the exact list, and the fact that every BAIRA member agency was told the same day.

RU1-120.claim: People concerned told Prothom Alo in November 2026 that until then a demand letter for up to seven workers needed no permission from the Expatriates' Welfare Ministry, that there are allegations this was used to bring in fake appointment letters in the name of sending workers, and that after the 4 November 2026 instruction every demand letter must be approved first.
RU1-120.target_section: Fake visa, demand letter or job offer
RU1-120.why_new: The loophole behind small-batch fake demand letters (seven workers or fewer needed no Ministry permission) and its closure.
RU1-120.h3: Fake visa, demand letter or job offer

RU1-121.claim: People in the sector told Prothom Alo in November 2026 that workers interested in jobs in the 12 countries should hold back from any payment or final decision until the appointment letter, the Ministry's approval and the emigration clearance have all been confirmed.
RU1-121.why_new: Attributed advice on the order of events for the 12 countries: three confirmations before any money.

RU1-122.claim: Volunteers of several organisations working on migration told Prothom Alo in November 2026 that getting a visa or a job offer through a recruiting agency is not by itself a guarantee of legal and safe migration, and that the real job opportunities in the country, the employer's identity, the job contract, pay and allowances, the visa type and Bangladesh government approval all need to be verified.
RU1-122.target_section: When the visa, the agency and the clearance are all real
RU1-122.why_new: States the section's premise in the words of people in the field, with the six things they say to verify.
RU1-122.h3: When the visa, the agency and the clearance are all real

RU1-123.claim: Volunteers of migration organisations told Prothom Alo in November 2026 that in several countries, particularly Cambodia, Laos and Vietnam, people have been forcibly held in online-fraud and scam compounds and made to do fraudulent work, and that many Bangladeshis who went to these countries for jobs became victims of fraud, exploitation, confinement and trafficking.
RU1-123.target_section: Cambodia, Myanmar and Laos: scam compounds
RU1-123.why_new: Names Vietnam alongside Cambodia and Laos as a scam-compound destination.
RU1-123.h3: Cambodia, Myanmar and Laos: scam compounds

RU1-124.claim: The UN commission's report describes a professional athlete who was told Russia was taking foreign players and that he could sign a contract after arriving if he liked the work, and who was handed to the military on arrival; another recruit said he was a cook and did not want to be a soldier but ended up on the front line.
RU1-124.why_new: Two individual cases from the UN report showing the 'sign after you see the job' pitch and that a cook's job ends at the front.

RU1-125.claim: The UN commission sent 69 letters to various countries about the recruitment and received 6 replies, and its report says Russia did not answer 41 written requests.
RU1-125.why_new: How little governments, and Russia, cooperated with the UN inquiry.

RU1-126.claim: According to information from the families, besides Pabitra Chandra and Robin Mir the 18 others of the group of 30 killed on the battlefield are Sohel, Md Mehedi Hasan, Md Al Mamun, Md Abdullah Al Mamun, Md Nazmul Alam, Md Wasim Akram, Md Arif Hossain, Md Sayed Molla, Tarikul Islam Mintu, Sabbir Hossain, Mofiz, Md Arman Ali, Md Nazrul Islam, Md Aminur Islam, Kazi Rezaul Karim, Main Uddin, Ripon Hossain and Arif Hossain Patwari; Prothom Alo spoke to relatives of seven more of the 30 and said nearly all the families are low-income.
RU1-126.why_new: The names of the dead as the families give them, for the record; no official list exists.

RU1-127.claim: The six of the 30 still being made to fight in October 2026 are Roni Sheikh and Sourav Molla of Gopalganj, Al Amin Islam of Lalmonirhat, Kamal Hossain and Helal Sheikh of Madaripur and Abu Hanif of Kishoreganj, some of whom keep in contact with their families, Prothom Alo reported.
RU1-127.why_new: Names and home districts of the six still in the Russian army.

RU1-128.claim: Prothom Alo reported on 30 July 2026 that BMET had given more than 15,000 workers clearance for Cambodia in the previous year and a half, even as workers taken there for call-centre jobs were being made to do online fraud.
RU1-128.target_section: Cambodia, Myanmar and Laos: scam compounds
RU1-128.why_new: Corroborates the guide's 18-month figure (15,921) from a second report; add only as a supporting source.
RU1-128.h3: Cambodia, Myanmar and Laos: scam compounds

MY1-1.claim: Prothom Alo reported on 21 March 2024, citing Expatriates' Welfare Ministry sources, that Malaysia had stopped approving new applications to hire foreign workers, that visa applications for already-approved workers had to be filed by 31 March 2024, and that those with visas had to enter Malaysia by 31 May 2024.
MY1-1.target_section: MALAYSIA DOC: What closed it before
MY1-1.why_new: Adds the 31 March 2024 visa-application cut-off that preceded the 31 May entry deadline.
MY1-1.h3: Is it open now, and who can go?

MY1-2.claim: From 1 June 2024 no worker from any other source country could enter Malaysia either, and Prothom Alo reported that the other countries blamed the Bangladeshi syndicate for this.
MY1-2.target_section: MALAYSIA DOC: What closed it before
MY1-2.why_new: The 2024 stop applied to all source countries, not only Bangladesh.
MY1-2.h3: Is it open now, and who can go?

MY1-3.claim: Prothom Alo reported in March 2024 that Tk 1.5 lakh per Malaysia-bound worker had to be paid to the ring formed in the name of the 100 agencies, that a business in the name of medical tests ran under the same ring, and that a worker spent Tk 4 to 5 lakh on average to go, though many found no job on arrival.
MY1-3.target_section: MALAYSIA DOC: Where a Tk 5.5 lakh deal goes
MY1-3.why_new: Ties the per-worker toll and the medical-test business to the same ring of 100 agencies.
MY1-3.h3: What you pay, and what you earn and keep

MY1-4.claim: Members of BAIRA (the recruiting agencies' association) said in March 2024 that the ring alone took Tk 1.5 lakh per worker, more than Tk 6,000 crore on over four lakh workers, and that the Malaysia labour market generated Tk 18,000 crore of business in the previous year and a half.
MY1-4.target_section: MALAYSIA DOC: Where a Tk 5.5 lakh deal goes
MY1-4.why_new: Total size of the syndicate toll and of the trade, as claimed by BAIRA members.
MY1-4.h3: What you pay, and what you earn and keep

MY1-5.claim: BAIRA joint secretary general Fakhrul Islam told Prothom Alo in March 2024 that although a worker was supposed to go to Malaysia for Tk 80,000, nobody could go for less than Tk 4.5 lakh.
MY1-5.target_section: MALAYSIA DOC: What people really pay
MY1-5.why_new: A named industry official's floor price for 2022-24.
MY1-5.h3: What you pay, and what you earn and keep

MY1-6.claim: Prothom Alo reported that 25 Bangladeshi agencies were first given the Malaysia work in 2022, later raised to 100, and that a ring of private agencies in Malaysia assists this ring; BAIRA members said the MoU between the two countries gave Malaysia the job of finalising the agencies, which let one group trade illegally.
MY1-6.why_new: Growth from 25 to 100 agencies and the MoU clause that left agency selection to Malaysia.
MY1-6.h3: How a job reaches you, and who takes a cut

MY1-7.claim: Malaysia's High Commissioner in Dhaka, Haznah Md Hashim, told journalists on 12 March 2024 that one cause of the problem was syndicates active in both Bangladesh and Malaysia.
MY1-7.why_new: Malaysia's own envoy naming the syndicate as a cause.
MY1-7.h3: How a job reaches you, and who takes a cut

MY1-8.claim: Prothom Alo reported that in 2016 the online framework for recruiting workers to Malaysia went to a firm named Synerflux, whose owner the article names as Dato Seri Abdul bin Amin Nur, a Malaysian citizen of Bangladeshi origin, that with his help 10 Bangladeshi agencies formed a ring, that workers spent Tk 2 to 3.5 lakh against a set cost of Tk 33,375, and that the ring took about Tk 5,500 crore in two years.
MY1-8.target_section: MALAYSIA DOC: What closed it before
MY1-8.why_new: Names the 2016 system firm (Synerflux) and gives this article's figures for the 10-agency round (Tk 33,375 set cost; the guide has Tk 37,000 from another source).
MY1-8.h3: Is it open now, and who can go?

MY1-9.claim: According to BMET data cited by Prothom Alo, 12.5 lakh Bangladeshi workers went to Malaysia legally from 1992 to January 2024, more than 3.5 lakh of them in 2023 and 50,000 in 2022.
MY1-9.why_new: Cumulative and yearly BMET departure counts.
MY1-9.h3: Is it open now, and who can go?

MY1-10.claim: Two officials of the Bangladesh mission in Malaysia, speaking anonymously, told Prothom Alo in March 2024 that 1.5 to 2 lakh Bangladeshi workers there were unemployed and living in inhuman conditions, that many came to the mission regularly for help, and that the mission could do little.
MY1-10.why_new: The jobless estimate comes from mission officials themselves, with their admission that the mission can do little.
MY1-10.h3: How a job reaches you, and who takes a cut

MY1-11.claim: In March 2024 a member of the Facebook group 'Malaysia Probashi Bangladeshi' wrote that his brother, newly arrived in Malaysia, had found no work for four months.
MY1-11.why_new: A worker-side account of months without work after arrival.
MY1-11.h3: How a job reaches you, and who takes a cut

MY1-12.claim: A statement on 20 March 2024 by Bangladesh Civil Society for Migrants (BCSM), a platform of 23 organisations, demanded punishment of those responsible for the closure, and Tasneem Siddiqui, founding chair of RMMRU, told Prothom Alo that the agencies involved in past irregularities should have been held accountable and that the same recruitment process was repeated when the market reopened in 2022.
MY1-12.why_new: Records that the agencies from the 2016-18 round were not held to account before 2022.
MY1-12.h3: How a job reaches you, and who takes a cut

MY1-21.claim: Prothom Alo described the 'Malaysia syndicate' in May 2024 as an arrangement in which only a few agencies may send workers: 25 at the start, rising in three steps to 100; the ring's leaders are alleged to have taken large sums from each agency to put its name in, and the agencies inside received at least Tk 1.5 lakh 'syndicate fee' per worker while sitting idle, part of which went to the ring's controllers in Malaysia.
MY1-21.why_new: The entry payment to join the list and the split of the per-worker fee with Malaysia.
MY1-21.h3: How a job reaches you, and who takes a cut

MY1-22.claim: When the market reopened in July 2022 the Expatriates' Welfare Ministry sent Malaysia a list of 1,520 recruiting agencies and only 25 were chosen; Prothom Alo reported that there was no policy for the selection and that there are many allegations of influence and bribery in it.
MY1-22.why_new: 1,520 proposed against 25 chosen, with no selection policy.
MY1-22.h3: How a job reaches you, and who takes a cut

MY1-23.claim: Fourteen countries send workers to Malaysia, and Prothom Alo reported that no country except Bangladesh has such a syndicate arrangement.
MY1-23.why_new: Only Bangladesh's agencies are restricted this way.
MY1-23.h3: How a job reaches you, and who takes a cut

MY1-24.claim: Owners of three agencies outside the syndicate told Prothom Alo in May 2024 that they obtained worker demand themselves and sent people to Malaysia in a syndicate agency's name, paying that agency Tk 1 lakh 52 thousand to Tk 1 lakh 65 thousand per worker.
MY1-24.target_section: MALAYSIA DOC: The processing agency: the toll gate
MY1-24.why_new: First-hand figure for the 2022-24 toll, from agencies that paid it (the guide gives Tk 1.07 to 1.52 lakh).
MY1-24.h3: How a job reaches you, and who takes a cut

MY1-25.claim: Analysing a list obtained from relevant sources, Prothom Alo found that Five M International, whose managing director according to BAIRA's website is MP Lt Gen (retd) Masud Uddin Chowdhury, was the top single sender to Malaysia and alone obtained clearances for 8,592 workers, though BMET said it had sent about 2,500 workers to the Middle East since it was founded in 2015.
MY1-25.why_new: Named agency, owner and clearance count.
MY1-25.h3: How a job reaches you, and who takes a cut

MY1-26.claim: Snigdha Overseas Limited, the agency of Feni Awami League MP Nizam Uddin Hazari, took its licence in December 2018 and sent only 100 workers abroad in three and a half years, but after joining the syndicate about 8,000 workers went to Malaysia in its name in a year and a half, making it the fourth-largest sender; its executive director Shahela Parvin told Prothom Alo that various agencies had sent workers through it and that it took nothing beyond the government-fixed cost.
MY1-26.why_new: Named agency with before and after volumes and its reply.
MY1-26.h3: How a job reaches you, and who takes a cut

MY1-27.claim: Ahmed International, the firm of Dhaka-20 MP Benzir Ahmed, who was BAIRA president when the syndicate was formed, had sent only 238 workers abroad before the Malaysia market opened and then sent 7,849 to Malaysia, the fifth-highest; Orbitals Enterprise and Orbitals International, in the names of the wife (Kashmeri Kamal) and daughter (Nafisa Kamal) of then finance minister A H M Mustafa Kamal, sent 9,861 in total.
MY1-27.why_new: Named agencies and counts for two more politically connected owners.
MY1-27.h3: How a job reaches you, and who takes a cut

MY1-28.claim: Oishi International was second and New Age International third on the list of agencies sending workers to Malaysia, and relevant sources claimed to Prothom Alo that both were active members of the syndicate.
MY1-28.why_new: Names the second- and third-largest senders.
MY1-28.h3: How a job reaches you, and who takes a cut

MY1-29.claim: BAIRA members allege that former BAIRA secretary general Ruhul Amin, known as Swapan, led the forming of the 2022 syndicate, fixed the names of 69 of its 100 agencies and was the channel through which money was transacted in Malaysia; by BMET's count 7,102 workers went in the name of his agency Catharsis International, and he did not respond to Prothom Alo.
MY1-29.why_new: Adds the '69 of 100' allegation and Catharsis's own count.
MY1-29.h3: How a job reaches you, and who takes a cut

MY1-30.claim: The Nur Ali-Abul Bashar panel won BAIRA's 2022 election after campaigning against the Malaysia syndicate, yet BNS Overseas Limited (of BAIRA president Mohammad Abul Bashar's son Ishtiaque Ahmed) and PR Overseas (of his son-in-law Golam Rakib, licensed October 2021, more than 4,000 workers sent) joined the syndicate, as did Sadia International, the agency of Shamim Ahmed Chowdhury, who was elected BAIRA secretary general in the last election and later resigned; Bashar told Prothom Alo the ring listed the two firms for money to damage his image, while his son claimed no money changed hands.
MY1-30.why_new: The syndicate's opponents inside BAIRA ended up in it.
MY1-30.h3: How a job reaches you, and who takes a cut

MY1-31.claim: Agencies new to the trade became top Malaysia senders after joining the syndicate: Imperial Overseas (licensed March 2021; 344 workers sent by July 2022, more than 7,000 in the next year and a half), BM Travels Limited of Dhaka North ward 39 councillor Md Shafiqul Islam (7,225 clearances, no earlier Malaysia experience) and Ananya Apurba Recruiting Agency of Dhaka South Awami League joint general secretary Mohiuddin Ahmed (licensed July 2022, 2,600 clearances); two agencies confirmed to Prothom Alo that they sent workers through Imperial by paying the syndicate fee.
MY1-31.why_new: New, inexperienced agencies as fronts through which others sent workers.
MY1-31.h3: How a job reaches you, and who takes a cut

MY1-32.claim: Md Selim of Narayanganj, who went to Malaysia in March 2023, did not get the promised job and paid his own fare home in September 2023, told Prothom Alo he had sold his own auto-rickshaw and his wife's jewellery and borrowed from people to go, and was now destitute and in debt.
MY1-32.why_new: The guide uses Selim's job and injury; this adds how he financed the trip and the dates.

MY1-33.claim: People in the sector told Prothom Alo in May 2024 that sending about 4.5 lakh people to Malaysia in a year and a half generated Tk 24,000 crore of business, about Tk 20,000 crore of it above the government-fixed fee, including more than Tk 6,500 crore of syndicate fee at Tk 1.5 lakh a head.
MY1-33.target_section: MALAYSIA DOC: Where a Tk 5.5 lakh deal goes
MY1-33.h3: What you pay, and what you earn and keep

MY1-34.claim: By the Expatriates' Welfare Ministry's own count in May 2024, five thousand workers who went to Malaysia found no work, while long-settled Bangladeshis there told Prothom Alo that thousands were jobless, some selling goods on pavements or umbrellas in the rain to pay for food.
MY1-34.why_new: The government's own figure for workers without jobs, set against community accounts.
MY1-34.h3: How a job reaches you, and who takes a cut

MY1-35.claim: From January to 24 March 2024, 453 workers returned from Malaysia empty-handed and without passports, travelling on travel permits, Prothom Alo reported.
MY1-35.why_new: Count of workers coming home on travel permits without passports in early 2024.
MY1-35.h3: How a job reaches you, and who takes a cut

MY1-36.claim: Prothom Alo reported in May 2024 that the ministry had never taken action despite repeated allegations of syndicate-forming and overcharging, and that the state minister, Shafiqur Rahman Chowdhury, said on 11 May 2024 that Malaysia had set the list of agencies and that the complaints were being looked into.
MY1-36.why_new: The ministry's record of inaction as of May 2024.
MY1-36.h3: How a job reaches you, and who takes a cut

MY1-40.claim: Prothom Alo reported on 31 May 2024 that Malaysia's labour market had closed to Bangladesh three times in 15 years: in 2009, then (after reopening at the end of 2016 with a ring of 10 agencies) from September 2018 over allegations of corruption and irregularities, and again from 1 June 2024.
MY1-40.target_section: MALAYSIA DOC: What closed it before
MY1-40.why_new: Confirms the three closures and the end-2016 reopening.
MY1-40.h3: Is it open now, and who can go?

MY1-41.claim: Bestinet, the firm that owns Migram, the software of Malaysia's Foreign Workers Centralised Management System (FWCMS), has among its owners Aminul Islam bin Abdul Nor, known as Amin Nor, a Malaysian citizen of Bangladeshi origin; it is alleged that he controls the whole worker-sending trade from Malaysia, that former BAIRA secretary general Ruhul Amin, known as Swapan, acts as his representative in Bangladesh, and that the two decided who would be in the syndicate.
MY1-41.why_new: Names the software (Migram) and states the Amin-Swapan allegation as Prothom Alo printed it.
MY1-41.h3: How a job reaches you, and who takes a cut

MY1-42.claim: Once a Malaysian demand letter is finalised it is distributed through the FWCMS software among the approved agencies, not equally, and the workers must be sent through the agency in whose name it arrives; three agencies outside the list told Prothom Alo that demand letters they collected from Malaysian companies went to a listed agency because their own names were not in FWCMS, and they then had to pay that agency Tk 1 lakh 52 thousand to Tk 1 lakh 65 thousand per worker.
MY1-42.target_section: MALAYSIA DOC: The processing agency: the toll gate
MY1-42.why_new: The mechanism by which a listed agency earns on demand it did not collect.
MY1-42.h3: How a job reaches you, and who takes a cut

MY1-43.claim: Prothom Alo reported in May 2024 that government records showed the worker going in the name of a syndicate agency even when that agency did not send him, and that in several written undertakings it collected, the recruiting agency actually sending the worker as 'sub-agent' or representative promised to take responsibility if the worker got no job, or any responsibility, although its name appeared in no government record of the sending.
MY1-43.target_section: When the visa, the agency and the clearance are all real
MY1-43.why_new: Explains why the agency on a worker's BMET clearance may not be the one that took his money, and how liability is shifted by private undertaking.
MY1-43.h3: When the visa, the agency and the clearance are all real

MY1-44.claim: Sarkar International sent 7,745 workers to Malaysia as a single agency; its proprietor Mohammad Ali Sarkar told Prothom Alo that many who had obtained demand from Malaysia sent workers through his agency, that written undertakings on responsibility for the workers were taken from those agencies, and that only the government-fixed amount was taken.
MY1-44.target_section: MALAYSIA DOC: The processing agency: the toll gate
MY1-44.why_new: A listed agency's owner confirming the written-undertaking practice.
MY1-44.h3: How a job reaches you, and who takes a cut

MY1-45.claim: Several BAIRA members allege that part of each Malaysia worker's cost in 2022-24 went to Ruhul Amin, known as Swapan, and part of that was laundered to Malaysia through hundi, with the rest going to the agency in whose name the worker was sent, and that in every case the money changed hands in cash without any receipt; Ruhul Amin told Prothom Alo the allegations were false, that nothing was taken beyond the government-fixed Tk 78,990 and that no money was sent to Malaysia.
MY1-45.target_section: The staged-payment trap, and no receipts
MY1-45.why_new: Cash-without-receipt applied even between agencies, with the accused's denial.
MY1-45.h3: The staged-payment trap, and no receipts

MY1-46.claim: Agencies inside the syndicate told Prothom Alo that the workers' extra cost was the fault of agencies outside it, which bought demand letters from Malaysia at high prices in unhealthy competition; Five M International's managing director Masud Uddin Chowdhury said on 30 May 2024 that he had not bought even 100 jobs, that all came automatically through the software, that those whose jobs came sent workers through Five M, and that his agency only did visa processing and took only the government-fixed fee.
MY1-46.target_section: MALAYSIA DOC: Where a Tk 5.5 lakh deal goes
MY1-46.why_new: The listed agencies' own account: they only 'process', others buy the demand.
MY1-46.h3: What you pay, and what you earn and keep

MY1-47.claim: BAIRA joint secretary general Fakhrul Islam told Prothom Alo in May 2024 that there were no set rules for making the agency list, so some got on it with no experience of sending workers, in collusion with the ringleaders, and then earned money sitting at home at Tk 1 lakh 52 thousand per worker.
MY1-47.why_new: A named official on how inexperienced agencies got listed.
MY1-47.h3: How a job reaches you, and who takes a cut

MY1-48.claim: Nayem Uddin of Narsingdi went to Malaysia in November 2023 through a broker, spending Tk 5 lakh 20 thousand borrowed at interest; he told Prothom Alo he was promised work in a tiles factory but given construction work for a company, which stopped his work after 15 days, kept him in an office for another two and a half months and then suddenly sent him home, where he could not pay the loan instalments.
MY1-48.target_section: Contract substitution: a different job or wage on arrival
MY1-48.why_new: A dated Malaysia case of a different job on arrival ending in forced return.
MY1-48.h3: Contract substitution: a different job or wage on arrival

MY1-49.claim: As of 31 May 2024 the Expatriates' Welfare Ministry was not separately investigating the allegations about sending workers to Malaysia and wanted to discuss them at a meeting of the two countries' joint technical committee, for which it had written to Malaysia; no date had been fixed.
MY1-49.why_new: No separate ministry inquiry as of the deadline day.
MY1-49.h3: How a job reaches you, and who takes a cut

MY1-50.claim: BOESL, the government recruiting agency, had received demand for more than 10,000 workers for Malaysia but had taken only 1,467 clearances by 24 April 2024; two BOESL officials told Prothom Alo that workers went through BOESL free, at the employer's cost, while private agencies charged Tk 4 to 5 lakh, so obstacles came in many ways, including demand letters going into other agencies' names and taking time to bring back.
MY1-50.why_new: Why the zero-cost government channel sent so few: its demand letters were diverted to private agencies.
MY1-50.h3: Is it open now, and who can go?

MY1-51.claim: BAIRA member Mostafa Mahmud told Prothom Alo that in 2017 several agencies filed two separate complaints, with Bangladesh's ACC and Malaysia's MACC; he said the ACC did not proceed because the accused were from the private sector, and alleged that Amin Nor used influence to stop the Malaysian investigation.
MY1-51.why_new: Earlier complaints to both anti-corruption bodies and what became of them.
MY1-51.h3: How a job reaches you, and who takes a cut

MY1-52.claim: Malaysia's High Commissioner in Dhaka, Haznah Md Hashim, told journalists on 29 May 2024 that there may be syndicates beyond the control of both the Bangladesh and Malaysian governments.
MY1-52.why_new: Malaysia's envoy saying the syndicate is beyond both governments' control.
MY1-52.h3: How a job reaches you, and who takes a cut

MY1-16.claim: Lailul Haque (34) of Kafura village, Sherpur upazila, Bogura, told Prothom Alo in May 2024 that Abdul Alim, a businessman of the Sherua area who sends people abroad, sent him to Malaysia on a fake visa on 6 June 2023, and that he was sent back to Bangladesh after six days in jail.
MY1-16.target_section: Fake visa, demand letter or job offer
MY1-16.why_new: A dated Malaysia fake-visa case that ended in jail on arrival and return.
MY1-16.h3: Fake visa, demand letter or job offer

MY1-17.claim: A sub-inspector of Sherpur police station, Bogura, told Prothom Alo that Abdul Alim took Tk 5 lakh 70 thousand from Lailul Haque to send him to Malaysia as a worker, and Tk 2 lakh 30 thousand, Tk 3 lakh 14 thousand, Tk 2 lakh 70 thousand and Tk 3 lakh 50 thousand from four other young men; Lailul Haque put the total for the five at Tk 17 lakh 34 thousand.
MY1-17.target_section: Fake visa, demand letter or job offer
MY1-17.why_new: Amounts one local broker took from five men of two unions.
MY1-17.h3: Fake visa, demand letter or job offer

MY1-18.claim: Lailul Haque of Sherpur, Bogura, said that after he came back from Malaysia he went to Abdul Alim several times for his money, that Alim gave assurances but did not pay, then moved away from Sherpur and could not be reached by phone; local residents said Alim was staying in Tarash, Sirajganj.
MY1-18.target_section: Refund refusals after a failed departure
MY1-18.why_new: Shows the refund pattern: assurances, then the broker leaves the area.
MY1-18.h3: Refund refusals after a failed departure

MY1-19.claim: The five young men filed a written complaint at Sherpur police station, Bogura, on the night of 20 May 2024, having first gone to Abdul Alim at least a year and a half earlier, and the officer-in-charge said the necessary legal action would be taken; the article reports no case or arrest.
MY1-19.target_section: Refund refusals after a failed departure
MY1-19.why_new: What the police did at the point of reporting: a written complaint received, no case yet.
MY1-19.h3: Refund refusals after a failed departure

MY1-20.claim: The five Sherpur, Bogura, men who paid Abdul Alim for work abroad said some of them had borrowed and some had sold land and cattle to raise the money.
MY1-20.why_new: How the money for a failed Malaysia departure was raised.

MY1-13.claim: UN experts, in a statement published on the OHCHR website on 19 April 2024, said Bangladeshi workers were promised jobs before going to Malaysia but did not get the promised work after entering, and that many were forced to stay on after their visas expired, putting them at risk of arrest, detention, ill-treatment and deportation.
MY1-13.target_section: When the visa, the agency and the clearance are all real
MY1-13.why_new: The path from no job to overstaying and arrest, stated by UN special rapporteurs.
MY1-13.h3: When the visa, the agency and the clearance are all real

MY1-14.claim: The UN experts said in April 2024 that criminal networks in Bangladesh and Malaysia were defrauding migrant workers, who were recruited to companies that did not exist and fell into debt paying the networks for that recruitment.
MY1-14.target_section: When the visa, the agency and the clearance are all real
MY1-14.why_new: Recruitment to non-existent companies, from a UN statement.
MY1-14.h3: When the visa, the agency and the clearance are all real

MY1-15.claim: The UN experts said in April 2024 that high-level officials of the Bangladesh and Malaysian governments were involved with these networks, that little action had so far been taken against the firms involved in either country, and that victims who spoke about it faced reprisals and harassment.
MY1-15.target_section: When the visa, the agency and the clearance are all real
MY1-15.why_new: Official involvement, lack of action and reprisals against victims who speak.
MY1-15.h3: When the visa, the agency and the clearance are all real

MY1-37.claim: According to the case statement of Nurul Islam of Ujantia, Lohagara, Chattogram, on 20 June 2014 the accused lured him with a well-paid job in Malaysia and took him from Lohagara to the Dariyanagar coast in Cox's Bazar, where he and Helal Uddin of the same area were put on a ship by trawler; some days later the ship put them ashore on the Thai coast, where brokers tortured them and extracted Tk 4 lakh ransom before handing them to a broker in Malaysia.
MY1-37.why_new: A full boat-route case with departure point (Dariyanagar, Cox's Bazar), the trawler-to-ship transfer and the ransom in Thailand.

MY1-38.claim: Nurul Islam of Lohagara, Chattogram, who reached Malaysia by boat in 2014, was arrested by Malaysian police as an illegal immigrant in June 2017 and jailed, and the Bangladesh government brought him home in October 2018 after a year in prison, according to his case statement.
MY1-38.why_new: Where the boat route ended three years later: arrest, a year's jail, return.

MY1-39.claim: Nurul Islam filed a human trafficking case against six people on 29 October 2018 at a Chattogram tribunal, which issued arrest warrants; on 28 October 2019 the 12-year-old brother of the 22-year-old accused Alauddin was produced before a High Court bench in his place and given eight weeks' anticipatory bail, the family then went into hiding, and on 30 May 2024 the Chattogram Human Trafficking Tribunal ordered Ramu police to investigate who the real accused is and sent the man claiming to be Alauddin to jail.
MY1-39.why_new: How a boat-trafficking case stood nearly six years after filing: bail by impersonation, no verdict.

MY1-53.claim: The National Human Rights Commission took up the Malaysia situation on its own motion and, in orders announced on 3 June 2024, said the allegations of extra money taken by fraud, workers sent to name-only companies and workers finding no work in Malaysia must be investigated and action taken against those involved, called for identifying the firms and people responsible for workers with visas and clearance failing to go in time, and gave the Expatriates' Welfare Ministry secretary until 10 July 2024 to report.
MY1-53.target_section: When the visa, the agency and the clearance are all real
MY1-53.why_new: An official body's order naming 'name-only companies' and setting a reporting date.
MY1-53.h3: When the visa, the agency and the clearance are all real

MY1-54.claim: The National Human Rights Commission's orders, announced on 3 June 2024, cite an allegation that in the last 10 days of May about Tk 150 crore was taken from about 30,000 passengers in the name of air tickets, an extra Tk 50,000 from each in the name of airfare, and call for it to be investigated and legal action taken.
MY1-54.target_section: Refund refusals after a failed departure
MY1-54.why_new: A further charge laid on workers just before the deadline: the airfare surcharge.
MY1-54.h3: Refund refusals after a failed departure

MY1-55.claim: On 31 May 2024, the last day for entering Malaysia, thousands of people crowded Dhaka's Hazrat Shahjalal International Airport without tickets in a last attempt to go, according to the National Human Rights Commission.
MY1-55.target_section: When the visa, the agency and the clearance are all real
MY1-55.why_new: Workers with visas and clearance were sent to the airport without tickets.
MY1-55.h3: When the visa, the agency and the clearance are all real

MY1-56.claim: Counts of those who could not go to Malaysia by 31 May 2024 differ: the Expatriates' Welfare Ministry and BMET put those with final clearance at 16,970, a responsible BMET source said 31,304 in all could not go because of visa and approval complications, and BAIRA officials said the number would be about 40,000, according to a Prothom Alo column of 4 June 2024.
MY1-56.target_section: MALAYSIA DOC: What closed it before
MY1-56.why_new: The guide gives only 17,777; these are the early official count and the wider counts of those with visas or approvals but no clearance.
MY1-56.h3: Is it open now, and who can go?

MY1-57.claim: In a Prothom Alo video cited in a 4 June 2024 column, Mohammad Kolim from Barishal, standing on the airport road, said he had paid with a loan taken at interest and could not go to Malaysia, and Belal Hossain from Cox's Bazar said part of his money came from his father, part from uncles who mortgaged the homestead and part from selling cattle, and that all of it was lost.
MY1-57.why_new: How two of the stranded workers had raised the money.

MY1-58.claim: Tanvir Mia (22) of Akhaura, Brahmanbaria, who could not fly to Malaysia by the 31 May 2024 deadline, fell from the door of the Upakul Express train into the Meghna at the Bhairab rail bridge on his way home from the airport and went missing, Prothom Alo reported.
MY1-58.target_section: When the visa, the agency and the clearance are all real
MY1-58.why_new: A named consequence of the failed departures.
MY1-58.h3: When the visa, the agency and the clearance are all real

MY1-59.claim: A Prothom Alo column of 4 June 2024 said, citing newspaper and television reports, that workers had bought plane tickets at three to four times the price with money raised by selling or mortgaging land and livestock and borrowing at interest, and still could not go to Malaysia.
MY1-59.target_section: Refund refusals after a failed departure
MY1-59.why_new: Ticket prices in the last days before the deadline.
MY1-59.h3: Refund refusals after a failed departure

MY1-60.claim: On 14 October 2024 brokers who had put more than a hundred Rohingya from the Ukhiya camps in Cox's Bazar on a fishing trawler, promising to take them to Malaysia, set them down at dawn on Inani beach in Ukhiya after 10 days at sea; police and the Coast Guard detained 26 and the brokers went into hiding.
MY1-60.why_new: Answers the guide's open question: boats were still leaving the Teknaf and Cox's Bazar coast for Malaysia in late 2024, and some never left Bangladeshi waters.

MY1-61.claim: Khurshida Begum (24), a Rohingya woman from Moynarghona camp (Camp 17) in Ukhiya detained at Inani on 14 October 2024, told Prothom Alo she had paid a broker Tk 30,000 after he said she would get a good job in Malaysia; another passenger said the trawler had left from Teknaf, met the Myanmar navy south of St Martin's island and was turned back towards the deep sea.
MY1-61.why_new: The price paid and why the boat turned back.

MY1-62.claim: Police and local representatives in Cox's Bazar said in October 2024 that traffickers become active when the Bay of Bengal is calm, from October-November to March, that brokers lure Rohingya onto trawlers with good jobs in Malaysia and traffic girls on a promise of marriage there, and that they take Tk 20,000 to 30,000 a head before boarding.
MY1-62.why_new: The season, the two lures (job for men, marriage for women) and the up-front price.

MY1-63.claim: Police and local representatives said in October 2024 that trafficking by sea was increasing through the coasts of Teknaf, Ukhiya, Ramu, Cox's Bazar Sadar and Maheshkhali, the Anwara and Banshkhali coasts of Chattogram, and the Karnaphuli river.
MY1-63.why_new: Names the departure coasts for the sea route, which the guide's path lacks.

MY1-64.claim: Police said that on the night of 12 October 2024 the Coast Guard seized a trawler carrying 17 Rohingya from the Mochhoni camp in Teknaf at Shikalbaha in Karnaphuli upazila, Chattogram, and arrested three members of a trafficking ring: Fazal Karim alias Futu Majhi (47) of Kalamarchhara, Maheshkhali, Enamul Karim (37) of Jaliapalong, Ukhiya, and Golam Hossain (40) of Cox's Bazar Sadar.
MY1-64.why_new: A dated seizure with named arrests on the Karnaphuli river.

MY1-65.claim: Police said that from 2016 to 2023 law enforcers rescued 1,134 people being trafficked to Malaysia by sea, 95 per cent of them Rohingya, and that 85 cases were filed at Ukhiya and Teknaf police stations in that period naming 1,200 accused, of whom 508 were caught.
MY1-65.why_new: Rescue, case and arrest counts for the sea route; the section has no numbers on it.

MY1-66.claim: Lawyer Abdus Shukkur, president of the Human Rights Defenders Forum-Cox's Bazar, said in October 2024 that broker rings were targeting Rohingya, especially girls, and that in the past few years at least 300 people had died in more than 20 trawler sinkings during trafficking to Malaysia.
MY1-66.why_new: Deaths at sea on this route, from a named local rights lawyer.

MY1-67.claim: RAB rescued 31 people, 27 Rohingya from the Ukhiya and Teknaf camps and 4 Bangladeshis, on the night of 17 November 2024 from an abandoned den in the Kachchhapia hills of Baharchhara union, Teknaf; each had paid Tk 20,000 to be taken to Malaysia by sea, the young women having been promised marriage to good grooms and the young men well-paid jobs, and instead they were confined in the hills and pressed to get money from relatives.
MY1-67.why_new: The boat offer used as a front for confinement and ransom inside Bangladesh, with Bangladeshi victims too.

MY1-68.claim: Those rescued from the Teknaf hill den in November 2024 said during questioning that the traffickers pressed them to contact relatives for money and told them to say they were in Myanmar, that food was not given properly and they were tortured; one said he had been held for eight days and another had been held for more than 13.
MY1-68.why_new: How the ransom call is staged: the family is told the person is already in Myanmar.

MY1-69.claim: According to RAB, Ekhlas Mia of Mochhar Khola, Ukhiya, and his cousin were abducted by traffickers on 12 November 2024 while visiting the Kachchhapia area on the Marine Drive and held in a hilltop den where men, women and children were already confined and tortured for money; unable to pay ransom, he was brought to the beach on the night of 16 November with 15 to 20 other young people to be trafficked by sea, slipped away before boarding and asked RAB to rescue the rest.
MY1-69.why_new: A local Bangladeshi abducted and put in the boat queue because his family could not pay: people on this route are not all willing passengers.

MY1-70.claim: RAB arrested two men as traffickers in the November 2024 Teknaf rescue, Md Anwar (44) of Pankhali, Hnila, and Atiqur Rahman (32) of Uttar Lambari, Teknaf Sadar; the Teknaf police officer-in-charge said a case had been filed against the two under the human trafficking law and five days' remand would be sought for each.

MY1-71.claim: On 14 December 2024 Teknaf police rescued 30 people, 15 men, 3 women and 12 children from the Ukhiya and Teknaf Rohingya camps, from the house of Saiful Islam in Dakshin Lambari Para, Teknaf Sadar union, where they were being held for ransom after being gathered for trafficking to Malaysia with promises of good jobs and marriage; the ring's members fled and nobody was arrested.
MY1-71.why_new: A second holding-house case a month later, this time with no arrest.

MY1-72.claim: The officer-in-charge of Teknaf police station said in December 2024 that every winter broker rings hold Rohingya from the Ukhiya and Teknaf camps for ransom in the name of sending them to Malaysia by sea, and that sometimes they put them on a big trawler, sail around for several days, leave them in different parts of Cox's Bazar and run off with the money.
MY1-72.why_new: A police officer describing the fake voyage as a routine trick.

MY1-73.claim: RMMRU, a migration research body, said in its report 'Trends in labour migration from Bangladesh 2024', presented on 28 December 2024, that Dato Amin, owner of Malaysia's foreign-worker recruitment software, and his Bangladeshi associate Ruhul Amin jointly built the syndicate, which sent five and a half lakh workers and embezzled USD 200 crore (Tk 24,000 crore) from migrants.
MY1-73.why_new: A research body, not only the press, naming the two and putting a figure on the take.
MY1-73.h3: How a job reaches you, and who takes a cut

MY1-74.claim: According to RMMRU's December 2024 report, the Bangladesh government had started legal proceedings against four members of parliament for involvement with the Malaysia syndicate and had written to the Malaysian government asking it to hand over the syndicate's two ringleaders.
MY1-74.why_new: Action taken after August 2024: proceedings against the four MPs and the extradition request.
MY1-74.h3: How a job reaches you, and who takes a cut

MY1-75.claim: RMMRU's December 2024 report said no labour migration took place in 2024 to several countries including Oman, Bahrain, the United Arab Emirates and the Maldives, and that labour migration to Italy was stalled because of forged documents and to Serbia because the server of the application process was out of order.
MY1-75.target_section: Why won't BMET clear workers for some countries?
MY1-75.why_new: Which corridors were shut in 2024 and why Italy and Serbia stalled (dated; check against the section's current list).

MY1-76.claim: According to RMMRU, 9,06,355 workers went abroad from Bangladesh from January to November 2024 against 13,05,453 in the whole of 2023, and 54,696 of them were women, 6 per cent of the total and the lowest in ten years apart from the pandemic period.
MY1-76.target_section: Which countries can I go to for work right now?
MY1-76.why_new: 2024 departure totals and the women's share (dated figures).

MY1-77.claim: According to police and local representatives in Teknaf, Cox's Bazar, trafficking by sea rose again from January 2024 after six or seven years of being largely stopped, and in the past year (to January 2025) law enforcers rescued at least 600 people, including 45 traffickers, in eight or nine operations on the Teknaf coast, most of those rescued being Rohingya men, women and children.
MY1-77.why_new: Dates the revival of the Teknaf boat route to January 2024 and gives a one-year rescue count.

MY1-78.claim: Rafiq Ullah, a Rohingya leader at the Lambashia camp in Ukhiya, told Prothom Alo in January 2025 that more than five hundred young men and women of marriageable age had been sent towards Malaysia from that camp in the past year and that more than three hundred had been caught by law enforcers and come back.
MY1-78.why_new: Scale from a single camp, and the share caught.

MY1-79.claim: Kamal Hossain, a Rohingya leader at the Balukhali camp, said in January 2025 that before reaching Malaysia Rohingya are held at the Thailand or Myanmar border while ransom is demanded from their relatives in the camps in Bangladesh, and that if this fails there are attempts to abduct members of that family.
MY1-79.why_new: The ransom stage en route and what happens to the family at home if it is not paid.

MY1-80.claim: Police and local representatives said at least 193 people, 86 of them Rohingya, were abducted in Teknaf in a little over a year to January 2025 and at least 98 were freed on ransom; the district's additional superintendent of police said investigations of several of the abductions found a link to human trafficking and the involvement of some local residents of Teknaf.
MY1-80.why_new: Abduction for ransom around the Teknaf departure points, tied by police to trafficking.

MY1-81.claim: Prothom Alo reported in January 2025 that 20 abduction cases had been filed at Teknaf police station in the past year, and the station's officer-in-charge said that although releases on ransom are reported in the media, none of the victims wants to come to the station to complain or give information.
MY1-81.why_new: Why few cases follow: victims who paid ransom do not complain.

MY1-82.claim: On 11 March 2025 the Anti-Corruption Commission (ACC) filed cases against 32 owners and officials of 12 recruiting agencies, alleging they took five times the government-fixed Tk 78,990 from 67,380 Malaysia-bound workers and embezzled Tk 1,128 crore, its director general Md Akhtar Hossain told a press conference.
MY1-82.why_new: The first batch of ACC cases, with date, number of accused, workers and amount; the guide says only that cases were filed against dozens of agencies.
MY1-82.h3: How a job reaches you, and who takes a cut

MY1-83.claim: In the ACC's 11 March 2025 cases, M/s Orbital Enterprise (owner Kashmiri Kamal, wife of former finance minister A H M Mustafa Kamal) is alleged to have taken an extra Tk 100 crore 98 lakh 57 thousand 500 from 6,029 workers and M/s Orbital International (owner his daughter Nafisa Kamal) an extra Tk 50 crore 16 lakh 62 thousand from 2,995; Mustafa Kamal is an accused in both cases.
MY1-83.why_new: Per-agency allegation with worker count and amount.
MY1-83.h3: How a job reaches you, and who takes a cut

MY1-84.claim: In the ACC's 11 March 2025 cases, Snigdha Overseas Limited is alleged to have taken an extra Tk 111 crore 50 lakh 47 thousand 500 from 6,657 workers (accused: owner and former MP Nizam Uddin Hazari, his wife Nurjahan Begum and five staff) and Binimoy International an extra Tk 91 crore 42 lakh 15 thousand from 5,458 (accused: owner Abdus Sobhan Bhuiyan, former Chauddagram upazila chairman, and his wife Taslima Akter).
MY1-84.why_new: Per-agency allegation with worker count and amount.
MY1-84.h3: How a job reaches you, and who takes a cut

MY1-85.claim: In the ACC's 11 March 2025 cases, FiveM International is alleged to have taken an extra Tk 119 crore 32 lakh 70 thousand from 7,124 workers (accused: owner and former Feni MP Lt Gen (retd) Masud Uddin Chowdhury, his daughter Tasnia Masud and two others who worked there) and M/s Unique Eastern Private Limited Tk 63 crore 44 lakh 90 thousand from 3,788 (accused: owner Md Noor Ali, his wife Selina Ali, daughter Nabila Ali and former secretary Khondaker Shawkat Hossain).
MY1-85.why_new: Per-agency allegation with worker count and amount.
MY1-85.h3: How a job reaches you, and who takes a cut

MY1-86.claim: In the ACC's 11 March 2025 cases, Catharsis International Limited is alleged to have taken an extra Tk 130 crore 43 lakh 22 thousand 500 from 7,787 workers (accused: owner Mohammad Ruhul Amin and his wife Lutfur Nesa Shelly), M/s Ahmad International Tk 143 crore 91 lakh 60 thousand from 8,592 (accused: owner and former Dhaka-20 MP Benzir Ahmad) and BM Travels Limited Tk 135 crore 55 lakh 77 thousand 500 from 8,093 (accused: owner and former Dhaka North councillor Shafiqul Islam and his wife Mousumi Akter).
MY1-86.why_new: Per-agency allegation with worker count and amount.
MY1-86.h3: How a job reaches you, and who takes a cut

MY1-87.claim: In the ACC's 11 March 2025 cases, BNS Overseas Limited is alleged to have taken Tk 70 crore 60 lakh 12 thousand 500 from 4,215 workers (accused: owner and Jubo League leader Ishtiaque Ahmed Saikat and his wife Nasrun Nesa), Rubel Bangladesh Limited Tk 47 crore 65 lakh 37 thousand 500 from 2,845 (accused: owner Muhammad Mojibul Haque Rubel and his wife Kamrun Nahar Hiramoni) and The Ifti Overseas an extra Tk 63 crore 59 lakh 97 thousand 500 from 3,797 (accused: owners Md Rubel and Borhan Uddin Panna).
MY1-87.why_new: Per-agency allegation with worker count and amount.
MY1-87.h3: How a job reaches you, and who takes a cut

MY1-88.claim: According to an ISPR (armed forces' public relations) statement, on 8 April 2025 the navy ship Durjoy seized the fishing trawler FB Kulsuma in the Bay of Bengal 44 nautical miles south-west of St Martin's island with 214 passengers, 118 men, 68 women and 28 children, who were being sent illegally to Malaysia; the trawler had set out at about 2 a.m. after 7 April from Shaplapur beach in Baharchhara union, Teknaf, and had no minimum life-saving equipment or adequate food and water.
MY1-88.why_new: A dated 2025 boat interception: boats still leave Teknaf, with over 200 aboard a fishing trawler.

MY1-89.claim: A sub-inspector of the Shah Porir Dwip police outpost, citing the Rohingya rescued in April 2025, said several broker rings were active in stages, bringing people out of the camps, driving them to the Kachchhapia area of Teknaf and putting them on the trawler, which was to pass the St Martin's coast and reach Thailand through Myanmar waters, from where the passengers were promised they would be handed on and delivered to Malaysia.
MY1-89.why_new: The sea route step by step in 2025: camp, vehicle to Kachchhapia, trawler, Myanmar waters, Thailand, handover.

MY1-90.claim: The Shah Porir Dwip police sub-inspector said the Rohingya rescued in April 2025 had been promised good jobs in Malaysia or marriage to a suitable man, that many girls had been married over the phone, and that the broker rings had taken Tk 30,000 to 50,000 from most of them.
MY1-90.why_new: The 2025 price and the phone-marriage lure.

MY1-91.claim: A Rohingya young woman from the Balukhali camp (Camp 9) in Ukhiya, Cox's Bazar, was married over the phone on 3 April 2025 to a young man living in Malaysia whom she had never met, her parents having agreed at a broker's word; on 5 April she was handed to a broker, kept with other Rohingya women in a house in the Kachchhapia hills of Teknaf and put on a trawler for Malaysia that the navy seized on 8 April, and she said her family had spent about Tk 50,000 by the time she boarded.
MY1-91.why_new: A phone marriage to an unseen husband used to put a woman on a smuggling boat; the section has only China cases.

MY1-92.claim: A driver from Kotbazar, Ukhiya, rescued from the trawler seized in April 2025 said two men hired his auto-rickshaw on 2 April, held him at gunpoint in a deserted spot and took him to the Kachchhapia hills in Baharchhara, Teknaf, where he was kept for four days in a hut with 20 to 25 other men and women, and that he was forced onto the trawler on the night of 7 April.
MY1-92.why_new: A Bangladeshi abducted and forced onto the boat.

MY1-93.claim: After the April 2025 interception the 214 passengers were handed to Teknaf police on 9 April; the Refugee Relief and Repatriation Commissioner said legal action was being taken against 12 of the rescued Rohingya for involvement in various crimes and the rest were handed back to the camps.
MY1-93.why_new: What the authorities did with those intercepted.

MY1-94.claim: In a memorandum handed to the Chief Adviser's office on 5 May 2025, BAIRA members alleged that in the last round Tk 1 lakh 52 thousand per worker had to be paid to the syndicate, that agencies were made syndicate members for Tk 5 crore each, and that this time Tk 14 crore each was being collected.
MY1-94.why_new: A stated price for an agency's place on the list, last round and in 2025.
MY1-94.h3: How a job reaches you, and who takes a cut

MY1-95.claim: The BAIRA members' 5 May 2025 memorandum alleged that the syndicate's ringleaders, Bangladesh-born Malaysian citizen Amin Nor and the fugitive Ruhul Amin, known as Swapan, and their Awami League associates were currently active in forming a syndicate with some influential political leaders, and demanded that Malaysia be asked to scrap the disputed online recruitment software.
MY1-95.why_new: The allegation, a year before the 2026 list, that the same two were rebuilding the ring; Ruhul Amin described as a fugitive.
MY1-95.h3: How a job reaches you, and who takes a cut

MY1-96.claim: The memorandum of 5 May 2025 proposed an alternative: BMET would build a database of interested workers, recruiting agencies would take workers from it, the worker would deposit the government-fixed cost through a bank and BMET would supervise the whole process; 453 recruiting agency owners had signed a memorandum with the same demand submitted to the Expatriates' Welfare Ministry on 21 April 2025.
MY1-96.why_new: The agencies' own proposal to cut out brokers and cash, and how many agencies backed opening the market.
MY1-96.h3: How a job reaches you, and who takes a cut

MY1-97.claim: Writing in Prothom Alo on 2 June 2025, Dhaka University associate professor and RMMRU researcher Mohammad Rashed Alam Bhuiyan said that in a letter of 23 April 2025, reported by Bloomberg News, Azman Mohd Yusof, secretary general of Malaysia's human resources ministry, called on Bangladesh to review and withdraw 'unsubstantiated allegations' of wrongdoing in labour migration between the two countries in order to improve Malaysia's rating in the annual US trafficking report.
MY1-97.why_new: Malaysia's request that Bangladesh drop the allegations, relevant to how the cases ended.
MY1-97.h3: How a job reaches you, and who takes a cut

MY1-98.claim: The same June 2025 column said that Bangladesh's police and Anti-Corruption Commission had begun investigating the recruitment process, that a complaint under the human trafficking law was made against the syndicate, and that in October 2024 Bangladesh police asked the Malaysian government to arrest and return two migration businessmen accused of trafficking migrant workers, money laundering and embezzlement.
MY1-98.why_new: Dates the police request to Malaysia to October 2024 and records the trafficking-law complaint.
MY1-98.h3: How a job reaches you, and who takes a cut
