MY1-99.claim: According to the June 2025 column, Malaysia said about 11,000 people had been unable to go despite holding valid calling visas, the expatriates' welfare adviser said Malaysia would initially arrange work for about eight thousand of them, no visible step had yet been taken, and recruiting agency owners and the press put the number much higher.
MY1-99.target_section: MALAYSIA DOC: What closed it before
MY1-99.why_new: Malaysia's own count of the stranded (about 11,000) against Bangladesh's, as of mid-2025.
MY1-99.h3: Is it open now, and who can go?

MY1-100.claim: A revised notice from the Bangladesh High Commission in Malaysia on 1 August 2025 said the Malaysian authorities had approved employment through BOESL (Bangladesh Overseas Employment and Services Limited) for workers from among those who could not come by 31 May 2024, and that the Malaysian government had decided to hire them in the construction or tourism sectors.
MY1-100.target_section: MALAYSIA DOC: What closed it before
MY1-100.why_new: The sectors (construction or tourism) and the date of Malaysia's decision on the stranded workers.
MY1-100.h3: Is it open now, and who can go?

MY1-101.claim: Under the High Commission's 1 August 2025 notice, for tourism-sector workers all information on the attached checklist for attesting the demand letter is to be submitted on Malaysia's FWCMS online portal, applications for construction workers go through CLAB (Construction Labour Exchange Centre Berhad) onto the same portal, and the originals plus one set of photocopies of everything submitted are to be lodged with the High Commission.
MY1-101.target_section: MALAYSIA DOC: What closed it before
MY1-101.why_new: How the employer-side filing for the stranded workers was to be done (FWCMS, CLAB, hard copies to the mission).
MY1-101.h3: Is it open now, and who can go?

MY1-102.claim: Of the 16,970 workers who had final clearance but could not go to Malaysia in 2024, Prothom Alo reported that one part could not get air tickets and another part did not get the employer's final consent from Malaysia: the employer had not sent the assurance that it would receive them at the airport.
MY1-102.target_section: MALAYSIA DOC: What closed it before
MY1-102.why_new: The two reasons cleared workers did not fly, including the employer's missing airport-reception assurance.
MY1-102.h3: Is it open now, and who can go?

MY1-103.claim: In a warning posted on its Facebook page on 1 August 2025, the Bangladesh High Commission in Kuala Lumpur said an organised ring was collecting passports and cash from Bangladeshis by promising to send them to work in Malaysia's Sabah state, that there was no agreement or understanding between the two governments on recruiting for Sabah and no decision from the Sabah authorities to hire Bangladeshi workers, and that any permission would be announced on the High Commission's website.
MY1-103.why_new: The guide has the Sabah warning; this adds its date and where a real opening would be announced (the High Commission's website).
MY1-103.h3: Is it open now, and who can go?

MY1-104.claim: On 28 August 2025 a CID sub-inspector, Md Moniruzzaman, filed a money-laundering case at Banani police station against 33 people of the Malaysia labour-market syndicate, among them three former MPs, a former minister's wife and Ruhul Amin, known as Swapan; the case says an inquiry into laundering of money taken by fraud found preliminary evidence of the accused's involvement.
MY1-104.why_new: The CID's money-laundering case: date, station, number of accused.
MY1-104.h3: How a job reaches you, and who takes a cut

MY1-105.claim: The CID's case statement of 28 August 2025 alleges that the accused, in collusion, took money from 9,372 workers sent to Malaysia through Five M International, the recruiting agency of Lt Gen (retd) Masud Uddin Chowdhury, that Five M took Tk 1.5 lakh per worker, and that Tk 1 lakh 7 thousand 510 of this was laundered, more than Tk 100 crore in all, a figure that may change during investigation.
MY1-105.target_section: MALAYSIA DOC: Where a Tk 5.5 lakh deal goes
MY1-105.why_new: A police case putting numbers on the split of the per-worker toll: Tk 1.5 lakh taken, Tk 1,07,510 of it sent out.
MY1-105.h3: What you pay, and what you earn and keep

MY1-106.claim: The accused named in the CID's August 2025 money-laundering case include former Feni-3 MP Masud Uddin Chowdhury, his wife Jesmin Masud and daughter Tasnia Masud, Ahmed International's owner Benzir Ahmed, Snigdha Overseas Limited's proprietor Nizam Uddin Hazari, Kashmeri Kamal of Orbitals Enterprise, and Ruhul Amin, former BAIRA secretary general and owner of Catharsis International; the case was filed under the Money Laundering Prevention Act.
MY1-106.why_new: Who is named and under which Act.
MY1-106.h3: How a job reaches you, and who takes a cut

MY1-107.claim: On 4 November 2025 the Anti-Corruption Commission approved six cases against 11 owners and officials of six recruiting agencies, alleging that on average five times the government-fixed Tk 78,990 was collected from 31,331 Malaysia-bound workers and Tk 525 crore 22 lakh 97 thousand 500 embezzled and laundered, its director general Md Akhtar Hossain said on 6 November.
MY1-107.why_new: The third batch of ACC cases, with date, workers and amount.
MY1-107.h3: How a job reaches you, and who takes a cut

MY1-108.claim: The ACC cases approved in November 2025 allege extra collections by M/s Amin Tours and Travels (owner Ruhul Amin) of Tk 124 crore 45 lakh 25 thousand from 7,430 people, by M/s Merit Trade International Limited (chairman Hasan Ahmed Chowdhury Kiron) of Tk 58 crore 44 lakh 7 thousand 500 from 3,489, and by Sadia International (Shamim Ahmed Chowdhury alias Noman) of Tk 55 crore 62 lakh 67 thousand 500 from 3,321.
MY1-108.why_new: Per-agency allegation with worker count and amount.
MY1-108.h3: How a job reaches you, and who takes a cut

MY1-109.claim: The ACC cases approved in November 2025 also allege collections by Imperial Resource Limited (chairman Md Iqbal Hossain, managing director Badruddoza Chowdhury) of Tk 135 crore 69 lakh 17 thousand 500 from 8,101 people, by RRC Human Resource Service Limited (chairman Mohammad Moniruzzaman, managing director Md Alamgir Kabir) of an extra Tk 87 crore 13 lakh 35 thousand from 5,202, and by Thanex International Limited (former manager Abdullah Shahed, director Md Joynal Abedin Nomani, current manager Shamser Ahmed) of an extra Tk 63 crore 88 lakh 90 thousand from 3,788.
MY1-109.why_new: Per-agency allegation with worker count and amount.
MY1-109.h3: How a job reaches you, and who takes a cut

MY1-110.claim: Before the November 2025 cases the ACC had filed cases on 11 March 2025 against 32 people over Tk 1,128 crore and on 14 September 2025 against the top officials of 13 recruiting agencies over Tk 1,159 crore, all over sending workers to Malaysia.
MY1-110.why_new: Gives the three ACC batches together: 12, 13 and 6 agencies.
MY1-110.h3: How a job reaches you, and who takes a cut

MY1-111.claim: Dhaka Metropolitan Police's Detective Branch (DB) arrested Lt Gen (retd) Masud Uddin Chowdhury, a former Feni-3 MP who had obtained a recruiting licence, at his home in Baridhara DOHS, Dhaka, at midnight on a Monday (reported by Prothom Alo on 24 March 2026), and a court granted five days' remand in a human trafficking case of Paltan police station.
MY1-111.why_new: The first reported arrest of a syndicate agency owner; the guide records cases and licence cancellations but no arrest.
MY1-111.h3: How a job reaches you, and who takes a cut

MY1-112.claim: The Paltan police station case in which Masud Uddin Chowdhury was remanded was filed on 3 September 2025 by Altab Khan, owner of a firm named Afia Overseas, alleging embezzlement through a syndicate and human trafficking, and names 103 accused in all.
MY1-112.why_new: A trafficking case against the syndicate brought by another agency owner, with 103 accused.
MY1-112.h3: How a job reaches you, and who takes a cut

MY1-113.claim: A DB additional commissioner said in March 2026 that Masud Uddin Chowdhury faces 11 cases in Feni and Dhaka, including cases at Dhaka's Paltan, Banani, Kotwali, Mirpur and Hatirjheel police stations on charges including murder, attempted murder and human trafficking, and that the ACC and the CID are investigating several allegations against him; at the remand hearing the public prosecutor said the accused had made off with Tk 24,000 crore in the name of sending people abroad.
MY1-113.why_new: Number and kind of cases pending against one syndicate agency owner.
MY1-113.h3: How a job reaches you, and who takes a cut

MY1-114.claim: Prothom Alo reported that Masud Uddin Chowdhury went into business after retiring in 2014, later obtained a manpower-export (recruiting) licence, and was then accused of making huge sums through the syndicate for sending workers to Malaysia.
MY1-114.why_new: Background of the owner of the top Malaysia sender.
MY1-114.h3: How a job reaches you, and who takes a cut

MY1-115.claim: A law-enforcement source told Prothom Alo in March 2026 that the ACC has a case against Masud Uddin Chowdhury alleging embezzlement of Tk 119 crore and has applied to the court to show him arrested in it, and that the court fixed 9 April 2026 for an order; a DB joint commissioner said he was on remand in a specific case and that information obtained from him was being verified.
MY1-115.why_new: Where the ACC's Five M case stood a year after filing: the accused only now being shown arrested.
MY1-115.h3: How a job reaches you, and who takes a cut

MY1-116.claim: Sources involved in the questioning told Prothom Alo that Masud Uddin Chowdhury is being asked how he used the state machinery in starting a manpower-export business after retirement and in allegedly building a syndicate in the name of sending workers to Malaysia and embezzling large sums.
MY1-116.h3: How a job reaches you, and who takes a cut

OT1-1.claim: Prothom Alo reported on 10 February 2024 that BMET smart cards (emigration clearance) are issued both offline, directly by BMET and the district manpower offices, and online through Ami Probashi, a mobile app run by a private organisation, with all data kept on a server at the BMET office, and that a ring had recently taken out smart cards in two batches of 24 and 20.
OT1-1.target_section: Fake BMET cards and fake clearance
OT1-1.why_new: The section says rings obtain BMET cards for fake visas but not how cards are issued (two channels, one a private app) or this dated incident inside BMET's own system.
OT1-1.h3: Fake BMET cards and fake clearance

OT1-2.claim: According to sources cited by Prothom Alo, 20 smart card applications that had been rejected in the Ami Probashi app between 27 December 2023 and 4 January 2024 were later given clearance; BMET formed a six-member inquiry committee on 10 January 2024, which reported on 7 February.
OT1-2.target_section: Fake BMET cards and fake clearance
OT1-2.why_new: A dated case of rejected clearance applications being approved from inside the system; not in the guide.
OT1-2.h3: Fake BMET cards and fake clearance

OT1-3.claim: BMET's inquiry report on the 20 cards said they were approved through the account of BMET's Additional Director General: 19 from an Android phone through two separate IP addresses and one from the Additional Director General's own computer, on which his ID and password were kept saved.
OT1-3.target_section: Fake BMET cards and fake clearance
OT1-3.why_new: Shows the mechanism: a senior official's login was used to approve rejected applications.
OT1-3.h3: Fake BMET cards and fake clearance

OT1-4.claim: The inquiry committee, which included representatives of the Expatriates' Welfare Ministry, Ami Probashi and the Bangladesh Computer Council (BCC), did not finally hold anyone responsible; its report said the Ami Probashi system has no automatic session time-out and no one-time PIN (OTP) to protect passwords, and that hackers used these or other system flaws to approve the rejected cards with the Additional Director General's ID.
OT1-4.target_section: Fake BMET cards and fake clearance
OT1-4.why_new: What the authorities found and did not do (no one held responsible); the specific security gaps.
OT1-4.h3: Fake BMET cards and fake clearance

OT1-5.claim: A BMET source told Prothom Alo that the regular Additional Director General (Employment) was on leave at the time and Ashraful Islam, the Additional Director General (Training), was covering; he told the inquiry committee that to his knowledge he had not finalised any worker's rejected application and claimed the Ami Probashi system had been hacked before, while the app's chief technical officer told the committee that no one other than a system user, neither its own staff nor an outsider, could do such a thing.
OT1-5.target_section: Fake BMET cards and fake clearance
OT1-5.why_new: Both sides' accounts of who could have approved the cards.
OT1-5.h3: Fake BMET cards and fake clearance

OT1-6.claim: A BMET source told Prothom Alo that, of the 20 cards under inquiry, 8 were taken in the name of the recruiting agency Bangladesh Export Corporation (RL-803), 7 on 2 January and 1 on 3 January 2024, and 12 in the name of Saad International Limited (RL-1068), 7 on 1 January and 5 on 3 January.
OT1-6.target_section: Fake BMET cards and fake clearance
OT1-6.why_new: Names the agencies in whose names the cards were issued, with licence numbers and dates.
OT1-6.h3: Fake BMET cards and fake clearance

OT1-7.claim: Saad International's managing director Shamim Mahmud Patwari told Prothom Alo that no complaint had ever been made against his agency, that it applied and got clearance by the rules as always, that no one from BMET had contacted him and that he knew nothing of any irregularity; Prothom Alo could not get a comment from Bangladesh Export Corporation.
OT1-7.target_section: Fake BMET cards and fake clearance
OT1-7.why_new: The named agencies' response, needed if they are named.
OT1-7.h3: Fake BMET cards and fake clearance

OT1-8.claim: On 31 December 2023 the recruiting agency Alif Overseas (RL-847) took out smart cards for 24 Saudi Arabia-bound workers, Prothom Alo reported; BMET officials noticed in the third week of January 2024 while checking papers that no matching data for these cards could be found on the server, the Director General was told in writing on 28 January, and a senior source confirmed that BMET took no immediate action and did not cancel the cards.
OT1-8.target_section: Fake BMET cards and fake clearance
OT1-8.why_new: A dated case of real smart cards with no data behind them on BMET's server, and that the cards were not cancelled.
OT1-8.h3: Fake BMET cards and fake clearance

OT1-9.claim: On 5 February 2024 BMET's Director General Saleh Ahmed Mozaffar wrote to the Dhaka Metropolitan Police deputy commissioner for cyber crime investigation asking him to identify those involved, the letter saying Alif Overseas had taken 24 emigration clearances by hacking the system; the deputy commissioner told Prothom Alo the letter had not yet reached his office.
OT1-9.target_section: Fake BMET cards and fake clearance
OT1-9.why_new: What the authorities did: a referral to cyber police, not a case; no arrest or licence action is reported.
OT1-9.h3: Fake BMET cards and fake clearance

OT1-10.claim: Akib Jabed, son of Alif Overseas's owner Md Monirul Haque, told Prothom Alo that the agency has no ability to hack BMET's server, that it never applied for the 24 cards, and that someone inside BMET who took out cards in Alif Overseas's name may be involved.
OT1-10.target_section: Fake BMET cards and fake clearance
OT1-10.why_new: The agency's denial and its counter-allegation against BMET insiders.
OT1-10.h3: Fake BMET cards and fake clearance

OT1-11.claim: People concerned told Prothom Alo in February 2024 that the server kept at BMET's office could not be secured and ran on very old software, so fraud could not be stopped and those involved could not be identified; BMET was moving server management to the Bangladesh Computer Council, a third of the data had been moved, and two BMET officials said that once done, taking smart cards by server fraud would stop and any further fraud would be easy to detect.
OT1-11.target_section: Fake BMET cards and fake clearance
OT1-11.why_new: Why fake-data smart cards were possible and BMET's stated fix.
OT1-11.h3: Fake BMET cards and fake clearance

OT1-12.claim: A top BMET official told Prothom Alo, on condition of anonymity, that the cyber police had been asked to look into BMET server fraud as a whole and not only the 24 cards, and that the Bangladesh Computer Council had been asked a month and a half earlier to investigate BMET's server and submit an audit report.
OT1-12.target_section: Fake BMET cards and fake clearance
OT1-12.why_new: Shows the scale BMET itself suspected and the audit requested.
OT1-12.h3: Fake BMET cards and fake clearance

OT1-13.claim: BMET's inquiry committee made eight recommendations to prevent fraud through the Ami Probashi app, among them introducing OTP and session time-out, having the BCC test the system's weaknesses, an IT audit, and keeping all of the app's data on BMET's server.
OT1-13.target_section: Fake BMET cards and fake clearance
OT1-13.why_new: The official remedy proposed; useful for a Need-to-know on whether it was done.
OT1-13.h3: Fake BMET cards and fake clearance

OT1-14.claim: Tasneem Siddiqui, founding chair of RMMRU (the Refugee and Migratory Movements Research Unit), said in February 2024 that workers sent abroad without proper verification can be cheated, and that the agencies in whose names smart cards were fraudulently taken must be investigated and punished if guilty.
OT1-14.target_section: Fake BMET cards and fake clearance
OT1-14.why_new: Named expert on what an unverified clearance means for the worker.
OT1-14.h3: Fake BMET cards and fake clearance

OT1-15.claim: Sajal Baidya, 35, of Jagannathpur, Sunamganj, who had come home from Saudi Arabia about three years earlier, lost Tk 6 lakh a few months before March 2024 trying to go to Romania through a dalal and then engaged another dalal to go to Italy for Tk 13 lakh, a relative told Prothom Alo; he died under a train at Kulaura station, Moulvibazar, on 6 March 2024, and the railway police officer in charge said that, from talking to relatives, it appeared he had killed himself by jumping under the moving train.
OT1-15.why_new: A dated case of a Romania payment lost to a dalal followed by a second, larger payment to another dalal, ending in a death; no police action against the dalals is reported.

OT1-16.claim: The Maldives stopped issuing new work visas to Bangladeshis from April 2024 because Bangladesh had filled the cap of 100,000 workers from any single country set by a law passed under the previous Maldivian government, according to the Expatriates' Welfare Ministry, the Bangladesh High Commission and its first secretary (labour) Md Sohel Parvez; the High Commission announced the stop in a notice on 22 May 2024.
OT1-16.target_section: Refund refusals after a failed departure
OT1-16.why_new: A mechanism the section lacks: a destination closing mid-process (country quota) after people have paid.
OT1-16.h3: Refund refusals after a failed departure

OT1-17.claim: Monir Hossain of Chattogram told Prothom Alo in May 2024 that he paid Tk 2 lakh 60 thousand to go to the Maldives through an acquaintance, with Tk 2 lakh more due once the visa came; the visa was promised for March 2024 and had not come, he could not tell whether the Maldives would issue it at all, and he was paying monthly interest on a Tk 1 lakh loan.
OT1-17.target_section: Refund refusals after a failed departure
OT1-17.why_new: A named, dated case of money paid before a visa that the destination then stopped issuing.
OT1-17.h3: Refund refusals after a failed departure

OT1-18.claim: Sheikh Alamin of Chandpur said in May 2024 that he had paid Tk 35 thousand to a dalal he knew to go to the Maldives, that the market closed again only three months after reopening and many like him who had deposited money were left in uncertainty, and that the dalal was still giving various assurances.
OT1-18.target_section: Refund refusals after a failed departure
OT1-18.why_new: Shows the dalal keeping the money and offering assurances after the market closed.
OT1-18.h3: Refund refusals after a failed departure

OT1-19.claim: By 22 May 2024, 6,436 people had taken BMET clearance to go to the Maldives after unskilled workers began to be sent from January 2024, and a large share of them were stuck without visas, a number no one could confirm, Prothom Alo reported.
OT1-19.target_section: Refund refusals after a failed departure
OT1-19.why_new: Shows people holding BMET clearance and still stuck without a visa; the section has only the Malaysia 2024 figure.
OT1-19.h3: Refund refusals after a failed departure

OT1-20.claim: Prothom Alo reported in May 2024 that the Maldives gives Bangladeshi tourists a visa at the airport, that dalals use this to cheat workers, and that some workers went to the Maldives this way without the embassy's attestation and were being identified.
OT1-20.target_section: Visit and tourist visas sold as jobs
OT1-20.why_new: The section describes forged Maldives work visas; this adds the on-arrival tourist visa as the opening dalals use, and that such workers were being identified.
OT1-20.h3: Visit and tourist visas sold as jobs

OT1-21.claim: The Bangladesh High Commission in the Maldives warned in its notice of 22 May 2024 that there is no scope to work in the country outside the approved employer, and said a number of unskilled workers had been sent home for breaking this law.
OT1-21.target_section: Free visas and visa trading in the Gulf
OT1-21.why_new: An earlier dated warning, with the fact that deportations had already happened.
OT1-21.h3: Free visas and visa trading in the Gulf

OT1-22.claim: In May 2024 the Maldives had close to two lakh foreign workers, Bangladeshis being the largest group: one lakh legal Bangladeshi workers and possibly at least 30 thousand more irregular ones, Prothom Alo reported.
OT1-22.target_section: Visit and tourist visas sold as jobs
OT1-22.why_new: Scale of irregular Bangladeshi workers in the Maldives; not in the guide.
OT1-22.h3: Visit and tourist visas sold as jobs

OT1-23.claim: Prothom Alo reported in May 2024 that the Maldives labour market closed in 2019 (BMET data show 4,411 workers went that year), that after the pandemic began the Maldives started catching workers without valid papers and sending them home, with 16 thousand forced to return between March and December 2021, and that the Maldives regularised about 40 thousand irregular Bangladeshi workers over the following years before the market reopened in December 2023.
OT1-23.target_section: Visit and tourist visas sold as jobs
OT1-23.why_new: How irregular work in the Maldives has ended (forced returns) and the open-close history.
OT1-23.h3: Visit and tourist visas sold as jobs

OT1-24.claim: Studies of Bangladeshi workers in the Maldives by RMMRU with the Asia Foundation found that 96 percent of the workers who went there had gone through relatives or dalals, that irregular workers work for lower pay, and that a legal worker sends home more than Tk 3 lakh a year against more than Tk 2 lakh for an irregular one, Prothom Alo reported in May 2024.
OT1-24.why_new: A corridor-specific share of dalal or relative recruitment and the earnings gap for irregular workers.

OT1-25.claim: At the Mymensingh regional passport office, a passport application submitted through a dalal is called a "channel file" (চ্যানেল ফাইল): three dalals told Prothom Alo in 2024, on condition of anonymity, that every shop outside the office now does channel files for Tk 2,500 above the government fee, of which Tk 1,200 goes to the passport office and the rest to the dalals.
OT1-25.why_new: The trade term, the street price and the split between dalal and office; the guide has only TIB survey averages.

OT1-26.claim: The three dalals said a fake "nationality and character certificate" in the name of Mymensingh City Corporation is attached to a channel file with a special code on it, that the clerk taking applications knows from the code whose dalal sent it and accepts it without scrutiny, that the passport office keeps a daily count of coded forms, and that an office employee collects the money by that count every Wednesday.
OT1-26.why_new: The exact marking and weekly settlement system between dalals and office staff.

OT1-27.claim: On 4 May 2024 a Prothom Alo reporter saw the application of Hashem Ali of Phulpur, Mymensingh, accepted without any scrutiny at the Mymensingh regional passport office: his "nationality and character certificate" had the ward and neighbourhood fields blank and an unidentified signature, and carried a handwritten code of three capital English letters and the number 53 beside the serial number, a code the report says is given by the passport dalal.
OT1-27.why_new: An observed, dated instance of the code system working at the counter.

OT1-28.claim: There are at least 30 shops in front of the Mymensingh regional passport office in Maskanda that openly do computer typing, photocopying and online passport applications, and almost all secretly act as the office's dalals; the dalals said they used to roam in front of the office for customers but changed method because of occasional raids by the administration, and by their account at least Tk 5 lakh a day is taken from ordinary people this way.
OT1-28.why_new: Where the dalals sit now (shops, not the gate) and the scale claimed.

OT1-29.claim: Azharul Islam of Tarakanda, Mymensingh, went to the Mymensingh regional passport office on 24 April 2024, waited an hour and a half in line and had his application refused over an error in his papers; he failed on two days, with new errors found each time, and refused to use a dalal; on 28 April he went to the office's deputy assistant director Bachir Ahmed and asked why his application was not being taken when all papers were in order, the officer quickly accepted it, and he got his passport on 16 May.
OT1-29.why_new: A case showing what worked without a dalal: going to the office's deputy assistant director; with dates from refusal to delivery.

OT1-30.claim: On 4 May 2024 Sabbir Ahmed of Churkhai, Mymensingh Sadar, whose application was not accepted because of an "error", said all his papers were in order but he was told to come the next day; he then went with two friends to a shop outside the office to find a dalal.
OT1-30.why_new: Shows how a refused applicant is pushed to the shops.

OT1-31.claim: The Mymensingh office's deputy director Morad Chowdhury told Prothom Alo in June 2024 that some dalal-type people stay outside the office and applicants are told to beware of them, but that he did not know of code numbers on fake City Corporation certificates or whether any staff member takes money for it, and would look into it; the deputy assistant director also said he would look into it.
OT1-31.why_new: The office's response; no action is reported.

OT1-32.claim: Ali Yusuf, secretary of the Mymensingh city unit of SUJAN (Citizens for Good Governance), told Prothom Alo in June 2024 that everyone knows nothing gets done at the passport office without a dalal, and that his nephew had recently failed for a month to submit his application and got a passport only after applying through a dalal.
OT1-32.why_new: A named civil-society witness with a one-month example.

OT1-33.claim: On 20 November 2024 people under the banner "Victims: the ordinary people of Rajshahi" formed a human chain in front of the Rajshahi divisional passport and visa office in Shalbagan against files submitted through dalals being processed first, then met the deputy director and gave one month to end the irregularities, warning of a bigger programme otherwise.
OT1-33.why_new: A dated public protest against dalal-first processing at a named office.

OT1-34.claim: Speakers at the Rajshahi protest said they had observed that the special files coming through dalals are taken straight upstairs to the room of deputy director Rozy Khandaker, who signs them, that the assistant director enters them into the computer on the same floor, and that the files then come quickly down to the ground floor for the photograph, while people who do not pay a dalal stand for hours in the long ground-floor line.
OT1-34.why_new: The physical route of a dalal file inside the office (floor, room, order of steps), as alleged by protesters.

OT1-35.claim: The Rajshahi victims said that when a file comes without a dalal the officers only look for mistakes and when it comes through a dalal nothing is checked, and that the person who enters ordinary people's passport files on the ground floor is often not at his desk, so the ordinary line does not move.
OT1-35.why_new: Matches the Mymensingh pattern (errors found only in non-dalal files) at a second office.

OT1-36.claim: Deputy director Rozy Khandaker denied all the allegations of irregularity when the Rajshahi protesters met her and asked them to show proof of corruption, and told journalists she could not speak to the media without the permission of the passport department's Director General.
OT1-36.why_new: The official's denial, needed alongside the allegation.

OT1-37.claim: According to an intelligence agency report cited by Prothom Alo, a "G-25" syndicate of passport officers was built by the then director Toufiqul Islam under the patronage of Abu Asad when he was director (administration and finance); its 24 officers became known as G-25 because they allegedly collect at least Tk 25 lakh in bribes a day, the Anti-Corruption Commission questioned its members in 2021 on the basis of the report and filed cases against some of them, and victims in Rajshahi said in November 2024 that deputy director Rozy Khandaker is known as a member.
OT1-37.why_new: Names the alleged officer syndicate behind passport-office bribes and the ACC action; the guide has no named syndicate for passports.

OT1-38.claim: A study published on 18 February 2025 by IIED (the International Institute for Environment and Development), based on a survey of 648 households in 33 villages of Mathbaria, Pirojpur, and Gowainghat, Sylhet, found that a family spends Tk 4 lakh 61 thousand 220 in Pirojpur and Tk 4 lakh 13 thousand 667 in Sylhet to send a member abroad, raised by selling land or by high-interest loans, and that the migrants are not aware of their rights and so are easily cheated.
OT1-38.why_new: District-level cost-of-migration figures for 2025 and how the money is raised; the section has national figures only.

OT1-39.claim: The IIED study said people who migrate abroad are more helpless than internal migrants because they borrow to go and it is almost impossible for them to come home without repaying the loan, and that with the distance, the cost of travel and the wish to provide for the family they bear everything in silence.
OT1-39.why_new: Explains why the debt keeps a worker in a bad job abroad; the section lists borrowing but not this effect.

OT1-40.claim: The IIED study found that climate risk raised the likelihood of households in the surveyed areas of Pirojpur and Sylhet migrating abroad by 214 percent (against 161 percent for moving to another town inside Bangladesh), that most of those going abroad go to the Gulf countries, and that a third of them work as construction labourers in risky conditions.
OT1-40.why_new: Who is being pushed abroad and into which work; a driver the guide does not mention.

OT1-41.claim: The IIED study lists the seizure of migrants' visas and passports abroad, withheld wages, forced work, restriction of movement, threats and beatings, and excessive or unpaid work among the practices it counts as modern slavery.
OT1-41.target_section: The passport kept by the dalal
OT1-41.why_new: A research source classing passport seizure abroad as modern slavery.
OT1-41.h3: The passport kept by the dalal

OT1-42.claim: Shakirul Islam, chairman of OKUP (Ovibashi Karmi Unnayan Program), who was involved in the IIED study, told Prothom Alo in March 2025 that when disasters leave people no alternative work locally the decision to migrate is taken by the family and at least one member leaves in search of work, but there is no arrangement to protect these migrants.
OT1-42.why_new: Named expert on migration as a family decision under distress.

OT1-43.claim: At the Gazipur regional passport office in May 2025, applicants said that applying on their own meets harassment on various pretexts while through a dalal everything is done at once, for Tk 1,000 to 1,500 paid to the dalal; a Prothom Alo reporter saw people wait about an hour for document checks and two to two and a half hours for fingerprints and photo, while those paying Tk 1,000 to 1,500 more through a dalal went straight to the fingerprint and photo room.
OT1-43.why_new: A 2025 street price for skipping the biometric queue at a named office, observed by a reporter; TIB's survey says the biometric stage carries the highest bribe but gives no mechanism.

OT1-44.claim: Ariful Islam of Kapasia said he joined the line for fingerprints and photo at the Gazipur passport office at 9 am and finished at 1:30 pm, while those who had paid a dalal finished within 10 to 15 minutes of arriving.
OT1-44.why_new: Queue time with and without a dalal, in an applicant's words.

OT1-45.claim: Riad Mia of Tongi said he waited at the Gazipur passport office until 1:30 pm on a Wednesday in May 2025 without being able to submit his wife's file, came back on Thursday morning and finished after more than two hours, and that a man had asked him for Tk 1,000 to get the work done quickly, which he did not pay.
OT1-45.why_new: A case of the work being done without paying, at the cost of a second day.

OT1-46.claim: Some 25 to 30 small shops have grown up on both sides of the road in front of the Gazipur passport office, where dalals and their associates sit with computers, fill in applicants' passport forms and themselves deposit the bank fee, Prothom Alo reported in May 2025.
OT1-46.why_new: Shows the dalal handling the bank payment as well as the form, at a second office with the same shop set-up as Mymensingh.

OT1-47.claim: A Prothom Alo reporter posing as a customer in May 2025 was sent by a dalal named Masum to the shop Bismillah Computer in front of the Gazipur passport office, where a man named Md Jony said raising the age by one year on both the voter ID card and the passport would cost Tk 32,000, half in advance, with the passport delivered within a month, or within 15 days for Tk 2,000 more; the report says correcting the national ID properly takes several months.
OT1-47.why_new: A quoted 2025 price and turnaround for changing the age on the NID and passport; the "Changed ages" item has no price or place.

OT1-48.claim: Nasrin Parvin, deputy director of the Gazipur regional passport office, told Prothom Alo in May 2025 that pressure of applicants had risen in recent days so it could take some time, though not two to three hours, and that dalals may have been active before but since she arrived she has not let them inside under any circumstances.

OT1-49.claim: The ACC case of 3 July 2025 over women sent abroad on forged papers was filed by ACC assistant director Swapan Kumar Roy and names as accused BMET deputy director (emigration) Md Sazzad Hossain Sarkar, assistant director (emigration) Md Hossain Ullah Akanda, manpower survey officer Md Nizamuddin Patwari and office assistant and computer operator Md Azad Hossain, together with Md Anwar Hossain, managing partner of H A International, Md Salauddin, managing partner of K H Overseas, Md Jamal Hossain, proprietor of Makkah Overseas, Md Anwar Hossain Bhuiyan, managing partner of Tasnim Overseas, and Ekramul Haque, partner of S M Manpower.
OT1-49.target_section: BMET clearance and the smart card
OT1-49.why_new: The guide reports this case without the names of the officials and the five agencies.
OT1-49.h3: BMET clearance and the smart card

OT1-50.claim: In the same case the ACC alleges that the agencies colluded to use fake passports for women being sent to the Middle East as domestic workers, says the clearances for four women under 25 broke a ministry circular, and says in its complaint that the officials concerned gained financially from the forgery; the ACC said it was investigating further and would take legal action against those involved when the investigation ends.
OT1-50.target_section: BMET clearance and the smart card
OT1-50.why_new: Adds the collusion and financial-gain allegations and the status (investigation continuing; no verdict).
OT1-50.h3: BMET clearance and the smart card

OT1-51.claim: On 3 July 2025 the Anti-Corruption Commission filed a case against four BMET officials and the owners and officials of five agencies on a charge of trafficking women abroad on forged papers; it said its raid on BMET's Dhaka office on 29 May found proof of the ring's irregularities, and it alleges that applications were filed with another woman's passport number in place of the real applicant's and approved for clearance without a check against BMET's database.
OT1-51.target_section: Trafficking disguised as a job, especially for women
OT1-51.why_new: This section's cases do not include the ACC case, which the ACC itself frames as trafficking of women with officials' help; it is in the guide only under BMET clearance.
OT1-51.h3: Trafficking disguised as a job, especially for women

OT1-52.claim: A Prothom Alo guide for migrant workers published on 7 July 2025 said the Probashi Kallyan Bank migration loan needs no collateral and requires the applicant's photo, voter ID, address, certificates and copies of the passport, visa and smart card, the papers of one guarantor and three bank cheques, and that an account must first be opened at the bank.
OT1-52.placement: other: papers for the PKB loan
OT1-52.why_new: Lists the papers and the three cheques; note it says one guarantor where the guide (F0116) says two, so this needs checking against PKB before use.

OT1-53.claim: The same guide said the PKB loan is up to Tk 3 lakh for both a new visa and a re-entry visa, with terms of 3 years and 2 years respectively, repaid in monthly instalments after a two-month grace period at 9 percent simple interest.
OT1-53.why_new: Adds the re-entry visa loan, its 2-year term and the two-month grace period to what the guide gives.

OT1-54.claim: The Prothom Alo guide of 7 July 2025 said dalals usually press people by saying they will get the work done quickly, do not show proper papers and hide their own identity, and deceive with false visas, job offers and demands for extra money.
OT1-54.why_new: A published list of dalal behaviours; unattributed newspaper advice, so weaker than a case.

OT1-55.claim: Citing BMET's website, Prothom Alo wrote in July 2025 that a worker should leave with BMET's emigration clearance (smart card) by lawful means, and that going abroad by sea or any route other than the three international airports (Dhaka, Chattogram, Sylhet) is a punishable offence.
OT1-55.why_new: States the rule in the plain form BMET gives workers (three airports only); the guide gives section 34 without naming the exit points.

OT1-56.claim: The Ami Probashi app, which works with BMET, has a chat-based CV builder in Bangla and English that anyone wanting to go abroad can use free of charge, according to Prothom Alo in July 2025, which said a proper CV reduces dependence on dalals.
OT1-56.why_new: A free tool the guide does not mention; low priority.

OT1-57.claim: On 13 July 2025 at the Faridpur regional passport office, two local dalals, Siam Ahmed (27) and Rashed Khan (30), took Tk 30 thousand in all from a Rohingya couple on a promise of getting them passports, then started no passport work, threatened them and beat their son-in-law when he protested, according to local sources; he went into the office and asked the Ansar guards for help, and police detained the couple, the son-in-law and the two dalals.
OT1-57.why_new: A dated case of passport dalals taking money from people who cannot lawfully get a passport, with the dalals detained.

OT1-58.claim: The officer in charge of Faridpur Kotwali police station said in July 2025 that legal action was being taken against the two detained dalals, and that the three Rohingya would be sent to a camp if they were camp residents and otherwise back to where they live.
OT1-58.why_new: What the police did to the dalals and to the applicants.

OT1-59.claim: There are allegations that some sports federations and associations in Bangladesh have for many years sent fake players and officials abroad with their teams as a way of trafficking people, with most such allegations coming from the smaller sports and most cases staying hidden, Prothom Alo reported on 31 October 2025.
OT1-59.why_new: A form of impersonation the section lacks: travelling as a fake player or official in a national sports delegation.

OT1-60.claim: On 9 October 2025 the National Sports Council (NSC) told federations by letter that a proposal for the government order (GO) for any team going abroad must reach it at least 10 days before the flight, with proof of the selected players' fitness and performance; an NSC source said the rule was made mainly to stop such trafficking, and NSC director (sports) Aminul Ehsan said he would not say it was only to stop trafficking, but that the question of trafficking in the name of sport does come up in places.
OT1-60.why_new: The check that now exists and who runs it.

OT1-61.claim: Until the October 2025 rule, federations sent the NSC only the players' names for the government order, and whether a named person was really a player was not verified, Prothom Alo reported; Farhad Jesmin Liti, chair of the Bangladesh Olympic Association's athletes commission, said she often hears that some federations take fake players along.
OT1-61.why_new: Explains the gap that made it possible, with a named sports official.

OT1-62.claim: The Ministry of Foreign Affairs runs online apostille (attestation of public documents and certificates) on the MyGov portal, mygov.bd, of the a2i (Aspire to Innovate) programme, so people going abroad can get documents attested from home; a2i said on 13 December 2025 that about 17 lakh applications had been settled in the previous 11 months.
OT1-62.why_new: This section describes attestation in person only; the online apostille and its volume are missing here (the FAQ mentions mygov.bd).

OT1-63.claim: a2i said in a press release on 13 December 2025 that a ring is forging "apostille certificates" using several fake domains that resemble the government's, and that two such sites carrying forged certificates had been identified: apostillemygovbd.news and apostille-mygovbd.com.
OT1-63.target_section: Online job adverts, Facebook and WhatsApp scams, and fake government sites
OT1-63.why_new: Names the fake apostille domains; the section covers fake police-clearance sites but not fake apostille sites.
OT1-63.h3: Online job adverts, Facebook and WhatsApp scams, and fake government sites

OT1-64.claim: After the Ministry of Foreign Affairs wrote to Bangladesh Police in August 2025 asking for the fake domains to be shut and the forgers prosecuted, two of them, apostile.mygov-bd.com and apostiller-bd.com, were closed, and a2i said work to identify the forgers and close the other fake domains was continuing.
OT1-64.target_section: Online job adverts, Facebook and WhatsApp scams, and fake government sites
OT1-64.why_new: What the authorities did: two sites closed, no arrests reported.
OT1-64.h3: Online job adverts, Facebook and WhatsApp scams, and fake government sites

OT1-65.claim: a2i asked everyone not to open any suspicious link or website or give personal information on any site other than https://www.mygov.bd/ for apostille, saying the fraud could put the acceptance of Bangladesh government documents and citizens' lawful migration at risk.
OT1-65.target_section: Online job adverts, Facebook and WhatsApp scams, and fake government sites
OT1-65.why_new: An official warning naming the one genuine address.
OT1-65.h3: Online job adverts, Facebook and WhatsApp scams, and fake government sites

OT1-66.claim: From 21 January 2026, Bangladeshi citizens approved for a US business or tourist visa (B1/B2) must post a bond of up to USD 15,000, the US Embassy in Dhaka said in a notice on its verified Facebook page on 19 January 2026, and the condition does not apply to holders of valid B1/B2 visas issued before that date; Prothom Alo put USD 15,000 at about Tk 18 lakh 35 thousand at Tk 122.31 a dollar.
OT1-66.why_new: A new, large payment tied to a US visitor visa that the guide does not mention.

OT1-67.claim: The US Embassy in Dhaka warned on 19 January 2026: "Do not pay the bond before the interview. Paying a bond in advance does not guarantee a visa, and third-party websites may be fraudulent"; it said no money paid before the interview is refundable.
OT1-67.target_section: Online job adverts, Facebook and WhatsApp scams, and fake government sites
OT1-67.why_new: An embassy warning about third-party payment websites; the section has no US example.
OT1-67.h3: Online job adverts, Facebook and WhatsApp scams, and fake government sites

OT1-68.claim: The US State Department's travel website said on 6 January 2026 that citizens of 38 countries including Bangladesh must post a visa bond of up to USD 15,000 when applying to enter the United States, and the embassy's notice said the bond money is returned if the visa's conditions are properly followed.
OT1-68.why_new: Scope of the bond and the refund condition.

OT1-69.claim: The US Embassy in Dhaka said in a Facebook post on 26 January 2026 that an applicant found eligible after the visa interview is given payment instructions by the consular officer with a direct link to pay.gov, and must pay the bond within 30 days.
OT1-69.why_new: Says how and where the genuine payment is made (only after the interview, on the link the consular officer gives), which is the check against a fake payment site.

OT1-70.claim: Under the visa bond pilot programme the visa issued is single-entry and valid for at most three months, the holder must enter the United States through certain designated ports of entry, and the bond is cancelled automatically and the money returned after the holder comes home if all the visa's conditions are met, among them not working in the United States and returning within the set time, the embassy said.
OT1-70.why_new: The conditions under which the bond is lost: working in the US or overstaying.

OT1-71.claim: On 23 March 2026 Dhaka's detective police (DB) arrested Lt Gen (retd) Masud Uddin Chowdhury, a former member of parliament for Feni-3 and managing director of M International Limited, in Baridhara, and on 24 March a Dhaka metropolitan magistrate granted five days' remand in a human trafficking case at Paltan police station; police said there are 11 cases against him in Feni and Dhaka.
OT1-71.target_section: When the visa, the agency and the clearance are all real
OT1-71.why_new: An arrest of a named agency owner in a recruiting-syndicate case; the guide's syndicate item names no one and reports no arrest. The article does not name the destination country, so the link to the Malaysia syndicate must be confirmed from another source before it is placed in that item.
OT1-71.h3: When the visa, the agency and the clearance are all real

OT1-72.claim: The Paltan case was filed on 3 September by Altab Khan, owner of a firm named Afia Overseas, on charges of embezzlement through a syndicate and human trafficking, and names 103 accused, among them Masud Uddin Chowdhury, former expatriates' welfare minister Imran Ahmed, former secretary Ahmed Munirus Salehin, Benjir Ahmed, a former member of parliament and owner of Ahmed International, and Md Ruhul Amin Swapan, owner of Catharsis International.
OT1-72.target_section: When the visa, the agency and the clearance are all real
OT1-72.why_new: Names the accused, including a former minister and secretary; the article gives the filing date without the year.
OT1-72.h3: When the visa, the agency and the clearance are all real

OT1-73.claim: The case alleges that although there are more than two thousand recruiting agents in manpower export, the accused formed a syndicate and discriminated among them, and that by intimidation and force they took from the complainant an extra Tk 1.5 lakh per person for 841 people, Tk 12 crore 56 lakh 1 thousand in all, and collected about Tk 24 thousand crore from other businessmen and embezzled it.
OT1-73.target_section: When the visa, the agency and the clearance are all real
OT1-73.why_new: The alleged per-worker levy (Tk 1.5 lakh) the syndicate took from another agency, in a court case; a cut the guide's cost chain does not show.
OT1-73.h3: When the visa, the agency and the clearance are all real

OT1-74.claim: The case alleges that former secretary Ahmed Munirus Salehin, while in government service, used his son as a member of the syndicate under his own ministry, and that former minister Imran Ahmed helped the ring by irregularly approving the launch of an app named "Probashi" for his wife's elder brother's son.
OT1-74.target_section: When the visa, the agency and the clearance are all real
OT1-74.why_new: Alleged involvement of the ministry's top officials and of the private app used for clearance, as a court-case allegation.
OT1-74.h3: When the visa, the agency and the clearance are all real

OT1-75.claim: At the remand hearing on 24 March 2026 the public prosecutor Omar Faruq Faruqi told the court that the accused had taken Tk 24 thousand crore in the name of sending people abroad and that remand was needed to learn who shared the money and where it was laundered; the investigating officer's application sought the recovery of embezzled and extorted money and the arrest of absconding accused.
OT1-75.target_section: When the visa, the agency and the clearance are all real
OT1-75.why_new: The state's stated figure and aim in court.
OT1-75.h3: When the visa, the agency and the clearance are all real

OT1-76.claim: Masud Uddin Chowdhury was remanded a second time on 29 March 2026 and, after six days, a third time for three days on 4 April 2026 in the Paltan trafficking case; prosecutors told the court that the accused formed a syndicate and traded in commissions from more than two thousand recruiting agencies, which got no work unless they paid, and that every member of the syndicate except him was absconding.
OT1-76.target_section: When the visa, the agency and the clearance are all real
OT1-76.why_new: Status of the case in April 2026 (remand stage, others absconding) and the prosecution's description of the commission system.
OT1-76.h3: When the visa, the agency and the clearance are all real

OT1-77.claim: His lawyer Touhidul Islam told the court on 4 April 2026 that after 11 days of remand in two spells the investigating officer's application recorded no progress in the investigation, that recovering embezzled money cannot be a ground for remand, and that the investigator was busy with other matters instead of establishing the trafficking; he said his client is over 72 and has had brain surgery and two heart stents.
OT1-77.target_section: When the visa, the agency and the clearance are all real
OT1-77.why_new: The defence position, needed alongside the allegation; no charge sheet or verdict is reported.
OT1-77.h3: When the visa, the agency and the clearance are all real

OT1-78.claim: In a column in Prothom Alo on 27 March 2026, Dr Delwar Arif, an associate professor at Canisius University in New York, wrote that according to reports aired by ABC's Channel 7, MSN and Bangla channels in the United States, a Bangladeshi in New York who posed as an immigration lawyer without being one, and his firm, took millions of dollars from Bangladeshi and other legal and illegal immigration-seekers in the United States, USD 60 thousand from one person alone.
OT1-78.why_new: A fake-immigration-lawyer fraud against Bangladeshis already in the US; a pattern the guide lacks. Source is an opinion column citing US media, so weaker than a news report.

OT1-79.claim: The same column says the ring also took crores of taka from thousands of people in the name of sending them to the United States, through well-furnished offices in upmarket areas of Dhaka and eye-catching advertisements.
OT1-79.why_new: Shows the Dhaka end: a smart office and advertising as the lure.

OT1-80.claim: According to the column, the fraudsters' advertisements say "Do you want to settle in America?" (আপনি কি আমেরিকায় স্থায়ী হতে চান?) and "Get a green card in America by investing only Tk 50 to 60 lakh"; the writer says they take Tk 50 to 60 lakh a head only to bring a person across the southern or northern border of the United States, and that the dalals and traffickers do not care what happens after arrival or whether the person is caught.
OT1-80.why_new: The exact advertising lines and the price, with what is actually delivered (a border crossing, not a green card).

OT1-81.claim: The columnist writes that in his nearly two decades in the United States he has heard of many cases of people being cheated through Bangladeshi immigration lawyers, that many highly educated Bangladeshis are among the victims, and that US embassies could protect would-be migrants through public awareness campaigns and joint work with local law enforcement.
OT1-81.why_new: Who gets caught (including the educated); opinion of a named academic.

OT1-82.claim: Marina Sultana, director (programme) of RMMRU, told a Prothom Alo and Democracy International roundtable in Cumilla on 11 April 2026 that 31 percent of the people who go abroad are cheated, which she attributed to the lack of a law for the intermediaries or sub-agents.
OT1-82.why_new: A headline share of migrants cheated, from a named researcher; target is the In one minute of the Dalal scams chapter. Her "no law" premise conflicts with the guide (sub-agent registration has been in the Act since 2023); see the next draft.

OT1-83.claim: At the same roundtable the administrator of Cumilla City Corporation, Md Yusuf Molla, said most people who are cheated abroad are cheated because of the persons who act as intermediaries, and that Bangladesh has no law for intermediaries in the migration process and needs one at once.
OT1-83.placement: other: what officials believe (conflicts with the guide)
OT1-83.why_new: Evidence that local officials in a high-migration district did not know of the 2023 sub-agent provisions the guide describes; not to be stated as fact.

OT1-84.claim: Farzana Alam Majumdar, a sub-agent and member of BAIRA, told the Cumilla roundtable that the main problems in the sub-agent and recruitment system are false promises, cheating in cash transactions and keeping the contract hidden, and recommended that BMET bring all sub-agents under registration and that the ministry frame rules for the system.
OT1-84.why_new: A working sub-agent naming the three main abuses, including hiding the contract, and saying in April 2026 that sub-agents still need to be registered.

OT1-85.claim: Cumilla's additional deputy commissioner (general) Md Saiful Islam said in April 2026 that migrants have long demanded a one-stop service, and that people choose dalals because the government has not yet managed to provide it and the dalal or intermediary provides that service.
OT1-85.why_new: An official's own explanation of what the dalal sells: the one-stop service the state lacks.

OT1-86.claim: Cumilla's additional superintendent of police (Sadar circle) Saiful Malik said in April 2026 that people are cheated and fall into dalals' hands more because they do not know the rules, and that in his duties he has seen that those who go abroad through illegal channels are mostly the ones who face more problems.
OT1-86.why_new: A named police officer's field observation; general, low priority.

OT1-87.claim: Rawnak Jahan, a senior officer of Probashi Kallyan Bank's Cumilla region, said in April 2026 that the bank has only 4 branches for Cumilla's 17 upazilas, that the Tomsom Bridge branch has three staff and must serve 9 upazilas, and that shortage of staff and limited operations cause problems in giving and recovering loans in many cases.
OT1-87.why_new: Why the government loan is hard to get in one of the biggest migrant districts: branch and staff numbers from the bank itself.

OT1-88.claim: At the Cumilla roundtable the principal of the Cumilla Technical Training Centre, Kamruzzaman, recommended making sub-agent registration compulsory, activating union-level complaint settlement committees, expanding airport help desks, opening one-stop service centres and making lawful banking transactions compulsory, and the officer in charge of WARBE Development Foundation's Cumilla centre called for migration information services and a "migration corner" at union level.
OT1-88.target_section: Where to complain and get help
OT1-88.why_new: Shows that union-level complaint committees exist but are inactive, in officials' words; recommendations, not decisions.
OT1-88.h3: Where to complain and get help

OT1-89.claim: A union parishad member from Amratoli, Cumilla Sadar, named torture, excessive workload, withheld wages and getting no help with complaints as the main problems, and WARBE's Cumilla officer listed going without skills, dalal fraud, excess cost, not getting wages or papers abroad, and limited rehabilitation on return.
OT1-89.target_section: Where to complain and get help
OT1-89.why_new: Local-level list of problems, including no help with complaints; general.
OT1-89.h3: Where to complain and get help

OT1-90.claim: The state minister for expatriates' welfare, Md Nurul Haque, said at a Prothom Alo roundtable on 5 May 2026 that insecurity for women migrants is more frequent in some Middle Eastern countries, that the scope for legal remedy used to be limited, and that agreements with some countries have now created scope to file cases and recover compensation; he said there are problems with syndicates, tests and recruitment in Malaysia, Korea, Saudi Arabia and other countries and that complaints of irregularities and excess cost do come.
OT1-90.target_section: Where to complain and get help
OT1-90.why_new: The minister's own admission of syndicate and overcharging problems by country, and his claim of new legal remedies abroad (he does not name the countries).
OT1-90.h3: Where to complain and get help

OT1-91.claim: The state minister said in May 2026 that the government will bring the district manpower office, Probashi Kallyan Bank and the welfare centre into one building for a one-stop service, introduce a "Probashi card", fix a standard migration cost, and introduce a grading system to identify good recruiting agencies; he also said law firms would be appointed to protect women workers abroad and a special fund created to rehabilitate returnees.
OT1-91.why_new: Announced, not done: an agency grading system would be the first public rating of agencies; worth a Need-to-know on whether it exists yet.

OT1-92.claim: Dr A T M Mahbub-ul Karim, joint secretary and director (finance and budget) of the Wage Earners' Welfare Board, said in May 2026 that anyone, documented or undocumented, can become a member of the Board for Tk 400, and that if a worker abroad falls ill, is jailed or is in danger the Board gives legal help through the labour wing.
OT1-92.target_section: Where victims and families get help
OT1-92.why_new: Says undocumented workers can also join the Welfare Board, and the fee; the section does not say who is eligible.
OT1-92.h3: Where victims and families get help

OT1-93.claim: The Welfare Board official said a worker who applies because of illness within one year of returning home gets a one-time grant of up to Tk 2 lakh, and that a family gets Tk 2,000 a month for up to seven years for each disabled child, for at most two children.
OT1-93.target_section: Where victims and families get help
OT1-93.why_new: Two Board benefits with amounts and time limits that this section does not list.
OT1-93.h3: Where victims and families get help

OT1-94.claim: The same official said a worker injured or maimed abroad gets up to Tk 4 lakh against a Tk 500 premium, that there is a five-year life insurance policy for Tk 1,000, and that on a death, with a Tk 300 membership, the body is brought home from any country and Tk 35 thousand is paid for burial and transport, a further Tk 3 lakh goes to the heirs, and up to Tk 10 lakh more is paid if there is insurance.
OT1-94.target_section: Where victims and families get help
OT1-94.why_new: The injury benefit (Tk 4 lakh against a Tk 500 premium) is not in the guide; the death amounts match the FAQ. He gives the membership fee as Tk 400 in one sentence and Tk 300 in another, which needs checking.
OT1-94.h3: Where victims and families get help

OT1-95.claim: The Welfare Board helps recover dues owed abroad through 22 law firms in 12 countries, and under its reintegration policy more than 2 lakh 39 thousand people have so far been given training, counselling and financial help, its director (finance and budget) said in May 2026.
OT1-95.target_section: Where victims and families get help
OT1-95.why_new: A route for unpaid wages (law firms retained abroad) and the scale of reintegration help; neither is in the section.
OT1-95.h3: Where victims and families get help

OT1-96.claim: Nu-Emong Marma Mong, deputy manager (overseas recruitment) of BOESL, said in May 2026 that BOESL has sent women workers to Jordan's garment sector entirely free of cost since 2010, with its officers handling everything from the medical and pre-departure training to getting to the airport, and that BOESL tells workers the fixed migration cost for each country in advance.
OT1-96.why_new: BOESL's own statement that the Jordan garment channel is wholly free, including the medical and training, since 2010; supports the section's red flag with what the free channel covers.

OT1-97.claim: BOESL's deputy manager described its process: it starts with a government-to-government agreement or an employer giving BOESL the recruitment, labour wing officers at the Bangladesh embassy verify the employer's demand, the information is then published as a notice and a test is held with the employer or its local representative present, and BOESL helps with all the legal steps of going abroad after the test.
OT1-97.why_new: The genuine sequence of a BOESL recruitment (verified demand, public notice, test with the employer present), against which a fake "BOESL" offer can be checked.

OT1-98.claim: Rahnuma Salam Khan, senior national programme manager of the ILO, said in May 2026 that the government clearly set out in a 2025 set of rules what the responsibility and accountability of recruiting agencies and sub-agents will be, but that effective implementation or enforcement of these rules has not yet begun.
OT1-98.why_new: Answers part of the section's Need to know: as of May 2026 the 2025 licence and sub-agent rules were not being applied, according to the ILO.

OT1-99.claim: Marina Sultana, programme director of RMMRU, said in May 2026 that RMMRU helped the government frame the rules that later provided in law for the registration of sub-agents, but that this has still not been fully implemented, and that it also worked on alternative dispute resolution so that BMET's arbitration process becomes more transparent.
OT1-99.why_new: A second named source that sub-agent registration was not fully implemented by May 2026.

OT1-100.claim: Sheikh Romana, general secretary of the Bangladesh Ovibashi Mohila Sramik Association (an association of women migrant workers), said in May 2026 that of about 2,200 agencies 1,100 are valid, and that ethical recruitment has still not become real.
OT1-100.why_new: A count of agencies and how many are valid, from a workers' association leader; unsourced by her, so to be checked against BMET's licence list.

OT1-101.claim: Jasiya Khatun, director of WARBE Development Foundation, said in May 2026 that according to Wage Earners' Welfare Board data about 799 to 800 women migrants have come home dead in the past eight years, that in most cases the cause is given as heart attack or illness and sometimes suicide, and that the real cause is not known.
OT1-101.why_new: A count of women migrants' deaths and the doubt over recorded causes.

OT1-102.claim: According to BMET data cited at the roundtable, more than 10 lakh Bangladeshi women were working abroad in May 2026, though the number of women migrating has fallen in the last few years, and more than 10 lakh 95 thousand women went abroad between 2001 and 2022; RMMRU's programme director said women are about 13.5 percent of total migration.
OT1-102.why_new: Size of women's migration; the two speakers differ on whether the trend is falling or still rising.

OT1-103.claim: A 2025 study by Badabon Sangha, an organisation working on women migrant workers' rights, in Dhaka, Manikganj, Gopalganj, Sunamganj, Narsingdi, Cumilla and Pabna found that 27.6 percent of women migrated without having any source of income, which its programme manager Fariha Jesmin said points to forced migration; she said many took high-interest loans or sold assets, and that abroad they face low pay, loss of control of their passports, long hours and abuse.
OT1-103.target_section: Trafficking disguised as a job, especially for women
OT1-103.why_new: A survey figure on distress migration by women, with the debt and passport-control pattern.
OT1-103.h3: Trafficking disguised as a job, especially for women

OT1-104.claim: S K Mojibul Haque, director of BNSK, said in May 2026 that most women workers have to work 12 to 14 hours instead of 8.
OT1-104.why_new: Working hours as reported by a women migrants' organisation.

OT1-105.claim: Mahmuda Sultana, general secretary of the Ovibashi Nari Sramik Federation (a federation of women migrant workers), said in May 2026 that the three-day basic training given at the district employment office before departure mainly covers some first notions of the language, the culture and rules, and gives no in-depth training on the reality of the work, the risks or the long-term situation; a UNDP gender expert, Sharmin Islam, said language, culture and practical work skills cannot be acquired in three days.
OT1-105.target_section: BMET clearance and the smart card
OT1-105.placement: other: the pre-departure training in practice
OT1-105.why_new: What the compulsory 3-day course does and does not teach, from a returnee leader; the guide describes the course but not its limits.
OT1-105.h3: BMET clearance and the smart card

OT1-106.claim: A UNDP Bangladesh gender expert, Sharmin Islam, said in May 2026 that women workers are often seen standing confused at the airport with no idea of what they have to do, and that the same problem affects male workers.
OT1-106.why_new: An observation on first-time workers at departure; general.

OT1-107.claim: Mahmuda Sultana said women who come home after harassment and abuse abroad get hardly any rehabilitation help and find it hard to fit back into family and society, and that those who return aged 45 to 50 are in a pitiable state; Sheikh Romana said many women return after abuse abroad with a child, and questioned how many returnees really get the rehabilitation help that exists.
OT1-107.why_new: Returnee leaders' account that the listed help does not reach them, set against the Board's figures.

OT1-108.claim: Farzana Shahnaz, a national programme officer of IOM, said in May 2026 that for lack of correct and reliable information people at village level depend on dalals for information, and that a pilot initiative funded by the Italian government has been taken to deliver information through Union Digital Centres (UDCs, the government's grassroots-level service centres).
OT1-108.why_new: Names an alternative information point at union level (UDC pilot); the article does not say in which unions.

OT1-109.claim: IOM's Farzana Shahnaz said in May 2026 that people often go abroad at high cost on borrowed money and their income is almost used up repaying the loan, so a person needs to understand beforehand what going will cost, what they will earn, how long they will stay and what gain is left at the end.
OT1-109.why_new: A named IOM officer confirming that earnings go on loan repayment; the section has this from a former secretary only.

OT1-110.claim: The ILO's Rahnuma Salam Khan said an assessment of 40 technical training centres (TTCs) found that the training at TTCs under BMET is in many cases not fully in line with the demand of labour markets abroad.
OT1-110.why_new: An assessment finding on government training centres; context for why workers go unskilled.

OT1-111.claim: S K Mojibul Haque of BNSK linked state monitoring of digital media to stopping people falling for false publicity by dalals and recruiting agents (the printed sentence is garbled), and said women who come to DEMO offices, TTCs and expatriate welfare centres often do not get the service they want.
OT1-111.target_section: Online job adverts, Facebook and WhatsApp scams, and fake government sites
OT1-111.why_new: A named NGO director on false online publicity and on women being turned away at government offices; the sentence in the article is garbled, so the claim is limited to what is clear.
OT1-111.h3: Online job adverts, Facebook and WhatsApp scams, and fake government sites

OT2-1.claim: Shahriar Ahmed Emon, a 22-year-old Bangladeshi who had enrolled a few months earlier at a private university in Larnaca, Cyprus, told his flatmates on 12 June 2026 that he was going to join a factory job in Kofinou, his first day at work, left home at about 6:30 pm and disappeared after sending a friend a location pin.
OT2-1.target_section: Student visas used as work routes
OT2-1.why_new: The section has no Cyprus entry and no case of a student lured by a job offer.
OT2-1.h3: Student visas used as work routes

OT2-2.claim: Investigators found that the accused had met Shahriar on a bus five days before the killing, was angered by a remark of his and then trapped him with the lure of a job; according to police sources, the accused admitted luring him from his Oroklini home to a deserted area of Kofinou, where he was stabbed several times in the neck and back and killed that same evening.
OT2-2.target_section: Student visas used as work routes
OT2-2.why_new: Shows a job offer from a stranger used to lure a student; not in the guide.
OT2-2.h3: Student visas used as work routes

OT2-3.claim: After Shahriar disappeared in June 2026, unknown people contacted his father, who lives in Greece, demanding ransom, and social-media posts, which police were still verifying, demanded EUR 10,000 one day and EUR 25,000 the next and threatened that he would never see his son again if the authorities were told; according to police sources, the accused admitted killing Shahriar, stealing his phone and staging a fake kidnapping to get money from the family.
OT2-3.target_section: Student visas used as work routes
OT2-3.why_new: A ransom demand to the family for a person already dead; the guide's ransom cases are all real captivity.
OT2-3.h3: Student visas used as work routes

OT2-4.claim: The family reported the ransom demand and the location pin to the police; Cypriot police arrested the suspect on Sunday 21 June 2026, he led Larnaca CID to the body near the Kofinou migrant reception centre and a local slaughterhouse, and he was due before Larnaca District Court for a remand hearing on 22 June.
OT2-4.target_section: Student visas used as work routes
OT2-4.why_new: Outcome and what the family did; the authorities' response.
OT2-4.h3: Student visas used as work routes

OT2-5.claim: According to his brother Nur Hossain, Zakir Hossain of Banshkhali, Chattogram, unemployed and with a criminal case at the police station, needed a police clearance to go abroad but did not apply to the police directly because of the case, and went instead to an acquaintance working at a travel agency in Banshkhali.
OT2-5.why_new: Shows who buys a forged PCC and why (a pending criminal case); the guide has no case.

OT2-6.claim: According to Nur Hossain, the acquaintance, Abdur Rahman, said he could get the police clearance for Tk 1 lakh 23 thousand; the family paid Tk 80,000 in advance on 21 July 2026 and the rest after receiving the forged certificate on 12 August 2026.
OT2-6.why_new: A street price for a 'fast' PCC through a broker (answers the section's Need to know), against the Tk 1,500 fee.

OT2-7.claim: Police said the ring took Tk 1 lakh 23 thousand from Zakir Hossain on a promise of a quick police clearance, while making the certificate and showing it on the fake website cost Tk 3,000 in all, leaving Tk 1 lakh 20 thousand as profit.
OT2-7.why_new: The ring's cost and margin; not in the guide.

OT2-8.claim: The forged police clearance certificates sold in Chattogram in 2026 carried the signatures and seals of the relevant police officers and a QR code which, when scanned, showed the certificate on a clone of the Bangladesh Police website, so that, police said, it could not be told apart from a real one by looking.
OT2-8.why_new: Adds the forged signatures and seals and that the site is a clone; the guide says only 'counterfeit QR codes linking to a fake website'. Also implies scanning the QR code is no check.

OT2-9.claim: Chattogram's Additional Superintendent of Police (Special Branch) Junayed Kausar said the forged police clearance ring had several layers of people: some were brokers and some worked online and were skilled at making QR codes and websites.

OT2-10.claim: The forgery was detected when Zakir Hossain submitted the certificate to a travel agency; he then made a written complaint to the Chattogram District Superintendent of Police's office, and a case was filed at Banshkhali police station with his brother Nur Hossain as plaintiff.
OT2-10.why_new: Where the forgery was detected and the complaint route that worked.

OT2-11.claim: Police arrested four members of the forged police clearance ring on the night of Sunday 16 August 2026 in Chattogram city and Banshkhali: Md. Ashraf Ali Khan (36), Md. Nishan (36), Mohammad Abdullah Al Mamun (48) and Md. Abdur Rahman (46); police said the four were mainly brokers and that the hunt for the others continued.
OT2-11.why_new: The enforcement outcome; the guide gives no arrests for the PCC ring.

OT2-12.claim: Chattogram District Superintendent of Police Masud Alam asked people going abroad not to get a police clearance through any broker or illegal middleman but to follow the set government process, and called forging officers' signatures and using a fake website and QR code to make the document believable a very serious crime.

OT2-13.claim: Laos's Ministry of Labour and Social Welfare, in a directive issued on 9 September 2026 and reported by The Laotian Times on 14 September, suspended new work permits, labour import plans and labour project approvals for Bangladeshis from 1 September to the end of 2026, citing illegal entry, human trafficking, unauthorised labour suppliers and employers who evade responsibility after bringing workers in, though it gave no specific reason for singling out Bangladeshis.
OT2-13.target_section: Cambodia, Myanmar and Laos: scam compounds
OT2-13.why_new: Adds the issuing ministry, directive date and stated reasons; the guide has only the suspension dates.
OT2-13.h3: Cambodia, Myanmar and Laos: scam compounds

OT2-14.claim: Under the Lao directive, no person, company, employer or labour supplier may on its own let Bangladeshis enter or work in Laos, approval of the labour visa (LA-B2) for Bangladeshis stays closed until the end of 2026, and large government-approved priority projects with contracted work schedules are exempt.
OT2-14.target_section: Cambodia, Myanmar and Laos: scam compounds
OT2-14.why_new: Names the LA-B2 visa and the exemption; a worker told a 'project' job is still open can check this.
OT2-14.h3: Cambodia, Myanmar and Laos: scam compounds

OT2-15.claim: In Laos from September 2026, a worker found working outside his designated workplace without approval is fined 1 million kip (USD 44) per incident and sent home within 30 days at the cost of the employer or the party that broke the rule; employers are fined 2.5 million kip (USD 110) per worker per incident for bringing in or hiring a worker without approval, and 2 million kip (USD 89) for using a worker assigned to another unit, with fines tripled for a repeat offence.
OT2-15.target_section: Cambodia, Myanmar and Laos: scam compounds
OT2-15.why_new: What happens to a worker caught outside his workplace in Laos; not in the guide.
OT2-15.h3: Cambodia, Myanmar and Laos: scam compounds

OT2-16.claim: Asked about the Lao suspension in September 2026, Expatriates' Welfare Minister Ariful Haque Chowdhury told Prothom Alo that nothing was officially known and that the matter would be looked into.
OT2-16.target_section: Cambodia, Myanmar and Laos: scam compounds
OT2-16.placement: other: Where to get help / The law (Bangladesh response)
OT2-16.why_new: What Bangladesh did (nothing official at the time).
OT2-16.h3: Cambodia, Myanmar and Laos: scam compounds

OT2-17.claim: According to BMET sources, about 3,000 Bangladeshi workers took clearance for Laos in the first eight months of 2026, making it the 13th destination that year, against 3,835 in 2025 when it ranked 16th; Prothom Alo reports that the workers going to Laos mainly work in construction and manufacturing.
OT2-17.target_section: Cambodia, Myanmar and Laos: scam compounds
OT2-17.why_new: Year-by-year clearances and sectors; the guide has only a 21-month total.
OT2-17.h3: Cambodia, Myanmar and Laos: scam compounds

OT2-18.claim: On Tuesday 6 October 2026, UK Home Office immigration officers raided several London addresses and arrested two people on suspicion of fraud and immigration offences, accused of making fake documents, including staged photos and forged papers, that presented asylum seekers as gay, for up to £4,500 each; phones, jewellery and thousands of pounds were seized and a third person was arrested on suspicion of staying illegally.
OT2-18.target_section: NEW: Asylum claims built on a false story
OT2-18.why_new: The guide has no case of a bought asylum story.
OT2-18.h3: NEW: Asylum claims built on a false story

OT2-19.claim: The ring is believed to have helped prepare dozens of asylum claims by Bangladeshi men saying they were gay and that their lives would be in danger if returned, and the Home Office said many Bangladeshi men first claimed asylum on political grounds and, after refusal, claimed again as gay.
OT2-19.target_section: NEW: Asylum claims built on a false story
OT2-19.why_new: The mechanism: a second, invented claim after a refused political claim.
OT2-19.h3: NEW: Asylum claims built on a false story

OT2-20.claim: Chris Foster, regional head of the Home Office's criminal investigations, said intelligence showed the suspects charged each asylum seeker at least £1,000 and at most £4,500 for fake papers, which could include support letters from 'Apnajon', a Bangladeshi LGBT organisation based in Whitechapel, east London, staged photos meant to show the applicant as gay, and letters from someone claiming to be in a same-sex relationship with the applicant.
OT2-20.target_section: NEW: Asylum claims built on a false story
