OT2-20.why_new: The price and what the package contains.
OT2-20.h3: NEW: Asylum claims built on a false story

OT2-21.claim: According to Chris Foster, the October 2026 arrests centred on fake asylum claims linked to 'Apnajon', and the organisation came under suspicion after caseworkers saw the same kind of information repeated across several suspicious claims, followed by months of investigation.
OT2-21.target_section: NEW: Asylum claims built on a false story
OT2-21.why_new: How such claims are detected: identical stories across files.
OT2-21.h3: NEW: Asylum claims built on a false story

OT2-22.claim: The UK Home Office was reviewing more than a hundred asylum claims linked to the ring in October 2026, and Chris Foster said some fake claims had undoubtedly already been approved.
OT2-22.target_section: NEW: Asylum claims built on a false story
OT2-22.why_new: Even approved claims are being reopened.
OT2-22.h3: NEW: Asylum claims built on a false story

OT2-23.claim: A BBC investigation published in April 2026 reported that lawyers and advisers were helping some migrants claim asylum as gay, and secretly recorded a legal adviser, Tanisa Khan, saying she could arrange a 'full package' including photos taken at gay clubs and other evidence.
OT2-23.target_section: NEW: Asylum claims built on a false story
OT2-23.h3: NEW: Asylum claims built on a false story

OT2-24.claim: UK Home Secretary Shabana Mahmood said that those who profited from asylum fraud would be prosecuted, their illegal earnings seized and all their operations in the country shut, and that fraudulent asylum claims would be cancelled and the claimants removed from the country; the UK government says conviction for asylum fraud can carry up to 10 years in prison.
OT2-24.target_section: NEW: Asylum claims built on a false story
OT2-24.why_new: Consequence for the applicant, not only the seller.
OT2-24.h3: NEW: Asylum claims built on a false story

OT2-25.claim: In two of the cases documented by Amnesty International in Saudi Arabia, the accused said they had been forced to carry banned drugs, but the court neither examined nor accepted that, Prothom Alo reported in October 2026.
OT2-25.placement: other: add to the drug-packet warning
OT2-25.why_new: Being forced to carry drugs is no defence in practice; the guide only says drug offences can carry death.

OT2-26.claim: According to ESOHR (European Saudi Organisation for Human Rights, Berlin), 59 of the 108 people executed in Saudi Arabia from January to June 2026 (about 54%) were foreigners, including 49 of the 71 executed for drug offences, and Bangladeshis were among the 108, though how many is not known.
OT2-26.target_section: NEW: Arrested abroad: trials, drug charges and the death penalty
OT2-26.why_new: Execution numbers including Bangladeshis; nothing in the guide.
OT2-26.h3: NEW: Arrested abroad: trials, drug charges and the death penalty

OT2-27.claim: According to Amnesty International, 597 people were executed in Saudi Arabia for drug offences alone from January 2014 to June 2025, about 75% of them foreigners, in a country where about 44% of the 3 crore 53 lakh population is foreign.
OT2-27.target_section: NEW: Arrested abroad: trials, drug charges and the death penalty
OT2-27.h3: NEW: Arrested abroad: trials, drug charges and the death penalty

OT2-28.claim: Two Bangladeshis convicted of an 'immoral act' in a mosque in Mecca were executed in Saudi Arabia shortly before October 2026, outside the January to June 2026 count.
OT2-28.target_section: NEW: Arrested abroad: trials, drug charges and the death penalty
OT2-28.h3: NEW: Arrested abroad: trials, drug charges and the death penalty

OT2-29.claim: Bangladeshis are the largest group of foreign workers in Saudi Arabia, at least 25 lakh, followed by Indians, Pakistanis, Yemenis and Egyptians, yet ESOHR said it could learn or record nothing about 91 of the 108 cases (84.2%) executed in early 2026 before the execution, so there is no answer on how many Bangladeshis are held, on what charges, or whether they had lawyers, interpreters or consular help.
OT2-29.target_section: NEW: Arrested abroad: trials, drug charges and the death penalty
OT2-29.why_new: Size of exposure and the information gap (a Need to know).
OT2-29.h3: NEW: Arrested abroad: trials, drug charges and the death penalty

OT2-30.claim: According to Prothom Alo, Saudi Arabia's 2013 Law of Criminal Procedure gives accused people the right to legal help at both the investigation and trial stages and bans torture, but ESOHR documented that death-row prisoners in Khamis Mushait, Najran and Tabuk prisons had no professional interpreter or legal help, did not understand the proceedings, and often did not know when their sentence was upheld or their plea for pardon rejected.
OT2-30.target_section: NEW: Arrested abroad: trials, drug charges and the death penalty
OT2-30.why_new: The right on paper against practice.
OT2-30.h3: NEW: Arrested abroad: trials, drug charges and the death penalty

OT2-31.claim: Amnesty International documented 25 foreign nationals convicted of drug offences in Saudi Arabia (from Egypt, Ethiopia, Jordan, Pakistan and Somalia) and found many went through the system alone, without understanding or receiving the court papers or charges, without consular help, and at risk of confessions taken without an adequate interpreter or lawyer.
OT2-31.target_section: NEW: Arrested abroad: trials, drug charges and the death penalty
OT2-31.why_new: What an arrested migrant faces in court.
OT2-31.h3: NEW: Arrested abroad: trials, drug charges and the death penalty

OT2-32.claim: Amnesty International says Saudi law has no clear rule on advance notice of an execution to the prisoner or family; families said the prisoner may at most phone 24 hours before, some were told by prison officers the day before 'your turn has come', and many families learned of an execution from other prisoners' calls or from the state news agency.
OT2-32.target_section: NEW: Arrested abroad: trials, drug charges and the death penalty
OT2-32.why_new: What families should expect; nothing in the guide.
OT2-32.h3: NEW: Arrested abroad: trials, drug charges and the death penalty

OT2-33.claim: Saudi law does not guarantee return of the body after an execution, and in all three of the 25 Amnesty-documented cases executed between January and June 2025, Saudi Arabia neither returned the body to the family nor told them where it was buried.
OT2-33.target_section: NEW: Arrested abroad: trials, drug charges and the death penalty
OT2-33.why_new: Body repatriation does not happen after execution; relevant to 'How is the body brought home?'.
OT2-33.h3: NEW: Arrested abroad: trials, drug charges and the death penalty

OT2-34.claim: Amnesty's review found that low education, poor language skills and lack of money harm these migrants twice: first in migration, when they are cheated or exploited by brokers from the very start of going to Saudi Arabia, and then if they face legal trouble there, when they cannot hire a good lawyer or defend themselves properly and in most cases have reduced access to consular help.
OT2-34.target_section: NEW: Arrested abroad: trials, drug charges and the death penalty
OT2-34.why_new: Links dalal exploitation to later legal vulnerability.
OT2-34.h3: NEW: Arrested abroad: trials, drug charges and the death penalty

OT2-35.claim: Amnesty International's documentation says migrant workers in Saudi Arabia have been cheated by recruitment brokers, forced to work extra hours and had wages stolen, in some cases probably amounting to trafficking for labour exploitation; IOM lists irregular migration, hidden work such as domestic, sea or informal work, undue employer control, recruitment corruption and dependence on third-party brokers among the risk factors for migrants in Saudi Arabia.
OT2-35.target_section: Free visas and visa trading in the Gulf
OT2-35.why_new: Named-organisation statement on Saudi recruitment abuse; weak but usable context.
OT2-35.h3: Free visas and visa trading in the Gulf

OT2-36.claim: In December 2024 the UN Committee on the Elimination of Racial Discrimination found racial and ethnic discrimination in Saudi Arabia's criminal justice system, with migrant workers and domestic workers, including women, subjected to arbitrary detention, torture and ill-treatment, and called on Saudi Arabia to impose a moratorium on the death penalty.
OT2-36.target_section: NEW: Arrested abroad: trials, drug charges and the death penalty
OT2-36.why_new: UN finding; likely fluff for the guide unless the new section is kept.
OT2-36.h3: NEW: Arrested abroad: trials, drug charges and the death penalty

OT2-37.claim: Prothom Alo's October 2026 article lists among its sources Amnesty International's report 'If We Had Money and a Lawyer, Maybe My Brother Would Be Alive': Saudi Arabia's Execution Crisis (7 July 2025), ESOHR's '108 Saudi Arabia: Executions in the First Half of 2026', and a joint MENA Rights Group, ALQST and ESOHR submission dated 10 March 2026 to the UN Special Rapporteur on extrajudicial, summary or arbitrary executions.
OT2-37.target_section: NEW: Arrested abroad: trials, drug charges and the death penalty
OT2-37.h3: NEW: Arrested abroad: trials, drug charges and the death penalty

MY2-1.claim: At a roundtable on sea journeys abroad organised by BRAC and Prothom Alo in Cox's Bazar (reported by Prothom Alo on 6 June 2026), Bangladesh Coast Guard East Zone (Chattogram) zonal commander Captain Mohammad Mizanur Rahman said Cox's Bazar is one route for sea journeys abroad: people brought from different parts of the country are kept in the hills and other places there, taken in small boats to a large trawler or ship when the moment suits, and the torture begins once they are on board.
MY2-1.why_new: The section describes only the Cambodia-Thailand land route and the 2012-15 boats; this gives the 2026 mechanics of the Cox's Bazar sea departure (hill hideouts, small boats to a trawler) from a named official, and answers part of the section's Need to know on whether boats still leave.

MY2-2.claim: Tarekur Rahman of Maheshkhali, Cox's Bazar, who came back from the Malaysia route, told the June 2026 Cox's Bazar roundtable that a broker put him on a ship with talk of a good job in Malaysia, took him to Myanmar and took Tk 1 lakh from his family, then took Tk 7 lakh more in Thailand, and that he was caught at the border on the way to Malaysia, served a jail term and came home.
MY2-2.why_new: A named survivor case of the sea route with the amounts taken at each stage. Note: the fuller transcript (article 533a06e4) gives his account differently (held and jailed in Myanmar for about seven months, no Thailand stage); the two versions should be reconciled before use.

MY2-3.claim: Aung Aung U Jewel told the June 2026 Cox's Bazar roundtable that brokers caught him while he was a college student with an offer to take him to Australia by way of Malaysia for Tk 12 lakh, took him first from Cox's Bazar to Myanmar, where police arrested him and he was jailed, and that he later came home with the embassy's help.
MY2-3.why_new: A second named case: the "Australia via Malaysia" pitch, its price (Tk 12 lakh) and the fact that the journey ended in a Myanmar jail, none of which the section has.

MY2-4.claim: Suraiya Akter Sweety, a deputy secretary and camp-in-charge at the Refugee Relief and Repatriation Commission, said at the June 2026 Cox's Bazar roundtable that the tendency to go abroad by sea is high among Rohingya as well as Bangladeshis, especially teenage girls, who are taken by sea to Malaysia and Indonesia with the lure of a "better husband", and that many women are trafficked this way.
MY2-4.why_new: The section has no account of how girls and women are recruited for the boats; this is the marriage lure, from a named camp official.

MY2-5.claim: Citing accounts given by victims and families who come to the ministry, the state minister for expatriates' welfare, Md Nurul Haque, said at the June 2026 Cox's Bazar roundtable that on illegal sea journeys brokers hold people hostage and extract large sums from their families, do not give them even minimal food and water, many die on the way, and those who reach a shore are detained by police there.
MY2-5.why_new: An official statement of what happens on the boats (hostage-taking for ransom, no food or water, deaths, arrest on landing); the section's "What happens" covers only arrests on the land route. The minister was speaking of sea routes generally, not Malaysia alone.

MY2-6.claim: Shariful Islam Hasan of BRAC's Migration Programme said at the June 2026 Cox's Bazar roundtable that the dead found in the mass graves discovered in Thailand and Malaysia in 2015 had no names or identities and their graves were marked only with numbers.
MY2-6.placement: other: The path (the older boat route)
MY2-6.why_new: The section mentions the 2015 mass graves but not that the bodies were never identified and the graves carry numbers only.

MY2-7.claim: The Deputy Commissioner of Cox's Bazar, Md A Mannan, said at the 6 June 2026 Cox's Bazar roundtable that the sea off Cox's Bazar is calm in winter, so the risk of trafficking by sea rises then.
MY2-7.why_new: Gives the season of the boat departures, which the section lacks.

MY2-8.claim: The Deputy Commissioner of Cox's Bazar said at the 6 June 2026 roundtable that families who lose a member on a sea journey abroad, or are cheated, often do not want to admit what happened, which makes it hard to investigate the crime and identify the offenders.
MY2-8.why_new: Explains, from the district administration, why boat cases go uninvestigated; not in the section.

MY2-9.claim: The Coast Guard's East Zone commander said at the 6 June 2026 Cox's Bazar roundtable that traffickers bring people from around the country to hilly areas and try to send them out by sea in the dark of night, and that Bangladesh's coastline is 710 km long and a boat can be launched from any point on it.
MY2-9.why_new: Adds night departures and that launches are not tied to one landing point; complements MY2-1 from the fuller transcript.

MY2-10.claim: The Coast Guard's East Zone commander said at the 6 June 2026 Cox's Bazar roundtable that on the trafficking boats there is no food, clean water or toilet, that deaths happen and the bodies are thrown into the sea.
MY2-10.why_new: Conditions on the boats and the disposal of bodies at sea, stated by the Coast Guard; not in the section.

MY2-11.claim: The Coast Guard's East Zone commander said at the 6 June 2026 Cox's Bazar roundtable that even when cases are filed against traffickers, in many instances they get out of jail and go back to the same work.
MY2-11.why_new: What does not happen after a case is filed: the section's "The law" covers only Malaysian and Thai law, nothing on outcomes in Bangladesh.

MY2-12.claim: The Superintendent of Police of Cox's Bazar, A N M Sajedur Rahman, said at the 6 June 2026 roundtable that traffickers there build friendships through social media, invite people to come for a visit and then abduct or traffic them, and that some fishermen think they can earn more by trafficking people than by fishing.
MY2-12.why_new: Two mechanisms the section lacks: the social-media friendship and "come for a visit" lure that ends in abduction, and fishermen as the boat crews.

MY2-13.claim: Shariful Islam Hasan of BRAC, who reported as a journalist on sea trafficking and the Thailand-Malaysia border mass graves between 2012 and 2015, said at the 6 June 2026 Cox's Bazar roundtable that about one lakh people were trafficked in that period, and that in 2015 rescued Bangladeshis, many of them teenagers, were sent home with their hands and feet in chains.
MY2-13.placement: other: The path (the older boat route)
MY2-13.why_new: The section says "thousands" tried the boats in 2012-15; this gives an eyewitness estimate of about one lakh and how the rescued were returned.

MY2-14.claim: Shariful Islam Hasan of BRAC said at the 6 June 2026 Cox's Bazar roundtable that about two lakh people have crossed the Bay of Bengal in the past decade and many have gone missing, and that although brokers promise Malaysia or Australia, many are tortured and ransom is extracted.
MY2-14.why_new: The section has no figure for the Bay of Bengal route; he gives no source for the figure.

MY2-15.claim: Astrid Castelein, UNHCR's assistant representative (protection), said at the 6 June 2026 Cox's Bazar roundtable that in 2023 alone about 5,787 people went missing during illegal sea journeys abroad, about 25% of them women and children, and that half of the missing were Rohingya and half Bangladeshi citizens.
MY2-15.why_new: A UNHCR figure for the sea route. Caution: the transcript's numbers look garbled (the next sentence gives 39% women and 50% children for the same group); check against UNHCR's own publication before using.

MY2-16.claim: Shariful Islam Hasan of BRAC's Migration Programme said at a 6 June 2026 roundtable in Cox's Bazar that about one lakh Bangladeshis have been detained while trying to cross the Mediterranean in the past 16 years, and that about six and a half lakh Bangladeshis currently have asylum applications lodged in various countries.
MY2-16.why_new: Two aggregate figures from BRAC (16-year Mediterranean detentions; pending asylum applications); he gives no source for either.

MY2-17.claim: Shariful Islam Hasan of BRAC said at the 6 June 2026 Cox's Bazar roundtable that about a lakh people go abroad legally each month, yet many still try risky routes because the legal process is complicated, expensive and in many cases controlled by broker rings.
MY2-17.why_new: A named expert's explanation of why people choose irregular routes, linking them to the cost and broker control of the legal one.

MY2-18.claim: Liton Kanti Chowdhury, assistant director of the Cox's Bazar District Employment and Manpower Office (DEMO), said at the 6 June 2026 roundtable that about 30 complaints lodged with BMET and the Cox's Bazar DEMO had been settled under the grievance system and reports sent on them.
MY2-18.why_new: Shows a district DEMO actually handling complaints, with a count; the section says a complaint can be handed in at the DEMO but gives no evidence of what one does. He gives no period for the 30.
MY2-18.h3: Where to complain and get help

MY2-19.claim: The assistant director of the Cox's Bazar DEMO said at the 6 June 2026 roundtable that a District Migration Coordination Committee and a District Vigilance Task Force Committee are active against unsafe migration, that upazilas have been instructed to form the same committees, and that a pilot pre-decision programme for people thinking of going abroad is running in Chakaria.
MY2-19.target_section: Where victims and families get help
MY2-19.why_new: Names district-level bodies (vigilance task force, migration coordination committee) the help list does not mention. The article does not say how a worker reaches them.
MY2-19.h3: Where victims and families get help

MY2-20.claim: Mohammad Shahidul Islam, regional head of the NGO YPSA, said at the 6 June 2026 Cox's Bazar roundtable that there are counter-trafficking committees at district, upazila and union level and that they need to be made active.
MY2-20.target_section: Where victims and families get help
MY2-20.why_new: The help list does not mention the counter-trafficking committees; the speaker's own point is that they are not active.
MY2-20.h3: Where victims and families get help

MY2-21.claim: Mobarak Hossain, assistant director of the Cox's Bazar regional passport office, said at the 6 June 2026 roundtable that since e-passports began in 2020 no passport can be issued without online verification of the national ID and birth registration data, and that the gaps which earlier let some people get more than one passport are now easily detected.
MY2-21.why_new: The section gives the NID-match rule but not that a second passport is now detected; relevant to brokers who offer a new passport with changed details.

MY2-22.claim: The assistant director of the Cox's Bazar regional passport office said at the 6 June 2026 roundtable that some people first get a passport with wrong information and later try to change it, that under a February 2025 circular the national ID data is the basis of the passport, and that responsibility for any mismatch lies with the person concerned.
MY2-22.target_section: The agent wants to change my age on the passport. Is that a problem?
MY2-22.why_new: Adds the February 2025 circular and who bears the consequence of wrong passport data: the holder, not the agent who arranged it.

MY2-23.claim: Md Shah Jalal, principal of the Technical Training Centre at Ramu, Cox's Bazar, said at the 6 June 2026 roundtable that a skill verification test centre for employment in Saudi Arabia has opened in Cox's Bazar, that passing the test makes it easier to get a job there with a chance of higher pay, and that the Ramu centre runs pre-departure training and three-month technical courses.
MY2-23.target_section: Do I need a skill test?
MY2-23.why_new: A Saudi skill-test centre in Cox's Bazar and where pre-departure training is given in the district; check whether the Saudi doc's list of test centres has it.

MY2-24.claim: Biswajit Bhowmik, an advocate with the Bangladesh National Women Lawyers' Association (BNWLA), said at the 6 June 2026 Cox's Bazar roundtable that many people from Cox's Bazar go abroad by air holding a passport, visa and BMET card but are sent on 90-day visas, and after arriving get neither permission to stay nor any work and are forced to come home empty-handed.
MY2-24.target_section: A visit or tourist visa sold as a job
MY2-24.why_new: A lawyer handling returnees' cases describes workers who hold a BMET card yet travel on a 90-day visa; also belongs in "When the visa, the agency and the clearance are all real". He names no destination country.
MY2-24.h3: A visit or tourist visa sold as a job

MY2-25.claim: A BNWLA advocate said at the 6 June 2026 Cox's Bazar roundtable that the association is conducting the cases of about 100 returnees from abroad in the Cox's Bazar court, and that about 465 human trafficking cases are pending.
MY2-25.why_new: BNWLA is not in the free-legal-help list; this shows it runs returnees' court cases in Cox's Bazar. The article gives no contact details, and does not say whether the 465 pending cases are in Cox's Bazar or BNWLA's own.
MY2-25.h3: Where to complain and get help

MY2-26.claim: Tarekur Rahman told the 6 June 2026 Cox's Bazar roundtable that a broker, promising an easy Malaysian visa, trafficked him and others from Maheshkhali to Myanmar, where they were beaten, Tk 1 lakh was taken from the family and they were moved to another hidden place, tortured and threatened with death.
MY2-26.why_new: First-person account of the ransom stage in Myanmar; the section has no survivor account of the sea route.

MY2-27.claim: Tarekur Rahman said that under torture his family was forced to sell their house to pay the traffickers, that even then food sometimes came only after three or four days, and that after taking another large sum on a false promise of sending them to Malaysia the traffickers took them towards the border, where they were caught and held in a Myanmar prison for about seven months.
MY2-27.why_new: How the money keeps being extracted (house sold, second payment for the "onward" leg) and where it ended: seven months in a Myanmar prison. Differs from the news report of the same event (article 300ce3de), which has a Tk 7 lakh payment in Thailand.

MY2-28.claim: Tarekur Rahman said that while he was in the Myanmar prison he and the others got no real help from the Bangladesh embassy, and that they finally got home on money sent by their families.
MY2-28.why_new: Evidence of what the embassy route delivered in practice for one detainee in Myanmar (nothing, by his account); the section lists only embassy contacts. Aung Aung U Jewel, at the same event, said he returned with embassy help.

MY2-29.claim: Aung Aung U Jewel told the 6 June 2026 Cox's Bazar roundtable that he could not afford the language tests needed to go legally, so he set off when brokers promised an easy, cheap route to Australia by way of Malaysia; he later realised they had entered Myanmar, and after several days walking over hills they were detained, and he spent a month on remand and several months in prison.
MY2-29.why_new: Why he took the route (the cost of the legal one) and that the "Malaysia" leg was in fact an overland walk into Myanmar; fuller than the news report's version.

MY2-30.claim: Aung Aung U Jewel said he had no contact with his family while detained in Myanmar, managed to send a letter to his mother through a Myanmar police officer, and later learned that the brokers had also taken money from his family as the cost of rescuing him.
MY2-30.why_new: A second charge by the same brokers: money taken from the family as a "rescue cost" while the man sat in a foreign prison. Also relevant to "People who offer to get your money back".

MY2-31.claim: Aung Aung U Jewel said that when fighting began while he was held in Thandwe prison in Myanmar, the prisoners were moved elsewhere and forced to do various work, and that he later returned home with the help of the Bangladesh embassy.
MY2-31.why_new: Names the prison (Thandwe) and what happened to detainees when the fighting reached it; shows the embassy did arrange this return.

MY2-32.claim: On 19 July 2026 the Expatriates' Welfare Ministry issued a notification withdrawing the licences of 49 recruiting agencies, including agencies of former Awami League MPs, that Prothom Alo linked to the Malaysia syndicate; the notification says charge sheets against them under sections 406, 420, 385, 386, 427 and 34 of the Penal Code 1860 were filed in court and accepted, and that the licences were withdrawn under the migration Act for that reason.
MY2-32.why_new: The Malaysia doc says 49 licences were cancelled in July 2026; this adds the exact date, the legal ground (an accepted charge sheet) and the Penal Code sections. The date 19 July is confirmed by article 2ec8c523.
MY2-32.h3: How a job reaches you, and who takes a cut

MY2-33.claim: On 19 July 2026 the Expatriates' Welfare Ministry withdrew the licences of 49 recruiting agencies, which Prothom Alo described as linked to the Malaysia labour-market syndicate, because charge sheets against them under Penal Code 1860 sections 406, 420, 385, 386, 427 and 34 had been filed and accepted in court.
MY2-33.target_section: When the visa, the agency and the clearance are all real
MY2-33.why_new: The section's Malaysia item says what happened to workers but not what was done to the agencies; this is the licence action, with its legal basis.
MY2-33.h3: When the visa, the agency and the clearance are all real

MY2-34.claim: Among the 49 agencies whose licences were withdrawn on 19 July 2026 are Orbitals Enterprise and Orbital International, owned by the wife and daughter of former Awami League finance minister A H M Mustafa Kamal; Ahmed International of Benzir Ahmed, MP for Dhaka-20; Snigdha Overseas Limited of former Feni-2 MP Nizam Uddin Hazari; and Five M International of former Feni-3 MP Lt Gen (retd) Masud Uddin Chowdhury.
MY2-34.why_new: The Malaysia doc names only Catharsis among the 49; these are the politically owned agencies, named with their owners.
MY2-34.h3: How a job reaches you, and who takes a cut

MY2-35.claim: The 49 agencies whose licences were withdrawn on 19 July 2026 also include Unique Eastern Private Limited, of Noor Ali, whom Prothom Alo calls a much-discussed manpower businessman, and Catharsis International, of Ruhul Amin alias Swapan, whom it calls one of the members of the Malaysia syndicate.
MY2-35.why_new: Adds Unique Eastern (Noor Ali) to the named withdrawals; Catharsis is already in the doc.
MY2-35.h3: How a job reaches you, and who takes a cut

MY2-36.claim: The other agencies whose licences the Ministry withdrew on 19 July 2026, as named by Prothom Alo, include: M/s Shaheen Travels, Irving Enterprise, Hridoy Trade International, Rabbi International, Jahrat International, 4 Site International, Binimoy International, Akash Bhraman Limited, QK Quick Express Limited, United Export Limited, GMG Trading Private Limited, Sadia International, The Super Eastern Limited, Elegants Overseas Limited, Midway Overseas Limited, Madina Overseas, Al Khamis International, New Age International, Damashi Corporation Limited, Galaxy Corporation, Sultan Overseas, Provati International, Manispower Corporation, Amin Tours and Travels, ISMT Human Resource Development, Darbar Global Overseas, Natasha Overseas, Aparajita Overseas, Stanford Employment Private Limited, Jannat Overseas, BM Travels, BNS Overseas Limited, Rubel Bangladesh Limited.
MY2-36.placement: other: Action in Bangladesh (list of the 49; belongs with the agency records)
MY2-36.why_new: The doc points to agency records for the syndicate agencies but names none of the 49; this is the printed list (42 names besides the seven named with their owners). English spellings are transliterated from the Bangla and should be matched to RL numbers on OEP; the article prints no licence numbers.
MY2-36.h3: How a job reaches you, and who takes a cut

MY2-37.claim: The other agencies whose licences the Ministry withdrew on 19 July 2026, as named by Prothom Alo, include: Trans Asia Integrate Services Limited, Al Farah Human Resources and Consultancy, Brothers International, Thanex International Limited, JG Alfalah Management, Imperial Resources Limited, PR Overseas Limited, MEF Global Bangladesh Limited, Ananya Apurba Recruiting Agency.
MY2-37.placement: other: Action in Bangladesh (list of the 49; belongs with the agency records)
MY2-37.why_new: The doc points to agency records for the syndicate agencies but names none of the 49; this is the printed list (42 names besides the seven named with their owners). English spellings are transliterated from the Bangla and should be matched to RL numbers on OEP; the article prints no licence numbers.
MY2-37.h3: How a job reaches you, and who takes a cut

MY2-38.claim: Expatriates' Welfare Ministry sources told Prothom Alo in July 2026 that an agency's licence is cancelled when it breaks the licence conditions and is withdrawn when it commits a serious offence or is a threat to national security, and that getting a withdrawn licence back may require a legal fight.
MY2-38.target_section: The Overseas Employment and Migrants Act 2013
MY2-38.why_new: The guide treats "cancelled" as one status; the ministry distinguishes cancellation (breach of conditions) from withdrawal (serious offence), which explains the two words a reader sees in orders and news.

MY2-39.claim: When Malaysia reopened in July 2022 after nearly four years, the selection of agencies was left to the Malaysian government, to which the Ministry sent a list of 1,520 recruiting agencies; the syndicate began with 25 agencies and grew in three steps to 100, and it is alleged that a large sum was taken from each agency to get its name in.
MY2-39.placement: other: how the 2022-24 syndicate was formed
MY2-39.why_new: The doc describes the 2026 list of 25 but not the 2022 numbers: 1,520 proposed, 25 chosen, then 100, with an alleged entry payment by each agency.
MY2-39.h3: How a job reaches you, and who takes a cut

MY2-40.claim: Prothom Alo reported in July 2026 that about four and a half lakh workers were sent to Malaysia in a year and a half, making a trade of Tk 24,000 crore, with workers spending Tk 5,44,000 on average against a government-set maximum of Tk 78,990, and that agencies of former MPs, Awami League leaders and a city corporation councillor, and many firms new to the sector, sent large numbers of workers after getting into the syndicate.
MY2-40.target_section: MALAYSIA DOC: What people really pay
MY2-40.why_new: The doc has the per-worker figures but not the total (Tk 24,000 crore) or who the new entrants were.
MY2-40.h3: What you pay, and what you earn and keep

MY2-41.claim: A Prothom Alo editorial of 22 July 2026 said that although 14 countries including Bangladesh send workers to Malaysia, a syndicate system grew up only for Bangladesh, and that the UN human rights office (OHCHR) had issued a statement on the plight of Bangladeshi workers in Malaysia.
MY2-41.target_section: MALAYSIA DOC: What closed it before
MY2-41.why_new: States that the syndicate arrangement was unique to Bangladesh among source countries. Conflict to resolve: this editorial prints 14 source countries, the 2 Sept 2026 report (ede539c0) prints 11.
MY2-41.h3: Is it open now, and who can go?

MY2-42.claim: A Prothom Alo editorial of 22 July 2026 said the Malaysian labour market was reopening to Bangladeshis after talks between Prime Minister Tarique Rahman and Malaysia's Prime Minister Anwar Ibrahim during Tarique Rahman's visit to Malaysia the previous month.
MY2-42.why_new: The doc's Status timeline starts at the 15 October 2026 announcement; this gives the political step before it (the June 2026 prime ministers' talks).
MY2-42.h3: Is it open now, and who can go?

MY2-43.claim: On 30 July 2026 the state minister for expatriates' welfare, Md Nurul Haque, asked how agencies take Tk 12 to 15 lakh from a person going to Singapore, and said the Singapore authority does not take that money: six training institutes have been authorised, they charge, and by doing business as a syndicate they are becoming owners of hundreds of crores of taka.
MY2-43.why_new: The section covers Saudi and Jordan only; this is the Singapore training-centre route, with a price (Tk 12-15 lakh) and the number of authorised centres (six), from the state minister. He does not name the six.

MY2-44.claim: The state minister for expatriates' welfare said on 30 July 2026 that most of the country's roughly three thousand recruiting licence holders are involved in irregularities, and that if the rules were properly followed no more than four or five hundred licences would survive; he also said many agencies renew their licences without being qualified to.
MY2-44.target_section: Is there a list of good agencies?
MY2-44.why_new: The minister's own estimate of how many licensed agencies would pass their licence conditions; supports the guide's point that a valid licence proves little.

MY2-45.claim: The state minister for expatriates' welfare said on 30 July 2026 that advertising on social media to send people abroad without the Ministry's permission is plainly against the law, that the government has ordered tough action against those posting flashy, fake adverts for Malaysia and other countries, and he urged BMET to run mobile courts against them.
MY2-45.target_section: Online job adverts, Facebook and WhatsApp scams, and fake government sites
MY2-45.why_new: The section cites section 32 for unapproved adverts; this adds a dated statement by the state minister applying it to social media adverts, and the remedy he named (BMET mobile courts).
MY2-45.h3: Online job adverts, Facebook and WhatsApp scams, and fake government sites

MY2-46.claim: Professor Tasneem Siddiqui, executive director of RMMRU (the Refugee and Migratory Movements Research Unit), said on 30 July 2026, citing a study by the organisation, that about 51% of migrants are cheated in one way or another, 19% paid and still could not go abroad, and 32% were tortured after going abroad.
MY2-46.target_section: Dalal scams: the usual tricks and how to spot them
MY2-46.why_new: Three prevalence figures from RMMRU; the 19% who paid and never went belongs in "Refund refusals after a failed departure". The article gives no year or sample for the study.
MY2-46.h3: H2:Dalal scams: the usual tricks and how to spot them

MY2-47.claim: Professor Tasneem Siddiqui of RMMRU said on 30 July 2026 that, because of various kinds of fraud, the number of women migrating fell by about 41% in 2025 compared with 2022.
MY2-47.target_section: Trafficking disguised as a job, especially for women
MY2-47.why_new: A trend figure for women's migration with the cause RMMRU attributes it to; the section has only CID case counts.
MY2-47.h3: Trafficking disguised as a job, especially for women

MY2-48.claim: BMET's Director General, Jamil Ahmed, said on 30 July 2026 that in 2025 BMET settled 500 complaints by the manual process and obtained Tk 10 crore in compensation for migrants.
MY2-48.why_new: BMET's own count of complaints settled and money recovered in a year; the section has only OKUP's and RMMRU's figures on outcomes.
MY2-48.h3: Where to complain and get help

MY2-49.claim: Prothom Alo reported that the Online Complaint Management Module on the Overseas Employment Platform, developed jointly by BMET and RMMRU and launched on 30 July 2026, lets migrant workers and their family members file a complaint online, upload evidence, follow its progress and receive notifications at each stage, and will bring every District Employment and Manpower Office (DEMO) and BMET's central complaint handling into one digital framework.
MY2-49.why_new: The guide already has the module and its launch date; this adds that family members can file, that it sends stage notifications, and that DEMO complaints are in the same system.
MY2-49.h3: Where to complain and get help

MY2-50.claim: The Expatriates' Welfare Ministry's secretary, Md Mokhtar Ahmed, said on 30 July 2026 that most of the complaints the Ministry receives from migrants turn out to be true, and that the most common are money taken on a promise of sending someone abroad, a migrant's property at home being seized, and a person going missing abroad.
MY2-50.why_new: The Ministry's own ranking of complaint types, not in the section.
MY2-50.h3: Where to complain and get help

MY2-51.claim: Malaysia published the names of the 25 Bangladeshi recruiting agencies on FWCMS, its online foreign-worker management platform, on Friday 21 August 2026, and the opposition parties Jamaat-e-Islami and the National Citizen Party (NCP) issued statements of concern on 22 and 23 August.
MY2-51.target_section: MALAYSIA DOC: The processing agency: the toll gate
MY2-51.why_new: Gives the date the list of 25 appeared on FWCMS. The date is derived from "last Friday" in an article published Sunday 23 August 2026.
MY2-51.h3: How a job reaches you, and who takes a cut

MY2-52.claim: The NCP's spokesperson, Asif Mahmud, said in a statement on 22 August 2026 that the Bangladesh government had earlier sent Malaysia a list of 423 recruiting agencies that met Malaysia's conditions, and that the process, criteria and basis on which only 25 were chosen from it were still not clear.
MY2-52.why_new: The doc says a Malaysian committee chose the 25 but not that they came from a Bangladesh-approved list of 423, or that the selection criteria were never published.
MY2-52.h3: How a job reaches you, and who takes a cut

MY2-53.claim: Jamaat-e-Islami said in a statement on 23 August 2026 that it feared the arrangement of 25 agencies could push a worker's cost of going to Malaysia to Tk 6 to 7 lakh, and that Bangladesh has more than two thousand valid recruiting agencies.
MY2-53.target_section: MALAYSIA DOC: What people really pay
MY2-53.why_new: A third source for the Tk 6-7 lakh expectation (the doc has it from brokers and an agency owner); a political party's fear, not a measured price.
MY2-53.h3: What you pay, and what you earn and keep

MY2-54.claim: Bhaluka Overseas, one of the 25 agencies chosen for Malaysia, was licensed in 2022 and had taken clearance for 235 workers up to 23 August 2026, none of them for Malaysia; its proprietor, Md Abu Sohag Khan, told Prothom Alo he had earlier sent more than a thousand workers to Malaysia in the names of various other agencies, was selected automatically from Malaysia and paid no one for it.
MY2-54.target_section: MALAYSIA DOC: Step 1: Find a real job
MY2-54.why_new: The doc lists the eight agencies with a Malaysia record and Goodness among the 17 without; Bhaluka is not named. The owner's own statement also documents the practice of sending workers under other agencies' licences.

MY2-55.claim: The 17 of the 25 agencies with no record of sending workers to Malaysia in BMET data from January 2004 to 23 August 2026 are, as printed by Prothom Alo: Tania Trade, Satkhira International, A-Plus, Al Hayat Overseas, Valley Trade, Khan Jahan Ali Overseas, Bengal Human Resource, Earth Smart, At Taqwa, Motherland, Mangrove, Jewel Rinku Enterprise, Bangladesh One Overseas, Annesha Air, Chandpur International, Godness Services and Bhaluka Overseas.
MY2-55.target_section: MALAYSIA DOC: Step 1: Find a real job
MY2-55.why_new: The doc gives the count (17) and names only Goodness; these are all 17 names. Spellings are transliterated; match to the FWCMS list and RL numbers.

MY2-56.claim: Of the eight agencies among the 25 that had sent workers to Malaysia, BMET data analysed by Prothom Alo show five sent 11, 74, 100, 150 and 202 workers and the other three 436, 333 and 306; Bangladesh One Overseas Limited, also on the list, had taken clearance for 795 workers in all and none for Malaysia.
MY2-56.target_section: MALAYSIA DOC: Step 1: Find a real job
MY2-56.why_new: The doc has the total (1,612 across eight) but not how thin each agency's record is; the largest sent 436 in about 23 years. The article does not say which agency sent which number, except The Anchor Care (11).

MY2-57.claim: United Gulf Services, on the list of 25, is owned by Laila Arzuman Banu; Greenland Overseas, the firm of her husband Abdul Hai, was a member of the previous syndicate and is now run by their daughter Rehana Arzuman Hai; Laila Arzuman Banu did not answer Prothom Alo's several calls and her daughter also did not answer.
MY2-57.target_section: MALAYSIA DOC: Step 1: Find a real job
MY2-57.why_new: The doc has the link between United Gulf and Greenland but not the three names or that the daughter now runs Greenland.

MY2-58.claim: Several members of BAIRA, the recruiting agency owners' association, told Prothom Alo in September 2026 that the earlier syndicate agencies and the firms of ministers or MPs are not directly on the new list, but that the old ringleaders of the syndicate are behind the unfamiliar agencies, and that workers may have to spend Tk 6 to 7 lakh to go this time.
MY2-58.why_new: Explains, as BAIRA members allege it, why the 2026 list is made of unknown agencies: they front for the earlier organisers.
MY2-58.h3: How a job reaches you, and who takes a cut

MY2-59.claim: BAIRA members told Prothom Alo in September 2026 that on top of a syndicate fee of RM5,500 (Tk 1,68,000), bringing each demand letter, that is buying each visa, will cost RM8,000 to 9,000 (Tk 2,65,000 to 2,75,000), so that more than Tk 4,30,000 per worker will be siphoned off to Malaysia.
MY2-59.target_section: MALAYSIA DOC: Where a Tk 5.5 lakh deal goes
MY2-59.why_new: The doc has the RM5,500 toll and a demand-letter range of RM8,000-12,000 from another source; this adds BAIRA members' RM8,000-9,000 figure and their total of over Tk 4.3 lakh a worker leaving for Malaysia.
MY2-59.h3: What you pay, and what you earn and keep

MY2-60.claim: Prothom Alo reported in September 2026 that Ruhul Amin alias Swapan, a former BAIRA secretary general alleged to act in Bangladesh as the representative of Amin Nur, has been in hiding abroad since the fall of the Awami League in the 2024 uprising, that his agency's licence has been withdrawn, a case against him is under way and the ACC is also investigating.
MY2-60.why_new: The doc says police sought his extradition; this adds that he is abroad in hiding and the state of the proceedings as of September 2026.
MY2-60.h3: How a job reaches you, and who takes a cut

MY2-61.claim: Prothom Alo reported in September 2026 that Bestinet owns Migrams, the software of Malaysia's FWCMS recruitment system, and is owned by Aminul Islam bin Abdul Nur, a Malaysian citizen of Bangladeshi origin known as Amin Nur.
MY2-61.why_new: Adds the software's name (Migrams) and the name "Amin Nur" by which he is known in the Bangla press; the doc calls him "Amin".
MY2-61.h3: How a job reaches you, and who takes a cut

MY2-62.claim: The state minister for expatriates' welfare, Md Nurul Haque, told Prothom Alo in September 2026 that the Ministry would set a cost ceiling for sending workers to Malaysia, and that if any agency accused of trafficking or corruption is on the list Malaysia would be told and its licence withdrawn.
MY2-62.why_new: A dated commitment by the state minister on two open points in the doc: a cost cap, and removal of accused agencies from the list.
MY2-62.h3: How a job reaches you, and who takes a cut

MY2-63.claim: In a letter to BMET on 23 July 2026 seeking information on 57 agencies, the Anti-Corruption Commission (ACC) said it had filed a case in June 2025 against five agencies for acquiring illegal wealth by trafficking women abroad with forged papers made in collusion with dishonest BMET officials, and that the investigation had found allegations against 52 more agencies.
MY2-63.target_section: Trafficking disguised as a job, especially for women
MY2-63.why_new: The cross-country guide has no ACC case on trafficking women; this one alleges forged papers made with BMET officials' collusion and covers 57 agencies. The Malaysia doc already uses it for three listed agencies.
MY2-63.h3: Trafficking disguised as a job, especially for women

MY2-64.claim: In a notice of 28 August 2026 the Expatriates' Welfare Ministry said the agencies were vetted by a high-level joint committee of Malaysia's human resources, foreign and home ministries, its anti-corruption commission and law enforcement agencies, with not the slightest involvement of the Bangladesh government.
MY2-64.why_new: The doc says "a Malaysian committee"; this gives its composition and the date of the Ministry's notice. Note: the same notice, as printed, dates the MoU to 18 December 2022.
MY2-64.h3: How a job reaches you, and who takes a cut

MY2-65.claim: Prothom Alo reported that Malaysia set 10 conditions for the agency list, that 163 agencies first qualified, and that after Malaysia relaxed three conditions and then one more at Bangladesh's request, the Ministry under the interim government sent Malaysia a final list of 423.
MY2-65.why_new: How the long list was made (10 conditions, 163 qualifying, 423 after four conditions were relaxed); not in the doc. The article does not say what the conditions were.
MY2-65.h3: How a job reaches you, and who takes a cut

MY2-66.claim: Prothom Alo reported in September 2026 that Malaysia approved 25 agencies each for Nepal and Bangladesh and 10 each for India, Pakistan and Myanmar, that the agency owners' associations of four countries protested in a joint statement, that everyone on the lists sent by countries such as Sri Lanka and the Philippines was approved, and that Nepal has begun an investigation into its list of 25.
MY2-66.why_new: Comparison with other source countries in 2026, absent from the doc: the limited list is no longer unique to Bangladesh, and Nepal is investigating its own.
MY2-66.h3: How a job reaches you, and who takes a cut

MY2-67.claim: Prothom Alo reported in September 2026 that 11 countries including Bangladesh are on the list of countries sending workers to Malaysia, and that no country other than Bangladesh had had such a syndicate system.
MY2-67.target_section: MALAYSIA DOC: What closed it before
MY2-67.why_new: Same point as the 22 July editorial but with 11 source countries, not 14; one of the two figures is wrong.
MY2-67.h3: Is it open now, and who can go?

MY2-68.claim: Prothom Alo reported that in the 2022-24 round the agencies inside the syndicate, without doing anything, took at least Tk 1.5 lakh in "syndicate fee" for each worker, an allegation the ACC is investigating; four owners of agencies outside the list said Malaysian companies sent demand letters to them because of their long business there, and they then had to go to a syndicate agency and pay Tk 1,52,000 per worker to send the workers.
MY2-68.target_section: MALAYSIA DOC: The processing agency: the toll gate
MY2-68.placement: other: how the toll worked in 2022-24
MY2-68.why_new: The doc has the toll range; this adds who actually held the demand (experienced agencies outside the list) and that the listed agency's only role was to collect the fee, from four agency owners.
MY2-68.h3: How a job reaches you, and who takes a cut

MY2-69.claim: The four agency owners told Prothom Alo that an associate agency's position in 2026 will be the same, since it cannot send workers directly, and that listed agencies approved without experience are unknown to Malaysian employers, so they will send workers through experienced agencies and take the syndicate fee in return.
MY2-69.target_section: MALAYSIA DOC: The processing agency: the toll gate
MY2-69.why_new: Agency owners' prediction of how the 17 inexperienced agencies will operate: as fee collectors for others' workers.
MY2-69.h3: How a job reaches you, and who takes a cut

MY2-70.claim: Riazul Islam, BAIRA's immediate past senior vice-president, told Prothom Alo that no agency applied to be an associate, they were simply made associates, that jobs will come in the names of the 25 and not of the associates, and that at least 817 agencies sent workers in the earlier round by paying the syndicate fee.
MY2-70.target_section: MALAYSIA DOC: The processing agency: the toll gate
MY2-70.why_new: Adds that associate status was assigned, not applied for; check whether the doc's existing 817 figure is this one.
MY2-70.h3: How a job reaches you, and who takes a cut

MY2-71.claim: BAIRA members told Prothom Alo that about 1,400 Bangladeshi agencies were once listed on FWCMS, but only 10 were approved in 2016 and, in 2022, 25 at first and finally 100.
MY2-71.target_section: MALAYSIA DOC: The processing agency: the toll gate
MY2-71.why_new: Shows the narrowing from about 1,400 listed agencies to 10, then 25 and 100; not in the doc.
MY2-71.h3: How a job reaches you, and who takes a cut

MY2-72.claim: Prothom Alo reported on 2 September 2026 that the Expatriates' Welfare Ministry, warning people against brokers and fraud rings, said the process of sending workers to Malaysia was not final, that it would announce it by notice in due time, and that no one should make any payment before then.
MY2-72.why_new: An earlier (by early September 2026) official warning not to pay, before the October announcement the myth entry starts from.

MY2-73.claim: Prothom Alo reported that in 2022 BOESL received demand for more than 10,000 workers for Malaysia but sent about one and a half thousand; two responsible BOESL officials said that because its workers went free, at the employer's cost, obstacles came in various ways, and that BOESL itself had to spend money to get demand letters for employer-paid recruitment.
MY2-73.why_new: The doc says BOESL sent only 1,381; this adds the demand it had (over 10,000) and BOESL officials' explanation of the shortfall.
MY2-73.h3: Is it open now, and who can go?

MY2-74.claim: Prothom Alo reported that agencies of three Awami League-era MPs and of one MP's family member, with agencies of Awami League leaders and a city corporation councillor, did business inside the 2022-24 Malaysia syndicate, and that these agencies themselves said publicly that they had sent no workers: other agencies sent workers in their names.
MY2-74.target_section: When the visa, the agency and the clearance are all real
MY2-74.why_new: Mechanism the section lacks: the agency named on a worker's clearance may not be the one that recruited him, because listed agencies lent their names. Also fits MALAYSIA DOC: Who controls it.
MY2-74.h3: When the visa, the agency and the clearance are all real

MY2-75.claim: Shariful Hasan, associate director and head of BRAC's migration programme, told Prothom Alo in September 2026 that the choice of 25 agencies proved the syndicate is stronger than the two governments, and that workers are again being recruited through Amin Nur's system.
MY2-75.why_new: A named expert's assessment that the 2026 arrangement runs on the same system as 2022-24.
MY2-75.h3: How a job reaches you, and who takes a cut

MY2-76.claim: Dr Selim Reza of North South University's Centre for Migration Studies wrote in Prothom Alo on 4 September 2026 that, according to the government, the plan is to send the first 10,000 workers through BOESL on special chartered flights free of every cost including airfare, that more workers are to follow, and that various statements have mentioned the possibility of about two lakh workers.
MY2-76.why_new: Adds the chartered-flight plan and the two-lakh figure in circulation; check against the doc's Status, which already records the dispute over whether airfare is included.
MY2-76.h3: Is it open now, and who can go?

MY2-77.claim: Dr Selim Reza wrote on 4 September 2026 that if information on who may apply for the 10,000 zero-cost places, what qualifications are needed, how they are chosen and where to apply is not published, the scheme could become a new line of business for brokers, that a claim that paying money will get a name onto the list of 10,000 should be treated as likely fraud, and that the Ministry's warning not to hand over money, a medical test or a passport until government instructions come must be enforced.
MY2-77.why_new: A named academic's warning about the specific pitch of selling a place on the 10,000 list. He describes a risk, not a reported case.

MY2-78.claim: Dr Selim Reza wrote in Prothom Alo on 9 September 2026 that recent newspaper reports describe several hundred would-be migrants from Munshiganj and Cumilla who were lured through Facebook with "free visa" jobs in Saudi Arabia and paid about Tk 4 to 6 lakh each; the adverts carried the hiring company's logo and forged signatures, and many later learned their visa was not a work permit at all.
MY2-78.target_section: Online job adverts, Facebook and WhatsApp scams, and fake government sites
MY2-78.why_new: A Saudi "free visa" Facebook case with a scale (several hundred people) and price; the section's cases are Cambodia and fake police clearances. Second-hand: the author cites unnamed newspaper reports, so trace the original before use.
MY2-78.h3: Online job adverts, Facebook and WhatsApp scams, and fake government sites

MY2-79.claim: Dr Selim Reza wrote on 9 September 2026 that, as far as he and his colleagues have learned, thousands of Bangladeshis were cheated in the name of jobs in Malaysia over the past five years, after large sums were taken from them on the promise of factory jobs abroad.
MY2-79.target_section: Online job adverts, Facebook and WhatsApp scams, and fake government sites
MY2-79.why_new: Weak (no source or count): only supports that the Malaysia factory-job promise is a common pitch. Could be dropped.
MY2-79.h3: Online job adverts, Facebook and WhatsApp scams, and fake government sites

MY2-80.claim: Dr Selim Reza wrote on 9 September 2026 that online brokering has created new ways to take money under names such as "registration", "visa processing" and "document verification".
MY2-80.target_section: Online job adverts, Facebook and WhatsApp scams, and fake government sites
MY2-80.why_new: The section lists the slogans used in adverts but not the fee labels under which money is first taken.
MY2-80.h3: Online job adverts, Facebook and WhatsApp scams, and fake government sites

MY2-81.claim: Dr Selim Reza wrote on 9 September 2026 that IOM's recent warnings and data say fake online job adverts are not only a way to take money but sometimes the first door to trafficking and to being used in forced criminality.
MY2-81.target_section: Online job adverts, Facebook and WhatsApp scams, and fake government sites
MY2-81.why_new: Links the online advert to trafficking and forced criminality, citing IOM; second-hand, so cite IOM's own warning if it can be found.
MY2-81.h3: Online job adverts, Facebook and WhatsApp scams, and fake government sites

MY2-82.claim: Dr Selim Reza wrote on 9 September 2026 that brokers' networks show flashy YouTube videos of an easy way to Europe and use Facebook, imo and WhatsApp groups to make the offer, keep contact and pass on travel information, and that a Prothom Alo investigation about four years earlier had found Facebook groups used for sending people to Europe across the Mediterranean.
MY2-82.why_new: Names the apps used to sell the Europe route (YouTube, Facebook, imo, WhatsApp); second-hand reference to an earlier Prothom Alo investigation.

MY2-83.claim: Dr Selim Reza wrote on 9 September 2026 that more than two thousand recruiting agencies have been added to RAIMS (the Recruitment Agents Information System), that a 2024 amendment brought recruitment sub-agents and intermediaries under the Overseas Employment and Migrants Act, and that a 2025 code of conduct also provides for holding sub-agents to account.
MY2-83.target_section: How do I check whether an agency is real?
MY2-83.why_new: RAIMS is not mentioned in the guide. Conflict to check: the guide dates the sub-agent amendment to 2023, this article says 2024. The article does not say whether the public can search RAIMS.

MY2-84.claim: Dr Selim Reza wrote on 9 September 2026 that recent studies show a large share of people waiting to go abroad have not finished secondary education and most rely on relatives, local brokers, sub-agents and informal networks instead of licensed recruiting agencies, adding that these are indications of a trend, not exact national statistics; by government figures, he wrote, 8 to 9 lakh of the roughly 22 to 23 lakh young people entering the labour market each year have to look for work abroad.
MY2-84.why_new: Context figures; low priority, since the section already has survey percentages for broker use. The studies are not named.

MY2-85.claim: After the special mobile court at Triple A Overseas (RL-2630) on 10 September 2026, led by a BMET executive magistrate on the minister's instruction, the Expatriates' Welfare Ministry said the three boxes of passports taken irregularly from Malaysia-bound workers were in BMET's custody, and that returning them to their real owners through legal process and taking legal action against the agency were under way.
MY2-85.target_section: The passport kept by the dalal
MY2-85.why_new: The guide has the raid, fine and seizure; it does not say where the passports went (BMET custody) or that owners are to get them back through a legal process. The article does not say how an owner claims one.
MY2-85.h3: The passport kept by the dalal

MY2-86.claim: On 4 October 2026 the Appellate Division's chamber judge, Justice Md Rezaul Haque, stayed a High Court order that had suspended the Ministry's 19 July 2026 notification, so the withdrawal of the 49 recruiting agencies' licences remains in force.
MY2-86.why_new: The doc records the July withdrawal but not that agencies challenged it and that it was upheld (so far) at the Appellate Division in October 2026.
MY2-86.h3: How a job reaches you, and who takes a cut

MY2-87.claim: The Attorney General, Md Ruhul Quddus Kajal, said that after one agency challenged the withdrawal by writ the High Court issued a rule and stayed the notification on 15 September 2026, the chamber court stayed that order on 30 September, and 11 more agencies then obtained a stay from a vacation bench in a second writ, which the chamber court also stayed; Prothom Alo names New Age International among the agencies that filed writs.
MY2-87.why_new: The sequence of court orders: for two weeks in September 2026 the withdrawal was suspended, which matters to anyone checking whether one of the 49 could legally recruit on a given date.
MY2-87.h3: How a job reaches you, and who takes a cut

MY2-88.claim: The withdrawal of 49 recruiting agencies' licences on 19 July 2026 was suspended by a High Court order on 15 September 2026 and restored when the Appellate Division's chamber court stayed that order on 30 September, according to the Attorney General.
MY2-88.target_section: How do I check whether an agency is real?
MY2-88.why_new: Shows that an agency's licence status can change back and forth with court orders, which the answer (read the status on OEP) does not mention.

MY2-89.claim: The Attorney General, Md Ruhul Quddus Kajal, told reporters on 4 October 2026 that Bangladesh's labour market in Malaysia collapsed because of money taken beyond the fixed fees, people promised one job and given another, and fake visas, and that cases were filed during the interim government against those involved and charge sheets submitted after investigation.
MY2-89.target_section: Contract substitution: a different job or wage on arrival
MY2-89.why_new: The state's chief law officer names job substitution and fake visas, with overcharging, as the grounds of the Malaysia cases; the section has no Malaysia entry.
MY2-89.h3: Contract substitution: a different job or wage on arrival

AB1-1.claim: A Home Ministry report on human trafficking dated November 2023 says that in January to September 2023 courts disposed of 332 cases under the trafficking act and all the accused were acquitted in 316 of them, 95.18% of the total.
AB1-1.why_new: The section gives penalties but no conviction or acquittal rate.

AB1-2.claim: According to the same Home Ministry report, 12,279 accused were acquitted in the cases disposed of in January to September 2023, and in the 16 cases that ended in punishment 56 people were sentenced, only two of them to life imprisonment.
AB1-2.why_new: Number of people acquitted against number punished; not in the guide.

AB1-3.claim: Home Ministry sources told Prothom Alo in January 2024 that no accused was convicted in a single trafficking case in 2021 and 2022.
AB1-3.why_new: Two full years with no conviction; not in the guide.

AB1-4.claim: According to Home Ministry sources, 683 new trafficking cases were filed in the nine months to September 2023, charge sheets were given in 31 of them and final reports in 18; of 30,539 cases under the trafficking act in courts up to September 2023, 25,000 were under trial and 5,327 more under investigation.
AB1-4.why_new: Size of the backlog. Note for the editor: the same article also says 49 cases were disposed of "in this period", which does not match the 332 disposed cases it gives from the ministry report; only the figures quoted here are used.

AB1-5.claim: According to Home Ministry sources cited by Prothom Alo in January 2024, cases under the trafficking act have been filed against 289,472 people, of whom 132,638 have been arrested.
AB1-5.why_new: Accused against arrested; not in the guide.

AB1-6.claim: Experts who work against trafficking told Prothom Alo in January 2024 that accused are acquitted because cases are not investigated properly, witnesses cannot be produced in court, and cases are compromised with the trafficking rings for money.
AB1-6.why_new: The reasons cases collapse; the guide says only that workers cannot keep a case going.

AB1-7.claim: Salma Ali, president of the Bangladesh National Women Lawyers' Association (BNWLA), told Prothom Alo in January 2024 that trafficking cases are very profitable for the police: investigating officers take money from both the victim and the accused and hold up the investigation for a long time, and ring members threaten victims into a compromise.
AB1-7.why_new: A named lawyer on how investigations are stalled and victims pressured to settle; relevant to the 2026 Act offence of pressuring a victim to settle.

AB1-8.claim: After no convictions in 2021 and 2022 the Home Ministry issued an instruction on investigating trafficking cases which says the crime takes place in six stages from going abroad to returning, and tells investigators to collect who trafficked the victim, who introduced the victim to the ring, whether the victim was threatened, abducted by force or trafficked by exploiting a vulnerability, and by what route the ring moved the victim.
AB1-8.placement: other: what an investigation must establish
AB1-8.why_new: Tells a victim or family what facts investigators are instructed to gather (recruiter, introducer, means, route).

AB1-9.claim: A 28-year-old woman from Savar who was told she would be sent to Canada was trafficked to Nadia district in West Bengal, India, and came home after seven months in a jail there, Prothom Alo reported in January 2024.
AB1-9.target_section: NEW: India: women and girls taken across the land border
AB1-9.why_new: A Canada promise that ended in an Indian jail; no India case in the guide.
AB1-9.h3: NEW: India: women and girls taken across the land border

AB1-10.claim: The Savar woman's father, who filed the trafficking case, told Prothom Alo in January 2024 that the accused then filed a false case against him at Savar police station, that he was arrested and spent four months in jail, that it cost him Tk 5 to 6 lakh, and that he had now heard all the accused in his case had been acquitted.
AB1-10.why_new: A counter-case against the complainant and an acquittal: what did not work.

AB1-11.claim: The Savar father said the investigating officer told him many times that he would be taken to court to testify but never took him, and that two of the acquitted accused were back in the area; the Savar police sub-inspector who had investigated said the case had long since gone to the CID and he had no update.
AB1-11.why_new: Shows the complainant was never produced as a witness, one of the reasons experts give for acquittals.

AB1-12.claim: A 34-year-old Narayanganj woman went to Saudi Arabia in July 2022 after being told she would do housework for Tk 30,000 a month, and was physically and mentally abused there; her husband said the people who had sent her demanded Tk 3 lakh 20 thousand to bring her back, and that she was put out of the house after threatening suicide and then came home.
AB1-12.target_section: Trafficking disguised as a job, especially for women
AB1-12.why_new: A demand for money from the senders to bring an abused domestic worker home; the section has no such mechanism.
AB1-12.h3: Trafficking disguised as a job, especially for women

AB1-13.claim: The Narayanganj woman's husband said he filed a case at Hatirjheel police station on 24 November 2022 naming three men as traffickers; in January 2024 the police investigation was still unfinished, and the investigating sub-inspector said he had written to several institutions for information and had not received it.
AB1-13.target_section: Trafficking disguised as a job, especially for women
AB1-13.why_new: Outcome: more than a year on, no charge sheet.
AB1-13.h3: Trafficking disguised as a job, especially for women

AB1-14.claim: A ring trafficked women to India in the name of TikTok; one young woman escaped from India to Bangladesh on 7 May 2021 and on 1 June filed a case at Hatirjheel police station naming 12 people, and Rifadul Islam alias Hridoy (26), known as 'TikTok Hridoy', was involved in trafficking her.
AB1-14.target_section: NEW: India: women and girls taken across the land border
AB1-14.why_new: TikTok as the bait for trafficking to India; not in the guide.
AB1-14.h3: NEW: India: women and girls taken across the land border

AB1-15.claim: Prothom Alo reported in January 2024 that three years on, the investigation of the TikTok trafficking case filed at Hatirjheel police station was not finished, although accused arrested in India over the same incident had already been tried and punished there; Salma Ali of BNWLA said the lack of accountability of those investigating is why accused are not properly punished.
AB1-15.target_section: NEW: India: women and girls taken across the land border
AB1-15.why_new: Same crime: punished in India, still under investigation in Bangladesh.
AB1-15.h3: NEW: India: women and girls taken across the land border

AB1-16.claim: Of more than 13 lakh workers who went abroad in 2023, 77,263 were women; BMET data show the most women in one year, 121,925, went in 2017, and the yearly figure stayed above one lakh until 2019.
AB1-16.target_section: Which countries can a woman go to?
AB1-16.why_new: Yearly totals of women migrants; the FAQ gives only 2025-26 country counts.

AB1-17.claim: Bangladesh began sending women workers abroad in 1991; Saudi Arabia signed its agreement with Bangladesh in 2015, after Indonesia and the Philippines stopped sending domestic workers over allegations of abuse, and most Bangladeshi women migrants go to Saudi Arabia as domestic workers.
AB1-17.target_section: Which countries can a woman go to?
AB1-17.why_new: Why the Saudi domestic-worker channel opened to Bangladesh.

AB1-18.claim: Government agencies keep no count of workers who come back, except those who return on an outpass after losing their passport, whom the Wage Earners' Welfare Board's desk at the airport records; according to sources cited by Prothom Alo, 86,621 workers came back empty-handed from various countries in 2023, 2,902 of them women, including 249 women in December.
AB1-18.why_new: A yearly count of outpass returnees and who keeps it; the section has only country examples.

AB1-19.claim: Officials of several government bodies told Prothom Alo in January 2024 that most women who leave a Saudi household before the two-year contract ends run away and take shelter in the embassy's safe home, from where they are sent to the Saudi government's safe home, and the Saudi government pays for sending them home; if a woman wants to return within three months of arriving, her return is arranged through the Saudi company that recruited her.
AB1-19.target_section: What if I'm abused? Where can I go?
AB1-19.why_new: The actual path home (embassy safe home, then Saudi government safe home, who pays, the three-month rule); the FAQ only says safe homes exist.

AB1-20.claim: Lutfa Begum of Brahmanbaria went to Saudi Arabia as a domestic worker in March 2020 and worked 1 month 5 days; she told Prothom Alo she had to work in two neighbouring houses and the men of the house behaved badly, that she asked the person who had sent her for work elsewhere and did not get it, and that when she asked to go home she was sent to a shelter, where she stayed about three months before returning.
AB1-20.target_section: What if I'm abused? Where can I go?
AB1-20.why_new: A named account of work in two houses and three months in a safe home.

AB1-21.claim: Lutfa Begum said she was paid no wages for her work in Saudi Arabia in 2020, and that after coming home she received Tk 30,000 in cash assistance in two instalments.
AB1-21.target_section: What if I'm abused? Where can I go?
AB1-21.why_new: What a returnee actually received (Tk 30,000, source of the money not stated in the article).

AB1-22.claim: People in the migration sector told Prothom Alo in January 2024 that training before a woman is sent to Saudi Arabia is compulsory but is not followed in some cases, and that the quality of the training is also questioned.
AB1-22.why_new: The compulsory course is sometimes skipped.

AB1-23.claim: BRAC's Migration Programme said in January 2024 that women who go to Saudi Arabia as domestic workers keep coming home after abuse by employers, that some who were sexually abused return pregnant, and that women domestic workers are forced to return from Saudi Arabia almost every month.
AB1-23.target_section: Trafficking disguised as a job, especially for women
AB1-23.why_new: BRAC on the pattern of returns; the section has cases but no statement of how regular it is.
AB1-23.h3: Trafficking disguised as a job, especially for women

AB1-24.claim: Farida Yasmin, a Supreme Court lawyer and adviser to the Bangladesh Migrant Women Workers Association (বাংলাদেশ অভিবাসী নারী শ্রমিক অ্যাসোসিয়েশন), told Prothom Alo in January 2024 that although the migrants' law had been amended it does not separately address the protection of women.
AB1-24.why_new: A named lawyer on what the amended OEM Act lacks.

AB1-25.claim: Tipu Sultan, joint secretary general of BAIRA, told Prothom Alo in January 2024 that Saudi employers want workers quickly once they place a demand, that because of delays the women cannot be sent, and that the employers are therefore taking workers from other countries.
AB1-25.target_section: Which countries can a woman go to?
AB1-25.why_new: The agencies' association's explanation for the fall in women going.

AB1-26.claim: A Prothom Alo editorial of 16 January 2024 said many women back from Saudi Arabia say the roughly month-long training given before departure is not enough, that some cannot read or write and many cannot sign their name and can only give a thumbprint, and that the language of the country they go to is unknown to them.
AB1-26.why_new: Returnees on the length of the course, and that many sign contracts by thumbprint.

AB1-27.claim: A Prothom Alo editorial of 16 January 2024 said there is almost no example of action being taken against the accused recruiting agencies after women workers come back empty-handed and abused.
AB1-27.target_section: Trafficking disguised as a job, especially for women
AB1-27.why_new: What did not happen to agencies; it is the newspaper's own assessment and should be attributed as such.
AB1-27.h3: Trafficking disguised as a job, especially for women

AB1-28.claim: A US Embassy official filed a case at Gulshan police station, Dhaka, on the Monday before 14 February 2024 against five Bangladeshis on charges of involvement in human trafficking; the case says two of them, Mofizur Rahman (54) and Ashraful Alam Bhuiyan (33), went for US visa interviews on 11 February and admitted during the interviews that they are involved in trafficking people from Bangladesh to various countries and work mainly as dalals.
AB1-28.target_section: NEW: The United States through South America and Mexico
AB1-28.why_new: An embassy itself filing a trafficking case after a visa interview; not in the guide.
AB1-28.h3: NEW: The United States through South America and Mexico

AB1-29.claim: According to the US Embassy's case statement of February 2024, Mofizur Rahman traffics people from Bangladesh to Dubai and, with other dalals, to the United States, and sent his own brother from Bangladesh first through India to Suriname in South America, from where the brother went to the United States across the Mexico border.
AB1-29.target_section: NEW: The United States through South America and Mexico
AB1-29.why_new: A named route: India, Suriname, the Mexico border.
AB1-29.h3: NEW: The United States through South America and Mexico

AB1-30.claim: According to the same case statement, Ashraful Alam Bhuiyan said in his interview that he helps traffic people to the United States through Paraguay in South America.
AB1-30.target_section: NEW: The United States through South America and Mexico
AB1-30.h3: NEW: The United States through South America and Mexico

AB1-31.claim: According to the US Embassy's February 2024 case statement, Ashraful Alam Bhuiyan said an immigration officer at Shahjalal International Airport helps him with trafficking in return for money.
AB1-31.why_new: An alleged paid helper inside airport immigration, as stated by an accused broker.

AB1-32.claim: According to the US Embassy's February 2024 case statement, the two accused dalals submitted fake documents for their own US visa applications and described themselves in them as garment businessmen.
AB1-32.why_new: Fake papers detected at a visa interview led to a police case in Dhaka.

AB1-33.claim: The US Embassy's case names two associates, Mohammad Zaman and Bhasani, and says a man named Mohammad Nur Alam heads the ring; the police Counter Terrorism and Transnational Crime (CTTC) unit was given the investigation, and its deputy commissioner said in February 2024 that the process of formally taking over the case file from Gulshan police station had begun.
AB1-33.target_section: NEW: The United States through South America and Mexico
AB1-33.why_new: Which police unit investigates this kind of case.
AB1-33.h3: NEW: The United States through South America and Mexico

AB1-34.claim: Md Shanto Khan of Jamira village, Phultala, Khulna, went to Saudi Arabia through a dalal in 2020 at a cost of Tk 4 lakh 20 thousand, on the understanding that he would work as a cleaner in a bank; he said he was first given work at a petrol pump and then in a date garden, and did not get the monthly wage he had been promised.
AB1-34.target_section: Contract substitution: a different job or wage on arrival
AB1-34.why_new: A dated, named Saudi case: bank cleaner promised, petrol pump and date garden given.
AB1-34.h3: Contract substitution: a different job or wage on arrival

AB1-35.claim: Shanto Khan fell ill within two years, came home in mid-2023 by what he described as more or less running away, and said in October 2024 that the bank loan his father took and the money borrowed from relatives for the trip were still unpaid.
AB1-35.target_section: Contract substitution: a different job or wage on arrival
AB1-35.why_new: How the case ended: return after about three years with the debt unpaid.
AB1-35.h3: Contract substitution: a different job or wage on arrival

AB1-36.claim: Islam Hossain of Dumuria upazila, who told his story at a workshop in Khulna, said that in Oman he was not given the wage and the work he had been promised and was made to work 12 to 15 hours; he stayed five years and came home in 2020 during the Covid pandemic.
AB1-36.target_section: Contract substitution: a different job or wage on arrival
AB1-36.why_new: An Oman case; the section has none.
AB1-36.h3: Contract substitution: a different job or wage on arrival

AB1-37.claim: At a BRAC Migration Programme workshop in Khulna on 31 October 2024, attended by Khulna's additional deputy commissioner, a Khulna Metropolitan Police deputy commissioner and chaired by the assistant director of the Khulna manpower and employment office, speakers said migrants are cheated most when they go through brokers, that many keep no proof of the money they hand over when going abroad, and advised keeping proof of every transaction.
AB1-37.target_section: The staged-payment trap, and no receipts
AB1-37.why_new: Advice from officials at a named event that matches the section; adds a 2024 source.
AB1-37.h3: The staged-payment trap, and no receipts

AB1-38.claim: Tarek Aziz of Khanatua village, Manoharganj, Cumilla, alleged at a press conference on 1 March 2025 that Ashek Elahi, a former president of Cumilla South district Chhatra Shibir, took him to Nepal on the promise of taking him to the United States, held him hostage there and took Tk 45 lakh from his family; Ashek Elahi denied it at his own press conference on 3 March 2025, said the allegation was baseless and that he was himself a victim of the same fraud.
AB1-38.target_section: A flight to a different country first
AB1-38.why_new: The guide tells this Nepal case from the victim's side without names; this adds the accused's denial.
AB1-38.h3: A flight to a different country first

AB1-39.claim: By Ashek Elahi's account, a man named Jobayer Hossain of Chhatarpaiya, Senbag, Noakhali, an acquaintance of Tarek Aziz's father, was the one who sent people to America; Ashek, Tarek and several others went to Nepal with Jobayer on 7 December 2023, where Jobayer held several of them hostage and took their phones, passports and other papers.
AB1-39.target_section: A flight to a different country first
AB1-39.why_new: The accused names a different organiser; Tarek Aziz told Prothom Alo he does not know anyone of that name.
AB1-39.h3: A flight to a different country first
