AB1-40.claim: Ashek Elahi said that, in fear for their lives, the hostages told their families and his father paid Tk 40 lakh to Jobayer in cash and through a bank, after which what he called Jobayer's Nepali mafia ring let them go.
AB1-40.target_section: A flight to a different country first
AB1-40.why_new: A second ransom claimed in the same Nepal episode, paid partly through a bank.
AB1-40.h3: A flight to a different country first

AB1-41.claim: Ashek Elahi said the group came home after filing a complaint at the Bangladesh mission in Nepal (he called it the High Commission), and that at the time Tarek Aziz, as complainant, accused Jobayer of human trafficking to the Nepal police and to the mission in a complaint that bears Tarek Aziz's signature.
AB1-41.target_section: A flight to a different country first
AB1-41.why_new: Shows what hostages in Nepal did to get home: complaints to the Nepal police and the Bangladesh mission. It is the accused's account.
AB1-41.h3: A flight to a different country first

AB1-42.claim: Ashek Elahi said in March 2025 that a case under the human trafficking act had been filed against him and his family, that he and all the other accused in the case filed by Tarek Aziz were on bail, that Jobayer Hossain was not named as an accused, that he and several other victims had complained against Jobayer at Motijheel police station, and that Jobayer and a man named Masud of Kishoreganj were still absconding.
AB1-42.target_section: A flight to a different country first
AB1-42.why_new: State of the case in March 2025: accused on bail, a rival complaint, two named men absconding.
AB1-42.h3: A flight to a different country first

AB1-43.claim: Ashek Elahi alleged that on 14 December 2023 a group attacked his house and forcibly took his mother's signature on four blank bank cheques and 20 blank non-judicial stamp papers, that on 17 March 2024 Tarek Aziz's father took his uncle's signature on five blank stamp papers, that his family filed a court case to recover them, and that the cheques and stamps were then used to file the trafficking case against him.
AB1-43.why_new: The guide says only that the accused claimed his signature was taken by force; this gives his detailed claim about blank cheques and stamp papers and the counter-case.

AB1-44.claim: Tarek Aziz told Prothom Alo by phone on 3 March 2025 that his family knows nobody named Jobayer from Noakhali, that their contract was with Ashek Elahi, that Ashek Elahi took their money and that he has all the proof.
AB1-44.target_section: A flight to a different country first
AB1-44.why_new: The victim's reply to the accused's version.
AB1-44.h3: A flight to a different country first

AB1-45.claim: A 22-year-old woman living near the border in Jashore, about 30 km from Jashore town, told Prothom Alo in February 2025 that she was taken to India on the promise of a job and sold to a brothel, that Indian police rescued her two years later and she was sent back to Bangladesh, and that she saw three Bangladeshi girls in the brothel; BNWLA rehabilitated her after the rescue.
AB1-45.target_section: NEW: India: women and girls taken across the land border
AB1-45.why_new: A first-hand account of the job promise ending in an Indian brothel.
AB1-45.h3: NEW: India: women and girls taken across the land border

AB1-46.claim: Justice and Care, an organisation that works against trafficking, said the return of at least 10 women and girls trafficked across the border in the seven months from August 2024 to February 2025 was in process; Indian police had rescued them from brothels in Hyderabad, Maharashtra and Bengaluru.
AB1-46.target_section: NEW: India: women and girls taken across the land border
AB1-46.why_new: Where in India the women end up.
AB1-46.h3: NEW: India: women and girls taken across the land border

AB1-47.claim: By the count of Border Guard Bangladesh (BGB), 145 people, traffickers included, were detained while being trafficked illegally from August 2024 to January 2025, 55 of them women and children, and 162 people were repatriated from India in the same period.
AB1-47.target_section: NEW: India: women and girls taken across the land border
AB1-47.h3: NEW: India: women and girls taken across the land border

AB1-48.claim: Three girls in class eight at a Dhaka school said that in January 2025 one of them received a message from a Facebook ID named 'Nil Pakhi' saying 'Will you go to India to learn dance? Tk 50,000 a month salary'; the ID belonged to a girl of the same age whom she already knew, the girl's mother used the same ID, and that mother helped the three set off for India.
AB1-48.target_section: NEW: India: women and girls taken across the land border
AB1-48.why_new: The exact bait message and that it came from a known peer's account.
AB1-48.h3: NEW: India: women and girls taken across the land border

AB1-49.claim: The three girls said they boarded a bus from Dhaka to Jhenaidah on the morning of 10 February 2025; the bus conductor handed them to a man in Jhenaidah, who took them to a woman's house; in the evening they were put on a battery-run auto-rickshaw whose driver handed them to a man in the border area of Maheshpur.
AB1-49.target_section: NEW: India: women and girls taken across the land border
AB1-49.why_new: The relay of handlers, step by step.
AB1-49.h3: NEW: India: women and girls taken across the land border

AB1-50.claim: BGB members chased the three girls and the man taking them across the border at Maheshpur, Jhenaidah, on 10 February 2025; one girl tripped and fell, the BGB rescued all three, and the man, who had a gamcha (cotton towel) tied over his face, escaped.
AB1-50.target_section: NEW: India: women and girls taken across the land border
AB1-50.h3: NEW: India: women and girls taken across the land border

AB1-51.claim: One of the three girls filed a case at Maheshpur police station on 24 February 2025 under the Prevention and Suppression of Human Trafficking Act 2012; no one had been arrested in the case when Prothom Alo reported on 8 March 2025.
AB1-51.target_section: NEW: India: women and girls taken across the land border
AB1-51.h3: NEW: India: women and girls taken across the land border

AB1-52.claim: A 22-year-old divorced woman in Dhaka with cancer, whose treatment was costing a lot, was told by a woman neighbour that treatment is cheaper in India and that she could work there and pay for it herself; she was trafficked to India on 10 October 2024, and Hyderabad police rescued her from a brothel on 21 November.
AB1-52.target_section: NEW: India: women and girls taken across the land border
AB1-52.why_new: Cheap medical treatment as the bait, offered by a neighbour.
AB1-52.h3: NEW: India: women and girls taken across the land border

AB1-53.claim: A 15-year-old girl from a poor family wanted to go to India for work on the word of a cousin whom relatives believed to be a domestic worker in Maharashtra; she was trafficked on 11 February 2025, Maharashtra police rescued her on 23 February, and a Justice and Care programme officer said the girl had been used for sex work.
AB1-53.target_section: NEW: India: women and girls taken across the land border
AB1-53.why_new: A relative already in India as the recruiter.
AB1-53.h3: NEW: India: women and girls taken across the land border

AB1-54.claim: Prothom Alo reported in March 2025 that women have also been lured into a love affair, married and taken to India with a child and then forced into sex work; one woman said her six-month-old child was held hostage and dangled from a balcony with a threat to drop the child if she did not obey.
AB1-54.why_new: Marriage used for trafficking to India, with a child as hostage; the section covers China only.

AB1-55.claim: A Satkhira woman went to Saudi Arabia on 21 November 2024 after being told she would work as a cleaner; she was given domestic work in a house, said she was sexually abused there, and came back in January 2025.
AB1-55.target_section: Trafficking disguised as a job, especially for women
AB1-55.why_new: A cleaner job that turned into domestic work, with dates.
AB1-55.h3: Trafficking disguised as a job, especially for women

AB1-56.claim: The Satkhira woman filed a case in a Satkhira court on 16 February 2025; Monirul Islam, owner of Lamim Visa Care in Satkhira, was arrested in the case, while another accused, Md Rafiqul Islam, owner of M/s Siam Trade International in Dhaka, told Prothom Alo on 4 March that she came back because she was already ill and could not work.
AB1-56.target_section: Trafficking disguised as a job, especially for women
AB1-56.why_new: A court case leading to an arrest of a local visa-office owner, and the Dhaka firm's denial.
AB1-56.h3: Trafficking disguised as a job, especially for women

AB1-57.claim: People concerned told Prothom Alo in early 2025 that trafficking to India goes through Putkhali, Daulatpur, Gatipara, Sadipur and Rudrapur around Benapole in Jashore, through Maheshpur in Jhenaidah and through the Satkhira border, with scattered cases through Tamabil in Sylhet and the Cumilla border.
AB1-57.target_section: NEW: India: women and girls taken across the land border
AB1-57.h3: NEW: India: women and girls taken across the land border

AB1-58.claim: Binoy Krishna Mallick, executive director of Rights Jashore, said in early 2025 that traffickers now take Tk 15,000 to 20,000 per person just for getting someone across the border, far more than before, because checks have tightened; rescued women said that in the brothels they were told they had been bought for Tk 2 to 3 lakh.
AB1-58.target_section: NEW: India: women and girls taken across the land border
AB1-58.placement: The contract price and the final price
AB1-58.why_new: The crossing fee and the price a woman is told she was sold for.
AB1-58.h3: NEW: India: women and girls taken across the land border

AB1-59.claim: When someone trafficked from Bangladesh is rescued in India, the Indian Border Security Force (BSF) hands the person over to the BGB and immigration police at the 'zero line' of the Benapole border.
AB1-59.target_section: NEW: India: women and girls taken across the land border
AB1-59.why_new: How and where a rescued woman is handed back.
AB1-59.h3: NEW: India: women and girls taken across the land border

AB1-60.claim: Lt Col Saifullah Siddiqui, commander of the 49 Border Guard Battalion in Jashore, told Prothom Alo that each person in the trafficking process has a separate task, so the victims themselves cannot say who took them from which place.
AB1-60.target_section: NEW: India: women and girls taken across the land border
AB1-60.why_new: Why victims cannot name the chain; from a named BGB commander.
AB1-60.h3: NEW: India: women and girls taken across the land border

AB1-61.claim: Justice and Care's count of victims the BGB placed in its custody shows that in the 14 months from January 2024 to February 2025, 186 women and children were brought back across the Bangladesh-India border and 133 were rescued at the border; of these, between August 2024 and February 2025, 87 were brought back from India and 88 were rescued while being trafficked; the figures cover only the Jhenaidah, Chuadanga and Jashore areas.
AB1-61.target_section: NEW: India: women and girls taken across the land border
AB1-61.why_new: NGO count with its coverage limit stated.
AB1-61.h3: NEW: India: women and girls taken across the land border

AB1-62.claim: According to the US State Department's Trafficking in Persons report on Bangladesh for 2024, the government identified 1,210 trafficking victims in 2023 (210 of sex trafficking, 795 of forced labour and 205 of other kinds), while civil society and international organisations counted at least 10,135 victims, 1,784 of them of sex trafficking; the report says the government does not regularly publish anti-trafficking data.
AB1-62.why_new: Official against civil-society victim counts. Note for the editor: the article says "last year" for the 10,135 figure without restating the year.

AB1-63.claim: A UN global report on human trafficking published in 2024 said 452 women (228 of them trafficked abroad) and 63 girls were trafficked from Bangladesh from April 2023 to March 2024, more than in earlier years.
AB1-63.target_section: NEW: India: women and girls taken across the land border
AB1-63.why_new: UN count of women and girls.
AB1-63.h3: NEW: India: women and girls taken across the land border

AB1-64.claim: According to the Home Ministry, 1,135 trafficking cases were filed at police stations in 2024 and 4,291 cases in all were pending, 1,310 of them under investigation; one third of all the accused had been arrested; in 2024, after trials of earlier cases, five people were sentenced to life imprisonment and 55 to other terms, and 1,250 were acquitted.
AB1-64.why_new: 2024 case, conviction and acquittal figures; the guide has none.

AB1-65.claim: BNWLA (the Bangladesh National Women Lawyers' Association) rehabilitated a woman from near the Jashore border who was rescued from an Indian brothel, the BGB has handed victims it rescued to the custody of Justice and Care, and Justice and Care was arranging the return of women rescued by Indian police in early 2025.
AB1-65.target_section: Where victims and families get help
AB1-65.why_new: Two organisations shown actually handling women trafficked to India; the help list has neither for this purpose.
AB1-65.h3: Where victims and families get help

AB1-66.claim: Prothom Alo reported in March 2025 that traffickers usually target women from low-income families who are in financial trouble.
AB1-66.target_section: NEW: India: women and girls taken across the land border
AB1-66.h3: NEW: India: women and girls taken across the land border

AB1-67.claim: Abdullah Rubel of Padmapukur union, Shyamnagar, Satkhira, mortgaged his family's shrimp farm for a loan and went to Brunei in 2019; he found no work there, did all the household work in a Bangladeshi's home in return for food and lodging with no wages, and after nine months borrowed again to buy a ticket home.
AB1-67.why_new: A Brunei no-job case financed by mortgaging the family business.

AB1-68.claim: Abdullah Rubel told Prothom Alo in March 2025 that he had spent Tk 5 lakh to go abroad and still had not been able to repay the loan and recover the shrimp farm.
AB1-68.why_new: Six years on, the mortgaged asset is still not recovered.

AB1-69.claim: Hasan Gazi of Shyamnagar, Satkhira, went to Kuwait through India in 2018, spending Tk 5.5 lakh borrowed from relatives; he did various jobs in Kuwait for four years, was then detained by police and forced to return, and in 2025 was driving an auto-rickshaw in Keraniganj, Dhaka, and living in the rickshaw garage.
AB1-69.why_new: A Kuwait case that went through India and ended in detention and return.

AB1-70.claim: A study by OKUP and the International Institute for Environment and Development (IIED), 'Exposed and Exploited: Climate Change, Migration and Modern Slavery in Bangladesh', surveyed 648 households in 33 villages of Mathbaria, Pirojpur, and Gowainghat, Sylhet; it found people from Mathbaria who migrated abroad spent Tk 4 lakh 61 thousand 220 on average, raising 25% of the money by selling land and 18% from high-interest loans.
AB1-70.why_new: A local average cost and how it was financed (land sale 25%, high-interest loans 18%).

AB1-71.claim: The OKUP and IIED study says that people who go abroad on borrowed money are forced to accept any work, and found that 99% of the workers had faced at least one sign of modern slavery (low wages, withheld wages, physical and mental abuse, restrictions on movement) and 81% more than five.
AB1-71.why_new: Links the debt to what the worker has to accept abroad, with survey figures.

AB1-72.claim: Prothom Alo reported in March 2025 that there is no data on migrants who return, but figures are available for those who come back on an outpass (workers who became undocumented, have no passport, were detained by police and return empty-handed): about 89,000 came back this way in 2024 and more than 80,000 in 2023.

AB1-73.claim: Officials of BRAC's Migration Programme said in March 2025 that 250 to 300 migrant workers a day were coming back empty-handed, without proper clothes or money in their pockets, and that BRAC gives each Tk 1,000 for the fare home.
AB1-73.target_section: Where victims and families get help
AB1-73.why_new: The amount BRAC gives a destitute returnee for the fare home; the help list says "money to get home" without a figure.
AB1-73.h3: Where victims and families get help

AB1-74.claim: Prothom Alo reported in March 2025 that there is little activity for workers who come back: some projects were taken up after the Covid pandemic but not many workers benefit from them.
AB1-74.target_section: What help is there when I come back?
AB1-74.why_new: Sets the official list of return help against what reaches returnees.

AB1-75.claim: On the night of Monday 26 May 2025 the Airport Armed Police Battalion (APBn) arrested two Chinese nationals, Hu Junjun (30) and Zhang Leiji (54), and a Bangladeshi, Md Nayan Ali (30), in Bashundhara Residential Area, Dhaka, on charges of human trafficking, after a 19-year-old woman being taken through Shahjalal airport complained to the APBn at the roundabout by the airport's main entrance that the two Chinese men were trying to traffic her to China.
AB1-75.why_new: A 2025 China marriage case stopped at the airport by the woman's own verbal complaint, with where she complained.

AB1-76.claim: According to the APBn's press release of 28 May 2025, the two Chinese nationals had come to Bangladesh a year earlier, lived in Bashundhara and built ties with dalals around the country; with Nayan Ali's help the woman was persuaded by threats and inducements to marry, a passport and other papers were made in her name at a false address, and she was married to Hu Junjun in March 2025 with a denmohar (dower) of Tk 10 lakh.
AB1-76.why_new: Steps the section lacks: the foreigners settle in Dhaka first, work through local dalals, and get a passport made at a false address.

AB1-77.claim: The APBn said Zhang Leiji bought an air ticket in the woman's name to take her to China without telling her, and the arrested men took her by force from the house to Shahjalal airport.
AB1-77.why_new: The ticket bought without the bride's knowledge.

AB1-78.claim: From questioning the accused and from the woman's information the APBn confirmed that more local and foreign traffickers and women victims were in a house in Bashundhara Residential Area; a raid there arrested Nayan Ali, the others fled, and the police said they recovered important evidence and had initial proof that the ring had long been involved in trafficking.
AB1-78.why_new: A holding house in Dhaka with other women.

AB1-79.claim: On 28 May 2025 the woman's mother filed a case at Airport police station under sections 6(1), 6(2), 7, 8 and 10 of the Prevention and Suppression of Human Trafficking Act 2012.
AB1-79.why_new: Which sections were used and that a parent was the complainant.

AB1-80.claim: The Airport APBn's superintendent of police (operations), Mohammad Mozammel Haque, said in May 2025 that this was the second recent detention of Chinese nationals for trafficking at Shahjalal airport, and that some rings, with the help of local dalals, target women from simple, poor village families and try to traffic them to China with various inducements.
AB1-80.why_new: A named police officer on who is targeted and that it was the second such airport case.

AB1-81.claim: A Bangladeshi worker in Riyadh wrote in August 2025 that he learned only after reaching Saudi Arabia that his visa had passed through the hands of six dalals before it reached him, that he had had no way of knowing this while in Bangladesh, and that after he found no work in Saudi Arabia he spoke to five dalals.
AB1-81.target_section: The chain from the village to the visa seller
AB1-81.why_new: A worker's own count of the chain (six hands), matching the TIB figure with a first-hand account.

AB1-82.claim: The same worker wrote that the man through whom he went was from the next village, had lived in Saudi Arabia for about five years and was known locally as polite and decent; the man fixed the visa price at Tk 4 lakh and promised work at a good chocolate company, and when the worker's guardian asked him directly whether it was a chocolate factory he said to have faith and not worry.
AB1-82.target_section: Contract substitution: a different job or wage on arrival
AB1-82.why_new: What the seller said when asked to confirm the job. The article gives the man a pseudonym.
AB1-82.h3: Contract substitution: a different job or wage on arrival

AB1-83.claim: The worker wrote that he borrowed the Tk 4 lakh from relatives and paid the agency in instalments, sometimes Tk 50,000 and sometimes Tk 1 lakh, and that when he went to the agency's office in Dhaka to collect his papers before the flight he was treated very badly and the agency took more money from him on various pretexts.
AB1-83.target_section: The staged-payment trap, and no receipts
AB1-83.why_new: Extra money taken at the agency office on the day of the flight, after the full price was paid.
AB1-83.h3: The staged-payment trap, and no receipts

AB1-84.claim: He wrote that a driver took the group from King Khalid airport in Riyadh to a company room in Malaz, that he bought his own food for a month with no work, and that the man who sent him, who lived far away near the Yemen border, put him off for two months with 'today or tomorrow'; there was no chocolate factory.
AB1-84.target_section: Contract substitution: a different job or wage on arrival
AB1-84.why_new: What the first two months looked like.
AB1-84.h3: Contract substitution: a different job or wage on arrival

AB1-85.claim: The worker wrote that he later learned his visa belonged to a 'supply company' (a labour-supply firm) and that the villa he was housed in belonged to the same company; by his description, a supply company sells workers on to other places at a high price for its own profit, and the worker placed there is not paid.
AB1-85.why_new: The "supply company" visa, a term and mechanism the section does not have: the worker is hired out by the visa holder rather than left to find work.

AB1-86.claim: The worker wrote that he found out for himself and transferred to another company in Saudi Arabia, where he had been working for about four years on good pay.
AB1-86.why_new: A case where transferring employer worked.

AB1-87.claim: The same worker wrote from Riyadh in August 2025 that dalal rings bring workers from Bangladesh through various agencies on false promises but cannot give them work, so many have to hunt for work themselves; he said he had seen cheated workers sleeping on the street and one preparing to kill himself under the weight of debt.
AB1-87.target_section: Free visas and visa trading in the Gulf
AB1-87.why_new: An eyewitness account from inside Saudi Arabia.
AB1-87.h3: Free visas and visa trading in the Gulf

AB1-88.claim: The family of Shimul Sheikh (35) of Bichhali village, Narail Sadar, alleges that two neighbours, Khairul Islam (33) and Shariful Islam (28), promised that through them he would get a good job and an iqama (work permit) in Saudi Arabia for Tk 5 lakh; the family raised the money by selling a motorcycle, mortgaging land and borrowing at interest, and he went in May 2025.
AB1-88.why_new: A 2025 Saudi case sold by neighbours.

AB1-89.claim: Shimul Sheikh said by video call in September 2025 that he was told he would drive a company vehicle for Tk 70,000 to 80,000 a month and that the company would get him a licence, and that he was later asked for another Tk 1.5 lakh for the licence; according to the family no work was arranged, fresh money was demanded and, because they could not pay, no iqama was made.
AB1-89.why_new: The exact second demand (Tk 1.5 lakh "for the driving licence") after arrival, and no iqama when it was not paid.

AB1-90.claim: Shimul Sheikh's mother said that when the family could not pay again he was held and a man calling from an unknown number said he would be in danger unless money was paid, and that he escaped; in September 2025 he said he was on the run, hungry and had been chased by police the day before.
AB1-90.why_new: Held, family threatened from an unknown number, then undocumented and hiding from police.

AB1-91.claim: Shimul Sheikh's father said a village arbitration with local elders failed because the accused would not accept it; his mother filed a case in a Narail court (the article, published 29 September 2025, prints the date as 22 October), and the court ordered the Police Bureau of Investigation (PBI) in Jashore to investigate; the PBI sub-inspector said the investigation was continuing.
AB1-91.why_new: Arbitration failed; a court complaint was sent to the PBI. The printed case date is inconsistent with the publication date and needs checking.

AB1-92.claim: The accused Shariful Islam denied the allegations: he said Shimul was given a driving job as agreed but could not drive, was then placed with another company, ran away from it and is working with one of Shariful's cousins, that the iqama was made, and that the claims of a fresh demand for money and threats are false; Khairul Islam was not found at his house.

AB1-93.claim: Hossain, a rice farmer from Feni whose land had flooded repeatedly and who said ruling-party members were threatening him over his opposition politics, sold his land and borrowed about USD 33,000 from relatives and friends, raising USD 41,000 in all for travel and the dalal's costs, according to an investigation by Columbia Journalism Investigations (CJI) and Documented republished by Prothom Alo in October 2025.
AB1-93.target_section: NEW: The United States through South America and Mexico
AB1-93.placement: The contract price and the final price
AB1-93.why_new: A price for the US land route from a named-source investigation: USD 41,000.
AB1-93.h3: NEW: The United States through South America and Mexico

AB1-94.claim: Hossain left Bangladesh in February 2023 and crossed 11 countries by air and land over nine months before giving himself up to border officers in the US state of Arizona, who held him for three days in a room with 15 people and then released him.
AB1-94.target_section: NEW: The United States through South America and Mexico
AB1-94.why_new: Length of the journey and what happened at the border.
AB1-94.h3: NEW: The United States through South America and Mexico

AB1-95.claim: A legal firm in Manhattan filed Hossain's asylum application in April 2024 on the ground that he supports a Bangladeshi opposition party; the effect of climate-driven floods on his income and livelihood is not an accepted ground for asylum, and the investigation says the United States has no specific provision protecting people who flee climate disasters.
AB1-95.target_section: NEW: The United States through South America and Mexico
AB1-95.why_new: What an asylum claim can and cannot rest on.
AB1-95.h3: NEW: The United States through South America and Mexico

AB1-96.claim: While waiting for his hearing in the immigration court, Hossain got a US work permit after seven months; he worked first as a kitchen helper in a local restaurant, then delivering food by bike in Brooklyn, and in 2025 worked full time, six days a week, at a Bengali sweet shop and cafe in Kensington, Brooklyn, sharing a nearby basement apartment with two roommates.
AB1-96.target_section: NEW: The United States through South America and Mexico
AB1-96.why_new: What the person actually does after arrival.
AB1-96.h3: NEW: The United States through South America and Mexico

AB1-97.claim: Hossain had hoped that once granted asylum he could apply to bring his wife and daughter; he said that had he known how hard it now is, he would not have come to the United States.
AB1-97.target_section: NEW: The United States through South America and Mexico
AB1-97.why_new: The migrant's own verdict on the route.
AB1-97.h3: NEW: The United States through South America and Mexico

AB1-98.claim: The investigation reports that officers of US Immigration and Customs Enforcement (ICE) detained two Bangladeshis from Noakhali who were working in Buffalo, New York, and that Hossain keeps copies of his asylum application and court hearing notices to hand and his lawyer's number on speed dial in case ICE comes to his home.
AB1-98.target_section: NEW: The United States through South America and Mexico
AB1-98.why_new: Detention risk in 2025 even for those with a pending claim.
AB1-98.h3: NEW: The United States through South America and Mexico

AB1-99.claim: According to CJI and Documented's analysis of US Customs and Border Protection records, border crossings from Bangladesh rose 150% from 2019 to 2024; Noakhali is the top district of origin, with more than 30% of the Bangladeshis detained at the border, and Feni is among the top 10 Bangladeshi towns from which people reached the US-Mexico border.
AB1-99.target_section: NEW: The United States through South America and Mexico
AB1-99.why_new: Growth of the route and the home districts. The data record birthplace, not last residence, and about 35% of records leave birthplace blank, by the article's own account.
AB1-99.h3: NEW: The United States through South America and Mexico

AB1-100.claim: The same investigation says that among people detained in 2024 whose records it examined, about 100 were born in Bangladesh, against more than 520 born in Guatemala and about 350 in Senegal.
AB1-100.target_section: NEW: The United States through South America and Mexico
AB1-100.why_new: Printed count for 2024. Note for the editor: the article does not say what subset these figures cover and they look low for all detentions, so this needs checking against the original English investigation before use.
AB1-100.h3: NEW: The United States through South America and Mexico

AB1-101.claim: The investigation says Bangladeshi migrants arriving in New York first settle around the Bangladeshi grocery shops and restaurants of Kensington, Brooklyn, and that an estimated 1 lakh Bangladeshis live in New York City.
AB1-101.target_section: NEW: The United States through South America and Mexico
AB1-101.h3: NEW: The United States through South America and Mexico

AB1-102.claim: A Prothom Alo editorial of 24 October 2025 says that under ILO conventions there is no such thing as a free visa: it is a fraudulent arrangement in which the worker is only given permission to enter a country, or a sponsorship is sold, with no specific job arranged.
AB1-102.why_new: The guide cites BMET for "no such thing as a free visa"; this adds the ILO framing as stated by the newspaper. The OKUP survey figures in the editorial (five times the set cost, 72% loans, 11% mortgage, 6% asset sales, 43% no work, 7% through agencies) are already in the guide.

AB1-103.claim: A December 2025 Prothom Alo column by Nahid Hasan works through a Saudi pest-control job: the set wage is 700 riyals a month, which he gives as Tk 22,400, so two years of eight-hour days under the contract earn Tk 5 lakh 37 thousand 600, and after about Tk 2 lakh in living costs Tk 3 lakh 37 thousand 600 is left to send home.
AB1-103.target_section: How long will it take to pay back what I spend?
AB1-103.why_new: A worked example for one named job at SR 700; the FAQ example uses SR 800.

AB1-104.claim: The same column puts the cost of that Saudi job at about Tk 5 lakh 70 thousand: about Tk 4 lakh 60 thousand taken by the recruiting agency as its fee, about Tk 60,000 more for the passport, medical test, Takamol certificate, PDO training and police clearance, and roughly Tk 50,000 paid to sub-agents at various levels.
AB1-104.target_section: What people pay, and to whom
AB1-104.why_new: A three-way split (agency, papers, sub-agents) for a Saudi job; the section has a split only for a Cambodia case. It is a columnist's estimate, not a survey.

AB1-105.claim: By the column's arithmetic the worker is about Tk 2 lakh 32 thousand short of recovering the cost after two years, and in effect has to double the visa period and work four years for almost no gain.
AB1-105.target_section: How long will it take to pay back what I spend?
AB1-105.why_new: The conclusion of the worked example: the first contract does not repay the cost.

AB1-106.claim: The column says that under Saudi law employers are supposed to bear the worker's visa and recruitment costs but in practice this is often not followed, and that when Malaysia recruited government-to-government (G2G) many workers went for just Tk 35,000 in airfare, a system the writer says ended because of opposition from recruiting agencies.
AB1-106.target_section: Who pays for the air ticket?
AB1-106.why_new: What a no-broker channel cost (Tk 35,000) and why, by the writer's account, it ended.

AB1-107.claim: The column says there are very few legal recruiting agencies in the Rangpur region, so people there cannot even learn how going abroad works, and names lack of agencies, lack of a migrant network, inability to raise several lakh taka and fear of dalal fraud among the reasons few people go abroad from Rangpur division.
AB1-107.why_new: Regional gap in licensed agencies; low priority.

AB1-108.claim: A Prothom Alo editorial of 21 February 2026, citing the paper's own report, says an 18-year-old from Chandanaish, Chattogram, who hoped to go to South Africa, was sent abroad on a Tk 9 lakh loan that was beyond his family's means, and that his journey ended in his death in a foreign land.
AB1-108.why_new: A South Africa case; the guide has no South Africa route. The editorial gives no date, place or cause of death, so the underlying news report should be found before use.

AB1-109.claim: A Prothom Alo editorial of 21 February 2026 says, citing UNHCR data, that Bangladeshis were the largest group among migrants who crossed the Mediterranean to Italy from January to October 2024, as in 2023; the editorial also states, without naming a source, that more than 25,000 people drowned in the Mediterranean in the past decade, of whom at least 500 each year were Bangladeshi.
AB1-109.why_new: The guide has arrival counts for 2025-26 and deaths for 2024; it has no figure for Bangladeshi deaths. The 500-a-year figure is stated by the editorial without a clear source and needs checking.

AB1-110.claim: The editorial says local dalals win trust through social ties and point to relatives' success abroad, that the journey begins with a promise of a valid visa and safe travel and the route is changed midway, and that in many cases people are held in Libya or another country and videos of their torture are sent to the family to extract ransom.
AB1-110.why_new: Mostly already in the guide (ransom calls, route changes); adds the torture-video detail if the section lacks it. It is the newspaper's general description, not a case.

AB1-111.claim: Iqbal Mahmud, deputy team leader at The Asia Foundation, told a Prothom Alo roundtable in Cumilla published on 30 April 2026 that the 2023 amendment to the overseas employment law spoke of regularising dalals and rules were made in January 2025, but that in practice there has been little progress in registering dalals and bringing their work inside a structure.
AB1-111.placement: other: answers the Need to know on registration
AB1-111.why_new: Bears directly on the section's open question "Has BMET registered any sub-agents yet": as of April 2026 a named practitioner says little progress.

AB1-112.claim: Iqbal Mahmud said the recruiting agency completes the visa process but collecting workers and other important work is done through dalals; Kamruzzaman, principal of the Cumilla Technical Training Centre, said a clear decision is needed on which body (the ministry, BMET or another) regulates sub-agents and middlemen, and that with no defined structure they often take advantage.
AB1-112.why_new: A government training-centre head saying it is unclear who regulates sub-agents.

AB1-113.claim: Jesia Khatun, director of WARBE Development Foundation, said at the roundtable that because recruiting agencies are concentrated in Dhaka, dalals play the important role in the field; Farzana Alam Majumder, a BAIRA member from Cumilla, said the problems seen most are unlicensed dalals, false promises, cash transactions, fraud and keeping the contract paper hidden.
AB1-113.target_section: The chain from the village to the visa seller
AB1-113.placement: other: why dalals fill the gap
AB1-113.why_new: An agency-side speaker naming "keeping the contract hidden" and cash dealing as the commonest problems.

AB1-114.claim: Saiful Malik, additional superintendent of police (Sadar Circle), Cumilla, said at the roundtable that many people go abroad through dalals without a valid contract and later become undocumented, that complaints include not getting fair work or pay and even being held, and that action is hard to take because the necessary papers are missing.
AB1-114.target_section: Contract substitution: a different job or wage on arrival
AB1-114.why_new: A police officer saying cases fail for want of a written contract.
AB1-114.h3: Contract substitution: a different job or wage on arrival

AB1-115.claim: The same police officer said people should be encouraged to go through government channels such as BOESL, and that those who go that way are comparatively better off.
AB1-115.target_section: Can I go through the government agency, BOESL?
AB1-115.why_new: A district police officer's observation on BOESL migrants; an opinion, not data.

AB1-116.claim: The Cumilla additional superintendent of police said in April 2026 that although there are some complaints about police clearance, people with no case against them are getting it within the set time, and that if it takes longer the matter is resolved quickly on contacting the office concerned.
AB1-116.why_new: The police side on clearance delays, from one district.

AB1-117.claim: Md Atikur Rahman, assistant director of the Cumilla District Employment and Manpower Office, said at the roundtable that agencies do not fully follow the policy and in many cases take extra money from unskilled or uneducated people.
AB1-117.target_section: What people pay, and to whom
AB1-117.why_new: A DEMO official admitting agencies overcharge.

AB1-118.claim: Md Yusuf Molla, administrator of Cumilla City Corporation, said some dishonest agencies take everything people have on various inducements and then do not send them abroad as promised, and that politicians like him receive many such complaints and have to put pressure on the middlemen to do what they promised or return the money.
AB1-118.target_section: Refund refusals after a failed departure
AB1-118.why_new: How refunds are actually pursued locally: pressure through political figures, as stated by one.
AB1-118.h3: Refund refusals after a failed departure

AB1-119.claim: Jesia Khatun of WARBE Development Foundation said a significant amount of money had been recovered through mediation in the past three years, and Iqbal Mahmud of The Asia Foundation said grievance redress committees formed through municipalities, upazila and union parishads are working at district and local level but on a limited scale.
AB1-119.target_section: Refund refusals after a failed departure
AB1-119.why_new: Local mediation and grievance committees as a route to getting money back; the guide lists BMET, the ministry and courts only. No amount or contact is given.
AB1-119.h3: Refund refusals after a failed departure

AB1-120.claim: Md Main Uddin, assistant director of the Probashi Kallyan Centre in Cumilla, said the centre is the district-level office of the Wage Earners' Welfare Board and began work in July 2023, taking over services earlier given through the district manpower office; when a migrant is in trouble abroad, an application made through the centre gets legal help with the embassy's assistance.
AB1-120.target_section: Where victims and families get help
AB1-120.why_new: A district office families can apply through; the help list does not mention Probashi Kallyan Centres.
AB1-120.h3: Where victims and families get help

AB1-121.claim: The Cumilla Probashi Kallyan Centre's assistant director said in April 2026 that financial help for bringing a body home is given for BMET card holders, that a free ambulance takes the body from the airport to its destination, and that Tk 25,000 is paid after the body arrives and up to Tk 3 lakh in eligible cases.
AB1-121.target_section: If a worker dies abroad, what does the family get?
AB1-121.why_new: Conflict to resolve: the guide says a Tk 35,000 cheque at the airport; this official says Tk 25,000 after the body arrives.

AB1-122.claim: The same official said the Welfare Board gives education stipends to migrant workers' children and an allowance for disabled children, helps through the embassy to recover unpaid insurance and compensation abroad, offers overnight stay at the Wage Earners' dormitory near the airport, and that safe homes for women workers operate abroad and embassies can appoint lawyers for legal help.
AB1-122.target_section: Where victims and families get help
AB1-122.why_new: Services as listed by the district welfare office; most are in the FAQ, the disabled-child allowance and embassy lawyers may not be.
AB1-122.h3: Where victims and families get help

AB1-123.claim: Rawnak Jahan, a senior officer of Probashi Kallyan Bank in the Cumilla region, said a loan applicant must have a BMET card, a valid visa, a passport and a national ID card of his own area, plus a capable guarantor who will take on repayment if needed.
AB1-123.target_section: Can I get a government loan to go abroad?
AB1-123.placement: other: what the bank asks for and its reach
AB1-123.why_new: The papers as a branch officer states them (the FAQ says two guarantors; she says one capable guarantor).

AB1-124.claim: She said Cumilla, a district with many migrants and 17 upazilas, has only four Probashi Kallyan Bank branches, that the Cumilla branch in the Tomson Bridge area serves nine upazilas with only three officers, and that the bank often hears the complaint that it does not lend or asks for extra papers, while part of its borrowers are unwilling to repay on time, which makes lending to new customers harder.
AB1-124.target_section: Can I get a government loan to go abroad?
AB1-124.placement: other: what the bank asks for and its reach
AB1-124.why_new: Ground-level reach of PKB in one high-migration district: where the branch is and how thinly staffed.

AB1-125.claim: Marina Sultana, director (programme) of RMMRU, said at the roundtable that research shows about 31% of people who go abroad are cheated in one way or another, and that fraud happens at different steps starting from the passport.
AB1-125.target_section: Dalal scams: the usual tricks and how to spot them
AB1-125.why_new: A headline fraud rate for the Dalal scams chapter's "In one minute"; she does not name the study, so the source needs finding.
AB1-125.h3: H2:Dalal scams: the usual tricks and how to spot them

AB1-126.claim: Fatema Akter, a returnee woman worker, told the Cumilla roundtable that she worked in Oman for five years on a salary of only Tk 12,000, then went to Saudi Arabia and worked two years, where she said she received a salary of about Tk 3,000 for some of the time; she said food was not given properly, wages were not paid regularly and she was made to work all the time, and she came home ill.
AB1-126.target_section: Contract substitution: a different job or wage on arrival
AB1-126.why_new: A woman's wage figures for Oman and Saudi Arabia. Her wording on the Saudi pay is unclear (monthly or total) and is given as printed.
AB1-126.h3: Contract substitution: a different job or wage on arrival

AB1-127.claim: Fatema Akter said that her age has gone up and her passport also shows a higher age, and that despite many attempts she can no longer go abroad.
AB1-127.target_section: The agent wants to change my age on the passport. Is that a problem?
AB1-127.why_new: A returnee blocked from going again by the age shown on her passport.

AB1-128.claim: Kamruzzaman, principal of the Cumilla Technical Training Centre, said in April 2026 that attendance at women workers' training is now monitored online, and that the policy requirement that agencies take at least 10% trained workers must be enforced.
AB1-128.why_new: Online attendance monitoring answers the earlier complaint that the course is skipped.

AB1-129.claim: Cumilla City Corporation's administrator said some training centres have irregularities: training is given but a proper certificate is not, and employment is promised but does not happen.
AB1-129.why_new: A local official on training centres that promise jobs.

AB1-130.claim: Md Saiful Islam, additional deputy commissioner of Cumilla, said that because the government has not fully started a one-stop service many people turn to dalals, who handle the whole process of sending a person abroad from start to finish, and that the person often does not know how or at what cost he is going.
AB1-130.why_new: A district official on why the dalal wins: he does everything in one place.

AB1-131.claim: The additional deputy commissioner said that among the complaints from migrants that reach the Deputy Commissioner's office, embezzlement of money sent from abroad and family disputes are prominent, and that a person abroad cannot protect his family and property.
AB1-131.why_new: Remittance embezzlement at home as a leading complaint; no section covers it, so this placement is approximate.

AB1-132.claim: The Cumilla manpower office's assistant director said there is almost no psychological counselling service for migrant workers, especially women workers.
AB1-132.target_section: What if I'm abused? Where can I go?
AB1-132.why_new: What is not available at district level.

AB1-133.claim: Badrul Huda, president of the Multi-Party Advocacy Forum in Cumilla, said that information not reaching the family when someone dies or goes missing abroad is a major humanitarian problem.
AB1-133.target_section: If a worker dies abroad, what does the family get?
AB1-133.why_new: Families not being told of deaths, as raised by a local forum.
